en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Lineage of Buddhas in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya)

Prologue to the Book I pay homage to the Buddha, the abode of infinite knowledge and compassion, who has laid to rest all defilement, who is perfectly concentrated, and who brings about the welfare of others;
and to the Dhamma, the supreme restraint from existence; and to the Saṅgha, a mine of virtues, free from all blemish.
The best of the Conqueror’s disciples in wisdom, who was the General of the Dhamma and King of the Dhamma, questioned the Teacher—
who has gone from this shore to the further shore and is free from all defilements— in the midst of his circle of kinsmen. Herein,
within the lineage of the Fully Awakened Ones, is the history of the Buddhas, according to the pure lineage of the Leader.
That which was proclaimed by the Tathāgata while dwelling in concentration, having granted the opportunity [for its transmission],—
the sons of the Sugata have, until this very day, without allowing it to perish, compiled both the sequence of the Pāḷi and the meaning of the Pāḷi,
as well as the connections between the discourses, exactly as they had heard them.
Because this [work] proceeds according to the sequence of the commentary, which generates faith and wisdom for people who always desire to hear the word of that very Blessed One,
the Fully Enlightened One— [a word] which is the source of excellence and from which [this work] has arisen; [and because it was composed] by the Lion of Buddhas,
who delights in the True Dhamma with diligence and is exalted by virtues such as moral discipline.
I have been entreated for a very long time; therefore, I shall begin its praise.

For the sake of the long endurance of the Conqueror’s Dispensation—which is ever the seat of strife for people—and for the sake of the increase of the arising of merit for myself, as well as for the sake of inspiring confidence in the great multitude.
This commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*, which follows the textual tradition of the Mahāvihāra, is free from the fault of confusion; yet, in brief, it shall be the very essence.
For there is nothing else here concerning the narrative of the lineage of Buddhas that is worthy of being heard.
It is a means of inspiring confidence in those who delight in the qualities of the Buddha, and a cleansing of the great impurity of evil.
Therefore, being endowed with careful concentration, having abandoned distraction and focused the mind on nothing else,
listen to this sweet eulogy as it is being recited, placing your ears like refined gold.
"But having set aside all other duties, a wise person here, at all times,
should diligently listen to and also speak this discourse, for such a discourse is exceedingly rare.
In this regard, since it was stated that "the commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa* shall be the essence," the *Buddhavaṃsa* must first be established.

Herein, this is the analysis: the detailed account of the lineage, concerning the twenty-five Buddhas who appeared during the four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand additional eons prior to this, categorized by the specific eon of their appearance and so forth, should be understood as the "Buddhavamsa.
This [work] consists of the section on the eon, the section on the name, the section on the clan, the section on the birthplace, and the section on the city.
The section on the father, the section on the mother, the section on the Bodhi tree, the section on the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma,
the section on the clear realization, the section on the assembly of disciples, the section on the chief disciples, the section on the attendant, the section on the chief female disciples,
the section on the retinue of bhikkhus, the section on the rays of light, and the section on the dimensions of the physical relics.

It is defined and established by these twenty-two chapters found in the canonical text: the Chapter on the Bodhisatta’s Authority, the Chapter on the Prophecy, the Chapter on the Bodhisatta’s Striving, the Chapter on His Lifespan, and the Chapter on His Parinibbāna.
Furthermore, many sections not included in the canonical text should be brought in here, such as the Chapter on Living at Home and the Chapter on the Three Palaces.

It is established in ten sections: the section on the dancing women, the section on the chief queen, the section on the son, the section on the vehicle, the section on the Great Departure, the section on the striving, the section on the attendant, and the section on the monastery.
This [work], though consisting of many chapters, we shall [present] according to their respective places.
We shall proceed by showing [this] concisely in various places.
Now, once it has been thus defined:
By whom was this taught? Where was it taught? And for whose sake was it taught?
"For what purpose, when, for whom, and by whom was this word brought?
Having first briefly explained all these details,
I shall afterwards provide a commentary on the meaning of the *Buddhavaṃsa*."
In this regard, as for the question "By whom was this taught?": By whom was this *Buddhavaṃsa* taught?

It was taught by the Tathāgata—the All-Knowing One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the King of Dhamma, the Lord of Dhamma—who possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena, who is endowed with the ten powers, and who is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence.

Where was it taught? It was taught while walking upon the Jewel Walk (Ratanacaṅkama) in the Great Monastery of the Nigrodha Park in the great city of Kapilavatthu—a place of supreme beauty to behold, a site where the eyes of gods and humans were fixed.
For whose sake was it taught? It was taught for the sake of eighty-two thousand kinsmen and many millions of gods and humans.
For what purpose was it taught? It was taught for the purpose of crossing over the four floods (oghā).
When was it taught? For during his first enlightenment, the Blessed One lived for twenty years without a fixed residence, going and staying wherever it was comfortable. How so?
Having set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana in the first year and having caused eighteen koṭis of Brahmās to drink the draught of the Deathless, he remained in dependence upon Bārāṇasī.
He dwelt at Isipatana in the Deer Park. For the second year, he stayed near Rājagaha in the Mahāvihāra at Veḷuvana;
the third and fourth years were also there. The fifth year was spent near Vesālī in the Kūṭāgārasālā in the Great Forest.
The sixth year was at Makula-pabbata. The seventh year was in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The eighth year was at Saṃsumāragiri in the Bhagga country.
Relying on the Bhesakaḷā Grove. The ninth [was spoken] at Kosambī.
The tenth in the Pālileyyaka forest thicket. The eleventh at Nāḷā, the brahmin village. The twelfth at Verañjā. The thirteenth at Cāliya Mountain.
The fourteenth at the Great Monastery of Jetavana. The fifteenth in the great city of Kapilavatthu. The sixteenth after having subdued Āḷavaka.
Having caused eighty-four thousand living beings to drink the drink of the Deathless at Āḷavī, [the sixteenth year] was spent right at Rājagaha.
The seventeenth was also at Rājagaha, and the eighteenth likewise on Cāliya Mountain. Similarly, the nineteenth and twentieth years were spent right at Rājagaha.
Therefore it is said: "During his first twenty years of enlightenment, the Blessed One lived without a fixed residence; wherever..."
"Go and dwell wherever it is comfortable. From that time on, however, he resided near Sāvatthī itself, dwelling in the Jetavana Mahāvihāra and the Pubbārāma as a permanent resident.
But when the Teacher, having become a Buddha, had spent his first rains retreat at Isipatana in the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī...
Having completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā*, he went to Uruvelā. Staying there for three months, he subdued the three brothers who were matted-hair ascetics.
Surrounded by a retinue of one thousand bhikkhus, he went to Rājagaha on the full moon day of the month of Phussa and remained right there for two months.
At that time, five months had passed since his departure from Bārāṇasī; thus, the entire winter season was over.
Seven or eight days had passed since the arrival of the Elder Udāyī. On the full moon day of the month of Phagguna, he thought:
"The winter has passed; the spring season has arrived; it is time for the Tathāgata to go to Kapilavatthu.
Having thought thus, he praised the journey toward his native city with about sixty stanzas.
He praised [the Buddha]. Then, having heard his words, the Teacher, desiring to provide for his kinsmen,
set out from Rājagaha surrounded by twenty thousand monks whose taints were exhausted— ten thousand noble sons from Aṅga and Magadha and ten thousand from Kapilavatthu—
and traveling a *yojana* each day, he proceeded.

Having traveled sixty yojanas from Rājagaha to the city of Kapilavatthu in two months, he performed the Twin Miracle there for the purpose of making his kinsmen pay homage. At that time, this *Buddhavaṃsa* was taught.
Whose word is it? It is the word of the Fully Enlightened One alone, not shared by disciples or paccekabuddhas.

By whom was it brought down? It was brought down through a succession of teachers. For this [text] was brought down by the Elder Sāriputta, Bhaddaji, Tissa Kosiyaputta, Siggava Moggaliputta, Sudatta Dhammika, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, and Revata, and so forth, down to the time of the Third Council;

from then on, it was brought down by their respective disciples and grand-disciples. Thus, it should be understood that it has been brought down through a succession of teachers down to the present day.
To this extent—“By whom was this taught? Where was it taught? For whose sake was it taught?
For what purpose? When? To whom? And by whom was the word brought?”—it has been explained.
This verse has its meaning already explained.
The Introduction:
The External Introduction.
Now, for that which has been thus brought forward, there follows the commentary on its meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*).

This commentary, moreover, is said to be "well-commented" only when it is presented by showing these three origins: the distant origin (*dūrenidāna*), the not-distant origin (*avidūrenidāna*), and the proximate origin (*santikenidāna*).
And for those who hear it, it becomes "well-understood" because they comprehend it starting from its full accomplishment (*samudāgama*).
Therefore, we shall explain [the Jātaka] after first showing those causes (nidāna).
In this regard, first of all, the delimitation of those causes from the beginning must be understood. Herein, this is the brief exposition of the meaning:
from the time the Great Being made his resolution at the feet of the Ten-Powered One Dīpaṅkara, up until his existence as Vessantara.
The discourse occurring from the time he passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven is called the "remote origin" (*dūrenidāna*).

The discourse occurring from the time he passed away from the Tusita heaven until his attainment of omniscient knowledge at the seat of enlightenment is called the "not remote origin" (*avidūrenidāna*). For example:
"At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery."
Furthermore, such passages as “He dwelt at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground,” and “He dwelt at Vesālī in the Great Wood,

in the Gabled Hall,” should be understood as the *nidāna* (introductory setting) pertaining to each specific location where the Blessed One resided during the interval from his attainment of omniscience at the seat of Great Enlightenment until his final passing away on the bed of parinibbāna.
To this extent, the commentary on the external causes, by way of the three causes—distant, near-distant, and proximate—has been completed in brief.
[Now follows] the Internal Cause: 1.
Commentary on the Section on the Jewel Walk.
Now, however—“And Brahmā Sahampati, lord of the world, with palms joined, entreated the Unsurpassed One:
‘There are beings here whose eyes are scarcely dimmed by passion; teach the Dhamma, O Compassionate One, for the sake of these folk. —
There is an explanation of the meaning of the internal nidāna that has been set forth.
Herein, as in such suttantas as: “At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place,” [it is said]:
“At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park. Then...”
Why is it that, instead of stating the introduction (nidāna) by way of such passages as, "Then the venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One;

having approached, he asked the Blessed One about the lineage of the Buddhas," the introduction is stated by way of such passages as, "And Brahmā Sahampati, the lord of the world, with palms joined, entreated the Supreme One"? It is said: [Because of] the Blessed One’s...
It was stated for the purpose of demonstrating the Brahmā’s request for a teaching on the Dhamma, which served as the cause for the teaching of all phenomena.
[The question is: "When was the Victor requested by Brahmā for the sake of a Dhamma-teaching?
When, where, and by whom was this verse uttered?"
It is said: On the eighth day after the Blessed One had become a Buddha, he was requested and entreated by Brahmā to teach the Dhamma.

Regarding this, here is the sequential account: It is said that on the day of his Great Renunciation, the Mahāpurisa, having made his formal resolve, saw beds, seats, slave-girls, and female dancers that were exposed, manifest, and loathsome.
With an exceedingly agitated heart, he summoned Channa, who was stationed at a secluded spot, saying, "Bring the noble steed named Kaṇḍaka, the crusher of the foremost of enemies.

Having had Kaṇḍaka brought, and having mounted that excellent horse with Channa as his companion, he departed from the city when the city gate was opened by a deity residing there; thus he crossed over three kingdoms.
When the remainder of that night had passed, the Being Beyond the Ordinary stood on the bank of the river named Anomā and said this to Channa:
“Channa, take these ornaments, which are not shared by others, along with Kaṇḍaka, my excellent steed, and go to Kapilavatthu.
Having dismissed Channa, he cut off his own mass of hair with a sword that resembled a blue lotus from a pond of cool water.
Having cut [his hair] and tossed it into the air, and having taken the bowl and robes belonging to Devadatta, he himself went forth into homelessness.
Wandering by stages on his journey, he crossed the river Gaṅgā— which was free from obstruction and possessed waves and surges tossed up by the force of the wind—
and entered the city named Rājagaha, which shone with a network of rays from clusters of jewels, and there...
Like one mocking people intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty; like one inducing shame in people of arrogant appearance;
like one binding the hearts of the city folk to himself with the charms of his youth;
and like a mass of merit walking on foot, his physical beauty adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, he captivated the eyes of all people.
And like a mountain, detached from going about, with senses calmed and mind at peace,
looking only a yoke’s length ahead, he wandered for alms in Rājagaha; having taken a meal sufficient for his sustenance,

he departed from the city and sat down on a spot near the side of Paṇḍava Mountain— a place endowed with shade and water, a pure area, most delightful, secluded, and solitary— by the power of reflective contemplation.
Having partaken of the mixed meal, Bimbisāra, the Great King of Magadha, followed the voice from Mount Paṇḍava;
he approached the Great Man, inquired after his name and clan, and with a heart full of joy, invited him to the kingship, saying, "Accept a share of my kingdom.
To this, [the Great Man replied]: "Enough, Great King; I have no need for kingship; I have renounced the kingship."
Having said, "I have gone forth with the resolve, 'May I become a Buddha who has uncovered the veil from the world for the sake of the welfare of the world,'" and having been told by him,
"When you have become a Buddha, you should enter my realm first of all," he gave his promise, saying, "So be it. Then,
having approached Āḷāra and Udaka and finding no essence in their teaching of the Dhamma, [he departed].
Then, having departed from there, although he practiced austerities for six years at Uruvelā, being unable to attain the Deathless,
he nourished his body by partaking of substantial food.
At that time, in the village of Senānigama at Uruvelā, there was a daughter of a householder of Senānigama named Sujātā, who had reached marriageable age.
She made a vow at a banyan tree, saying: “If, after going to a family of equal caste, I obtain a son in my first pregnancy, I shall perform an offering. Her vow was fulfilled.
On the full-moon day of Vesākha, thinking, “Today I shall perform the offering,” she prepared, early in the morning, milk-rice that was effortlessly obtained and supremely sweet.
On that very day, the Bodhisatta, having attended to his physical needs and waiting for the time to go on almsround,
went early in the morning and sat down at the foot of that banyan tree. Then a female slave named Puṇṇā, who was the nurse for his mother,

went to clear the area around the tree root and saw the Bodhisatta sitting there, gazing toward the eastern world-system, his bodily splendor resembling the peak of a mountain of fine gold suffused with the light of twilight.

She saw the Sun of Sages, who had approached that excellent tree like the sun, the maker of day, which has emerged from the rift in the clouds and acts as a treasury that dispels the mass of darkness while causing the lotus groves to bloom.
And seeing that entire tree turned the color of gold by the radiance streaming forth from his body, this thought occurred to her: "Today our deity has descended from the tree..."
“Sitting there, she wished to receive the offering with her own hands. She went quickly and reported this matter to Sujātā.

Then Sujātā, having conceived faith, adorned herself with all her ornaments, filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand pieces with the most delicious honeyed milk-rice, covered it with another golden bowl, and took it upon her head.

She went toward the banyan tree. As she was walking, even from afar, she saw the Bodhisatta sitting there like a tree deity, having turned the entire tree golden-colored with the radiance of his body; he sat there like a mass of accumulated merit, endowed with beauty.
Filled with joy and gladness, Sujātā, perceiving him to be a "tree deity," [began] from the spot where she had first seen him...
Having gone down the slope and lowered the golden bowl from his head, he placed it in the hands of the Great Being, prostrated with the five-fold greeting, and said:
“Just as my own wish has been fulfilled, may yours likewise be fulfilled,” and then he departed.
Then the Bodhisatta, taking the golden bowl, went to the bank of the river Nerañjarā and stood upon Suppatiṭṭha.
Having placed a golden bowl on the bank of the river Nammada, bathed, and come out, he ate that milk-rice while forming it into forty-nine mouthfuls.
Then, saying, "If I am to become a Buddha today, let this golden bowl go against the current," he threw it.
That bowl went against the current and reached the abode of the nāga king named Kāḷa.
Having entered, he lifted up the bowls of the three Buddhas and stood beneath them.
The Great Being, having spent the day’s rest right there in that forest grove, at the time of evening,
took the eight handfuls of grass given by a grass-cutter named Sotthiya after the latter had recognized the marks of a Great Man, and ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
He stood in the southern direction, but that spot trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
The Great Being thought, "This place is unable to sustain my virtue," and went toward the western direction;
it trembled in the same way. Again he went toward the northern direction; it trembled in the same way. Again...
He went toward the eastern direction. There, the spot the size of a cross-legged seat remained motionless.
The Great Man, having reached the conclusion that "this place is the site for the destruction of the defilements," took those blades of grass by their tips and shook them.
They became as if cut off by the edge of a razor. The Bodhisatta thought, "Without having attained enlightenment..."
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture," he resolved, and having established the fourfold energy,
he sat down facing east with his legs folded in the full lotus position, placing the trunk of the Bodhi tree behind him.
At that very moment, Māra, the one who assails the whole world, manifested a thousand arms and appeared like a peak of the Snowy Mountains measuring one hundred and fifty yojanas.
Mounting his excellent elephant named Girimekhala— the best of adversaries and a formidable beast— and surrounded by an exceedingly vast army of Māra consisting of nine *yojanas* in extent,
including bows, swords, spears, javelins, and clubs, he approached the Great Being like a mountain enveloping everything around it or like a great predator approaching its prey.
Even while the sun was still shining, the Great Man scattered the host of Māra, which had come to cause a tumult, like a blossoming *jayasumana* flower.

Being honored as if by joy itself through the sprouts of the Bodhi tree—which fell upon his robe, beautiful to behold and resembling red coral shoots—he attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives during the first watch;

purified the knowledge of the divine eye during the middle watch; and, having applied the knowledge of dependent origination during the last watch, [perceived] the cycle of existence and its cessation.
Reflecting thus at the break of dawn, having become a Buddha, he said:
“Through many births in saṃsāra I have wandered without finding rest, seeking the builder of the house; for birth again and again is suffering.”
“House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered.
The mind has reached the unconditioned; it has attained the destruction of craving.”
Having uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) and spent seven days experiencing the bliss of liberation, on the eighth day he emerged from his meditative attainment.
Knowing the doubts of the deities, and for the purpose of dispelling those doubts, he rose into the air and displayed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
Having dispelled their doubts, he shifted slightly from his cross-legged posture toward the east.
Standing in the northern direction, he spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at both the Bodhi tree and the seat upon which he had realized omniscience— thinking, "On this very seat, indeed,
I have penetrated all-knowing wisdom"— the place where he attained the fruit of the perfections fulfilled over four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand kalpas. That...
That place became known as the Animisa Cetiya.

Then, walking back and forth on the Jewel Walk (Ratanacaṅkama), which extended from east to west between the site of the throne and the site where he stood, he passed seven days; that place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya. From there...
In the western quarter, the deities constructed the shrine named Ratanaghara;
there, sitting cross-legged, he spent seven days investigating the Abhidhammapitaka, and specifically the *Anantanaya-samantapadṭṭhāna*.
That place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya. Thus, having spent four weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, he remained there.
In the fifth week, he went from the foot of the Bodhi tree to the Goatherd’s Banyan tree;
there too, while investigating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he spent seven days at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree.
Then, for another seven days, he sat at the Mucalinda tree. As soon as the Blessed One had sat down there, throughout the entire interior of the world-system...
A great untimely cloud arose, filling the sky. When it appeared, Mucalinda the Naga King thought:
"This great cloud has arisen just as the Teacher has entered my abode; he ought to receive a dwelling place.
Although he was capable of creating a divine mansion made of the seven precious gems, resembling a celestial palace, [he chose instead to provide a shelter].

When this was done, thinking, "This will not be of great fruit for me; I shall perform bodily service for the One Possessed of the Ten Powers," he assumed an exceedingly vast body, surrounded the Teacher seven times with his coils, and stood with a great hood spread over him.
Then the Blessed One, in the great space within that enclosure, which was composed entirely of jewels—

He dwelt as if residing in a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi), furnished with a most costly couch and canopied by a canopy of various fragrant flower-garlands hanging down above, and perfumed with various sweet scents.
Having thus spent those seven days there, the Blessed One sat for the next seven days at Rājāyatana. There too, he experienced only the bliss of liberation. At this point—
Seven weeks were fully completed. During this interval, the Blessed One spent his time in the bliss of *jhāna* and the bliss of the fruit [of liberation].
Then, after the seven weeks had passed, the thought arose in him: "I shall wash my face.
Sakka, the lord of the gods, brought and gave him *agada* and *harītaka*. Then Sakka also provided him with a *nāga*-creeper tooth-stick and water for washing the face.
He gave it. Then the Blessed One, having chewed the tooth-stick and rinsed his mouth with the water of Lake Anotatta, sat down at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree.

At that time, having accepted and consumed the fine flour-mash and honey-cake from the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika, which had been brought in exquisite stone bowls by the four World-Protectors, he returned to the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree.

He sat down. Then, as soon as he had sat there, while reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma he had realized, there arose in him—due to that state of mind common to all Buddhas—the reluctance to teach the Dhamma to others, [born of the thought]:
"This Dhamma I have realized is profound, hard to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise."
Then a reflection arose in the mind of Brahmā Sahampati. Knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, he uttered these words:
"Alas, the world is perishing! Alas, the world is being destroyed! Thus he spoke, surrounded by a host of Brahmas from ten thousand world-systems.
Accompanied by the devas of the Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, and Paranimmitavasavatti realms, he arrived and appeared before the Blessed One.
Having fashioned the earth as a place for himself to stand upon,
he knelt with his right knee on the ground and joined his ten fingers in a radiant añjali, resembling a cluster of fresh, stainless, and unblemished lotus buds.
Placing his head [at the Blessed One’s feet], he said: “May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma, may the Sugata teach the Dhamma!
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, through not hearing the Dhamma, are falling away; there will be those who understand the Dhamma.
“In former times, O Magadhans, the Dhamma appeared, impure, conceived by those still stained with defilement.”
Open this door to the Deathless! Let them hear the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One.
Just as one standing on the summit of a rocky mountain might see the people all around, even so, O wise one with eyes everywhere, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, look upon the world.
Free from sorrow, look upon the people overcome by sorrow, who are oppressed by birth and old age.
“Arise, O Hero, victor in battle! O Caravan-leader, free from debt, wander through the world.
Teach the Dhamma, Blessed One; there will be those who understand.”
“Is it not so that you said: ‘The Buddha shall awaken; having crossed over, I shall help others cross; being liberated, I shall liberate others’?
“What need have I for anonymity? Having realized the Dhamma here, and having attained omniscience, I shall help cross over the world together with its devas.”
Having made his aspiration and fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he attained omniscience;
and with many such methods as, "If you do not teach the Dhamma, who else indeed will teach it? What other refuge, protection, shelter, or final resort can there be for the world?
he entreated the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma. Therefore it was said: "To him who had become a Buddha..."
"But on the eighth week after the Blessed One’s passing, the Teacher was requested by Brahmā for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
Now, the opportunity has arrived to answer these questions: "When, where, and by whom was this verse uttered?
Regarding that, when was it spoken? It was spoken at the time of the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti). The First Great Council...
This [method] is to be understood according to the very manner stated in the *Saṅgītikhandha*.

Where and by whom was it spoken? It is said that after the Blessed One had attained final *parinibbāna*, at the gate of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the slope of Mount Vebhāra in the city of Rājagaha, King Ajātasattu of Magadha—who had conquered all enemies—caused [the council] to be held for the purpose of the recitation of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgāyana*) in a hall resembling the full orb of the moon.

It should be understood that this verse, beginning with "Brahmā, the lord of the world," was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda Thera while seated upon the Dhamma throne in the pavilion which is the very essence of all that is to be seen.
This is the connection of the verses here.
Up to this point—
“When was this Victor requested by Brahmā for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma?
When, where, and by whom was this verse uttered?”—this verse also has its meaning already explained.
Now, we shall provide an explanation of the words not yet analyzed in this verse, which was spoken according to this connection.

In this context, "Brahmā" means one who has been expanded (*brūhita*) by various specific qualities; thus, he is a Brahmā. Furthermore, this word *brahma* is seen used for Mahābrahmā, a brahmin, the mother and father of a Tathāgata, a merchant-chief, and others.
For instance, in such passages as "the Brahmā of two thousand [worlds]," it is intended to mean Mahābrahmā. Likewise:
"The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the all-seeing, who has reached the end of the world and transcended all states of existence..."

“The one free from taints, who has abandoned all suffering, who is called Truth—O Brahmā, he has been attended upon by me. Here it refers to a *brāhmaṇa*. “‘Brahmā,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata. Here it refers to the Tathāgata. “‘Brahmā’ refers to mother and father, and they are called the first teachers. Here it refers to mother and father. “He sets in motion the Wheel of Brahmā. Here it refers to the Dhamma. Thus, the term “Brahmā” is used in these five senses. Furthermore, there are these ten meanings of “Brahmā”: the Brahmā realm, the Brahmā world, the Brahmā state, the Brahmā abode, the Brahmā vehicle, the Brahmā path, the Brahmā fruit, the Brahmā goal, the Brahmā person, and the one named Brahmā. What is the Brahmā world? It is the world of the Great Brahmās. What is the Brahmā state? It is the state of the Great Brahmās. What is the one named Brahmā? It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. These are the four meanings of “Brahmā. Furthermore, there are these three meanings of “Brahmā”: the Brahmā realm, the Brahmā world, and the one named Brahmā. What is the Brahmā realm? It is the realm of the Great Brahmās. What is the Brahmā world? It is the world of the Great Brahmās. What is the one named Brahmā? It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. These are the three meanings of “Brahmā. Furthermore, there is this single meaning of “Brahmā”:

the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Fully Awakened One, the All-Knowing One, the All-Seeing One, the All-Wise One, the All-Pervading One, the All-Illuminating One, the All-Light One, the All-Splendid One, the All-Glorious One, the All-Victorious One, the All-Conquering One, the All-Powerful One, the All-Masterful One, the All-Ruler, the All-Subduer, the All-Tamer, the All-Subjugator, the All-Overcomer, the All-Conqueror, the All-Extinguisher, the All-Cool One, the All-Peaceful One, the All-Happy One, the All-Blessed One, the All-Auspicious One, the All-Refuge, the All-Island, the All-Light, the All-Shelter, the All-Protector, the All-Support, the All-Reliance, the All-Resort, the All-Abode, the All-Home, the All-Source, the All-Origin, the All-Basis, the All-Foundation, the All-Root, the All-Summit, the All-Pinnacle, the All-Crest, the All-Top, the All-Head, the All-Crown, the All-Utmost, the All-Highest, the All-Supreme, the All-Excellent, the All-Unsurpassed, the All-Incomparable,

Here, the "best" is intended. But here, having developed the first jhāna to a refined degree, one who has been reborn in the plane of the first jhāna as a Great Brahmā with a lifespan of an eon is intended.

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of inclusion; the meaning is "Brahmā and others," that is, the Brahmās in ten thousand world-systems—or it may simply serve to complete the meter. "Lord of the world" (*lokādhipati*)...

Here, "world" (*loka*) refers to three worlds: the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*), the world of beings (*satta-loka*), and the world of space (*okāsa-loka*). Among these, it is the world of beings that is intended here.

Its lord or master is the "Lord of the World" (*lokādhipati*); furthermore, one who is the master even of a portion of the world is also called a "Lord of the World," just as there are "Lords of Devas" (*devādhipati*) and "Lords of Men" (*narādhipati*).

Regarding "Sahampati": it is said that in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was an elder named Sahaka who, having attained the first jhāna and not falling away from that attainment, was reborn at the end of his life as a Great Brahmā with a lifespan of an eon in the plane of the first jhāna.
There, they know him as "Brahmā Sahampati. Although he should have been called "Sahakapati," [he is known by the latter name].
Having made "Sahampati" a conventional designation (*ruḷhī*) based on his lineage, they call him "Sahampati.
"With palms joined" (*katañjali*) means one who has joined the palms; the sense is that he placed his hollowed hands upon his head. "Anadhivaram":

one who has no superior excellence (*adhivara*) is "anadhivara"; or, because there is no excellence greater than his, he is "anadhivara," meaning "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*); [he entreated] that unsurpassed one. "Ayācatha" means you entreated (*ayācittha*), you besought (*ajjhesi*).
Now, in order to show the purpose for which he requested this of the Blessed One, the passage beginning with "There are beings here" was spoken.
In that context, *santi* means they exist, they are found; the sense is that they are present, coming within the range of the Buddha’s vision.
*Idha* is a particle used to designate a location. This term is sometimes used with reference to the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
As it is said: “Right here, monks, is the ascetic; right here is the second ascetic; right here is the third ascetic;
right here is the fourth ascetic; empty are the doctrines of others of other ascetics. And in some places, there is scope [for another], as it is said:
“While remaining right here, even though I have become a deva...”
“Furthermore, O Noble Ones, my life has been regained; know it thus.
In some cases, [the particle] serves merely to fill out the verse, as it is said: “In this case, monks, I would have finished eating and been invited to stop.
In some cases, it refers to the world, as it is said: “In this world, the Tathāgata arises for the welfare of many people.”
"For the happiness of many people. Here too, it should be understood that this is stated with reference to the world itself; therefore, the meaning is "in this world of beings" (*sattaloka*).

As for "beings" (*satta*): they are called "beings" because they are attached, bound, clung to, stuck, and fastened by desire and lust (*chandarāga*) toward the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsadda*), however, this designation applies even to those who are free from lust.
“Of those whose nature is with little dust in their eyes”: in the eye consisting of wisdom (*paññāmaya-akkhi*), there is little—that is, limited—dust of passion, hatred, and delusion;

they are of such a nature, thus they are “of a nature with little dust. Alternatively, those who have little dust, namely passion and so forth, are “those with little dust”; being of a nature with little dust, they are “of a nature with little dust.
This is how the meaning should be understood here. “Of those beings” refers to those of a nature with little dust.
Having changed the case ending and connecting it with the phrase "teach the Dhamma," the meaning should be understood as follows.
"Teach" (*desehi*) is a word of entreaty; its meaning is: teach, speak, point out.

Regarding the word "Dhamma" (*dhamma*): here this term *dhamma* [applies] to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), nature (*pakati*), intrinsic being (*sabhāva*), emptiness (*suññatā*), merit (*puñña*), offenses (*āpatti*), the knowable (*ñeyya*), the Four Truths (*catusacca*), and so forth.
It is seen [in various senses]. For instance: in such passages as, "Here, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma—the discourses (*sutta*), mixed prose and verse (*geyya*), expositions (*veyyākaraṇa*)...

and questions-and-answers (*vedalla*)," it is seen in the sense of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). In such passages as, "Those Blessed Ones were of such a nature (*evaṃdhammā*)," it is seen in the sense of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
And: "O Lord of Monkeys, he who possesses these four qualities, just as you do... [is seen in the sense of a quality (*dhamma*)].
In such passages as “Truth, the Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity—he transcends what is seen,” it refers to wisdom (*paññā*).
In such passages as “Subject to birth, subject to aging, and likewise subject to death,” it refers to nature (*pakati*).

In such passages as “Wholesome phenomena (*dhammā*), unwholesome phenomena, and indeterminate phenomena,” it refers to intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). At that time, however... [the rest of the passage continues].
In such passages as “they are *dhammas*, they are aggregates (*khandhas*)”, it refers to emptiness (*suññatā*). In “The Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness”, it refers to merit (*puñña*).
In “Two indeterminate *dhammas*”, it refers to an offense (*āpatti*).

In “All *dhammas* in all their aspects come within the range of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddha”, it refers to the knowable (*ñeyya*). In “One who has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma”, it refers to... [the Dhamma].
Regarding the Dhamma of the Four Truths: here too, it should be understood as the Dhamma of the Four Truths. "Have compassion" means: exercise compassion and pity.
By saying "this," he is pointing out the *pajā* (the generation). It is called *pajā* because it has been born;
that *pajā*, meaning the multitude of beings—his intention is: "liberate them from the suffering of *saṃsāra*. However, some [commentators] say:
“The Blessed One, the Lord of the World, the Supreme among Men,
with palms joined, was entreated by the hosts of Brahmās”—
thus they recite. To this extent, the meaning of this verse is entirely explained.
Then, having heard that request of the Brahmā Sahampati, great compassion arose in the Blessed One— the possessor of the ten powers,
whose strength of compassion had been accumulated over immeasurable eons, and whose course of wisdom was skillful in accomplishing the welfare of others—
merely by making an opening for all beings. And regarding that arising of compassion in the Blessed One, the compilers at the time of the recitation, while demonstrating it, said:
“For the Tathāgata, the peerless individual, who has perfected true knowledge and conduct,
who is suchlike, who bears the radiance [of wisdom], and who wears his final body— compassion arose for all beings.
This verse was placed here.
In that context, "one whose knowledge and conduct are perfected" (*sampannavijjācaraṇa*): perfection is threefold, by way of being complete, possessed, and sweet. Regarding this, it is said:
"Kosiya, crows eat the ripe rice-ears;
O Brahmā, I inform you of this, yet I am unable to prevent it."

This is called "endowed with perfection. "By means of this Pātimokkha restraint, he is endowed, well-endowed, approached, well-approached, perfected, and possessed"—this is called "endowed with possession.
"'Venerable sir, the lower surface of this great earth is endowed [with sweetness], having a flavor like fresh, non-dark honey"—this is called "endowed with sweetness."
[This is] the name. Here, it is appropriate [to understand it] as "complete and perfect" (*paripuṇṇa-sampanna*) and as "endowed with the factors" (*samaṅgi-sampanna*).
"Knowledge" (*vijjā*) is so called in the sense of piercing through opposing states, in the sense of making things known, and in the sense of that which is to be found.

Furthermore, those three knowledges and eight knowledges should be understood according to the method presented in the *Bhayabherava Sutta* for the three knowledges, and in the *Aṃbaṭṭha Sutta* for the eight.
For in that context, having included the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) along with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and mind-made psychic power (*manomaya-iddhi*),
eight clear knowledges (*vijjā*) are spoken of. "Conduct" (*caraṇa*) refers to restraint by virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness,
faith, moral shame, moral dread, erudition, the arousal of energy, established mindfulness, and perfection of wisdom.
The four fine-material-sphere jhānas—these fifteen states are to be understood.
Indeed, it is because the noble disciple moves by means of these fifteen states and goes toward the deathless state that they are called "conduct" (*caraṇa*).
As it is said: "Here, Mahānāma, the noble disciple is virtuous," and so forth, according to the method explained throughout the *Majjhima Paṇṇāsa*.

It should be understood as follows: *vijjā* (clear vision) and *caraṇa* (conduct) are "clear vision and conduct. One who has perfected and fulfilled clear vision and conduct is "one perfected in clear vision and conduct" (*sampannavijjācaraṇo*).
Alternatively, he is "one perfected in clear vision and conduct" because he is endowed with, possessed of, or equipped with clear vision and conduct.
In either case, the meaning is indeed appropriate; [this refers] to that one perfected in clear vision and conduct.

"Tādin" means one who possesses the characteristic of "suchness" (tādi) as it appears in the *Mahāniddesa* in the manner of the passage beginning, "He is such toward the desirable, he is such toward the undesirable.
The meaning is: of one who is "such" (tādisa), that is, one who is unchanging toward the desirable, the undesirable, and so forth. "Jutindharassa" means "of the radiant one";
the meaning is: of one who possesses a mass of bodily radiance more brilliant than the sun risen during the autumn season on Mount Yugandhara.
Or it is appropriate to say: “Of him who bears the lamp of wisdom. For this has been said:
“Four lamps exist in the world, and a fifth is not found here:
The sun shines by day, and the moon radiates at night.”
“Then the fire shines there and there, day and night;
the Fully Awakened One is the best of those who glow—this is the unsurpassed radiance.

Therefore, the meaning is that he possesses the power of both the physical body and the expansion of wisdom. “Bearing his final body” means bearing his very last physical form; the meaning is that there is no further becoming.
Regarding the term "Tathāgata": here, the Blessed One is called "Tathāgata" for eight reasons. Which eight?

He is a Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) in such a way (tathā); he is a Tathāgata because he has gone (gata) in such a way; he is a Tathāgata because he has come to the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇa);

he is a Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to (abhisambuddha) the true dhammas as they really are; he is a Tathāgata because of his seeing things as they truly are; he is a Tathāgata because of his speaking things as they truly are... [and so forth].
The Tathāgata is so called because of his acting accordingly; he is the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.

How is the Blessed One the Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) in that way? It is because he came by means of that same resolve (*abhinīhāra*) with which, having fulfilled the perfection of giving, he fulfilled the perfections of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truth, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these ten [perfections].

The Tathāgata is so called because, having fulfilled the thirty perfections—namely the ten perfections (*pāramī*), the ten near-perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*)—and having practiced the five great renunciations, namely the renunciation of limbs, the renunciation of life, and the renunciation of wealth, kingdom, children, and wife, he has come just as the Perfectly Enlightened Ones such as Vipassī and others have come;
thus, our Blessed One has also come in that same way. As it is said:
“Just as Vipassī and the other sages attained omniscience here in this world, so too has this Sage of the Sakyas arrived;
therefore, the Visionary One is called ‘Tathāgata.
How is he a Tathāgata by virtue of having thus gone? Just as Vipassī and the others, immediately upon birth, [stood] with level feet upon the earth...
Having been established, she walked seven steps facing north; likewise, our Blessed One has gone thus, and therefore he is the Tathāgata. As it is said:
"Just as the Lord of Bulls, immediately after birth, touched the earth with his even feet..."
Thus Gotama took seven steps, and the Maruts held up a white parasol for him.
Having taken those seven steps, Gotama surveyed the quarters all around.
He uttered a voice endowed with eight factors, like a lion standing upon a mountain peak.

How is it that he is called a *Tathāgata* because he has come to the characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*)? He is a *Tathāgata* because he has come to, reached, and awakened to the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena—both material and immaterial—as they truly are, without error, in accordance with the range of knowledge.
As it is said: “Because he has come exactly to the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are, therefore the Teacher is a *Tathāgata*.”
How is he the Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of things as they really are (*yāthāvato*)?
The "true nature of things" (*tathadhammā*) refers to the Four Noble Truths. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, these four are true, not false, and not otherwise.
Which four? 'This is suffering,' bhikkhus—this is true, this is not false, this is not otherwise."
The detailed explanation follows. The Blessed One has fully awakened to these [truths]; therefore, because he has fully awakened to them as they truly are, he is called the "Tathāgata.
For in this context, the word *gata* carries the sense of "fully awakened" (*abhisambuddha*).
"The Leader fully awakened to those truths that are such; therefore he is the Tathāgata."
"Therefore, because he has perfectly awakened to those truths, he is the Tathāgata.

How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they truly are? For the Blessed One, regarding the objects of form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena that come within the range of the doors of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind of immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems—[he sees them as they truly are].
The Tathāgata knows and sees in every way; thus, he is the "Tathāgata" because of his seeing things as they truly are (*tathadassitā*).
Alternatively, whatever is true (*tatha*) in the world, he shows that to the world exactly as it is. For this reason also, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata.
Here, the derivation of the term "Tathāgata" should be understood in the sense of "one who sees things as they truly are."

Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are drenched, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are saturated thoroughly, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are completely filled, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are fully occupied, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are entirely taken up, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are completely grasped, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are perfectly held, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are firmly established, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are securely grounded, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are well-supported, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are well-maintained, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are well-preserved, and not otherwise. Therefore, by virtue of his truthful speech, he is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, whatever he said was in accordance with the way things are well-guarded, and not otherwise.

Whatever has been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata, comprised within the ninefold division of the scriptures beginning with the Suttas—all that is as true and not otherwise, just as if it had been weighed on a single balance. Therefore he said:
"Cunda, between the night when the Tathāgata awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and the night [when he passes away]..."
“He attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue. Whatever he speaks, utters, or explains during this interval—all that is exactly so and not otherwise.
Therefore, he is called the ‘Tathāgata. In this context, however, the word *gata* has the sense of *gada* (speaking).

Thus, he is a “Tathāgata” because of his speaking truthfully (*tathāvādita*). *Āgada* means speaking; the meaning is “speech. He is a “Tathāgata” because his speech (*āgada*) is true (*tatha*), that is, non-erroneous. It is stated thus by changing the letter *da* to the letter *ta*.
“Because the Victor speaks thus, because he proclaims the Dhamma thus, and because his way of speaking is thus, therefore the Buddha is called the Tathāgata.

How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly? For whatever word the Blessed One spoke, that very thing he performed with his body; his body conforms to his speech, and his speech conforms to his body. Therefore it was said:
“Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks... [etc. ...therefore he is called ‘Tathāgata.
Furthermore, just as his speech has gone, so his body has gone; just as his body has gone, so his speech has gone. Thus, by virtue of acting accordingly, he is a Tathāgata.
‘Since his body has gone in the same way that his speech has gone,’... [etc.]”
"Because he speaks thus, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Teacher, is therefore called the Tathāgata.

How is he the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? Having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below his limits, he overcomes all beings throughout the immeasurable world-systems across the horizontal, by means of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
Even with regard to liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is no measure or limit for him;
rather, he is incomparable, immeasurable, and unsurpassed. Therefore it was said:
"In the world with its devas, bhikkhus... the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power; therefore he is called 'Tathāgata'."

In this regard, the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: it is like a medicine (*agada*), thus it is "medicine" (*agada*). But what is this? It is both the splendor of the teaching and the accumulation of merit.
For by means of these, this physician of great power overcomes all proponents of other doctrines and the world with its devas—just as one would [overcome] snakes with a divine medicine.
Thus, because it overcomes the entire world, it is the splendor of the teaching and the accumulation of merit, which are unerring.
And because he is "an antidote" (*agada*), by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, he should be understood as the "Tathāgata. Thus, in the sense of overcoming, he is the Tathāgata:
"That Teacher whose doctrine is true and unerring, and who is an antidote, being one who has mastery—by that reason he is the Teacher, the Tathāgata."

"Appaṭipuggalassa" means being without a counterpart; there is no other person capable of giving such a promise as "I am the Buddha"—thus he is "without a counterpart" (appaṭipuggala), [the word] "of him, the one without a counterpart.

"Uppajji" means he arose, he appeared. "Kāruññatā" is the state of compassion (karuṇā); it is the abstract noun from karuṇā. "Sabbasatte" is a term that includes all sentient beings without exception.
The meaning is: "among all classes of beings. At this point, the meaning of this verse has been explained.

Then the Blessed One, having been requested by Brahmā for the sake of teaching the Dhamma, and desiring to teach the Dhamma after generating compassion for sentient beings, addressed Mahābrahmā with a verse:
"Open are the doors to the Deathless for those who have ears; let them release their faith!"
“Perceiving violence, O Brahmā, I did not speak the refined, sublime Dhamma among human beings. Then Brahmā Sahampati,
knowing that he had been granted permission by the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma, joined his ten fingers in a resplendent añjali at his head,
paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed surrounded by a host of Brahmās.
He departed. Then the Teacher, having given his promise to that Brahmā, thought, "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?
As he reflected, the thought arose in him, "Āḷāra Kālāma is wise; he will quickly understand this Dhamma.
But looking further, he perceived that Āḷāra had passed away seven days prior, and that Udaka had passed away three days ago.
Having understood this, he further wondered, "Where are the monks of the group of five currently dwelling?
Directing his attention toward them, he perceived that they were at the Deer Park in Isipatana near Bārāṇasī.
Then, when the night of the month of Āsāḷha had dawned, he took his bowl and robe early in the morning and set out upon the eighteen-league road; on the way, he encountered an Ājīvaka named Upaka.
Having seen him and revealed his own state as a Buddha, he went to Isipatana that very day at the time of evening.
There, having declared his state as a Buddha to the group of five monks and having taken his place upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him,
he addressed the five bhikkhus and taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.

Among them, the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña directed his knowledge according to the course of the teaching, and at the conclusion of the discourse, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās.

The Teacher entered the rains retreat right there, and on the following day, he established the Elder Vappa in the fruit of stream-entry. By this same method, he established all of them in the fruit of stream-entry.
Having established them [in the fruits], he again assembled those five elders on the fifth day of the fortnight and taught the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*.
At the conclusion of the teaching, all five elders were established in Arahatship.
Then, the Teacher, seeing right there the spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) of the young man Yasa, [perceived him] as one who had gone forth, having abandoned the household life.
Having seen him, the Teacher called out, "Come, Yasa," and on that very night established him in the fruit of stream-entry;

on the following day, he established him in Arahatship. Furthermore, having ordained his forty-four companions through the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-pabbajjā*), he established them in Arahatship.
Thus, when sixty-one Arahants had arisen in the world, the Teacher—
Having completed the rains retreat and performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), he addressed the monks and said this:
“O monks, for the sake of others and for your own welfare, while treading upon this earth and speaking to human beings, practice the Dhamma.”
“Dwell in solitude, upon mountains and in forests,
constantly proclaiming the True Dhamma to the world for me.
Performing the duty of a messenger of the Dhamma, make it known, O monks.”
For the welfare of beings, those of good conduct should heed my words:
“O you who are free from taints, close all the doors to the states of misery;
open wide the door to the path of heaven and liberation, O you who are equanimous.”
“Through teaching and practice, you who are the abode of qualities such as compassion,
may you cause wisdom and faith in the world to increase in every way.
By constantly giving material gifts to laypeople who assist you,”
“Render them a service in return by giving the gift of the Dhamma.
Exalt the True Dhamma by teaching it to those who are born of the lineage of the Seers.
Having performed the duties that ought to be done, proceed toward the supreme goal.”
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One dispatched those monks in various directions;
proceeding himself toward Uruvelā, he converted thirty youths of the Bhaddavaggiya group in a cottonwood grove along the way.

Among them, the very last was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and the very best was a non-returner (*anāgāmī*); not even one among them was an arahant or an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*). All of them—
Having ordained them by the "Come, monk" formula and dispatched them in various directions, he himself went to Uruvelā. There, after displaying three thousand five hundred miracles,
he tamed the three brothers who were matted-hair ascetics, including Uruvelakassapa and his retinue of one thousand,
and having ordained them by the "Come, monk" formula, he seated them at Gayāsīsa and [taught] the discourse on the Simile of the Burning Fire.

Having established them in Arahatship, the Blessed One, surrounded by those one thousand Arahants, went to the grove named Laṭṭhivana on the outskirts of the city of Rājagaha, thinking, "I shall fulfill my promise to King Bimbisāra. Then the park-keeper informed the king.
Upon hearing that "the Teacher has arrived," the king, together with twelve hundred thousand brahmins and householders, [set out].
Surrounded [by his retinue], he approached the One of Ten Powers— the sun among the best of sages who had entered the forest thicket like the sun emerging from a dense cloud—
and having bowed his head, which was illuminated by the radiance of the jewels in his crown, at the feet of the One of Ten Powers— feet whose soles were adorned with wheels and as soft as pure,
unblemished lotuses— he sat down to one side together with his assembly.
Then it occurred to those brahmin householders: "Does the Great Ascetic lead the holy life under Uruvelā Kassapa, or does Uruvelā Kassapa lead the holy life under the Great Ascetic?
Then the Blessed One, knowing the reflection in their minds, addressed the Elder with a verse:
“Having seen what, O dweller of Uruvelā, did you, who are known as ‘the emaciated one,’ abandon the fire?
I ask you, Kassapa, about this matter: how was your fire-sacrifice abandoned?
The Elder, having understood the Blessed One’s intention—
“Sacrifices proclaim forms, sounds, tastes, and desirable women;
knowing this to be a stain among acquisitions, therefore I have no delight in sacrificing or offering oblations.
Having spoken this verse, in order to manifest his status as a disciple, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata.
—“The Blessed One is my Teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple,” he said, and having ascended into the air to the height of one palm tree, two palm trees...
[and so on] up to seven palm trees, he performed a miracle seven times. Then, descending from the sky and bowing to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Thereupon, the great multitude, having witnessed that miracle, exclaimed: “Oh, how truly majestic are the Buddhas! Thus...”

He spoke in praise of the virtues of the One Possessing Ten Powers, saying, "Even Uruvelakassapa, who was firmly rooted in wrong views and who imagined himself to be an 'Arahant,' was subdued by the Tathāgata after he had torn asunder the net of his views.
Hearing this, the Teacher said, "It is not only now that I am subduing this Uruvelakassapa; in the past, too, he was subdued by me. Then that great multitude...
Rising from his seat, paying homage to the Blessed One, and raising his joined palms to his head, he said:
"Venerable Sir, we have now seen this one tamed by you; but how was he tamed by the Blessed One in the past?
Then the Teacher, being requested by that great multitude, recounted the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka, which had been concealed by another existence, and [expounded] the four...

He proclaimed the Noble Truths. Then, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, King Bimbisāra, together with eleven hundred thousand followers, was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), and one hundred thousand declared themselves lay disciples (*upāsaka*).
Having gone for refuge, the king invited the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, for the following day, and [honored] the Blessed One three times...
Having performed a circumambulation and paid homage, he departed.

On the following day, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha surrounded by a thousand bhikkhus—like the king of the gods with his thousand eyes surrounded by hosts of Maruts, or like Mahābrahmā surrounded by hosts of Brahmās. The King [attended] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having given the gift, at the conclusion of the meal, he said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I shall not be able to live without the Three Jewels;
whether it be the right time or the wrong time, I will come into the presence of the Blessed One.
The Bamboo Grove is indeed very far away, but this park of ours called Veḷuvana is suitable for those who desire seclusion."
Not too far and not too near, convenient for coming and going, free from the bustle of people, possessing the bliss of seclusion, endowed with shade and water,
adorned with cool stone slabs, a most delightful region, densely covered with excellent fragrant flowering trees, and beautifully decorated with lovely palaces,
watchtowers, celestial mansions, monasteries, pleasure groves, and pavilions. This, venerable sir, is mine.

Taking jewel-colored water scented with fragrant flowers from a golden pitcher that resembled glowing embers of fresh fire, the Blessed One accepted it as Anāthapiṇḍika was offering the Veḷuvana monastery;
he poured the water into the hand of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
At the acceptance of that monastery, those who had attained the state of joy, thinking, "The roots of the Buddha’s teaching have been planted," began to dance.
This great earth trembled as if it were shaking. Indeed, apart from the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana in Jambudīpa, there is no other dwelling place that has been taken by causing the earth to quake.
Then, having accepted the Veḷuvana monastery, the Teacher offered words of appreciation for the King’s gift of the monastery.
“Who indeed, other than the Buddhas, the Lords of the World,
would be capable of describing the benefits of giving a dwelling-place, even with ten million mouths?
Longevity, beauty, happiness, strength, excellence, renown, and eloquence— ”
He is called a "giver" who gives a monastery to the Saṅgha.
"The giver [provides] shelter from cold and other such dangers to life;
yet because he protects the lifespan of that [recipient], the virtuous say he is the producer of that lifespan."
“While dwelling in a residence that is too hot or too cold, one lacks strength, beauty, and eloquence.
Therefore, the donor of a monastery gives strength, beauty, and indeed eloquence.
[He gives] against the suffering in the world arising from cold, heat, reptiles, wind, sun, and so forth.”
The donor of a monastery constantly provides protection against many kinds of things and is a bringer of happiness.
Because the donor of a monastery wards off the suffering caused by cold, heat, wind, sun, dust, rain, reptiles, gravel,
wild beasts, and so forth, he finds happiness in the life hereafter.
“He who, with a clear mind, gives for the sake of existence and enjoyment that delightful abode which gladdens the heart—
to those exalted by virtues such as morality— he is called a ‘giver of all.
Having abandoned the stain of stinginess along with greed, he gives to those who are the very dwelling place of virtues.”
He is indeed cast there among others in heaven, born according to his deserts, free from sorrow:
“A man should cause beautiful and sublime monasteries to be built and have monks dwell therein;
with a mind full of faith, he should constantly and respectfully give them food, drink, and clothing.”
“Therefore, O Great King, having experienced existence and wealth that are exceedingly delightful,
you shall later attain peaceful happiness free from sorrow through the fruit of the gift of this monastery.
Having thus expressed his appreciation for King Bimbisāra’s gift of the monastery, the King of Sages rose from his seat, surrounded by the community of monks.
With his own bodily radiance, which was most beautiful to behold, making the city, the forest, the celestial mansions, and so forth appear as if sprinkled with liquid gold,
he entered the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana with the incomparable grace of a Buddha and the infinite splendor of a Buddha.
“In the monastery of Veḷuvana, which is delightful to the mind, the Tathāgata [dwelt] there.”
The Wise One dwelt in various abodes, looking out for those who were ready to be trained.
Now, while the Blessed One was dwelling in this manner, King Suddhodana thought:

"My son, having performed austerities for six years, attained supreme perfect enlightenment, and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, has arrived at Rājagaha and is staying at the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana."
Having heard that [the Bodhisatta] was dwelling there, he addressed a certain high minister:
"Come, my good man, go to Rājagaha with a retinue of one thousand men and, speaking in my name, say: 'Your father, the Great King Suddhodana, desires to see you.
Then, taking my son with you, return. Having assented to the king, saying "Very well, Your Majesty," he set out with a retinue of one thousand men.
Having traveled a road of sixty yojanas, he entered the monastery at the time for the preaching of the Dhamma.

Thinking, "Let the message sent by the king wait for now," he stood at the edge of the assembly and, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, attained Arahantship right where he stood;
together with his thousand men, he requested the going-forth. The Blessed One said, "Come, monks," and extended his hand.

He extended [his hand]. At that very moment, they all became endowed with proper deportment like elder monks of sixty years' standing, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (*iddhimaya*), and they surrounded the Blessed One.
The king, thinking, "He has not returned, nor is any message heard," dispatched his ministers nine times in the same manner. Among those nine thousand men—
Not even one informed the king, nor did anyone send a message. Having all attained *arahantship*, they went forth into homelessness.
Then the king thought, "Who indeed will carry out my command? Looking over his entire royal army, he saw Udāyin.
It is said that he was the king’s minister who accomplished all his objectives, an intimate and most trusted confidant of the Bodhisatta.
He was born on the very same day as [the prince], a companion who had played in the dust with him. Then the king addressed him:
"Dear Udāyin, desiring to see my son, I dispatched nine thousand men; yet not even a single man has returned to report so much as a message.
Indeed, the threat to my life is difficult to discern; while I am still alive—"
“I wish to see my son. Will you be able to show my son to me?
He replied, “I shall be able to do so, Your Majesty, if I am permitted to go forth. “Dear one, whether you go forth or not, show my son to me.
Saying, “Very well, Your Majesty,” he took the king’s message and went to Rājagaha to the Teacher.

Having heard the teaching on the Dhamma, together with the thousand men, he attained arahantship, was established in the state of "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu), and on the full moon day of the month of Phagguna, he thought:
"The winter has passed; the spring season has arrived; the forest groves are in full bloom;
the road is fit for travel; it is time for the One of Ten Powers to perform an act of kindness toward his kinsmen. Having thus reflected, he—
Having approached the Blessed One, he praised the journey for the sake of going to the Blessed One’s native city with about sixty verses:
“Now the trees are like glowing coals, O Blessed One; bearing fruit, they have shed their foliage.”
They shine forth like those possessed of radiance; this is the season of the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
The trees, variegated and resplendent with red sprouts and tender leaves, resemble pavilions brilliant with jewels;
this is the season of the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
“Their tips are in full bloom, adorned with flowers; they are delightful, possessing pure and noble fragrances.
The trees shine forth on both sides; O Great Hero, Aṅgīrasa, this is the right time.
With various trees flourishing with many fruits, the space on both sides is magnificent.”
They dispel hunger and thirst; this is the season of the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
Adorned with variegated garlands and pure sprouts, resembling a peacock’s plumage, the trees shine on both sides; this is the season of the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
“Shining with fruits and sprouts, well-adorned as a dwelling for those who reside there, it truly gladdens beings weary from their journey;
this is the season, O Great Hero, of the Aṅgīrasas.
With their tips in full bloom, many creepers clinging to the forest thickets are resplendent.”
They gladden beings like jeweled pavilions; this is the time for the Great Heroes, the sons of Aṅgīrasa.
Like various creepers clinging to trees, or like a bride accompanied by her loved ones, they entice with their sweet fragrance;
this is the time for the Great Heroes, the sons of Aṅgīrasa.
“Birds of various lovely colors, such as blue and others, warbling all around, delight us with their sweet voices and pleasures;
this is the season of the Aṅgīrasas, O Great Hero.
And deer of many kinds, shining brightly, with tall ears and charming eyes,”
They run forth in all directions: "The time has come for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas!
The earth on every side is delightful, shining with green grass and young shoots;
the trees are well-flowered and adorned like crests—this is the time for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas!"
“Wells-prepared sand made of jewels, well-settled and giving a lovely touch, shines forth in all directions;
it is the time for the Great Hero among the Aṅgīrasas.
The level ground is smooth to the touch and pure, perfumed by the fragrance of delightful blossoms.”
“O Great Hero, Angīrasa, the time has come for those who shine with pure and beautiful splendor.
O Great Hero, Angīrasa, the time has come for those who are like the well-adorned Nandana grove, decorated with clusters of various colorful trees, where the breeze is fragrant and most delightful.”
“The lakes are variegated, diverse, and delightful, well-adorned with lotuses and white water-lilies;
filled with clear, cool, and beautiful water—it is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
Shining with various kinds of fully blossomed lotuses, they are fragrant with pure scents.”
“O Great Hero, this is the time for the Aṅgīrasas to gladden both humans and gods.
“Seated upon fully blossomed lotuses, the birds on all sides warble their songs;
they rejoice together with their mates—O Great Hero, this is the time for the Aṅgīrasas.”
“Having taken up pollen from fully blossomed flowers, bees fly about humming;
the fragrance of honey wafts in every direction—this is the season for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
The trumpeting of rutting elephants and the torrents of water flowing from the mountains [are also present].”
The rivers flow as if adorned by heroes; this is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
The mountains appear on all sides like the necks of peacocks, blue in color;
the quarters of the world shine like kings of the earth; this is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
“Flocks of peacocks dance upon the mountain peak, accompanied by female birds;
they warble with various sweet notes—this is the season for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
Many beautiful birds of lovely song, resplendent with their variegated plumage, [sing].”
Standing upon the mountain, they resound: "The time has come, O Great Hero, for the sons of Aṅgīrasa!
"The mountains shine forth in all directions, strewn with blossoming flowers and adorned with various fragrant blooms; the time has come, O Great Hero, for the sons of Aṅgīrasa!"
“The reservoirs possess manifold fragrant scents, like the reservoirs in the palaces of the Lord of Gods;
rivers flow with great splendor—this is the season for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
Adorned with variegated bathing-places, they are delightful with various deer and birds.”
The rivers shine, flowing beautifully together; this is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
On both sides, at the reservoirs, stand trees in full bloom, lovely and sweetly fragrant;
the tips are adorned and there are beautiful, fair women; this is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
“The forest, strewn with clusters of various fragrant trees, is variegated like the Nandana grove of the gods;
it is ever delightful to the mind for those of noble lineage. O Great Hero, this is the time for the Aṅgīrasas.
Abounding in various pure foods and drinks, provided with condiments and endowed with delicious flavors;”
On the paths in the village, pleasant flowers are easily found; this is the season for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas.
The earth has shone forth on all sides with variegated colors like a seat of flowers;
adorned as if by red lotuses, this is the season for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas.
“Endowed with qualities such as pure faith and aspiring toward the King of Perfect Buddhas, many people from all around gathered right there.
‘O Great Hero, this is the time for the Aṅgīrasas!
[This place] is filled with various groves and beautiful lotus ponds, covered with diverse kinds of lotuses.’”
The time has come, O Great Hero, for the Aṅgīrasas, when they distill the essence like milk from stalks.
Adorned with variegated blue canopies, the delightful trees stand on both sides;
risen up, they have become a multitude of sevenfold beings—the time has come, O Great Hero, for the Aṅgīrasas.
“The forest is long-stretched like a variegated blue cloud, like the Nandana grove in the world of the Lord of Gods;
with flowers of every season, fragrant and beautiful, this is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
In every league there is pure water, and pleasant villages with abundant food are easy to find.”
“Crowded with people, with food and drink easily obtained—this is the time for the Great Hero, the sons of Aṅgīrasa.
Abounding in shade and water, delightful, providing all happiness to those who dwell there;
with many spacious halls and assembly-houses—this is the time for the Great Hero, the sons of Aṅgīrasa.”

“Adorned with various groves of diverse trees, with delightful parks and beautiful lotus ponds, well-laid out and fragrant with the scent of noble perfumes—this is the season for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
The wind is gentle, cool, and pleasant; the sky is clear, with clouds dispersed on all sides.”
All directions shine brightly; this is the time for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas.
On the road, dust rises up; at night, there falls a gentle rain;
the sun in the sky is mild in its heat; this is the time for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas.
“Intoxicated elephants with rut-flowing temples sport joyfully with herds of female elephants;
trumpeting, they run through all directions. This is the time for the great heroes of the Aṅgīrasas.
The forest is deep blue and beautiful to behold, as lovely as a peak of blue clouds.”
To those who behold it, it is most wonderful: this is the time for the great heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
The sky is pure like a cloudless vault, most delightful, as if adorned with jewels;
all directions shine forth brilliantly: this is the time for the great heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
“Gandhabbas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras, with sweet voices and beautiful songs, wander in that most delightful grove;
it is the season for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas.
This forest is frequented by hosts of ascetics who have cast off the shackles of the defilements.”
“The time has come for the Aṅgīrasas, O Great Hero, when the monasteries and groves have flourished.
With their forest borders abounding in various fruits, free from turmoil, and eternally delightful to the mind, they cause concentration and rapture to increase;
the time has come for the Aṅgīrasas, O Great Hero.”
“Constantly frequented by many brahmins, dwelling continually from village to village, there are excellent villages in every town;
this is the season for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
Clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, perfumes, garlands, and ointments—”
