There, the people were prosperous and numerous; that was the time of the Great Heroes, the descendants of Aṅgīrasa.
Through the power of merit, all those people had attained the highest heaven;
they lived there happy and prosperous, possessing abundant wealth of various kinds; that was the time of the Great Heroes, the descendants of Aṅgīrasa.
“The sky is of most pure hue, free from clouds, and the moon illuminates all directions;
the night air is soft and cool—this is the season for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
When the moon rises, all people are delighted, conversing with various talk upon their own courtyards.”
They rejoice together with those they love; this is the time for the Aṅgīrasas, O Great Hero.
The sky shines with the rays of the moon, and the earth has a pure and pleasing hue;
all directions are perfectly clear—this is the time for the Aṅgīrasas, O Great Hero.
“Having seen from afar the excellent moonbeams, flowers blossomed upon the surface of the earth.
For those who seek the quality of fragrance from all sides, it is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
As if smeared by the rays of the moon, the earth is adorned on every side with blossoms.”
It shone like a woman adorned with garlands of every limb; such was the season for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas.
“Even elephants, intoxicated with rut, trumpet; and birds with variegated plumage [resound] on all sides.
They let out their cries in the most delightful forest; such was the season for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas.”
“The entire road is fit for travel, and the kingdom is prosperous, wealthy, and well-provided with enjoyments;
it is praised by all and bestows every happiness—the time has come, O Great Hero, for the Aṅgīrasas.
And the entire forest is of most varied beauty, like the well-constructed Nandana grove.”
It constantly generates joy for ascetics—this is the time, O Great Hero, of the Aṅgīrasas.
“Kapilavatthu by name, adorned and delightful like the city of the gods;
this glorious family city—this is the time, O Great Hero, of the Aṅgīrasas.”
“With its charming watchtowers and variegated forms, adorned with clusters of blossoming lotuses, and with its beautiful moats, the city is most delightful;
it is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
With its variegated walls and gateways, and its beautiful courtyards, it has become like a dwelling place for the gods.”
The delightful street, resembling the world of the gods— this was the time for the Great Hero,
the Aṅgīrasas. The sons of the Sākya king, adorned with excellent ornaments,
shone resplendently like the sons of the gods in the world of the Lord of Suras— this was the time for the Great Hero, the Aṅgīrasas.
“Suddhodana sent ten of his ministers’ sons to behold the best of sages;
together with a great force, O Lord of Sages, it was the appointed time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas.
But he saw neither one who had come nor any word from the best of men, the Hero, who was overcome by sorrow.”
“I wish to please the lord of men; O Great Hero, it is the time for the Aṅgīrasas.
“Seeing him, there was a surge of wonderful joy in those looking toward the Lord of Bipeds;
please him, O Lord of Sages, supreme in virtue; O Great Hero, it is the time for the Aṅgīrasas.”
“Out of hope the field is ploughed, out of hope the seed is sown;
out of hope merchants go forth to sea, carrying wealth as their prize.
May that hope for which I stand be fulfilled for me.”
“Neither too cold nor too hot, neither too plagued by famine nor drought;
the earth is verdant and green—this is the time, O Great Sage.
Then the Teacher said to him, “Udāyī, why do you praise the journey? [He replied: “Venerable sir, for you...”
“Father, the Great King Suddhodana wishes to see you; perform the gathering of your kinsmen,” he said.
“Very well, Udāyin, I shall perform the gathering of my kinsmen. In that case, announce it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, so that they may fulfill the duties of those traveling.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Elder replied, and he announced it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

The Teacher, surrounded by twenty thousand bhikkhus whose taints were exhausted— ten thousand from among the noble sons dwelling in Aṅga and Magadha, and ten thousand from among those dwelling in Kapilavatthu—
departed from Rājagaha and, traveling a league each day, reached the city of Kapilavatthu in two months.
As soon as the Blessed One had arrived, the Sākiyas, thinking, "We shall see our foremost kinsman," sought out the place where the Blessed One was staying.
Having observed that the Nigrodha Sāka’s monastery was delightful, they had all the preparations for its reception carried out;
then, with their bodies adorned with every ornament, they went forth to meet him, carrying perfumes and flowers in their hands.
Honoring the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, powders, and other offerings, they proceeded ahead of him toward the Nigrodha Monastery.
There, the Blessed One sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him, surrounded by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were exhausted.
But the Sakyans, being of a proud nature and stiff with pride, thought: “Prince Siddhattha is younger than we; he is our—”
Thinking, "He is my younger brother, my son, my nephew, and my grandson," they said to the very young princes, "You should pay homage;

we shall sit behind you, one after another. When they were seated in this manner, the Blessed One, observing their disposition, thought: "These relatives do not pay homage to me because of their own futile old age."
But they do not know what a Buddha is like, nor what the power of a Buddha is like; nor do they know that "a Buddha is such-and-such," or that "the power of a Buddha is such-and-such.

Therefore, let me display my own power as a Buddha and my power of psychic potency (*iddhi*), and perform a miracle by creating in the sky a walking-path (*caṅkama*) made of all kinds of jewels, extending across ten thousand world-systems.
“Having built it, while walking there, he should observe the inclinations of the great multitude and teach the Dhamma,” he thought.
Therefore, for the purpose of showing the Blessed One’s reflection, the compilers of the collection said:
“Neither these gods nor humans know: ‘What kind of person is this Buddha, the supreme among men?’”
What is the power of psychic potency and what is the power of wisdom? What is the power of a Buddha for the welfare of the world?
"Neither gods nor humans know these things: that this Buddha is such a supreme among men;
that his power of psychic potency is such, his power of wisdom is such, and his power as a Buddha for the welfare of the world is such."
“Come now, I shall display the unsurpassed power of a Buddha;
I will fashion a walkway in the sky adorned with jewels.
In this context, *na hete jānanti* means “for these do not know. The word *na* has the sense of negation (*paṭisedhattho*). The word *hi* has the sense of a reason (*kāraṇatthe*).

This is a particle. However, because these relatives of mine and other gods and humans do not know—so long as my power as a Buddha and my power of psychic potency (*iddhi*) have not been revealed—that "the Buddha is such, and his power of psychic potency is such," therefore the meaning is: "I shall show my power as a Buddha and my power of psychic potency.
Regarding the term *sadevamānusā* (together with gods and humans): here, "gods" refers specifically to those gods born by rebirth (*upapatti-deva*). "Together with gods" means...
"Together with the gods" (*sadevā*). Who are they? Humans; "together with the gods" means humans together with the gods.
Alternatively, "god" (*deva*) refers to a conventional god (*sammutideva*), namely King Suddhodana. "Together with the god," that is, with King Suddhodana, means "together with the gods.

"Humans" (*mānusā*) refers to kinsmen who are human. "Together with the gods, together with the humans" means together with King Suddhodana; or, these kinsmen of mine, together with the king, constitute my strength.
The meaning is "they do not understand. The remaining deities are also included. All deities are called "deities" (*devā*) in the sense of "shining" (*devana*).
"Shining" refers to the meaning of the verbal root, such as play and so forth. Alternatively, "deities and humans" is *devamānusā*;
"together with deities and humans" is *sadevamānusā*. Who are they? The ellipsis must be understood as "the worlds" (*loka*). "Buddha" [refers to] the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths...
The Buddha is so called because he has awakened after [others] have awakened. As it is said:
"What was to be directly known has been directly known; what was to be developed has been developed;
what was to be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, O Brahmins, I am the Buddha."
Furthermore, here the derivation of the word *buddha* should be understood in the sense of the agent (*kattukāraka*).
Because he has been awakened to and known by gods and humans who have attained distinction as "Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddho*), he is called *buddha*.

Here, the derivation of the word *buddha* should be understood in the sense of the object (*kammakāraka*). Or, he is *buddha* because awakening (*buddha*) belongs to him; the meaning is "one possessed of awakening" (*buddhavanto*).
All of that should be understood according to the rules of grammar (*saddasattha*). "Of what kind" (*kīdisako*) means:
of what sort, resembling what, like what, of what color, of what shape, or whether long or short—this is the meaning.
"Supreme among men" (*naruttamo*): he is the highest, the most excellent, the best among men or for men; thus, he is "supreme among men. "Power of psychic potency" (*iddhibala*): here...

Success (*iddhi*) is so called in the sense of succeeding and in the sense of attainment. Alternatively, it is success because by means of it beings succeed, become successful, and reach the pinnacle of excellence;
thus it is success. That, moreover, is tenfold. As it is said: "Successes:
there are ten successes. Which ten? Success through resolve, success through transformation, success consisting of mind..."

“Supernormal power (iddhi): supernormal power through the exercise of knowledge, supernormal power through the exercise of concentration, noble supernormal power, supernormal power born of the ripening of kamma, supernormal power of one possessing merit, supernormal power consisting of science, and supernormal power in the sense of succeeding through the condition of right application in this or that case.
This is their distinction: by nature, one person adverts to many things—having adverted to a hundred or a thousand—
Having analyzed it thus, one resolves with knowledge, "May I become many.
This supernormal power (iddhi), being accomplished by way of resolution, is called "resolution-iddhi" (adhiṭṭhānā iddhi). Its meaning is as follows:

having entered the fourth jhāna as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) and emerged from it, if one desires to become a hundred, one does so with sense-sphere preparatory thoughts (parikamma-citta), thinking, "I am a hundred, I am a hundred."

Having performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*), he again enters the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññāpādaka-jhāna*). Emerging from that, he adverts once more and resolves.
Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, there are a hundred [beings]. This same method applies to a thousand and so forth.
In this context, the mind of the foundational jhāna has the sign (*nimitta*) as its object, while the preliminary minds have a hundred or a thousand and so forth as their objects.
Or they have various objects, and those are by way of color, not by way of designation. The resolving consciousness also has a single object;
however, like the absorption consciousness, it arises immediately after the change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhū) and belongs to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
Having abandoned its natural appearance, it displays the form of a youth, or it displays the form of a nāga, or the form of a supaṇṇa.

Or... pe... or he displays various military arrays—thus, the psychic power (iddhi) arrived at in this way is called "power of transformation" (vikubbaniddhi) because it proceeds by means of changing one's natural appearance.
"Here, a bhikkhu creates from this body another body, material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts..."

The supernormal power (iddhi) described by this method as "with unimpaired faculties" is called "mind-made supernormal power" (manomayiddhi) because it proceeds by way of producing another mind-made body within one's own very body.
By the power of the knowledge of Arahatship to be attained through that personal existence— whether prior to the arising of that knowledge, subsequent to it, or at that very moment—

A specific excellence produced through the expansion of knowledge is called "success by the expansion of knowledge" (*ñāṇavipphārā iddhi*). This refers to the success by the expansion of knowledge of the Venerable Bākula and the Venerable Saṅkicca;
their story should be told here as an illustration.

A specific excellence produced through the power of serenity (*samatha*), whether before, after, or at the very moment of concentration, is "success by the expansion of concentration" (*samādhivipphārā*).

Regarding "supernormal power" (iddhi): there is the supernormal power of the venerable Sāriputta arising from the expansion of concentration; the supernormal power of the venerable Sañjīva arising from the expansion of concentration;
the supernormal power of the venerable Khāṇu-koṇḍañña arising from the expansion of concentration; the supernormal power of the female lay follower Uttarā arising from the expansion of concentration;
and the supernormal power of the female lay follower Sāmāvatī arising from the expansion of concentration—the accounts of these instances should be related here.
However, I have not explained them in detail here for the purpose of avoiding the fault of excessive prolixity.
What is noble supernormal power (*ariyā iddhi*)? Here, a bhikkhu, if he so desires, "May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive," dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive;
if he so desires, "May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive," [he dwells there perceiving the repulsive].
“He dwells there perceiving repulsiveness... he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending.
This is called noble supernormal power (*ariyā iddhi*), because it occurs only for noble ones who have attained mastery over the mind.
What is supernormal power born of the ripening of kamma? It belongs to all birds, all deities, and the beings of the first eon.
The psychic power born of the ripening of kamma for certain humans and for those in the states of deprivation, such as traveling through the air, is called *iddhi*.
What is the psychic power of one possessing merit? A wheel-turning monarch travels through the air together with his fourfold army.
For the householder Jaṭilaka, a golden mountain eighty cubits high appeared. This is called the psychic power of one possessing merit. [As was the case] for Ghosaka...
The state of being free from illness even when attempts are made to kill one by householders in seven ways is the supernormal power (iddhi) of the meritorious.
The appearance of rams made of the seven precious gems over an area of eight karīsas for the merchant Meṇḍaka is the supernormal power of the meritorious.
What is the supernormal power consisting of science (vijjāmayā iddhi)? Having recited the spells, the holders of science travel through the air, in the sky, in the firmament.
"Showing even an elephant... [and so on]... showing various military arrays"—this is called success consisting of science (*vijjāmaya-iddhi*), which proceeds according to such a method.
The excellence produced by performing this or that action is "success in the sense of succeeding through the condition of right application.
This is what is meant by "success" in each respective case in the sense of succeeding through the condition of right application. Of these ten kinds—
The power of supernormal success (*iddhi*) is called "the power of success" (*iddhibala*); the meaning is: "They do not know this power of success of mine.
Regarding "the power of wisdom" (*paññābala*), what is intended is the power of wisdom of the path to Arhatship, which bestows all mundane and supramundane distinctions of excellence;
they do not know that either. Some say: "This 'power of wisdom' is a designation for the six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*)."
They say: "The power of a Buddha" (*buddhabala*) here refers either to the majesty of a Buddha (*buddhānubhāva*) or to the ten powers of knowledge (*dasabalañāṇa*).

Among these, the ten powers of knowledge are: the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇa*); the knowledge of knowing the ripening of kamma in the past, future, and present; the knowledge of the path leading everywhere (*sabbatthagāminipaṭipadāñāṇa*);
the knowledge of knowing the world with its many elements and various elements (*anekadhātunānādhātulokajānanañāṇa*); and the knowledge of various inclinations (*nānādhimuttikañāṇa*).

The knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies; the knowledge of things as they really are regarding the defilement, purification, and emergence from the meditative absorptions (jhāna), liberations (vimokkha), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti);
the knowledge of recollecting past lives; the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava)—these are the ten.
"Buddha-power" is a designation for these ten knowledges. *Edisaṃ* means "of such a kind"; or rather, *īdisaṃ* is the reading.
*Handā* is a particle used in the sense of relinquishing. *Aham* refers to himself. What is meant?

Since these relatives of mine do not know the power of the Buddha or his qualities, but merely out of pride based on their own state of vain old age do not pay homage to me—the eldest and most excellent in all the world—therefore they possess the banner of conceit.
The meaning is: having broken it, he would display the power of a Buddha for the sake of paying homage. "I shall display" (*dassayissāmi*) means "I would display" (*dasseyyaṃ*).

There is also the reading "I shall show" (*dassesāmi*), which has the same meaning. "Buddha-power" (*buddhabalaṃ*) refers either to the majesty of a Buddha or to the excellence of a Buddha’s knowledge.
"Unsurpassed" (*anuttaraṃ*) means without superior. "Walks" (*caṅkamanti*) refers to the place where one should walk. "I shall measure out" (*māpayissāmi*)— [End of fragment]
“I shall have it built. There is also the reading “I shall have a walkway (caṅkamana) built,” which has the same meaning. “In the sky” means in the air.

“Adorned with all kinds of jewels” means adorned and decorated with all those things that produce delight—by way of being jewels—in the form of pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, masāragalla, and ruby;
thus it is “adorned with all kinds of jewels,” and that is what is meant by “adorned with all kinds of jewels. “In the sky... [text continues].
Some read it as "ratanamaṇḍitan"ti.

Then, as soon as the Blessed One had thought this, the earth-dwelling and other deities inhabiting the ten thousand world-systems, their hearts filled with joy, gave their approval. To clarify this matter, the compilers of the collection [said]:
"The earth-dwellers, the Mahārājikas, the Tāvatiṃsas, the Yāma gods, the Tusitas, and the Nimmita gods;..."
"Even those who are mind-made (Paranimmita) and the Brahmakāyika gods raised a vast cry of joy"—thus it should be understood that these opening verses have been placed [there].

In this context, "of the earth" (bhummā) means those dwelling on the earth, situated upon rocks, mountains, forests, trees, and so forth. "Belonging to the Great Kings" (Mahārājikā) means those who are followers of the Great Kings.
Having heard the sound of the earth-dwelling deities, the space-dwelling deities [heard it]; from them, the cloud-deities of the rain-clouds;
from them, the cloud-deities of heat; from them, the cloud-deities of cold; from them, the cloud-deities of rain; from them, the cloud-deities of wind;
from them, the Four Great Kings; from them, the Tāvatiṃsa gods; from them, the Yāma gods; from them, the Tusita gods.
Then the Nimmānarati [heaven], then the Paranimmitavasavatti [heaven], then the Brahmakāyika [heaven], then the Brahmapurohita [heaven],
then the Mahābrahmā [heaven], then the Parittābha [heaven], then the Appamāṇābha [heaven], then the Ābhassara [heaven], then the Parittasubha [heaven],
then the Appamāṇasubha [heaven], then the Subhakiṇha [heaven], then the Vehapphala [heaven], then the Aviha [heaven], then the Atappa [heaven], then...
The Sudassā, then the Sudassī, and then the Akaniṭṭha deities, having heard the sound, made a great noise.

With the exception of non-percipient beings and those beings belonging to the formless realm, all gods, humans, nāgas, and others—in every place where the ear-sphere functions—raised a shout of acclamation with their hearts overcome by joy;
this is the meaning. "Delighted" means with joyful hearts, having given rise to rapture and gladness.
The meaning is "having offered. "Vipula" means broad.

Then, immediately after the thought [had arisen], the Teacher entered the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the white-kasiṇa and resolved: "Let there be light throughout ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
Simultaneously with that mind of resolution, light appeared, starting from the earth.
As far as the Akaniṭṭha realm. Therefore it was said:
“The earth, together with its devas, was illuminated, And the vast, unconfined spaces between the worlds;
The intense darkness was dispelled at that time, Upon seeing this marvelous miracle.”

In this context, "illuminated" means made manifest. Regarding "earth": here this earth is fourfold—solid earth (*kakkhaḷa-pathavī*), constituent earth (*sasambhāra-pathavī*), sign earth (*nimitta-pathavī*), and conventional earth (*sammuti-pathavī*).
Among these, the solid earth is that which is spoken of in such passages as: "And what, friends, is the internal earth element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, that is hard and solid."

[The term] *nāma*. In such passages as, “Whatever bhikkhu should dig the earth or cause it to be dug,” the “earth with its constituents” (*sasambhāra-pathavī*) is mentioned—namely, the twenty parts beginning with head-hair, as well as external things such as iron and copper.

This is called “earth with its constituents” because it is earth together with its constituent factors, such as color and so forth. In such passages as, “One person perceives the earth-kasina,” it refers to the “sign-earth” (*nimitta-pathavī*).

It is also called "the earth as an object. One who has attained the jhāna of the earth-kasiṇa and is reborn in the world of the gods receives the name "earth-deva" (pathavīdeva) by way of his arrival there. For this is said: "The water-gods and the earth-gods," and so forth;

in such passages, this should be understood as conventional earth, the earth as a designation. However, in the present context, the earth consisting of material components (sasambhāra-pathavī) is intended.

“Together with the devas” means together with the world of the devas. There is also a reading “together with the devas,” which is even better; the meaning is that the human world, along with the devas, was illuminated.
“Many” means numerous. “The intermediate spaces between the worlds” (lokantarikā) is a designation for the asura hosts and the hells;
however, there is one intermediate space between three world-systems (cakkavāḷa), just as there is a space between the three wheels of a cart.
Each individual Lokantarika hell is like a space in the midst of those standing shoulder-to-shoulder;

in extent, it is eight thousand *yojanas*. "Uncovered" (*asaṃvutā*) means having no foundation below. "Darkness" (*tamo*) means gloom. "Intense" (*tibbo*) means thick and dense. Due to the absence of the light of the moon and sun, it is perpetually dark.
"Distressed" (*vihato*) means shattered. "Then" (*tadā*) refers to when the Blessed One felt compassion for sentient beings.
He emitted light for the purpose of performing a miracle; at that time, the intense darkness standing in the intermediate spaces between worlds was dispelled and shattered—this is the meaning.
"A marvel" (*acchariya*) means worthy of being seized by a *accharā* (a celestial nymph); the meaning is that it is worthy of being struck with the fingers due to its quality of causing wonder.

*Pāṭihīra* is so called because it removes opposing factors (*paṭipakkha-haraṇato*). Alternatively, it is *pāṭihīra* because it strikes back (*paṭiharati*) the minds of beings that have fallen into views and conceit;
or it is *pāṭihīra* because it brings back (*paṭi-āharati*) confidence in beings who lack it.
There is also the reading *pāṭihera*, which has the same meaning. Here, this is a designation for a particular kind of manifestation of light. Having seen...

The meaning should be understood by citing this passage: "It was a wonderful miracle" (*accherakaṃ pāṭihīraṃ*), whereby gods, humans, and even beings born in the intermediate spaces of the world, upon seeing that miracle of the Blessed One, attained supreme joy and gladness.
Otherwise, neither the former would be consistent with the latter, nor the latter with the former.
Now, in order to show that light exists not only in the human world, but that light indeed prevails everywhere throughout the threefold world—
comprising formations, beings, and space— it is said: “O gods, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas,
a sublime and vast radiance has arisen!”
"In this world and in the next, both together, below, above, and across—thus it is spread out. This verse was spoken.
Therein, "devas" includes all devas: conventional devas (*sammutideva*), devas by birth (*upapattideva*), and devas by purification (*visuddhideva*).

Devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas—these are the deva-gandhabba-human-rakkhasas. Together with the devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas is "together with devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas" (sadevagandhabbamanussarakkhaso).
What, then, is that? It is the world; in that world together with devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas.
"Ābhā" means light. Regarding the word *uḷāra*, this term is seen used in the senses of sweet, excellent, abundant, and so forth.
For this term is seen in the sense of "sweet" in such passages as, "They are eating and consuming choice hard foods and soft foods";
in the sense of "excellent" in such passages as, "But Master Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with an excellent praise";
and in the sense of "vast" in such passages as, "Transcending the divine majesty of the devas, there was an immeasurable, vast radiance. And here it [is used]...
It should be understood as "supreme. "Vipula" means immeasurable. "Ajāyata" means it arose, appeared, and came into being.
"In this world and in the next" means in this human world and in that divine world; such is the meaning.
"In both" refers to those two together, to be understood in the same way as in the case of "internal and external" and so forth. "Below" refers to the hells, such as Avīci and others.
It rises even above the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) and even into the hairless space (*ajaṭākāsa*). "And across" means across as well, throughout ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Extensive" means spread out. The meaning is that, having dispelled the darkness and having overspread the aforementioned world and region, the radiance proceeded.
Alternatively, "and across, extensive" means extensive and vast in the transverse direction.
The meaning is that he remained after having pervaded an immeasurable region with light.
Then the Blessed One, having performed the pervasion of light throughout the ten thousand world-systems, entered the fourth jhāna which serves as the basis for direct knowledge;
emerging from that, having adverted his mind and resolved with a mind of determination, he rose up into the air before those kinsmen.
As if scattering the dust from his feet upon their heads, he displays the Twin Miracle in the midst of a great assembly of gods and humans.
This, moreover, should be understood from the text itself:
"What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the Twin Miracle? Here, the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle."
Unshared with his disciples, from the upper part of his body a mass of fire issues forth, and from the lower part of his body a stream of water issues forth.
From the lower part of his body a mass of fire issues forth, and from the upper part of his body a stream of water issues forth...
[and so on] ...from the front part of his body a mass of fire issues forth, and from the back part of his body a stream of water issues forth. From the back part of his body...
A mass of fire proceeds from the front part of the body, and a stream of water proceeds from [the back]... pe ...
a mass of fire proceeds from the right eye, and a stream of water proceeds from the left eye.
A mass of fire proceeds from the left eye, and a stream of water proceeds from the right eye... pe ... a mass of fire proceeds from the right ear canal.
A stream of water flows from the left ear-canal; a mass of fire issues from the left ear-canal, while a stream of water flows from the right ear-canal...
[and so on] ...a mass of fire issues from the right nostril, while a stream of water flows from the left nostril.
A mass of fire issues from the left nostril, while [a stream of water flows] from the right nostril.
A stream of water issues forth... [and so on] ...a mass of fire issues from the right shoulder-peak, and a stream of water issues from the left shoulder-peak.
A mass of fire issues from the left shoulder-peak, and a stream of water issues from the right shoulder-peak...
[and so on] ...a mass of fire issues from the right hand, and a stream of water issues from the left hand.
From his left hand a mass of fire issues forth, and from his right hand a stream of water issues forth... [and so on]...
From his right side a mass of fire issues forth, and from his left side a stream of water issues forth.
From his left side a mass of fire issues forth, and from his right side a stream of water issues forth... [and so on]... From his right foot a mass of fire issues forth.
A stream of water issues from the left foot; a mass of fire issues from the left foot, and a stream of water issues from the right foot...
[and so on] ...a mass of fire issues from each finger, and streams of water issue from the spaces between the fingers;
streams of water issue from the spaces between the fingers, and a mass of fire issues from each finger... [and so on].
From each single pore a mass of fire issues forth, and from each single pore a stream of water issues forth.
From every single pore a mass of fire issues forth, and from every single pore a stream of water issues forth—of six colors:
blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and translucent.
“The Blessed One walks while the emanation stands, sits, or lies down. The Blessed One stands while the emanation walks, sits, or lies down.
The Blessed One sits while the emanation walks, stands, or lies down. The Blessed One lies down while the emanation walks, stands, or sits.”
or sits down. The emanation walks back and forth while the Blessed One stands, or sits down, or lies down.
The emanation stands while the Blessed One walks back and forth, or sits down, or lies down.
The emanation sits down while the Blessed One walks back and forth, or stands, or lies down. The emanation lies down while the Blessed One...
Whether he walks, stands, or sits—this should be understood as the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s Twin Miracle.
Furthermore, by means of his attainment of the fire-kasiṇa, a mass of fire issues from the upper part of that Blessed One’s body;
and by means of his attainment of the water-kasiṇa, a stream of water issues from the lower part of his body. Thus, again, by means of the stream of water...

It should be understood that it was said, "A mass of fire issues from the lower part of the body, and a stream of water issues from the upper part of the body," in order to show that a stream of water issues from the place where a mass of fire issues, and a mass of fire issues from the place where a stream of water issues.
This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. Furthermore, in this context, the mass of fire [is compared] to the stream of water...

It was entirely unmixed. Likewise, the stream of water [was unmixed] with the mass of fire. As for the rays, however, each successive ray proceeds simultaneously with its predecessor like a pair of twins.

Although there is no such thing as the simultaneous occurrence of two consciousnesses, in the case of the Buddhas, due to the lightness of the subsistence in the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and their mastery through five modes of practice, [this occurs].
These rays proceed as if simultaneously; however, the preliminary work (*parikamma*), the adverting (*āvajjana*), and the resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for each ray are distinct.
For the sake of the blue ray, the Blessed One enters the attainment of the blue kasiṇa; for the sake of the yellow ray and the others, he enters the attainment of the yellow kasiṇa and so forth.
Thus, while the Bhagavā’s Twin Miracle was being performed, it was as if the entire ten-thousandfold world-system were being adorned. Therefore it is said:
“The Teacher, the unsurpassed leader, the supreme guide, honored by gods and men;
possessed of great majesty and the marks of a hundred merits, displayed this wondrous miracle.”

In this context, *sattuttama* means "the supreme among beings. He is the supreme, the most excellent, and the best among all beings by virtue of his own qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth;

thus he is *sattuttama*. Alternatively, *sattuttama* means "the supreme of beings. For *satta* is a name for knowledge (*ñāṇa*); therefore, because he is the best and supreme by means of that knowledge—consisting of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the six unique knowledges—he is *sattuttama*.
Or, according to grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇa*), he is *sattuttama* because he is a being (*satta*) who is supreme (*uttama*).
If this were the case, one should have said "uttamasatto," because of the rule that places the word *uttama* first in a compound.
However, this variation should not be viewed as irregular, due to the principle of frequent usage (*bahulavacanato*), just like the terms *naruttama*, *purisuttama*, and *nara-vara*.
Alternatively, it may be analyzed as "he whose being (*satta*) is supreme (*uttama*)," thus "one of supreme being" (*sattuttama*); and here too, the word *uttama* is placed first in the compound.
It occurs. There is no fault here because of the rule of placing the qualifying term first in the compound *uttamasatta*, as in the case of *cittagū* and *paddhagū*.
Alternatively, it should be understood as a dual qualification, like the reading *āhitaggi* and so forth.

He is called a *vināyaka* because he leads (*vineti*) and tames (*dameti*) beings through many means of guidance. He is a *satthā* (Teacher) by virtue of [teaching] matters pertaining to this life and the life to come.
He is a Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs beings according to what is appropriate for them. "Ahū" means "there was. He is "honored by gods and humans" (*devamanussapūjita*):

they are called "gods" (*deva*) because they shine and sport with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure; they are called "humans" (*manussa*) because of their abundance of mind (*manassa ussannattā*).

Thus, "gods and humans" are *devamanussā*, and one who is honored by gods and humans is *devamanussapūjita*. He is honored both by the offering of flowers and the like, and by the offering of requisites.

The meaning is "honored. But why is it that only gods and humans are mentioned? Is it not true that the Blessed One was indeed honored even by animals—such as Āḷavaka, Kāḷāpa, Dhanapāla, Pālileyyaka, and the nāgas—as well as by those fallen into the lower realms, such as Sātāgira, Āḷāvaka, Hemavata, Sūciloma, and Kharaloma?
This is certainly true; however, [the text] does so by way of an inclusive limit, that is, by way of including all categories of persons.
It should be understood that this has been said. "Of great majesty" means endowed with the great majesty of a Buddha.

"Possessing the marks of a hundred merits": if all beings in infinite world-systems were each to perform a meritorious deed a hundred times, the Bodhisatta was reborn having himself performed a hundredfold the merit produced by all those people acting together. Therefore, he is called "possessing the marks of a hundred merits."
It is said. However, some say that "each single characteristic is produced by a hundredfold meritorious deed.
If that were so, it would follow that anyone could become a Buddha; therefore, that view has been rejected in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
"He showed" means he displayed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), which causes extreme wonder in all gods and humans.
Then the Teacher, having performed a miracle in the sky and observed the mental disposition of the great multitude,
desiring to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma suited to their inclinations while walking, fashioned in the sky a jeweled cloister made of all kinds of gems,
extending across ten thousand world-systems. Thus it is said:

“Thus requested by the best of gods, the Visionary One, the Supreme among Men, having then considered the purpose, the Leader of the World had a walkway constructed, perfectly finished and fashioned from all kinds of jewels.
In this passage, “He” refers to that Teacher. “Requested” means he was requested for the teaching of the Dhamma at the very beginning, on the eighth day.
The meaning is as follows. By "Devavara" is meant Sahampati Brahmā. Regarding the term "Cakkhumā": here, that which sees (*cakkhati*) is "vision" (*cakkhu*);
the meaning is that it discerns the even and the uneven. That vision, moreover, is twofold: the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*) and the physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*).
Therein, the eye of knowledge is fivefold: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*), the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), and...

"Eye of wisdom" (paññācakkhu). Among these, the "Buddha-eye" (buddhacakkhu) refers to both the knowledge of the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions (*āsayānusayañāṇa*) and the knowledge of the degrees of maturity of the faculties in others (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*), which is mentioned in the passage:
"Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye. The "Dhamma-eye" (dhammacakkhu) refers to the three lower paths and the three fruits, which is mentioned in the passage:
"The dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose. The "Universal Eye" (*samantacakkhu*)...
The "eye of omniscience" (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is that which is described as: "Having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, O wise one, with eyes on all sides.
The "divine eye" (*dibbacakkhu*) is the knowledge associated with the supernormal consciousness (*abhiññā-citta*) arisen through the increase of light, as it is described:
"With the purified divine eye. The "eye of wisdom" (*paññācakkhu*) is that [knowledge] where it is said: "The eye arose, knowledge..."
In the passage, “...arose,” the knowledge of past lives and so forth is referred to as the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).
The "fleshly eye" (*maṃsa-cakkhu*) is the sensitive fleshly eye mentioned in the passage, “Dependent on the eye and forms.

That, however, is twofold: the eye with its constituent parts (*sasambhāra-cakkhu*) and the sensitive eye (*pasāda-cakkhu*). Of these two, that which [is located] in the eye-socket within the eye-lids...

The lump of flesh surrounded [by the elements] is that wherein there are, in brief, thirteen constituent factors: the four elements, color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, birth, life, existence, eye-sensitivity, and body-sensitivity.
In detail, however, there are thirty-six factors arising from the four origins—namely, those originating from kamma: birth, life, existence, eye-sensitivity, and body-sensitivity.
The four [factors] together with their constituent parts constitute what is called the "eye with its equipment.

However, that mere sensitivity capable of seeing forms, which is situated within the visible circle (diṭṭhamaṇḍala) surrounded by the black circle (kaṇhamaṇḍala) and demarcated by the white circle (setamaṇḍala), is called the "eye of sensitivity" (pasādacakkhu).
All these are of one kind when considered as impermanent and conditioned; they are of two kinds...

They are twofold as being with-taints (sāsava) and without-taints (anāsava), or mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara); threefold according to plane (bhūmi) and according to the triad of "clung-to" (upādiṇṇa);
fourfold according to whether their objects are exclusively limited (paritta), immeasurable (appamāṇa), or indefinite (aniyata);
fivefold by way of having form, Nibbāna, the formless, all things, or no object; and sixfold by way of the Buddha-eye and so forth. Such are the types of eyes belonging to him as thus described.
He is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he possesses these qualities; thus he is said to be "one who has eyes.

"Having scrutinized the matter" means that, having prepared the walking path (*caṅkama*), he examined and reflected for the sake of the welfare of gods and humans as a sign for the teaching of the Dhamma—this is the intended meaning.

"He laid out" (*māpayi*) means he caused it to be laid out. "Leader of the world" (*lokanāyaka*): he is called the leader of the world because he leads the world toward heaven and liberation. "Well-finished" (*suniṭṭhita*):...
"Thoroughly completed" means "finished. "Constructed from all kinds of gems" means made of the ten types of jewels.
Now, in order to demonstrate the Blessed One’s perfection of the threefold marvels:
"The Blessed One possessed mastery over the three marvels: The marvel of psychic power, the marvel of mind-reading, and the marvel of instruction."
"The Leader of the World had a walking path measured out, perfectly finished and fashioned from all kinds of gems"—so it was said.

In this context, "supernormal power" (*iddhi*) refers to the various modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha*), known as the miracle of supernormal power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*). This proceeds according to such methods as: being one, he becomes many;
being many, he becomes one; and so forth. "Mind-reading" (*ādesanā*) is the act of speaking after having known the mental disposition of another.

The miracle of direct communication (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) consists of the constant teaching of the Dhamma by both disciples and Buddhas. "Instruction" (*anusāsani*) refers to the miracle of instruction (*anusāsani-pāṭihāriya*), meaning advice given in accordance with the specific inclinations of each individual.

Thus, these are the three miracles. Among them, the miracle of instruction through the miracle of psychic power was the habitual practice of Mahāmoggallāna; the miracle of instruction through the miracle of direct communication—
The miracle of instruction belongs to the General of the Dhamma, whereas the constant teaching of the Dhamma belongs to the Buddhas.
"In the three miracles" means among these three types of miracles. "Bhagavā" is a designation for one who is distinguished by special qualities, the highest of beings, and worthy of reverence.
For this has been said by the ancients:
“‘Bhagavā’ is the best word; ‘Bhagavā’ is the supreme word;
he is worthy of heavy respect, therefore he is called ‘Bhagavā.
“Vasī” means one who has attained mastery (*vasippatta*) in these three kinds of miracles; the meaning is that he has practiced mastery. There are five kinds of mastery:
The masteries are fivefold, consisting of adverting, entering, resolving, emerging, and reviewing.

Among these, "mastery of adverting" (āvajjanavasi) refers to the capacity to advert quickly—that is, the absence of sluggishness in adverting—such that one can advert to whichever jhāna one desires, whenever one desires, and for as long as one desires. Likewise, [the same applies to] whichever jhāna one desires... pe... [and so forth].
The mastery of attainment (*samāpajjana-vasī*) is the capacity to enter [an attainment] swiftly, meaning there is no sluggishness in the act of entering.
The mastery of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vasī*) is the capacity to remain [in that state] for a long duration. Likewise, the mastery of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*) is the capacity to emerge quickly.
As for the mastery of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-vasī*), it consists precisely of the reviewing impulsion-moments (*paccavekkhaṇa-javana*).
Since these [mental states] arise immediately after the adverting consciousness (*āvajjanā*), they are said to be under the mastery of adverting.
Thus, one who has practiced mastery over these five kinds of mastery is called "one who has attained mastery" (*vasī*). Therefore it was said: "The Blessed One was masterful in the three wonders.
Now, in order to show the manner in which that Jewel Walkway (*ratana-caṅkama*) was fashioned:
“In the ten-thousandfold world system, upon the supreme mountain Sineru, he displayed, one after another like pillars, walkways made of jewels”—these are the opening verses that were spoken.
Therein, “in the ten-thousandfold world system” means in ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). “Upon the supreme mountain Sineru” refers to what is known as Mahāmeru.
"On Seṭṭhapabbata" means: "Like pillars"—having made the Sineru mountains in the ten thousand world-systems stand in succession like golden pillars, he constructed a walkway upon them and showed it;
this is the meaning. "Ratanāmaya" means "made of jewels."

13. “Having transcended ten thousand [world-systems]”: when the Blessed One was constructing the Jewel Walkway (*ratana-caṅkama*), he constructed it by making one end reach the entire limit of the eastern rim of the world-sphere (*cakravāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*) and the other end reaching the western rim of the world-sphere. Therefore, it is said:
“Having passed beyond ten thousand [yojanas], the Victor had a walking path constructed;
its sides were made entirely of gold, and the walking path itself was made of jewels.

In this context, “the Victor” (jina) is so called because he has conquered the enemies that are the defilements (kilesa). Regarding the phrase “its sides were made entirely of gold”: of that [path] thus fashioned...
On both sides of the walking path (caṅkama), there was a most delightful boundary ground made of gold; the intention is that the middle [of the path] was made of jewels.
14. "Sets of scales" (tulāsaṅghāṭa) refers to pairs of scales; they should be understood as being composed of various gems. "Corresponding" (anuvagga) means suitable.
"Covered with golden planks" (sovaṇṇaphalakatthata) means covered with golden planks; above the sets of scales, it was made of gold.
"Padaracchada" means a floor-covering. "Vedikā sabbasovaṇṇā" means that the railing is entirely made of gold;
the meaning is that this railing which encircles the walking path (*caṅkama*) is exclusively of gold and unmixed with any other jewels. "Dubhato passesu nimmitā" means constructed on both sides.
The letter *da* is used for metrical conjunction (*padasaṃdhikara*).
15. *Maṇimuttāvālukākiṇṇā* means strewn with sand made of jewels and pearls. Alternatively, *maṇi-muttā-vālukā* refers to jewels, pearls, and sand;
it is *maṇimuttāvālukākiṇṇā* because it is strewn and covered with those jewels, pearls, and sand.
*Nimmito* means fashioned or constructed in this manner. *Ratanāmaya* means consisting entirely of jewels; the meaning is "a walkway (*caṅkama*) made of all kinds of gems."
“Illumines all directions” means it illuminates and makes manifest all ten directions.

“Like the thousand-rayed one” means like the sun with its thousand rays. “Risen” means ascended. Just as the thousand-rayed sun, having risen, illuminates all ten directions, even so this walkway made of all kinds of jewels illuminates; such is the meaning.
Now, however, in order to show the Blessed One’s activity once the walkway was finished,
it is said: “On that walkway, the wise Victor, the Fully Awakened One, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks,
shone brightly as he paced back and forth.”
“Celestial mandārava flowers, lotuses, and pārichattaka trees—
all the gods, having gathered together, scatter these over the walking path.
The hosts of gods from the ten thousandfold world-system behold him with great joy.”
"Prostrating themselves, they fall down, joyful, elated, and filled with rapture"—these verses were spoken.

In this context, "the Wise One" (*dhīra*) means one endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*). "Possessing the thirty-two excellent marks" means being endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, such as having well-placed soles of the feet and so forth.
"Divine" (*dibba*) means that which exists or is born in the world of the gods. "Pāricchattaka" refers to [the tree] of the gods...
By the power of the *koviḷāra* tree of the Thirty-three [gods], a most beautiful *pāricchattaka* tree arose, measuring a hundred leagues in circumference.
When it was in bloom, the entire city of the gods was perfumed with a single fragrant scent;
its golden palaces, strewn with the pollen of its flowers, appeared as if they were tinged with gold. Of this—
However, it is said that both the flower of the *pāricchattaka* tree and the *pāricchattaka* tree itself [are meant].

"They scatter over the walkway" means they strew them upon that jeweled walkway; the meaning is that they worship the Blessed One as he walks upon that walkway with flowers of the aforementioned kind.
"All the gods" refers to the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth. Therefore, he said: "They see..."
"Those hosts of gods"—the meaning is that they see the Blessed One walking upon the Jewel Walk (Ratanacaṅkama), even within their own abodes.
"The ten-thousandfold world-system" is a nominative plural used in the sense of a locative; the meaning is that the hosts of gods in the ten-thousandfold world-system see him.
"Exultant" means delighted. "Falling down" means gathering together. "With joyful hearts" means they are thrilled with joy due to their rapture.
"Pamoditā" (rejoicing) should be understood as being connected with "together with the Tāvatiṃsa and other gods," who are to be mentioned now;
otherwise, one does not escape the fault of tautology. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Rejoicing, they behold that Blessed One; joyful and delighted, they gather here and there."
Now, in order to show those who saw and those who assembled in their true form:
“The Tāvatiṃsa gods and the Yāma gods, the Tusita deities as well;
the Nimmānarati gods and those gods who are masters of others’ creations.”
With uplifted hearts and joyful minds, they behold the Leader of the World.
"Devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and even kinnaras—
behold him who is compassionate for the welfare of the world, like the orb of the moon risen high in the sky."
“The deities of the Ābhassara, Subhakiṇha, Vehapphala, and Akaniṭṭha realms,
dressed in perfectly pure white garments, stand with palms joined in reverence.
They scatter five-colored flowers— mandārava blossoms mixed with sandalwood powder.”
Then I shook my robes and the sky, [saying]: “O, the Jina is compassionate for the welfare of the world!
These verses were spoken.
Therein, “with uplifted hearts” means with hearts uplifted by way of rapture and joy. “With glad minds” means precisely because their hearts were uplifted.
*Sumanā*. “*Lokahitānukampakaṃ*” means both one who is for the welfare of the world and one who is compassionate toward the world;
or, one who is compassionate by virtue of being for the welfare of the world. “*Nabheva accuggatacandamaṇḍalaṃ*”:
here the meaning is that she saw him shining with the glory of a Buddha, bringing joy to the eyes, like the orb of the moon in autumn—newly risen in the sky, full, and free from all calamities.

"Ābhassara" (Radiant) is stated by way of the highest limit; it should be understood that all those produced by the second jhāna—distinguished as Limited Radiance, Immeasurable Radiance, and Radiant, and further divided into inferior, medium, and superior—are included. "Subhakiṇha" (Wholly Pure) is likewise stated by way of the highest limit;
therefore, by means of the third jhāna, [all those] distinguished as Limited Beauty, Immeasurable Beauty, Wholly Pure, and so forth, are included.
It should be understood that all those who have been reborn there are included. "Vehapphalā" means those with vast fruits (*vipula-phala*).

They are born from the fourth jhāna and dwell on the same level as the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*). However, those born from the first jhāna, such as the Brahmakāyika deities and others, were already shown below;
therefore, they are not shown here. Furthermore, because they lack eyes and ears, the non-percipient beings and the formless beings (*arūpin*) are not mentioned here.
"And the deities of Akaniṭṭha"—here too, this is stated by way of the highest limit.
Therefore, it should be understood that all five Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa), namely Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassi, and Akaniṭṭha, are included.
"Wearing very pure white garments" means: very pure (*susuddha*) and white (*sukka*), that is, bright white; they have put on very pure white garments as both lower and upper robes.
And by those who were dressed in very clean white garments; the meaning is that they were clothed in perfectly pure, bright clothes.
There is also a reading, "susuddhasukkavasanā. With palms joined: having made the añjali gesture, resembling a lotus bud, and placing it upon their heads, they stood there.
“They scatter” means they sprinkle. “But the flower,” however, refers to the blossom (*kusuma*). There is also a reading, “or flowers” (*pupphāni vā*);
this should be seen as a change in the wording, but the meaning remains the same. “Five-colored” (*pañcavaṇṇika*) means five colors—five colors by way of blue, yellow, red, white, and madder-red.
“Mixed with sandalwood powder” means mixed with sandalwood dust. “They swirl the cloths” means they cause them to whirl.
“Robes! Oh, the Victor is compassionate for the welfare of the world! Thus they uttered words of praise such as, “Oh, the Victor is a benefactor to the world;
oh, he is compassionate for the welfare of the world; oh, he is merciful! The connection is: “They release flowers and wave their garments.
Now, in order to show the words of praise employed by them, these verses were spoken:
“You are the Teacher and the banner, the standard and the sacrificial post for living beings;
you are the refuge, the support, and the island—the supreme among bipeds.
The deities of the ten-thousandfold world system possess great psychic power.”
Surrounding him, they pay homage, joyful, elated,
and filled with rapture: "Devas and celestial maidens, serene and glad at heart,
worship the Bull among Men with flowers of five colors."
“Beholding him, the hosts of gods, with serene and joyful minds, worship the Bull among Men with flowers of five colors.
‘Oh, what a marvel in the world! A wonder that makes the hair stand on end!’”
Never before has there been such a marvel, a hair-raising wonder:
"The deities, sitting each in their own abode,
burst into great laughter upon seeing that miracle in the sky."
“Those dwelling in the sky and those dwelling on the earth, those who live along grassy paths—
joyful, thrilled, and delighted, they pay homage with palms joined.
Even those long-lived *nāgas*, possessed of merit and great psychic power,”
Delighted, they pay homage and worship the Supreme among Men.
They set up musical performances in the sky, as swift as the wind;
seeing that marvel in the heavens, they play instruments with leather-covered drums.
“Gongs and drums, and many kettledrums,
resounded in the sky upon seeing that marvel in the heavens.
‘Truly, a wonder has arisen for us today, causing our hair to stand on end!’”
“May we obtain the permanent accomplishment of our goal; the opportune moment has been granted to us.
Upon hearing the word “Buddha,” joy arose in them at that very instant.
Crying out, “A Buddha! A Buddha! they stood with their hands joined in reverence.
“With sounds of *hiṅkāra* and cries of ‘well done,’ with shouts of acclaim and cheering;
and various beings in the sky move about with palms joined.
They sing, clap their hands, play instruments, beat their arms, and dance.”
They release five-colored flowers— mandārava blossoms mixed with sandalwood powder—
[saying]: “Just as, O Great Hero, there is the wheel-mark upon your feet,
so too are they covered with banners, thunderbolts, flags, and increasing hooks.”
In this context, he is the Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs for the sake of welfare in this world and the next. He is the Banner (*ketu*);

in the sense of being worthy of honor as a banner, he is like a banner, thus "the Banner. He is the Standard (*dhaja*); in the sense of being a raised standard and in the sense of being beautiful to behold, you are like a standard, thus "the Standard.
Or alternatively, just as in the world, upon seeing anyone's standard, one thinks: "This is the standard..."

Just as one who possesses a banner is known as "the bannered one" (*dhajavā dhajī*), even so, upon seeing the Blessed One, the attainment of Nibbāna through wisdom is made manifest for the sake of attaining Nibbāna by means of that wisdom. Therefore it is said: "The banner and the sacrificial post.

This refers to the sacrificial post erected for the purpose of performing all the sacrifices mentioned in the *Kūṭadanta Sutta*, beginning with giving and ending with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*).
"Are" means "there is. "Refuge" (*parāyana*) means a resort. "A support" (*patiṭṭhā*):
just as the great earth is a support and a basis for all living beings by being their foundation, so too are you a support. "And a lamp" (*dīpo ca*): this refers to a lighted lamp.
Just as a lamp placed in the midst of the fourfold darkness serves to reveal forms for sentient beings wandering therein.
The meaning is: "You are a lamp that reveals the ultimate truth for beings wandering in the darkness of ignorance.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "Just as an island in the great ocean serves as a firm footing for beings whose ships have wrecked, so too are you like an island for living beings sinking in the ocean of saṃsāra where no footing can be found; thus, you are a 'lamp' (dīpa)."
"Supreme among bipeds" (*dvipaduttama*) means the highest among bipeds;

here, however, because there is an absence of the defining characteristic of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), there is no prohibition against the genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*). It is the genitive case characterized by selection that is prohibited from being compounded.
But the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*) is the supreme among footless beings, bipeds, quadrupeds, many-footed beings, those with form, and those without form.
He is indeed the supreme among those with perception, those without perception, and those with neither-perception-nor-non-perception. But why is he called "the supreme among bipeds" here?
It is by way of being the most excellent. For when one who is called "supreme" arises in this world, he does not arise even among those without feet, four-footed beings, or many-footed beings;
he arises only among bipeds. Among which bipeds? Among humans and among devas.
When arising among humans, he is reborn as a Buddha capable of exercising authority over a trichiliocosm (a system of three thousand great thousandfold world-systems).
When arising among the devas, he is reborn as a Mahābrahmā with power over ten thousand world-systems.
He becomes either his attendant or his monastery attendant (ārāmika). Thus, it is by way of being even more excellent than that...
“Supreme among bipeds”—thus it was said.
“In the ten-thousandfold world-system” means in the world-system reckoned as ten thousand. “Possessed of great psychic power” means endowed with great *iddhi*;
the sense is that they possess great majesty. “Surrounding” means having encircled the Blessed One on all sides.
*Pasannā* means one who has conceived faith. *Narāsabhaṃ* means the bull among men. *Aho acchariyaṃ*:
here, it is called *acchariyaṃ* because it is not constant—like a blind man’s climbing of a mountain—or because it is worthy of a *accharā* (a finger-snap);
the meaning is that it is fit to cause one to snap the fingers in wonder, thinking, "Aha! This is marvelous! *Abbhutaṃ* means that which was never before; it is what has not happened before.
“Abbhutaṃ” (wondrous) is a synonym for that which brings about amazement. “Lomahaṃsanaṃ” (hair-raising) means causing the hairs of the body to stand on end.

“Na me idaṃ bhūtapubbaṃ” means “such a thing has never happened before for me”; the meaning is that a wondrous thing has been seen. One should understand the word “diṭṭhaṃ” (seen) by supplying the verb “has been seen. “Accheraṃ” means a marvel.
"In their respective abodes" means in their own individual dwellings. "Having sat down" means having entered.
As for the word "deities," it should be understood that this term is common to both gods and goddesses.
"Laughing" means those deities laugh with a great laugh; because their hearts are overcome with joy, they do not merely smile, but let out a boisterous laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*).
The meaning is "laughing. *Nabheti* means "in the sky.
*Ākāsaṭṭhā* means "dwelling in the sky," that is, situated in celestial mansions (*vimāna*) and so forth; the same principle applies to those dwelling on the earth (*bhūmaṭṭha*).
*Tiṇapathanivāsino* means "those who dwell upon the tips of grass and on paths. *Puññavanto* means "possessors of great merit. *Mahiddhikā* means "possessors of great power."
“They perform musical concerts” means they perform the musical concerts of celestial dancers; the sense is that they employ them for the purpose of worshipping the Tathāgata.
“In the sky” (*ambare*) means in the atmosphere. “In the wind-path” (*anilañjase*) means on the path of the wind;

because the word *ambara* has multiple meanings, “in the wind-path” is stated as a synonym for the same thing as the previous term. “Strung with leather” (*cammanaddhāni*) means bound with leather. Or rather, this very reading [is preferred].
"Devadundubhiyo" means "divine drums. "Vādentī" means the deities are sounding them.
"Saṅkha" refers to conch shells made from bones. "Paṇava" refers to a specific type of thin-bodied percussion instrument. "Ḍiṇḍima" refers to small drums made of grass.
"Vajjanti" means they are sounding them. "Abbhuto vata no" means "truly wonderful for us. "Uppajji" means it has arisen.

"Lomahaṃsana" means causing horripilation. "Dhuvaṃ" (certainly) means: because this Teacher has arisen in the world as something wonderful, therefore the intention is, "We shall certainly obtain the accomplishment of our purpose.
"Labhāma" means we shall obtain. "Khaṇa" means the ninth moment, which is devoid of the eight inopportune moments. "No" means for us. "Paṭipādito" means obtained.
"Having heard 'Buddha' from them": having heard these words "Buddha," the five-colored rapture arose in those deities;
this is the meaning. "At that time" (*tāvade*): at that moment. "Hymns" (*hiṅkāra*): sounds of *hiṅkāra*; when spirits (*yakkha*) and others are overjoyed, they utter the sound *hiṃ*.
"Acclamations" (*sādhukāra*): sounds of "well done! (*sādhu*) also occurred. "Shouts of joy" (*ukkuṭṭhi*): the sound of *ukkuṭṭhi*.
And the meaning is "and the sound of loud shouting. "Creatures" (pajā) refers here to the gods and others. Some read: "Various banners move about in the sky.
"They sing" means they sing songs connected with the virtues of the Buddha.
"They shout" means they produce the sound of shouting with their mouths. "They play instruments" refers to the great *vipañcikā* lute, the crocodile-mouthed drum, and so forth.
They play and cause to be played lutes and musical instruments for the purpose of honoring the Tathāgata. "They clap their arms" means they strike their arms;
here, a change of gender (liṅgavipariyāsa) should be understood. "And they dance" means they cause others to dance and they themselves dance.

Just as in the case of the phrase, "O Great Hero, there is the mark of the wheel upon your feet," where *yathā* signifies "in whatever manner" or "just as. [The epithet] "Great Hero" (*mahāvīra*) refers to one of great power (*mahāvīriya*).

“By virtue of yoga, you are a Great Hero. Regarding the mark of the wheel on the feet: the meaning is that on both the soles of your feet, the mark of the wheel shines, complete in every aspect, with a thousand spokes, a rim, and a hub.

Furthermore, this word *cakra* (wheel) is seen in such contexts as prosperity, the parts of a chariot, modes of deportment, giving, gems, the Dharma, the hoof-wheel of a horse, and the mark of the wheel itself. “These four... [etc.]
In such passages as, "O monks, the wheels [of sovereignty] possessed by gods and humans," it appears in the sense of excellence (*sampatti*).

In such passages as, "Like the wheel of one who drives," it refers to a part of a chariot (*rathaṅga*). In such passages as, "The four-wheeled [body] with nine gates," it refers to the modes of deportment (*iriyāpatha*).
In the passage, "Give and enjoy, and do not be negligent; set the wheel in motion for all living beings," it refers to giving (*dāna*). "Divine..."

In the phrase "the wheel-treasure has appeared," it refers to the *ratana-cakka* (wheel-treasure). In the phrase "the wheel set in motion by me," however, it refers to the *dhamma-cakka* (wheel of Dhamma).
In the phrase "For the person struck by desire, the wheel spins upon his head," it refers to a razor-wheel;
the meaning is a weapon-wheel. In the phrase "wheels have grown on the soles of the feet," it refers to a mark (*lakkhaṇa*). Here too, it is the wheel as a mark (*lakkhaṇa-cakka*).

It should be seen. "Adorned with banners, thunderbolts, flags, the *vaḍḍhamāna* [turban], and hooks" means that it is covered, decorated, and surrounded by banners, thunderbolts, flags, the *vaḍḍhamāna*, and hooks; the meaning is that there are wheel-marks on the soles of the feet.
When the wheel-mark is grasped, the remaining marks are already grasped. Likewise, the eighty secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*).
And there was the fathom-wide radiance. Therefore, adorned with those thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-wide radiance,
the Blessed One’s body was like a *pāricchattaka* tree in full bloom,
like a lotus grove with blossoming lotuses, like a new golden archway variegated with diverse jewels, or like the vault of the sky resplendent with the rays of the stars.
Running hither and thither and quivering, emitting six-colored rays of light from a Buddha, he shines exceedingly.
Now, in order to show the perfection of the Blessed One’s physical body and his Dhamma-body:
“In form, virtue, concentration, and wisdom, he is peerless.”
"Unequaled in liberation, in setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion"—this verse was spoken.

Therein, the word *rūpa* (form) is seen in the sense of aggregates (*khandha*), existence (*bhava*), signs (*nimitta*), conditions (*paccaya*), body (*sarīra*), color (*vaṇṇa*), shape (*saṇṭhāna*), and so forth.
As it is said: "Whatever form, whether past, future, or present"—here it is seen in the sense of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).
In the phrase “he develops the path for rebirth in the form realm,” it refers to the form existence (*rūpabhava*).

In the phrase “perceiving the internal as formless, he sees forms externally,” it refers to the kasiṇa sign. In the phrase “Bhikkhus, it is with a form as condition that evil unwholesome states arise, not without a form,” it refers to the condition (*paccaya*).
In the phrase “space, when enclosed, comes to be designated simply as ‘form,’” [it refers to space].
“In this body”: in the physical frame. “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises”:
here it refers to color. “One who is measured by form and delighted by form”: here it refers to shape. Here too, it should be understood as referring to shape.
“In virtue”: in the fourfold virtue. “In concentration”: in the threefold concentration. “In wisdom”: in mundane and supramundane wisdom. “Peerless.”
"Unequaled and incomparable. "By liberation" means by the liberation that is the fruit (*phala-vimukti*). "Peerless among the peerless" means: those Buddhas of the past were peerless;

he is equal to those peerless Buddhas in virtue and other qualities, thus he is "equal to the peerless" (*asama-sama*). Up to this point, the excellence of the Blessed One’s form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) has been shown.
Now, in order to show the Blessed One’s bodily strength and so forth:
“Ten times the strength of an elephant is your natural bodily strength;
peerless by the power of your psychic potency (*iddhi*) in setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion”—thus it was said.

Therein, "ten times the strength of an elephant" means ten times the strength of the six-tusked elephant (*chaddanta-nāga*). For the Tathāgata’s strength is twofold: bodily strength and the strength of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*). Of these, the bodily strength is to be understood according to the lineage of elephants. How so?
“Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tambapiṅgala, Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta—these are the ten breeds of elephants.
These are the ten elephant breeds to be known. *Kāḷāvaka* is the ordinary breed of elephant. [That which belongs to] ten men...

The bodily strength of one [ordinary person] is equal to the strength of a single black-footed elephant (*kāḷāvaka*). The strength of ten black-footed elephants is equal to that of a single Ganges-elephant (*gaṅgeyya*);
by this same method, it should be carried on until the strength of the six-tusked elephant (*chaddanta*) is reached.
The strength of ten six-tusked elephants is the strength of a single Tathāgata; this alone is the Nārāyaṇa-strength, the diamond-strength (*vajirabala*).
It is said: by the standard of counting ordinary elephants, this is the strength of ten million times a thousand elephants;
by the standard of counting men, it is the strength of ten million times ten thousand men. This, first of all, is the Tathāgata’s natural physical strength;

as for his power of knowledge, however, it is immeasurable—the knowledge of the ten powers (*daśabala*), the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and the unshakable knowledge regarding the eight assemblies.
The power of knowledge includes such things as the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth, the knowledge that delimits the five destinations, and the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha.
However, in this context, it is the power of the body (*kāyabala*) that is intended.

Regarding the phrase "the natural power in your body," the meaning is: "that natural power which exists in your body. Therefore, "the strength of ten nāgas" means the strength of ten *Chaddanta* elephants.
Now, demonstrating the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), he said: "Unequaled in power through supernormal success (*iddhibala*) in setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.

In this context, "unequaled in power through supernormal success" means that by means of the power of supernormal success—such as transformation, resolution, and so forth—he is unequaled, peerless, and incomparable. "In setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion" means that he is likewise unequaled even in the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*).
Now, in order to demonstrate the injunction for paying homage to the Tathāgata—by way of saying, "The Teacher who is endowed with such qualities as these is the sole leader of the entire world;
pay homage to that Teacher"—it was said: "Thus, pay homage to the Great Sage, the compassionate Lord of the World, who is endowed with all virtues and has attained every excellence."
In this context, *evaṃ* is a particle used as a demonstrative indicating the manner already described. Regarding the phrase *sabbaguṇūpetaṃ*:
here, *sabba* is a term expressing "without remainder" (inclusive). As for the word *guṇa*, this term is seen in many senses.

For instance, in the passage, “I allow you, monks, a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) of unwashed cloth,” it is seen in the sense of a layer. [And in the passage: “The times pass; they carry one away... [it is seen in the sense of a quality].

In the phrase, “The nights, the qualities of youth, gradually pass away,” it has the sense of a collection (*rāsa*). In the phrase, “A gift endowed with a hundred qualities is to be expected,” it has the sense of a benefit (*ānisamsa*).
In the phrases, “The end, the intestinal cord” and “One should make many garland-strings,” it has the sense of binding (*bandhana*).
In the phrase, “Endowed with eight qualities, he brought forth the power of direct knowledge,” it has the sense of possession (*sampatti*). Here too, it has the sense of possession.
It should be understood thus: therefore, the meaning is that he is endowed and possessed of all mundane and supramundane qualities and all perfections.
"Possessed of all factors" (*sabbaṅgasamupāgata*) means arrived at or endowed with all the qualities of a Buddha, or with the constituent parts of those qualities.
He is called a "Great Sage" (*mahāmuni*) because, in comparison with other sages such as the *paccekabuddhas* and others, he is a sage of superior status.
"O Great Sage. "Compassionate" means compassionate because of his endowment with the quality of compassion (*karuṇā*). "Lord of the World" means the sole lord of the entire world;
the meaning is that he is thus entreated by all the worlds, saying, "He is the one who strikes down and pacifies our affliction and distress.
Now, in order to show the Blessed One’s worthiness (*arahabhāva*) through every possible mode of homage, [the author says]:
“Salutation, praise, homage, and commendation;
veneration and worship—all these you truly deserve.
Whatever beings in the world are worthy of being honored, those who are deserving of homage—you are they.”
"O Great Hero, most excellent of all, there is no one equal to you"—thus it was said.
In this context: "salutation" (abhivādana) means causing others to perform a salutation toward oneself; "praise" (thomana) means extolling in one's absence; "veneration" (vandana) means bowing down;
"commendation" (pasaṃsana) means praising in one's presence; and "reverence" (namassana) means joining the palms in homage.
Or "reverence with the mind. "Worship" means worship with garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth.
"All" means that you are worthy of, or fit for, all those aforementioned distinctions of honor; this is the meaning.

"Whoever in the world is worthy of homage" means whoever in the world should be saluted, who is venerable, and who deserves homage. "Who" (ye) refers to those who, moreover, in the world deserve homage.
This, however, is a synonym for the very first phrase. "The most excellent of all" means the best and supreme among them all;
the meaning is: "O Great Hero, no one like you exists in the world.
Then, after the Blessed One had displayed the Twin Miracle and created the Jewel Walkway, while he was walking back and forth there—
The Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain with a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus.
Then the Elder, looking toward the Blessed One, saw him walking upon the Jewel Walkway in the sky over Kapilavatthu. Thus it is said:
“Sāriputta of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna...”
“Standing right on Vulture Peak, he beholds the Leader of the World,” and so forth.
Therein, “Sāriputta” means the son of the brahmin woman named Rūpasārī, thus he is Sāriputta.
“Of great wisdom” means he is endowed with the sixteenfold great wisdom, thus he is of great wisdom. “Skilled in concentration and jhāna”: here, “concentration” (samādhi) refers to...
It is called *samādhi* because it places the mind evenly and establishes it upon the object. That *samādhi* is threefold:

*samādhi* with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*), *samādhi* without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakka-vicāramatta*), and *samādhi* without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*).
As for *jhāna*, by these [terms]—the first *jhāna*, second *jhāna*, third *jhāna*, and fourth *jhāna*—the *jhānas* of loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*) and so forth are also included.
There are two kinds of jhāna: contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*).
Among these, the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is called "contemplation of characteristics" because it contemplates the characteristics such as impermanence.

However, the first jhāna and so forth are called "jhāna" because they contemplate the object or because they burn away opposing states. And among the concentrations (*samādhi*), there are the jhānas...
And "skilled" (*kovidā*) means skilled in meditative absorption (*samādhi-jhāna*); the sense is that he is proficient in meditative absorption and jhāna.
"On Vulture Peak" (*gijjhakūṭe*): standing on the mountain of that name, he saw;

thus it is said "he saw. 44. "The king of sāl trees in full bloom": its trunk was perfectly symmetrical, and its branches were adorned with abundant, tender fruits, shoots, and sprouts that had emerged.

"He gazed upon the King of Sāla trees, which has all its fruits and flowers; whose root is virtue (sīla), whose trunk is concentration (samādhi), whose branches are wisdom (paññā), whose blossoms are the higher knowledges (abhiññā), and whose fruit is liberation (vimutti)—the King of Sāla trees that is the Ten Powers (dasabala).
This is the connection with the word "gazing" (oloka). "Just as the moon in the sky" means:
free from the afflictions of clouds, smoke, dust, and Rāhu, surrounded by a host of stars, and full during the autumn season.

The meaning is: "He gazes upon the moon-like Best of Sages, who dispels the darkness of all defilements and causes the lily grove of those people ready for training to blossom. *Yathā* is merely a particle. *Majjhanhikeva sūriyam* means:
shining like the sun at midday, which possesses a garland of rays more intense in its splendor. *Narāsabham* means: the bull among men.

45. "Flaming" means burning intensely; it refers to one whose beautiful face possesses the splendor of the full moon during the autumn season, whose excellent body is adorned with the primary and secondary marks (lakkhaṇa and anubyañjana), and who shines with the supreme glory of a Buddha—this is the meaning.
"Like a lamp-tree" means like a lamp-tree upon which a lamp has been placed. "Like the rising young sun" means like the newly risen sun.
The meaning is that they flow with a gentle nature. Furthermore, the youthful state of the sun is spoken of in relation to its rising;
