for unlike the moon, it possesses no waning or waxing. "Anointed with fathom-wide radiance" means colored by fathom-wide radiance.
"He beholds the steadfast Leader of the World" means he beholds the Leader, the sole steadfast one in all the world.
Then the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, standing upon Mount Gijjhakūṭa— whose peak was kissed by masses of clouds bearing exceedingly cool water, whose peak was perfumed by various fragrant tree flowers,
and whose peak was most beautiful and wonderful— beheld the Blessed One surrounded by hosts of devas and brahmas who had come from ten thousand world-systems,
endowed with the unsurpassed glory of a Buddha and the incomparable grace of a Buddha.

Seeing him walking upon a cloister made entirely of jewels, he thought: "Well now, let me approach the Blessed One and request a discourse illuminating the qualities of a Buddha and a teaching on the lineage of Buddhas.
Having thus reflected, he assembled the five hundred bhikkhus who lived with him. Thus it was said:
“He gathered in an instant five hundred bhikkhus— those who had done what was to be done,
the stable ones, whose taints were exhausted, and who were stainless. Regarding this,
in the phrase “of five hundred bhikkhus,” the genitive case should be understood in the sense of the accusative (i.e., “five hundred bhikkhus”).

"Of those who have done what was to be done" means that they have brought to completion the sixteen tasks by means of the four paths through the modes of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing regarding the four truths. "Of those whose taints are destroyed" means those for whom the four taints are completely exhausted.

"Of the stainless ones" means those from whom impurity has departed; or alternatively, because their taints are destroyed, they are stainless, meaning they possess a mental continuum that is supremely purified.
"At once" means at that very moment. "He caused to assemble" means he had them assembled.
Now, in order to show the reason for those bhikkhus' going to the assembly, [the text says]:
"He displayed a miracle called 'Delighting the World'."
“We too, having gone there, shall pay homage to the Jina.
“Come, let us all go; we shall empty [the hall] for the Jina;
we shall dispel our doubt after seeing the Leader of the World.”—these verses were spoken.
In this context, "inspiring confidence in the world" (*lokappasādana*) refers to a miracle called *pāṭihīra* because it produces confidence in the world.
There is also a reading, “inspiring confidence in what is looked up to” (*ullokappasādana*); the meaning of that is “the miracle of opening up the world.
Furthermore, having made a single expanse of light from the Akaniṭṭha realm above down to the Avīci hell below, within that interval—
It is said that for all beings, there is a resolve to see one another.
*Nidassayī* means he showed. *Amhepi* means "we too. *Tattha* means having gone to where the Blessed One was; this is the meaning.
*Vandissāma* means we shall pay homage to the feet of the Blessed One with our heads. In this context, however, regarding these two words, *amhepi* and *mayaṃ*:
The connection of the first word should be understood with the action of going, and that of the latter with the action of paying homage;
otherwise, one would not be freed from the fault of tautology.

Regarding "Come, we shall dispel your doubt": here it may be asked—since there is no doubt whatsoever for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), why did the Elder speak thus? This is true; yet [doubt] has been utterly eradicated by the first path itself. As it is said:

“Which phenomena are to be abandoned by vision? The four types of consciousness-arising associated with wrong view, consciousness-arising accompanied by doubt, greed leading to the states of misery, hatred, delusion, conceit, and the defilements associated with them.
But this doubt (kaṅkhā) termed “vicikicchā” is not [mere] uncertainty; rather, it is the non-comprehension of the conventional designation (paññatti).
However, the Elder wished to ask the Blessed One about the *Buddhavamsa* (Lineage of Buddhas), which is the domain of Buddhas alone, and not of Paccekabuddhas or the disciples of the Buddha.
Therefore, it should be understood that the Elder spoke thus because [the matter] was outside his domain. "I shall dispel" means "we shall dispel.
Then those bhikkhus, having heard the Elder’s words, each took his own bowl and robe;
like great elephants well-harnessed, with defilements shattered and bonds severed, they were of few desires, contented, secluded, and unattached.
Endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they assembled in haste. Therefore it was said:
“Having assented, saying ‘Very well,’ those who were prudent and possessed of restrained faculties, taking their bowls and robes, approached in haste.”
In this context, the word *sādhu* is seen in such senses as requesting, accepting, encouraging, and beauty. For instance, it is seen in the sense of requesting in passages such as:
"It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. It is also seen in the sense of acceptance in passages such as:
"‘Very well, venerable sir,’ that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words..."
In the context of acceptance: in such passages as “Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta,” it refers to encouragement.
“Excellent is King Dhammaruci; excellent is the man possessed of wisdom;
Excellent is one who does not deceive friends; the non-doing of evil is happiness.”—thus [it is used].
In the word *ādīsu*, it means "in beautiful things. Here, it means "in accepting. Therefore, the meaning is: "having accepted the Elder’s words, saying 'well' and 'very well.
*Nipakā* means wise and possessed of wisdom. *Saṃvutindriyā* means those who have guarded the doors of the sense faculties; the meaning is that they were endowed with restraint of the senses.
*Taramānā* means hurrying. *Upāgamiṃsu* means they approached the Elder.

50–1. Now, the compilers of the Council, in order to show the conduct of the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), spoke the verses beginning with “By those whose taints are destroyed, who are stainless...

In this context, “by the tamed” (*dantehi*) means by those tamed in body and mind. “In the supreme taming” (*uttame dame*) refers to Arahantship; the locative case here should be understood in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*).

“By those monks” (*tehi bhikkhūhi*) means by the five hundred monks. “The great leader of the group” (*mahāgaṇī*) [refers to him] because of his excellence in virtue and the other factors of the Noble Path.
He is called a *mahāgaṇī* because he possesses a great multitude (*mahāgaṇa*) by way of number;

or alternatively, it is a "great multitude" because it is a great assembly of virtues such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth due to its various members. He is a *mahāgaṇī* because he possesses such a great multitude.
"Sporting like a god in the sky" means that he approached the Blessed One in the vault of the sky, displaying his splendor through the play of supernormal power (*iddhivilāsa*).
52. Now, in order to show the manner of their approach with the words, “They approached him being in such a state,” the passage beginning with “coughing and spitting” is commenced.

Therein, “coughing” (*ukkāsita*) means the sound of coughing; “spitting” (*khipita*) means the sound of spitting. “Having looked on with equanimity” (*ajjhupekkhiya*) means having observed them with equanimity;
the intended meaning is that he did neither of those two things. “Of good vows” (*subbata*) means possessing the stainless qualities of the ascetic practices (*dhuta*).
"Sappatissā" means "possessing respectful deference"; the meaning is "those who live in humility.
(53) "Sayambhu" means one who has attained the state of Buddhahood by oneself alone, without the instruction of another, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs).
"Accuggataṃ" means "risen anew. "Candaṃ va" means "like the moon," [referring to] the Blessed One shining in the sky.
"Seeing [it] like the moon in the sky"—thus the connection between the words should be understood. Here too, the word *yathā* is merely a particle (*nipāta*).
54. "Or like lightning": as if it were a dense flash of lightning. The meaning is: "If its radiance were long-lasting, such as that.
"As in the sky" means as in the atmosphere; here too, the word *yathā* is merely a particle. In similar cases following this as well...
In these instances, the word "yathā" should be understood as a mere particle.
55. "Like a lake, perfectly serene": this means the water is untroubled and serene, like a great lake that is exceedingly deep and wide.
"Like a lotus in full bloom": the meaning should be understood as being like a lake with a grove of fully blossomed lotuses.
There is also a reading, “*suphullaṃ kamalaṃ yathā*,” for which the meaning is: “like a forest of lotuses in full bloom because of their loveliness.

(56) Then those bhikkhus, headed by the General of the Dhamma, placed their joined palms upon their heads and prostrated themselves at the feet of the One of Ten Powers, whose soles were marked with wheels;
this is the meaning. Therefore it was said: “Having raised their joined palms, joyful, elated, and delighted,” and so forth.
In that context, "they fell down" means they prostrated; this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "on the wheel-marked foot":
a foot upon which the wheel is the mark is a "wheel-marked foot," and it is on such a wheel-marked foot [that they fell]. It is said "on the foot" by way of its genus;
the meaning is that they fell at the Teacher’s feet, whose soles were adorned with wheels.
57. Now, in order to provide the names of certain elders, the verses beginning with “Sāriputta of great wisdom, resembling the *koraṇḍa* flower” were spoken.

Regarding that, “resembling the *koraṇḍa*” means having a complexion like the *koraṇḍaka* flower. If this is so, one might ask: “Should it not simply be said ‘like the *koraṇḍa*’ (*koraṇḍasamo*) or ‘similar to the *koraṇḍa*’ (*koraṇḍasadiso*)?
Why is the word ‘resembling’ (*samasādiso*) stated twice? It is not [the case that]...
"Dosa" (fault) refers to that which is like the *koraṇḍa* flower; by virtue of its similarity to the *koraṇḍa*, it is "equal and similar to the *koraṇḍa*.

The intention is not, however, to imply redundancy. Regarding the phrase "skilled in concentration and jhāna," here the word *kusala* is seen in such senses as health, blamelessness, dexterity, happiness, and result.
Indeed, this word is seen in the sense of health in passages such as: "Is it well with you, sir? Is it free from illness with you? and so forth.
“But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct? “That bodily conduct which is blameless, Great King”—in such passages as these, it refers to the blameless.
“You are skilled in the parts and components of the chariot”—in such passages as these, it refers to one who is clever.

“Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma”—in such passages as these, it refers to that which has a pleasant ripening. But here, however, it should be understood as referring to one who is clever. “He paid homage” means he paid homage.
58. "Gajjitā" means one who thunders; thus he is called Gajjitā. The intention is that he is like a dark cloud, a bearer of blue water, within the range of his supernormal power (*iddhivisaya*).
"Equal and similar to a blue lotus" means having a color like that of the blue *kuvalaya* lily.
The meaning here should be understood in the same manner as explained above. "Moggallāna" is the name obtained by way of his clan (*gotta*), [the son of] Kolita.
59. Regarding the phrase "Mahākassapa too": among Uruvelakassapa, Nadīkassapa, Gayākassapa, Kumārakassapa, and the other elders, both great and small, he was the greatest;
therefore, he is called "Mahākassapa. The particle *pi* (too/also) has the sense of inclusion and respect.

"Resembling molten gold" means his skin color was like that of heated, refined gold. Regarding the term "ascetic qualities" (*dhutaguṇa*), it is so called because they shake off (*dhunana*) the defilements.
"Dhamma" means ascetic; "ascetic quality" (*dhutaguṇa*) means an ascetic practice (*dhutadhamma*). What, then, is called an ascetic practice?

Meagerness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, and indifference to worldly affairs—these five qualities, which are the attendants of the volition for the ascetic practices, are called "ascetic practices" because of such statements as "relying on meagerness of wishes alone. Alternatively, [they are so called] regarding the defilements...

Knowledge arising from shaking off [defilements] is called *dhuta*; [the term refers to] that quality of asceticism (*dhutaguṇa*). “Placed at the head” means he was established as the foremost, the best, the most excellent, and the pinnacle.

The meaning is that he was established in a particular rank [with the words]: “This, monks, is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are exponents of the ascetic practices (*dhutavāda*), namely Mahākassapa.
Furthermore, this word *agga* (foremost) is seen used in the senses of beginning, pinnacle, portion, excellence, and so forth.
For instance, it is seen at the beginning in such passages as: “From this day forward, good gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs.

It is seen at the end in such passages as: “He might touch that fingertip with that very fingertip,” and “the tip of a sugarcane, the tip of a bamboo. It is seen in the sense of a portion or category in such passages as:
“Sour at the beginning or sweet at the beginning,” and “I allow you, monks, [to assign] by way of the monastery or by way of the courtyard.”
In such passages as “let him divide [it]...,” it refers to a portion. In such passages as, “Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, ...
[etc. ... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them,” it refers to the best. Here, however, it should be understood as meaning the best. It also applies in the sense of a limit.
The Elder is both the best and the limit in his own station. Therefore it is said: “placed at the head,” *agga*.
"Supreme" means he has reached the pinnacle. "Praised" means extolled by gods, humans, and others. "Commended by the Teacher" means praised and lauded by the Teacher;

he was commended through numerous methods of discourse such as: "Bhikkhus, Kassapa approaches families like the moon, with body withdrawn and mind withdrawn, ever-new among families, free from arrogance. Thus he was praised.
"Praised" means that he too pays homage to the Blessed One.
"Of those with the divine eye" (*dibbacakkhūnaṃ*): those who possess the divine eye are "those with the divine eye";
the meaning is that he is the foremost and best among those bhikkhus with the divine eye. As it was said: "This, monks, is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus..."
“Of those with the divine eye, this one is foremost, namely Anuruddha.
The Elder Anuruddha was the son of the Sakyan Amitodana, who was the younger brother of Mahānāma and the paternal uncle of the Blessed One. Possessing great merit, he was exceedingly delicate;
having gone forth from the home into homelessness as the seventh member of his family, his sequence of renunciation is recorded in the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
He has indeed arrived; he is near, in the very presence of the Blessed One.
61. Regarding "offenses and non-offenses": he is skilled in both what constitutes an offense and what does not. Regarding "curable and incurable":

the meaning is that it refers to both those with a remedy (*sappaṭikamma*) and those without a remedy (*appaṭikamma*). In this context, that which has a remedy is sixfold, while that which has no remedy is...
An offense involving defeat (*pārājikāpatti*). There is also a reading: “Skilled in what is an offense and what is not an offense, and in what is curable”;

it has the same meaning. “In the Vinaya” means in the Vinaya Piṭaka. “Placed at the head” means he was established in the position of the foremost, according to the passage: “This, monks, is the foremost among my disciples, the monks who are bearers of the Vinaya, namely Upāli. “Upāli” refers to the Elder Upāli. “Praised by the Teacher.”

He was praised and commended by the Teacher. It is said that the Elder, having learned the Vinaya Piṭaka in the very presence of the Tathāgata, recounted three cases—the Bhārukacchaka-vatthu, the Ajjuka-vatthu, and the Kumārakassapa-vatthu—correlating them with the knowledge of omniscience.
Therefore, he is said to have been "praised by the Teacher" in such a manner as, "the Elder is the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya."
62. *Sukhumanipuṇatthapaṭividdho* means one who has penetrated the subtle and refined meaning; the sense is that he has penetrated the meaning that is difficult to see and refined.
*Kathikānaṃ pavaro* means the best among those who preach the Dhamma. He was ranked in the *Etadagga* (Foremost) discourse as follows:
“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are preachers of the Dhamma, namely Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇī.”

Therefore it was said: "The most excellent among speakers. "A leader" (gaṇī) means one who has a community (saṅgha). It is said that five hundred sons of noble family went forth in the presence of the Elder.
All of them were born in the land where the One Possessing the Ten Powers appeared, residents of the kingdom where he was born;
all were those whose taints were destroyed, and all had attained the ten bases of discourse. Therefore it was said: "A leader. "A seer" (isī) means one who seeks or investigates.
"Wholesome states," says the Sage. "The son of Mantāṇī" means he was the son of a brahmin woman named Mantāṇī; "Puṇṇa" was his name.
"Renowned" means he was famous for his own qualities such as fewness of wishes.
As for the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña, however, after the Teacher had attained full enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, [he followed] by degrees...

Having come and been dwelling in dependence on Rājagaha, he went to Kapilavatthu, ordained his own nephew, a young brahmin named Puṇṇa, and after paying homage to the Blessed One and taking leave of him, he went himself to the Chaddanta Lake to dwell there.
Puṇṇa, however, having come with the Elder to see the Blessed One, thought: "My duty as one who has gone forth..."
Thinking, "I shall go into the presence of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers only after reaching the very summit," he remained right there in Kapilapura.
Applying systematic attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), he attained Arhatship before long and approached the Blessed One.
In this context, however, the two elders, the Thera Anuruddha and the Thera Upāli, having entered the city of Kapilavatthu on the day of the gathering of kinsmen—
[The text] appears as if describing those who have gone forth, yet that does not accord with the Khandhaka-pāḷi and its commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). It should be accepted after investigation.
Then the Teacher, having understood the mental dispositions of the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Elder Sāriputta, began to speak of his own virtues. Therefore it was said:
"Having understood their minds, the Sage, skilled in parables..."
“The Great Hero, the Dispeller of Doubt, spoke of his own virtues.
In this context, “skilled in similes” means one who is proficient in using analogies. “Dispeller of Doubt” means one who cuts through the uncertainty of all beings.
Now, he spoke of his own virtues; to demonstrate them—
“Four incalculables, the limit of which is not known;
the body of beings, space, and the world-systems are infinite;
the Buddha’s knowledge is immeasurable—it is not possible to comprehend these. Thus it was said.
In this context, "four" is a numerical limit. "These" indicates the subject matter that is about to be explained.
"Incalculable" (*asaṅkhyeyya*) means they are so called because they cannot be numbered; the meaning is that they have transcended the path of calculation.
"A crore," etc., refers to the end or boundary. "Of which" means of those four incalculables. "Is not known" means it is not discerned.
Now, in order to demonstrate those four incalculables (asaṅkhyeyya) of the kind already mentioned, the passage beginning with “the mass of beings” (sattakāya) was spoken.
“The mass of beings” means a collection of beings; the mass of beings is infinite, immeasurable, and unfathomable.
Likewise, space has no end; likewise, the world-systems (cakkavāḷa) are indeed infinite. The Buddha’s knowledge, the knowledge of omniscience, is unfathomable. It is not possible [to measure it].
"But as for the statement 'these can be known,' since these are infinite, they cannot be known.
65. Now, the Teacher, to those gods, humans, and others who had conceived a sense of wonder and amazement at his own display of psychic power, said:
"What is this marvel? There is a marvel and a wonder even more distinguished than this; listen to that from me."
Increasing his teaching of the Dhamma, he said:
"What is this wonder in the world, that my display of psychic power [is so great]?
There are many other wonders, marvelous, and hair-raising. And so forth.
In this context, *kinti* is a word of negation. *Etaṃ* refers to this supernormal transformation (*iddhi-vikubbana*).
*Yaṃ*: this word *yaṃ* is seen in the accusative case in such passages as, “That which we asked you, you have explained to us; we ask another thing, please speak on that. [And:
“It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that in one world-system...”
In the phrase "There were two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones," it is used in the sense of a cause. In the phrase "The Blessed One Vipassī arose in that eon," it is used in the locative sense.
In such passages as "Venerable sir, what I heard and received directly from the presence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, I report that to the Blessed One," it is used in the nominative sense;
here too, it should be understood as being in the nominative sense. Others...
He indicates that he possesses many wonderful and marvelous distinctions.
Now, showing those wonders, he says:
"When I was in the Tusita realm, I was then named Santusita."
“Ten thousand [gods] having gathered together, with palms joined, entreat me”—thus he spoke at the beginning.
Therein, “when” (*yadā*) means at which time. “Me” (*ahaṃ*) refers to himself. “In the Tusita body” (*tusite kāye*) means in the divine realm known as Tusita.
But when I, having fulfilled the thirty perfections (*pāramī*) and having relinquished the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*),...

Having reached the pinnacle of conduct for the benefit of relatives, conduct for the benefit of the world, and conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood, and having given seven hundred great alms-givings, he caused the earth to quake seven times;

then, passing away from the Vessantara existence, in his second thought-moment he was reborn in the Tusita heaven, where at that time he was the divine king named Santusita. "Ten thousand [worlds] assembled" means...
The meaning is: "the deities in the ten thousand world-systems having assembled. "They entreat me with palms joined" means that, having approached me, they say:
"O Noble One, these ten perfections were fulfilled by you not while aspiring for the status of Sakka, nor Māra, nor Brahmā, nor the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch;
rather, they were fulfilled while aspiring for Buddhahood for the sake of delivering the world. You..."
“Now is the time for you, dear sir; it is the moment for you, dear sir, to attain Buddhahood,” they entreated me. Therefore it was said:
“The time has come for you, O Great Hero; arise within a mother’s womb!
Delivering the world with its devas, awaken to the deathless state.”
In that context, *kālo te* means "it is time for you," or rather, the reading is simply *kālo*. *Uppajja* means "take rebirth"; there is also the reading *okkama*.
*Sadevakaṃ* means "the world together with its devas. Regarding *tārayanto*:

here, even while fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*), one is said to "cause others to cross over," and even while bringing the perfections to their ultimate consummation, one is said to "cause others to cross over. [This occurs] after passing away from the Vessantara existence...
Having taken rebirth in the Tusita heaven, even while remaining there for seventy-five billion years plus six million years,
he is said to "deliver" beings; likewise, when requested by the deities,
he takes rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā after performing the fivefold Great Survey, and even while dwelling in the womb for ten months, he delivers them.
Indeed, even while remaining in the midst of household life for twenty-nine years, he is said to deliver others.

On the very day Rāhulabhadda was born, although he departed on horseback with Channa as his companion, having crossed over three kingdoms and gone forth on the bank of the river named Anomā, he is still said to deliver others.
Even while practicing austerities for six years, on the full moon day of the month of Visākha—
Having ascended the great seat of enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa) and shattered the host of Māra, he recollects his past lives during the first watch of the night,
purifies his divine eye during the middle watch, and during the final watch, having comprehended the twelvefold dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in both forward and reverse order,
even while penetrating the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), he is said to "cross over," and likewise at the moment of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

At the moment of the path of once-returning, at the moment of the fruit of once-returning, at the moment of the path of non-returning, at the moment of the fruit of non-returning, at the moment of the path of arahantship, and at the moment of the fruit of arahantship, he is indeed called a "savior.

From the time he gave the drink of the Deathless to the group of five monks in the company of eighteen thousand crores of deities, he is said to have been a "savior" from then on. Therefore it was said:
“Delivering the world together with its gods, awaken to the deathless state!
Thus, although the Great Being was entreated by the deities, he did not grant them a formal promise;

instead, he performed the fivefold Great Observation known as the *mahāvilokana*, concerning the time, the continent, the country, the clan, the mother, and the limit of his lifespan. Therein, first, he considered: “Is it the right time, or is it not the right time?”
He observed the time. In that context, a lifespan exceeding one hundred thousand years is not called "the time. Why?
Because birth, aging, death, and so forth are not manifest; and the teaching of the Dhamma by Buddhas is never devoid of the three characteristics.
When they speak of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, people do not believe them, wondering, "What are these people talking about?"

Consequently, there is no realization; when that is absent, the teaching lacks the quality of leading to liberation. Therefore, that is an improper time. Even a lifespan less than one hundred years is not the proper time. Why?
Because at such a time, sentient beings have defilements in excess; and advice given to those with excessive defilements does not remain in its proper place.
Therefore, that too is an improper time. From a lifespan of one hundred thousand years onwards...

The period of human lifespan from one hundred years upwards is called "the time. Seeing that the lifespan of humans at present is one hundred years, the Bodhisatta perceived, "Now is the time for me to be born.
Then, surveying the continents, he saw that Buddhas are born only in Jambudvīpa; thus, he beheld Jambudvīpa.
“Indeed, this great land named Majjhimadesa is ten thousand yojanas in extent; in which region, then, do Buddhas take birth?
While surveying the region, he beheld the Middle Country (*majjhimadesa*). Then, surveying the families, he thought: “Buddhas are born into families esteemed by the world;
at present, the Kṣatriya family is esteemed by the world; I shall be born there. [He saw] Suddhodana...
Thinking, "The king shall be my father," he surveyed his lineage. Then, looking toward his mother, he reflected:

"The mother of a Buddha is not one who is lustful, addicted to liquor, or a gambler; she must possess the five precepts unbroken. Seeing that Queen Mahāmāyā was such a woman, he thought, "She shall be my mother.
As he contemplated how long her life would last, he perceived it to be ten months and seven days.
Having thus performed these fivefold observations, he gave his promise to the deities, saying, "The time for my becoming a Buddha has come, dear sirs.
Having remained there for the duration of his lifespan and passed away from that state, he took rebirth in the womb of Queen Māyā in the Sakyan royal family. Therefore it was said:
“When he descended from the Tusita realm and entered the womb, the ten-thousandfold world system, including the earth, trembled at that time”—and so forth.
In this context, *okkami* means he descended or entered. *Kucchiyam* means in the mother’s womb. *Dasasahassī lokadhātu* refers to the ten-thousandfold world system.
"Kampittha" means that the Bodhisatta, mindful and clearly comprehending as he descended into his mother’s womb,

took rebirth on the full moon of Āsāḷha under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha by means of a great resultant consciousness (mahāvipākacitta) similar to the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness— specifically, that wholesome, unprompted (asaṅkhārika), knowledge-associated, joy-accompanied consciousness belonging to the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā).

At that time, the entire ten-thousandfold world system trembled, shook, and quaked; this is the meaning. "Dharaṇī" means the earth, so called because it supports all things, both stationary and moving. 69.
"Mindful and clearly comprehending I went forth": here, when I was mindful and clearly comprehending as I emerged from my mother’s womb, like one descending from a Dhamma-seat...

Like a preacher descending from a pulpit, or like a man descending from a ladder, I emerged with my two hands and two feet outstretched, remaining unstained by any impurity born of the mother’s womb. "They uttered cries of 'Well done!
means they gave cries of "Well done!"; the sense is that they were offering applause. "It shook" means...
*Kampittha* means that even at his descent into the mother’s womb and at his emergence from the womb, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.

Then, having seen no one equal to himself regarding such events as the descent into the womb, the Blessed One spoke this verse—“In my descent, there is no equal”—in order to demonstrate his own marvelous nature. In that context, *okkantī* means...
In the phrase *gabbhokkantiyaṃ*, the word is in the nominative case used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is "at the descent into the womb.
*Me* means "by me. *Samo* means "there is no one equal. Regarding *jātito*: here, she is called "mother" (*mātā*) because one is born (*jāyati*) by her;
thus, the meaning of *jātito* is "from the mother. *Abhinikkhameti* means "at the emergence from the mother's womb," that is, when there is birth.
The meaning [of *sambodhi*] is as follows: here, *sambodhi* is "excellent and beautiful awakening" (*pasatthā sundarā bodhi*).
Furthermore, this word *bodhi* is seen in reference to a tree, a path, Nibbāna, omniscient knowledge, and so forth—for instance, in the passages:
"He was first fully awakened at the foot of the Bodhi tree," and "Between Gayā and Bodhi," the tree is called *bodhi*.
In the passage where it is said, “Bodhi is called the knowledge in the four paths,” it refers to the path (*magga*).

In the passage where it is said, “Having attained bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned,” it refers to Nibbāna. In the passage where it is said, “The one of excellent and vast intelligence attains bodhi,” it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
However, in this context, what is intended is the Blessed One’s knowledge of the path of Arahantship. Others, however, say it is “omniscient knowledge.”
The meaning is that among those forms of enlightenment, he says, "I am the best.
But why does the Blessed One praise himself by relying on his enlightenment? Because it is the giver of all qualities.
For the Blessed One’s enlightenment is the giver of all qualities; it bestows every single quality of a Buddha without exception, but not so for others.

For others, however, it grants to some the path to Arahatship and the fruit of Arahatship itself; to some, the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*); to some, the six supernormal powers (*cha abhiññā*);
to some, the four analytical knowledges (*catasso paṭisambhidā*); to some, the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*);
and to Paccekabuddhas, it grants only the knowledge of Paccekabodhi. But for Buddhas, it grants the attainment of all qualities. Therefore, the Blessed One...
Because he bestows all virtues, he praises himself, saying, "I am supreme in regard to full enlightenment.
Furthermore, because he attained full enlightenment after shaking the earth, he says, "I am supreme in regard to full enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "in the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma," the Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. Therein—

There is the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*), developed through wisdom, which brings about the noble fruit for oneself; and there is the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*), developed through compassion, which brings about the noble fruit for disciples.
The knowledge of penetration is supramundane (*lokuttara*), wholesome (*kusala*), accompanied by equanimity, and without applied or sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*).
The knowledge of teaching is mundane (*lokiya*) and indeterminate (*abyākata*). Both of these, moreover, are not shared with others. However, it is the knowledge of teaching that is intended here.

71. Now, having heard of the occurrence of the earthquake and other phenomena at the moment of the Blessed One’s descent into the womb, the deities uttered this verse, saying, "Oh, what a marvel in the world! In that regard, "the greatness of the Buddhas' qualities" means:
oh, the magnitude of the Buddhas' qualities; oh, the great power of the Buddhas. [It refers to] the ten-thousandfold world system, which shook in six ways.
"It shook" means that in ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), the great earth shook and trembled in six ways. How so?
It rose up in the east and sank down in the west; it rose up in the west and sank down in the east;
it rose up in the north and sank down in the south; it rose up in the south and sank down in the north.
It rises in the middle and sinks at the edges, or it rises at the edges and sinks in the middle;
thus, in these six ways, this great earth— though insentient, even though it is as thick as two hundred and forty thousand yojanas and bounded by the waters that support the world—
is, like a ship buffeted by the impact of waves stirred by the force of the wind, as if possessed of consciousness through joy.
The meaning is that they trembled as if dancing. "And there was a great radiance" means that there was a sublime radiance, surpassing even the divine power of the devas.
"A marvel, hair-raising" means that it was both a marvel and hair-raising. 72.
Now, while these wonders—such as the earthquake and the manifestation of light—were occurring, [the following is] for the purpose of showing the activity of the Blessed One:
The verses beginning with “At that time the Blessed One” were spoken. Therein, “the eldest in the world” means the best in the world.
“Together with the devas”: this should be understood as the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive (meaning “of the world together with its devas”).
“Displaying” means showing a miracle. 73. “While walking back and forth”: [he did so] upon that jeweled ground which stood pervading thousands of world-systems.
While walking back and forth on the walkway, he spoke. Then the Teacher, like a lion uttering a lion’s roar upon the surface of the ground of precious stone,
like a thundering rain-cloud, and like one causing the celestial Ganges to descend,

with a voice endowed with eight qualities— pleasing to hear, lovely, and a Brahma-voice— expounded the Dhamma variegated by various methods, connected with the Four Noble Truths, and struck by the three characteristics.
The meaning is that he delivered a discourse on the sweet Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase "he does not turn back midway, as on a four-cubit walking path":
here, of that walking path created by the Teacher, one end was at the eastern rim of the world-system (cakravāḷa) and the other at the western rim of the world-system.
While standing thus, as the Teacher walked upon that jeweled cloister, he would turn back only after reaching both ends;

he did not turn back in between, before reaching both ends. The meaning is: just as one walking on a four-cubit cloister turns back immediately upon reaching both ends, so too he did not turn back in between. But why?
Did the Blessed One shorten the walking path, which measured ten thousand *yojanas* in length, or did he manifest a physical form (*attabhāva*) of such great size?
He did not do so. The spiritual power (*buddhānubhāva*) of the Buddhas is inconceivable.
From the Akaniṭṭha realm down to the Avīci hell, it became a single level ground; and horizontally, ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) became a single level ground.
They existed. Devas saw humans, and humans also saw devas.

Just as all devas and humans see one walking about in their ordinary state, so too did they see the Blessed One walking about. Moreover, while walking about, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma and entered the intermediate attainment (*antarāsamāpatti*).
Then the Venerable Sāriputta beheld the Exalted One’s noble body,

adorned with the thirty-two excellent major marks produced by the power of wholesome kamma accumulated over immeasurable aeons, and resplendent with the eighty minor characteristics; it was like the full moon in autumn,
or like a *pāricchattaka* tree a hundred leagues high in full bloom, or like one eighteen cubits tall, graced by a halo of light extending a fathom in circumference.

He saw the Blessed One walking with the incomparable grace of a Buddha and the incomparable splendor of a Buddha’s majesty, like a moving mountain of excellent gold, surrounded by a host of ten thousand deities. Upon seeing him, [he thought]:
"This entire ten-thousandfold world system has assembled; there must be a great discourse on the Dhamma here, a teaching on the lineage of the Buddhas."

"However, they are of great benefit and inspire confidence in the Blessed One; what if I were now to inquire thoroughly about the lineage of the Buddhas, starting from the initial resolve of the One Possessing the Ten Powers?

Having thought thus, he adjusted his robe over one shoulder, approached the Blessed One, and placed his hands together in reverent salutation—hands as radiant as ten nails, resembling the unblemished bud of a lotus flower—at the crown of his head, and addressed the Blessed One.
He asked a series of questions beginning with, “Of what kind are those Great Heroes? Therefore it was said:
“Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna, Having reached perfection in discernment, asks the Leader of the World.”
“What was the nature of your resolve, O Great Hero, O Supreme among Men?
At what time, O Wise One, did you aspire for supreme enlightenment?”—and so forth.

What is this sequence called? It is called a sequence by way of question (*pucchānusandhi*). For there are three kinds of sequences: sequence by way of question, [sequence by way of answer, and sequence by way of connection].

“Connection by way of underlying intention” means “according to the sequence. In that regard, connection by way of question should be understood through the suttas answered by the Blessed One when they were asked, such as: “When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
‘Venerable sir, what is the near shore? What is the far shore? Thus it should be understood for those who ask.
Then, a certain bhikkhu had this reflection arise in his mind:
"So it seems, sirs, that form is non-self, feeling is non-self, perception is non-self, volitional formations are non-self, and consciousness is non-self;
yet how will actions performed by what is non-self affect a self? Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in that bhikkhu's mind, said:

He addressed the bhikkhus: “It is possible, bhikkhus, that some foolish man here, being ignorant and immersed in ignorance, with a mind dominated by craving, might think that he should go beyond the Teacher’s instruction, [thinking]:
‘Indeed, sirs, form is non-self, feeling is non-self, perception is non-self, volitional formations are non-self, consciousness is non-self.’”
‘If there is no self, and actions are performed by what is not-self, then what self will experience the result of those actions? … ‘What do you think, monks,

is form permanent or impermanent?’— thus, having understood the underlying disposition of others, the sequence of the discourse according to that disposition should be understood as spoken by the Blessed One.

However, the sequence of the discourse (yathānusandhi) should be understood by way of those suttas in which the subsequent teaching occurs—either by way of a doctrine corresponding to the doctrine with which the teaching began, or by way of its negation.
Therefore it was said: "the sequence of questions" (pucchānusandhi).
In this context, "one who has attained perfection in wisdom" means one who has reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s knowledge of the perfections (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*). "He asks" means he questioned.

Therein, questioning is fivefold: questioning for the illumination of what has not been seen, questioning for the corroboration of what has been seen, questioning for the cutting off of doubt, questioning for assent, and questioning out of a desire to speak. Of these, which kind was it for the Elder?

If you ask why: it is because this *Buddhavaṃsa* is not within the domain of Pacceka-buddhas who have accumulated a mass of merit over an incalculable aeon plus one hundred thousand aeons, nor of the two Chief Disciples who have accumulated a mass of merit over an incalculable aeon plus one hundred thousand aeons, nor of the other Great Disciples who have accumulated a mass of merit over one hundred thousand aeons; rather, it belongs exclusively to the Omniscient Buddhas.
This is the subject; therefore, it should be understood that for the Elder, this is a question concerning the demonstration of what was not previously seen (*adiṭṭhajotanā*).
"Of what kind? refers to the manner of questioning; the meaning is, "of what sort? "Your" (*te*) means "your. "Resolution" (*abhinīhāra*):
resolution (*abhinīhāra*) is the fixing of the mind for the sake of Buddhahood, having resolved upon energy (*vīriya*), thinking, "I shall not rise until I have received the prophecy of Buddhahood."
Lying down. Therefore it was said:
"O Great Hero, O Supreme among Men, what was the nature of your resolve?
At what time? At that time. "Aspired" means desired or longed for: "May I become a Buddha and awaken others; may I be liberated..."
By means of the method beginning with “moceyyan” (may I be liberated), he asked when the aspiration for Buddhahood was made.

“Bodhi” is the designation for both the knowledge of the path to Arahatship and omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). It is called “supreme” (*uttama*) because it is superior to the enlightenment of disciples (*sāvakabodhi*) and the enlightenment of paccekabuddhas.
The letter *m* between the two words serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*).
Now, asking about the qualities that bring about the state of Buddhahood:
“What is the nature of generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, and energy?
What is the nature of patience, truthfulness, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity?”
“O Wise One, Leader of the World, what are the ten perfections (pāramīs) like?
How is the near-perfection (upapāramī) fulfilled, and how is the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī)? Thus he spoke.

Regarding that, first, in the perfection of giving (dānapāramī), the relinquishing of external goods is called the perfection (pāramī); the relinquishing of one’s own limbs is the near-perfection (upapāramī).
The sacrifice of life is called the ultimate perfection (*paramatthapāramī*). This same method applies to the remaining perfections as well. Thus, there are thirty perfections in total:
ten perfections (*pāramī*), ten secondary perfections (*upapāramī*), and ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*).

Among these, there is no limit to the number of existences in which the Bodhisattva fulfilled the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). However, in the *Sasapaṇḍita-jātaka*, it is stated categorically: [that he gave away his body ninety-nine times].
“Seeing him who had approached for alms, I sacrificed my own life;
there is no one equal to me in giving—this is my perfection of giving.
Thus, for one who makes the sacrifice of their own life for another, the perfection of giving becomes what is called the perfection in the ultimate sense.
Likewise, there is no measure to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*). Indeed, it is stated exclusively of him in the *Saṅkhapāla Jātaka*:
"Even when being pierced with stakes or beaten with spears, I did not become angry at Bhojaputta; this is my perfection of virtue."
Thus, for one who practices self-sacrifice, the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī) becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī).

Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of renunciation (nekkhammapāramī) by abandoning great sovereignty. Indeed, in the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka, it is stated with absolute certainty:
"He cast away the great sovereignty that had come into his hands, like a globule of spittle."
“There is no clinging for one who has cast it off; this is my perfection of renunciation.
Thus, for him who went forth, casting aside his kingdom out of detachment, the perfection of renunciation became a perfection in the ultimate sense.

Likewise, there is no measure to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of wisdom during the time of the wise Mahosadha and others. However, it was in the time of the wise Sattubhattaka that—
“Investigating with wisdom, O Brahmin, I liberated you from suffering;
there is no one equal to me in wisdom—this is my perfection of wisdom.
Thus, for him who showed the snake that had entered inside his belly, the perfection of wisdom became known as the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī).
Likewise, there is no measure to the number of existences fulfilled through the perfection of energy (*vīriyapāramitā*). Regarding this, it is stated categorically in the Mahājanaka Jātaka:
“Those men were all destroyed in the midst of the waters, unable to see the further shore;
yet my mind did not waver—this is my perfection of energy.”
Thus, for one crossing the great ocean, the perfection of energy becomes known as the perfection in the ultimate sense.
Likewise, in the *Khantivādijātaka*:
“Even as they were hacking at me with a sharp axe, as if I were insentient...”
“I am not angry with the King of Kāsi; this is my perfection of patience.
Thus, for one who endures great suffering as if it were insentient, the perfection of patience becomes what is called the perfection in the ultimate sense.
Likewise, in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka—
“Protecting my word of truth, even at the cost of my own life, I liberated one hundred kṣatriyas;
this is my perfection of truth. Thus, for one who protects the truth by sacrificing his life, the perfection of truth becomes what is called the ultimate perfection.
Likewise, in the Mūgapakkha Jātaka:
“My mother and father are not to be given away, nor am I myself to be given away;
omniscience is dear to me, therefore I have resolved upon this vow.”
Thus, for one who resolves upon a vow even after renouncing life itself, that perfection of resolve (adhiṭṭhānapāramī) becomes known as the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī).
Likewise, in the Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka:
“No one terrifies me, nor do I fear anyone;”
“Strengthened by the power of loving-kindness, I then delighted in the forest.
Thus, disregarding even his own life while practicing loving-kindness, the perfection of loving-kindness became for him a perfection in the ultimate sense.
Then, in the *Lomahaṃsa Jātaka*:
“I make my bed in the charnel ground, with a skeleton as my pillow;
when the village girls approach, they display no small amount of beauty.”— Thus it was,
even while the village children were causing him pleasure and pain by spitting on him and so forth, and by offering him garlands and perfumes.
For one who does not overstep equanimity, the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī) is said to have become a perfection in the ultimate sense (paramattha-pāramī). This is the summary here;
the detailed account, however, should be taken from the Cariyāpiṭaka.
Now, the compilers [of the canon], showing the Blessed One’s reply to what was asked by the Elder, said:
Questioned by him, he replied with a voice as sweet as the karavīka bird’s, cooling the heart and gladdening the world together with its devas:
“It was taught by the Conquerors, the Buddhas of the past; it has been polished and handed down through the succession of Buddhas.”
"With an intelligence following after his former abodes, he revealed the welfare of the world, including the devas"—so it was said.
Regarding that, "being questioned by him, he answered": having been questioned by that Dhamma-general (Sāriputta), he answered him;
he recounted the entire lineage of the Buddhas (*buddhavaṃsa*), from his own initial aspiration up to the conclusion of his perfect enlightenment.
The meaning is as follows: “With a voice as sweet as the karavīka bird” means one whose speech is as sweet as that of the karavīka bird;
the sense is that his voice is as sweet and melodious as the karavīka. Herein, this is the sweetness of the karavīka birds’ voice:
it is said that when karavīka birds strike a ripe mango of sweet flavor with their beaks and drink the juice trickling from it, [they become intoxicated].
When the drum is struck with a hand-clap, the four-footed creatures, intoxicated as if by madness, begin to frolic and bellow;
even herds of quadrupeds intent on foraging cast aside the grass in their mouths to listen to that sound;
and predatory beasts pursuing small game stand as if painted in a picture, unable to lift their raised feet to set them down, while those being pursued likewise remain transfixed.
Having cast off the fear of death, even birds remaining in the air stand with their wings outspread;
even fish in the water remain listening to that sound without moving a fin. Such is the sweet voice of the karavīka bird.
"Cooling the heart" means [cooling] the minds of all people, which have been heated by the fire of the defilements, by means of the cooling stream of the Dhamma discourse.
The meaning is "producing a state of coolness. "Causing to laugh" means causing to rejoice. "Together with the devas" means the world together with its devas.

"Of the past Buddhas" means of the Buddhas of the past. Prior to the aspiration (*abhinīhāra*) of our Blessed One, however, four Buddhas—Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara—were born in a single eon (*kappa*).
Following them, there were twenty-three Buddhas beginning with Koṇḍañña; thus, all twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara are intended here by the term "past Buddhas" (*atītabuddhā*).
"Of those past Buddhas" (*tesaṃ atītabuddhānaṃ*): *jinānaṃ* is a synonym for that same term. "Taught" (*desitaṃ*) means spoken.
It refers to the discourse on the Dhamma connected with the Four Noble Truths delivered by the twenty-four Buddhas. "Composed" (*nikīlitaṃ*)...
Their conduct—including their eon, birth, clan, lifespan, awakening, assemblies of disciples, attendants, parents, children, wives, retinue, and so forth—is called "inscribed" (*nikīlita*).
"Transmitted through the succession of Buddhas" means that it has come down and been taught from the time of the Ten-Powered One Dīpaṅkara until the succession of Kassapa;
this is the meaning of "inscribed. "By means of an intelligence following after past lives" means even a single birth...
"Two births": thus, he has followed and approached the past lives (pubbenivāsa), which are defined as the continuity of the aggregates (khandha-santāna) previously inhabited;
the meaning is "by means of that wisdom following past lives," that is, by the knowledge of the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa).

"He proclaimed" means he explained. "The welfare of the world" refers to the lineage of Buddhas (buddhavaṃsa), which is for the benefit of the entire world. "In the world with its devas" means in the world together with the devas.
80. Then the Blessed One, with a heart cooled by compassion, spoke the words beginning with “generating joy and gladness,” while enjoining the world together with its devas to listen.
In this context, “generating joy and gladness” means that which produces joy and gladness;

it refers to gladness as the precursor to rapture (*pīti*), the meaning being the generation of fivefold rapture. “Dispelling the dart of sorrow” means the removal and destruction of the darts known as sorrow.
“Attainment of all success” (*sabbasampattipaṭilābha*) means that by means of this, one attains all forms of success, such as those of gods and humans;
thus, the meaning is “the teaching of the lineage of Buddhas (*buddhavaṃsa-desanā*) which is that attainment of all success.

“Having honored it” (*cittīkatvā*) means having placed it in the heart; the meaning is “having placed the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) before oneself. “Listen” (*suṇātha*) means “pay close attention.”
Understand this: "Me" means mine.
(81) "Madanimmadana" means that which effects the crushing of all forms of intoxication, such as the intoxication of birth and so forth. "Sokanuda" means that which dispels sorrow;

for "sorrow" (soka) is the burning of the mind when one is afflicted by the loss of relatives and the like. Although in its actual meaning it is simply mental distress (domanassa), [it is here termed sorrow].
Even so, it has the characteristic of inward brooding, the function of the mind’s intense brooding, and its manifestation is sorrowing.

It is called "dispeller of sorrow" (*sokanuda*) because it dispels that sorrow; thus, it is "that which dispels sorrow. "Liberation from saṃsāra" means that which effects complete liberation from the bonds of *saṃsāra*.
There is also a reading, "transcending *saṃsāra*," the meaning of which is "that which effects the transcending of *saṃsāra*."

Regarding the phrase "the destruction of all suffering" (*sabbadukkhakkhaya*): here, the word *dukkha* is seen in the sense of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*), the basis of suffering (*dukkhavatthu*), the object of suffering (*dukkhārammaṇa*), the condition for suffering (*dukkhapaccaya*), the locus of suffering (*dukkhaṭṭhāna*), and so forth. Indeed, in passages such as “with the abandoning of suffering” (*dukkhassa ca pahānā*), it is seen in the sense of painful feeling. In passages such as “birth is suffering, aging is suffering,” it is seen in the sense of the basis of suffering.
And in the passage: “For form, Mahāli, is suffering, it is beset by suffering... [it is seen in the sense of the object of suffering].
In such passages as “entered upon suffering,” it refers to the object of suffering. In such passages as “The accumulation of evil is suffering,” it refers to the condition for suffering.
In such passages as “To this extent, monks, it is not easy to reach by description how far suffering extends in the hells,” it refers to the locus of suffering.

Here, however, it should be understood both as the basis of suffering and as the condition for suffering. Therefore, it is that which brings about the destruction of all suffering, beginning with birth.

The meaning is as follows: "Path" (*magga*)—here it is called the teaching on the lineage of the Buddhas (*buddhavaṃsadesanā*) because it is sought after by those desiring what is wholesome, or because it goes while slaying the defilements (*kilesa*).

"That teaching on the lineage of the Buddhas, which constitutes the path to Nibbāna"—"carefully" (*sakkacca*) means with due honor, that is, having lent an attentive ear. "Practice" (*paṭipajjatha*) means establish yourselves [in it]; "listen" (*suṇātha*).

The meaning [is as follows]. Alternatively, having heard this teaching on the lineage of the Buddhas—which generates joy and gladness, dispels the dart of sorrow, and serves as the cause for attaining all perfections—[the Buddha exhorted them]:
"Now, apply yourselves to the path to Buddhahood, which brings about the destruction of all suffering and possesses such distinguished qualities as the subduing of intoxication.
Thus, he inspired all gods and humans to aspire toward Buddhahood.
He causes [them] to be born. The rest here is self-evident.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the Jewel-Walking (Ratanacaṅkamanakaṇḍa) in the Madhuratthavilāsinī, the commentary on the Buddhavaṃsa.
The commentary on the meaning of the internal nidāna has been completed in every respect.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Sumedhā’s Aspiration: Now—
“In a hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable [aeons], there was a city named Amara, beautiful and delightful.

Having reached this point, the opportunity has arrived for the commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*, which proceeds according to the method beginning with these words. And this commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*...

Since the exposition is made clear when explained after investigating the occasion for the delivery of the discourse (*suttanikkhepa*), the investigation of the occasions for the delivery of discourses should first be understood.

There are four occasions for the delivery of discourses: those arising from one’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), those arising from another’s inclination (*parajjhāsaya*), those prompted by a question (*pucchāvasika*), and those arising from a specific circumstance (*aṭṭhuppattika*).
Among these, those discourses which the Blessed One spoke solely out of his own inclination, without being requested by others, [are called "arising from one’s own inclination"].
For example, the *Ākaṅkheyya-sutta*, the *Vattha-sutta*, and so forth—these are instances of a formulation based on one’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*).
Alternatively, those such as: “Rāhula’s qualities conducive to the ripening of liberation have indeed matured;

what if I were now to train Rāhula further in the destruction of the taints?”—are instances [of formulations] based on the inclination, patience, intention, and capacity for understanding of others (*paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ khantiṃ manaṃ bujjhanakabhāvañca*).

These were spoken after having observed the inclinations of others. For example—the *Rāhulovāda Sutta*, the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*, and so forth—these have their "deposit" (*nikkhepa*) in the inclinations of others.

Having approached the Blessed One, various gods and humans ask him questions; those discourses spoken by the Blessed One when thus questioned, such as the *Devatāsaṃyutta* and the *Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta*, have their "deposit" in the occasion of the question.

Furthermore, those discourses taught in dependence upon a specific occasion that had arisen—such as the "Heirs of the Dhamma," the "Son's Flesh" simile, and so forth—have an *aṭṭhuppattika* (occasion-based) placement.
Thus, among these four types of sutta-placement, this *Buddhavaṃsa* has a placement based on a question (*pucchāvasika*).
For it was placed by the Blessed One by way of a question. By whose questioning?
Of the venerable elder Sāriputta. For this was said in this very introduction:
“Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna, having reached perfection in insight, questioned the Leader of the World.”
"Of what kind, O Great Hero, was your resolve, O Supreme among Men?"—and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that this teaching of the *Buddhavaṃsa* is based on a question.

In that context, regarding the phrase "in a hundred thousand aeons" (*kappe ca satasahasse*), this word *kappa* refers to conviction, conventional usage, time, designation, cutting off, alternative, a trace, omnipresence, a lifespan-aeon (*āyukappa*), a great aeon (*mahākappa*), and so on.

It is seen [in various senses]. Thus, in such passages as “This is to be trusted by Master Gotama, just as it is for an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One,” it is seen in the sense of *abhisaddahana* (firm conviction).
In such passages as “I allow you, monks, to consume fruit according to the five monastic conventions (*samaṇakappa*)”, it is seen in the sense of *vohāra* (convention or usage).

In such passages as “By which indeed I dwell constantly throughout my life (*niccakappa*)”, it is seen in the sense of *kāla* (time). And in the passage “Thus said the Venerable Kappa,” it is seen in the sense of a personal name.

And [the term *kappa* is used] in the sense of designation (paññatti), as in such passages as: “His name was Nigrodhakappa; this was done by you, O Blessed One, for the brahmin”; in the sense of cutting (chedana), as in:
“adorned, with hair and beard trimmed (*kappita*)”; in the sense of option (vikappa), as in: “it is allowable (*kappati*), it is a two-finger-breadth allowance (*dvaṅgulakappo*)”;
in the sense of a small portion (leśa), as in: “there is time (*kappa*) to lie down”; and in the sense of the entirety (sakala), as in: “having illuminated the whole of Jetavana (*kevalakappaṃ*)...”

In the sense of "all-encompassing" (*samantabhāve*): in the passage, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One remain for an eon; may the Sugata remain for an eon,” it refers to a life-span eon (*āyukappe*).
In the passage, “How long, venerable sir, is an eon? it refers to a great eon (*mahākappe*).

By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), [the meaning] in the passage, “Indeed, sir, while we were consulting with a disciple, we did not realize it was as if by the Teacher’s eon,” refers to a counterpart eon (*paṭibhāge*).
"In the phrase ‘The kappa is lost; the portion of the kappa that has been made is worn out,’ it refers to the *vinaya-kappa* (the disciplinary code).
But here, it should be understood as referring to a *mahākappa* (great eon). Therefore, the meaning of ‘a hundred thousand kappas’ is ‘a hundred thousand *mahākappas*.

And regarding the phrase ‘four incalculables (*asaṅkheyya*),’ it should be understood that the ellipsis of the words is ‘at the end of four incalculables. [This refers to] those exceeding a hundred thousand kappas..."
The meaning is: "at the summit of four incalculable eons. Regarding the city named Amara: there was a city that had received the names both "Amara" and "Amaravatī.
However, some here describe it in another manner; but what need is there for them? This is merely the name of that city.
"Worthy of being seen" (*dassaneyya*) means [endowed with] well-proportioned and variegated crossroads, gates, quadrangles, junctions, ramparts, enclosures, and palaces.
It is "worth seeing" because it is beautifully adorned with palaces and mansions. It is "delightful" because it gladdens the minds of gods,

humans, and others due to its level, pure, and most charming grounds, its abundance of shade and water, the ease with which food is obtained, and its prosperity through being endowed with all necessary requisites.

"Unfurnished with ten sounds" means it was never devoid of these ten sounds: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of kettledrums, the sound of conchs, the sound of clay drums, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of cymbals and clapping, and the tenth sound: "Eat! Drink!
Feast! It was thus unfurnished with these ten sounds, being at all times filled with incomparable festivals, assemblies, and theatrical performances.
The meaning is "they play. "Well-provided with food and drink" (*annapānasamāyuta*) means well-endowed (*suṭṭhu āyuta*) with both the fourfold food and drink;
by this, the state of having abundant alms-food is shown, meaning it is well-provided with much food and drink.
Now, in order to show those ten sounds according to their substance—
It is said: “The sound of elephants, the sound of horses, and the sounds of drums, conchs, and chariots—‘Eat! Drink! thus it resounds with food and drink.
In this context, “the sound of elephants” (hatthisaddaṃ) should be understood as the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental, meaning by means of the trumpeting sound of the elephants.
This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. “And the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, and chariots” means by the sound of kettledrums, the sound of conchs, and the sound of chariots.

It is stated with a change of grammatical gender; the meaning is that it was resounded and made to ring out with cries associated with food and drink, proceeding in such a manner as “Eat! Drink! and so forth. Here it is asked: But of those sounds...
Is it shown only in part, and not in its entirety? It is not merely a part; rather, the tenfold [splendor] is shown in its entirety. How so?
By the sound of the kettle-drum, the sound of the drum is included; by the sound of the conch, the sounds of the lute, song, cymbals, and clapping are included—thus, all ten are indeed shown.
Having thus described the prosperity of the city by way of one method, he speaks again in order to demonstrate that very same thing:
“A city endowed with all its parts, where every task is accomplished, possessing the seven treasures, crowded with various people;
flourishing like the city of the gods, an abode for those who perform meritorious deeds”—thus it was said.

Therein, "endowed with all its parts" means possessed of all the constituent elements of a city, such as walls, gate-towers, and watchtowers; and complete in all requisites of wealth, riches, grain, grass, firewood, and water.
Or it means "the purpose. *Sabbakammamupāgataṃ* means approached by all activities; the meaning is "one to whom all activities have fully approached.

*Sattaratanasampannaṃ* means possessing the seven jewels, such as pearls and so forth, which are complete; or, it means endowed with the seven jewels beginning with the elephant-jewel, from the perspective of being the dwelling place of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). *Nānājanasamākulaṃ* means crowded with people of various kinds and regional languages.
"Filled with people" means crowded with folk. "Prosperous" means flourishing and abundant with all the requisites for human enjoyment.
"Like a city of the gods" means it was as prosperous as a city of the gods, such as Ālakamandā or Amaravatī; this is what is meant. "A dwelling for those who perform meritorious deeds":
it is a "dwelling" (āvāsa) because those who perform meritorious deeds dwell there. Although it should be called "āvāso," the form "āvāsaṃ" is used here due to a change in grammatical gender.
It should be understood that this was said having made [this point]. It is called *puñña* because one shines forth by means of it;

the meaning is that one shines forth by way of noble birth, physical beauty, great wealth, and sovereignty. Alternatively, it is *puñña* because it purifies (*punāti*). Since meritorious action (*puñña-kamma*) carries away all the stains and dust of unwholesomeness, those who possess such meritorious action are "those with meritorious action" (*puñña-kammī*); the meaning is that it is the dwelling place for those with meritorious action.
There lived a brahmin named Sumedha, well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and his father’s side,
of pure descent back through seven generations of ancestors, unblemished and irreproachable by birth; he was handsome, pleasing to behold, inspiring confidence,
endowed with the highest beauty of complexion, and he had mastered the three Vedas, including the Nighaṇṭu and the Keṭubha.
He was well-versed in the Vedas, including the Itihāsas as the fifth, as well as the Padaka and the Veyyākaraṇa; he was also proficient in Lokāyata philosophy and the marks of a Great Man.
However, while he was still young, his parents passed away.
Then the treasurer, a minister, brought forth the register of wealth and opened the storehouses filled with various treasures such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls, saying: "This much..."

“Prince, this much wealth belongs to your mother, this much to your father, and this much to your grandfathers and great-grandfathers,” he said, enumerating the riches down through seven generations of his lineage, and then handed it over to him, saying, “Deal with this as you see fit.
He accepted it, saying, “Very well,” and dwelt at home performing meritorious deeds. Thus it was said:
“In the city of Amarāvatī, there was a brahmin named Sumedha,
who possessed a hoard of many millions and was abundant in wealth and grain.
He was a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, and one who had mastered the three Vedas.”
“He reached perfection in the characteristics, in history, and in his own doctrine.
Herein, “in the city of Amarāvatī” means in the city known as Amarāvatī. Regarding the name “Sumedha”:
here, “medhā” refers to wisdom (*paññā*). Because that wisdom was beautiful and praiseworthy in him, he became known as Sumedha. “Brāhmaṇa” [refers to one who has attained] the *brahma*...
One who breathes (*aṇati*) and trains (*sikkhati*) is a *brāhmaṇa*; the meaning is that he recites the mantras. However, etymologists say that a *brāhmaṇa* is "the offspring of Brahmā.
But the Noble Ones (*ariya*) are called *brāhmaṇas* because they have banished evil (*bāhitapāpa*). "Accumulation of many millions" (*anekakoṭisannicaya*):
an accumulation of millions is a "million-accumulation" (*koṭisannicaya*); one who has many such million-accumulations is "one with an accumulation of many millions" (*anekakoṭisannicaya*).
The meaning is "a collection of many millions of coins. "Possessing abundant wealth and grain" means possessing much wealth and grain.

It should be understood that the former [phrase] was stated with reference to wealth and grain stored underground or in storehouses, whereas this [phrase] was stated with reference to wealth and grain intended for constant personal use.
"Ajjhāyaka" means one who does not meditate (*na jhāyati*); the meaning is that he is devoid of the cultivation of *jhāna*. For this has been said:
"They do not meditate now; 'they do not meditate now,' Vāseṭṭha—this is how the third syllable, 'ajjhāyakā ajjhāyakā,' came to be applied.
Thus, [the term was used] for those brahmins of the first eon who were devoid of *jhāna*.
A word of reproach has arisen. Now, one who "meditates on the mantras" (mantaṃ jhāyati) is called an *ajjhāyaka*;
they employ this term as a word of praise in the sense of "one who recites the mantras. One who "bears the mantras" (*dhāreti*) is a *mantadhara*. Regarding the phrase "of the three Vedas":
it refers to the three Vedas, namely the *Iruveda*, the *Yajuveda*, and the *Sāmaveda*. Furthermore, this word *veda* [is used] in the senses of knowledge, joy, and books.

It is seen [in various senses]. For instance, in such passages as, “The brahmin one should know as a master of the Vedas (vedagu), who possesses nothing and is unattached to sensual existence,” it is seen in the sense of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

In such passages as, “Those born of the Vedas who wander the world,” it is seen in the sense of mental joy (*somanassa*). In such passages as, “One who has gone to the further shore of the three Vedas, together with the Nighaṇṭu and Keṭubha,” it is seen in the sense of the texts (*gantha*).
Here too, it is in the sense of the texts. “Gone to the further shore” means by the mere act of reciting the three Vedas from memory.
One who has gone to the further shore (*pāra*) is a "one who has reached the further shore" (*pāragū*). Regarding "characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa*):

it refers to characteristics such as the female characteristics, male characteristics, and the characteristics of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*). Regarding "legendary lore" (*itihāsa*): it means "thus it was" (*itiha āsa*), referring to specific ancient texts associated with such expressions.
Regarding "his own doctrine" (*sadhamma*): it refers to the Brāhmaṇas' own doctrine or their own traditional teaching. "One who has reached the perfection" (*pāramiṃ gata*)...
"Having reached the further shore, he became a teacher renowned in all directions"—this is the meaning.

Then one day, that wise Sumedha Paṇḍita, who had pleased the multitude with his tenfold virtues, sat alone on the excellent upper terrace of the palace, having folded his legs crosswise in the *pallaṅka* posture, and reflected: "The taking of rebirth-linking in a future existence is indeed suffering."
"Thus, in every place where I am reborn, there is the breaking up of the body; and I am subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, and subject to death.

It is fitting for me, being such as this, to seek the blissful, auspicious Nibbāna—which is without birth, without aging, without sickness, and without death—and surely, having been released from the prison of existence, I must find the one path leading to Nibbāna. Therefore it was said:
“Seated in seclusion, I then reflected thus:
‘Rebirth is indeed suffering, as is the dissolution of the body.
Subject to birth, subject to aging, and subject to sickness, I was then [afflicted].’”
I shall seek the unaging, deathless, secure state of Nibbāna.
"What if I were now to cast aside this putrid body, filled with various kinds of filth,
and go forth without longing or seeking after it?"
“There exists that path; it is not impossible for it to be found.
I shall seek that path for the sake of liberation from existence.
Here, however, we shall proceed after first explaining the connection between the verses and the meaning of the words not previously explained. In this context, “gone into seclusion” means:
"Having gone into seclusion, seated in a secluded place, I thought thus"—by saying "I thought thus," he shows the manner of his reflection.

"At that time" means at the time of the wise Sumedha. By saying "you thought thus," the Blessed One establishes the identity of the wise Sumedha with himself. Therefore, at that time, that Sumedha was none other than myself.
Explaining this, the Blessed One said, "Thus I thought then," speaking by way of the Supreme Person (*uttamapurisa*). "Subject to birth" (*jātidhamma*) means having the nature of birth.
This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Nibbuti" means Nibbāna.
"Yaṃnūna" is a particle used in the sense of reflection; the meaning is, "What if I were... "Pūtikāya" means a body that has become putrid.
The body. "Filled with various kinds of filth" means filled with many types of filth such as urine, feces, pus, blood, bile, phlegm, saliva, and nasal mucus.
"Without regard" means without attachment. "It exists" means it is necessarily found. "He will exist" means he will come to be; this is a word of conjecture.
"It is not possible that he would not be because of that cause" means it is not possible for him not to exist by means of that path. "But that path is indeed the cause."
"It does not fail to be the state of being a cause" means that it is indeed a cause. "From liberation from existence" means from liberation from the bondage of existence.
Now, in order to fulfill the purpose he had reflected upon himself, he said, "Just as," and so forth.
For just as in the world there exists what is called happiness, which is the opposite of suffering, so too, when existence (bhava) exists, there must also be its opposite, non-existence (vibhava).

It must exist; and just as when there is heat, there is also a coolness that serves as its pacification, so too there must be *nibbāna* by way of the pacification of the fires of lust and the other defilements.

And just as there exists a beautiful, blameless state (*dhamma*) which is the opposite of evil and base states, even so, while evil birth exists, [there must be a state] that casts off all forms of birth.
"Therefore, Nibbāna must indeed exist as that which is called 'unborn' (ajāta). Thus it was said:
'Just as when suffering exists, that which is called happiness also exists;
so too, while existence (bhava) exists, non-existence (vibhava) is something to be sought.'"
“Just as when heat exists, something cool also exists;
so when the threefold fire exists, Nibbāna is to be sought.
Just as when evil exists, the beautiful also exists;”

“In the same way, while birth exists, non-birth is to be sought. In this context, *yathāpi* is a particle used in the sense of a simile. *Sukhaṃ* means bodily and mental happiness; it is called *sukha* because it thoroughly (*su*) cuts away (*khana-ti*) suffering. *Bhava* means arising. *Vibhava* means non-arising; even though arising exists, that which has the nature of non-arising— *...* [The remainder of the passage follows] ...is what is meant. Thus, the meaning is: “Just as one who desires happiness would seek for non-birth while birth exists, so too, while the world of becoming exists, one should seek for the state of non-becoming. Therefore, it is said: “While birth exists, non-birth is to be sought. Herein, *jāti* (birth) refers to the manifestation of the aggregates. *Ajāti* (non-birth) refers to the cessation of those same aggregates. *Pucchitabbaṃ* (to be sought) means to be investigated or to be aimed at. *Kantanti* means desired or wished for. The meaning is: “Just as one who desires happiness would seek for non-birth while birth exists, so too, while the world of becoming exists, one should seek for the state of non-becoming. Thus, it is said: “While birth exists, non-birth is to be sought. Herein, *jāti* (birth) refers to the manifestation of the aggregates. *Ajāti* (non-birth) refers to the cessation of those same aggregates. *Pucchitabbaṃ* (to be sought) means to be investigated or to be aimed at. *Kantanti* means desired or wished for. The meaning is: “Just as one who desires happiness would seek for non-birth while birth exists, so too, while the world of becoming exists, one should seek for the state of non-becoming. Thus, it is said: “While birth exists, non-birth is to be sought. Herein, *jāti* (birth) refers to the manifestation of the aggregates. *Ajāti* (non-birth) refers to the cessation of those same aggregates. *Pucchitabbaṃ* (to be sought) means to be investigated or to be aimed at. *Kantanti* means desired or wished for. The meaning is: “Just as one who desires happiness would seek for non-birth while birth exists, so too, while the world of becoming exists, one should seek for the state of non-becoming.”
It should be desired. "The threefold fire exists" means that the threefold fire, beginning with lust (*rāga*), is present.
