"Nibbāna" means the extinguishing, the pacification, and the Nibbāna of those three fires of lust and so forth; this too should be desired. "Brings to" means it causes one to reach what is unwholesome (*akusala*) and base.
"Even the beautiful" means even the wholesome (*kusala*). "Just so" means in exactly this way. "Birth exists" refers to birth.

The meaning is "while it exists. This was stated by changing the gender and omitting the case ending. "Even non-arising" means that even the unarisen Nirvana should be desired as the cessation of birth.
Then I thought further: "Just as if a man were submerged in a heap of excrement and [saw] from afar a pond adorned with clusters of lotuses, blue water-lilies, and white lotuses..."
Upon seeing a pond of pure water, it is appropriate to search for that pond, thinking, "By what path should one go there?
That one does not search for it is not the fault of that pond; it is the fault of that person alone.
In the same way, while the great pond of the Deathless exists for the washing away of the stains of the defilements, that one does not search for it—[is not the fault of the pond].
This is a fault of the great lake of Nibbāna, which is designated as the Deathless; it is a fault of the person, just like the fault of a man.
For example, if a man surrounded by thieves does not flee even though a path of escape exists, that is not a fault of the path, but a fault of that man alone.
In the same way, for a person who has been surrounded and seized by the thieves of the defilements...
When the auspicious great highway leading to the great city of Nibbāna exists right here,
the failure to seek out that path is not the fault of the path, but rather the fault of the person.
Just as when a man afflicted by disease does not seek out a physician who is available and have that physician treat his ailment, it is not the fault of the physician.

"The fault lies with that man alone. In the same way, the fault lies with him who, being afflicted by the disease of the defilements (*kilesa*), does not seek out a teacher who exists and is skilled in the path that pacifies those defilements; it is not the fault of the teacher who is the healer of the disease of the defilements.
Thus it was said.
“Just as a man who has fallen into excrement, upon seeing a pond full [of water],
does not seek out that pond— it is no fault of the pond. So too,
while the pond of the Deathless exists, one is defiled by the stains of the afflictions.”
He does not search for that pond; there is no fault in the pond of the Deathless.
Just as a man besieged by enemies, though a path for travel exists, does not flee—there is no fault in the straight road.
“Thus obstructed by defilements, though the auspicious path exists, one does not seek that way; yet there is no fault in the supreme bliss.
Just as a man who is diseased, though a physician is present...”
“He does not have that disease treated; there is no fault in the physician.
‘Thus, one who is afflicted and oppressed by the diseases of the defilements does not seek out such a teacher; there is no fault in the Guide.’”
In this context, *gūthagata* means having entered a cesspool, or being covered and defiled by excrement. *Kilesamaladhovaṃ* refers to the cleansing of the stains of the defilements;
the word is in the nominative case used in the sense of the locative. *Amatantaḷe* should be understood as a locative used in the sense of the genitive, meaning "in the lake known as the Deathless";
it is stated thus because one has thrown in a lotus stalk. *Arihi* means by enemies. *Pariruddho* means surrounded on all sides.

"Obstructed" (*niruddho*). "On the path of going" (*gamanapatha*) means on the way of departure. This was said after he had performed the act of returning in order to prevent the destruction of his desire.
"He does not flee" (*na palāyati*) means if he were not to flee. "That man" (*so puriso*) refers to the man who was surrounded by the thieves.
"Of the straight course" (*añjasassa*) means of the path; for regarding the path—
“Road, path, way, track, straight course, highway, vehicle;
boat, ford, bridge, raft, float, and crossing”—these are its many names.

Here, however, it is spoken of by the name "straight course" (*añjasa*). "Auspicious" (*siva*) means auspicious because of the absence of all calamities. "Straight course to the auspicious" (*sivamañjase*)—
The meaning is "for the straight path of Śiva. *Tikicchake* means "in a physician. *Na tikicchāpeti* means "he does not have [himself] treated.
*Na doso so tikicchake* means there is no fault in the physician; the meaning is that the fault lies only with the one who is ill.
*Dukkhito* means "one who has experienced physical and mental suffering. *Ācariyam* refers to the teacher of the path to liberation (*mokkhamaggācariya*). *Vināyake* refers to the teacher.
Having reflected thus, I further thought:

"Just as a man accustomed to adornment, having cast off a corpse hanging from his neck, would go away happy, so too must I, casting off this putrid body, enter the great city of Nibbāna without looking back.
And just as men and women [discard] excrement and urine in a dungheap..."
They do not go taking it on their lap or wrapping it in the hem of their garment; rather, loathing it and unwilling even to look at it, they cast it away without regard and depart.
In the same way, it is fitting for me also to cast away this putrid body without regard and enter the deathless city of Nibbāna. And just as those called boatmen [abandon] a dilapidated...
Just as people abandon a boat that travels upon the water and depart without looking back,
so too shall I abandon this body, which exudes from nine openings, and enter the great city of Nibbāna without looking back.
And just as a certain man, having taken various kinds of jewels such as pearls, gems, and beryl, while traveling on a road with bandits—
Just as one, out of fear for the destruction of one’s own treasure, abandons those thieves and takes the safe path, so too is this putrid body like a thief who plunders treasures.
If I were to develop craving for it, the treasures of the noble path and the wholesome qualities would be lost to me;
therefore, having abandoned this physical body which is like a great thief, [one should seek] the great city of Nibbāna.
"It is fitting to enter. Therefore it was said:
"Just as a man, loathing a corpse tied around his neck, might set it free and go away happy, independent, and self-mastered."
“Just so, having cast aside this putrid body— a heap of various kinds of filth—
I would go away, indifferent and without desire for it.
Just as men and women [discard] excrement in a place for refuse...”
"Having abandoned it, they go away, indifferent and having no further need for it.
In this very way, I shall abandon this body, filled with various kinds of filth,
and go away, just as one leaves a hut after having relieved oneself."
“Just as people abandon a dilapidated boat, leaking and taking on water,
and depart without looking back, having no further need for it;
even so do I regard this body, with its nine openings, constantly oozing.”
"I shall go away, having abandoned it, just as owners leave behind a worn-out boat.
"Just as a man traveling with thieves, taking merchandise along with him,
sees the danger of the goods being seized and goes on his way after abandoning them."
“In this very way, this body is like a great thief;
having abandoned it, I shall go away for fear of the destruction of my wholesome qualities.
In that regard, “just as a man [might carry] a corpse” means just as a young man, in the prime of his youth and fond of adornment, might [carry] a snake’s carcass...
Or, having become terrified, ashamed, and disgusted by a dog’s corpse or a human corpse hanging from his neck, he would release that corpse and go away.
"Happy" means being happy. "Independent" means living according to one's own will. "A heap of various corpses" means a place filled with many kinds of corpses;
there is also a reading: "filled with various corpses."

"In the place of excrement" (*uccāraṭṭhāne*): it is "excrement" (*uccāra*) because they discharge feces there; it is "the place of excrement" (*uccāraṭṭhāna*) because it is both that excrement and a place.
Alternatively, it is "excrement" (*ussāsa*) because it is emitted; this is a name for feces. Its place is the "place of excrement" (*ussāsaṭṭhāna*);
in that place of excrement, which means "in the place of waste. "Just as after having discharged feces [one builds] a hut": having discharged feces.
The meaning is that men and women go to the hut.
"Jajjaranti" means worn out; "palugganti" means they fall apart, which is to say they crumble away. "Udagāhinim" means water-absorbing.
"Sāmī" refers to the owners of the boat. "Navacchiddam" means having nine openings—the nine wound-like apertures such as the eyes, ears, and so forth.
"Without a gap" means it is joined together. "Flowing from the permanent" means the outflow of the permanent; the meaning is that it is impure, constantly trickling.
"He takes up goods" means he takes up whatever goods there may be, such as jewels and so forth.
"Seeing the fear of having his goods snatched away" means seeing the fear arising from the theft of his goods. "In this very way" means like that man who was going along after taking up the goods.
"This body" (*kāya*): it is called "body" because it is the source (*āya*) of things that are vile and supremely loathsome.
*Āya* means a place of origin. Because they arise from there, they are called *āya*; thus, it is the "body" (*kāya*) because it is the source of the vile things such as hair and so forth.
Like a great thief: through the eyes and other sense faculties, by way of attachment to pleasant forms and the like, one is a thief of killing, stealing, and so on.
"Having sacrificed it, one robs all that is wholesome"—thus it is like a great thief. Therefore, the connection of the meaning is as follows:

"Just as that man who, having taken precious goods and traveling with thieves, abandons those thieves and goes on his way, even so shall I abandon this body, which is like a great thief, and go forth to seek the path that brings about my own security."
It should be understood. "From the fear of cutting off what is wholesome" means from the fear of destroying wholesome states.
Then, having reflected upon the reasons for renunciation through various similes, the wise Sumedha thought again:
"Having accumulated this great heap of wealth, my father, grandfather, and the rest departed for the next world without taking even a single kahāpaṇa with them."
“Others have taken it and departed, but since I have taken it, it is fitting that I should provide the means for my departure. Having gone, he reported to the king:
“Great King, my heart is oppressed by birth, old age, and the like, and I shall go forth from the household life into homelessness.
I possess wealth amounting to many hundreds of thousands of millions; may Your Majesty accept this. The king said: “No.”
“I have need of that wealth; you yourself may do with it as you wish.

He replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and after having the drum beaten throughout the city and giving alms to the great multitude, he abandoned both material desires and the desires of the defilements.
Departing from Amarāvatī—which was like the supreme city of the immortals—he went forth all alone into a forest abounding in various herds of wild animals.

In the Himavat mountains, having established a hermitage by the mountain named Dhammika, built a leaf-hut there, and prepared a walking-path (caṅkama) free from the five faults, he went forth into homelessness.

Having cast off his garment which possessed nine defects, and having donned a bark-cloth (vākacīra) endowed with twelve virtues, he attained the power of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) equipped with eight qualities. Thus he—
Having gone forth and abandoned a leaf-hut beset with eight faults, he approached the foot of a tree endowed with ten advantages;
having abandoned all varieties of grain, he became one who eats only fallen fruit, and while exerting himself through sitting, standing, and walking,
within seven days alone he attained the eight meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
He became a recipient [of this fruit]. Therefore it was said:
“Having thus reflected, and having given wealth amounting to many hundreds of millions to both those with protectors and those without, I went to the Himālaya.”
"Not far from the Himālaya mountains is a mountain named Dhammika;
there my well-constructed hermitage stands, with its leaf-hut beautifully arranged.
There I constructed a walking-path, free from the five defects."
I acquired the power of direct knowledge endowed with eight qualities. There,
I cast off my cloth garment, which had come to possess nine faults,
and I donned a bark robe, which possessed twelve qualities.
“I abandoned the leaf-hut, which was beset by eight defects,
and approached the foot of a tree, endowed with ten virtues.
I abandoned entirely the grain that had been sown and planted.”
“I took ripe fruit endowed with manifold virtues. There,
having established myself in exertion at the place of relinquishment and the walking path,
within seven days I attained the powers of direct knowledge.”
In this context, *evāhaṃ* means "thus I," that is, having reflected in the manner described below.

*Nāthānāthānaṃ* means to those with protectors and those without protectors, both the wealthy and the poor; the meaning is that he gave it together with the storehouses, saying, "Let those who need it take it.
*Himavantassāvidūre* means not far from, in the vicinity of Himavanta, the king of mountains. *Dhammiko*...
“Nāma pabbato” means a mountain with such a name. But why was it called “Dhammika”?

For the most part, Bodhisattas, having gone forth as forest-dwelling ascetics (isipabbajjā), relied upon that mountain to develop supernormal powers (abhiññā) and practiced the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma).
Therefore, because it served as the support for the duty of a recluse, it became well known specifically as “Dhammika. [It was] an hermitage (assama).
In such passages as "Well-constructed by me," it is stated that the wise Sumedha personally built the hermitage, the leaf-huts, and the walking-paths;
yet they were not actually built by his own hand, but were fashioned by the divine son Vissakamma, sent by the god Sakka.
However, the Blessed One, at that time, spoke with reference to that perfection which had arisen through the power of his own merit.
“Sāriputta, on that mountain he said:
‘My hermitage is well-prepared, the leaf-hut is well-constructed;
there I have built a walking-path, free from the five defects. Thus he spoke at the beginning.
In this context, "leaf-hut" (*paṇṇasālā*) means a hut with a roof of leaves. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that hermitage grove.
"Free from the five faults" means devoid of the five defects of walking-paths (*caṅkama*). What are the five so-called defects of walking-paths?
They are: rigidity and unevenness, trees within [the path], being overgrown by thickets, being too narrow, and being too wide—[it is free] from these five defects.
"Free from": by way of the maximum limit, a walking path (*caṅkama*) sixty *ratana*s in length and one and a half *ratana*s in width is mentioned.
Alternatively, "free from the five faults" means free from the defects of the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*);

this should be understood as being connected with the subsequent phrase, "bringing forth the power of direct knowledge (*abhiññābala*), which is devoid [of those faults]. "Endowed with eight qualities."

“When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability”—the meaning is that he brought forth, or led forth, the power of direct knowledge (abhiññā-bala) endowed with these eight qualities.

Some, however, say it is "endowed with the eight joys of a recluse" (*samaṇa-sukha*); these eight joys of a recluse are as follows: the absence of concern for wealth, grain, and possessions; [and so on].
The state of seeking almsfood blamelessly; the state of consuming almsfood with tranquility;
the absence of the defilement of oppressing the country when royal agents are seizing wealth, grain, and so forth;
the absence of desire or lust for requisites; fearlessness toward robbery by thieves; non-association with kings, royal ministers, and high officials; and being unopposed in the four directions.
They say, making a connection with the hermitage, “He built a hermitage endowed and fully equipped with these eight ascetic pleasures”;
however, that does not accord with the text.
*Sāṭaka* means a garment. *Tattha* means in that hermitage. *Navadosamupāgataṃ*, Sāriputta, there—
Vasanta gave up and renounced the costly robe he was wearing.
By giving up the robe, it is shown that he did so having seen nine faults in it. For nine faults regarding the robe are declared for those who have gone forth into the ascetic life.
What are the nine? The high cost of the robe, its dependence on others, and [the fact of] its being used...
It is easily soiled; once soiled, it must be washed and dyed again; through use, it becomes worn out;
when worn out, one must have it mended with patches or provide it with new linings; it is difficult to obtain again through renewed seeking;
it is unsuitable for the ascetic life of renunciation; and it is common property shared with enemies.

It is shown that one should discard the cloth (*sāṭaka*)—which is beset by these nine faults, namely: that it must be guarded so that enemies do not seize it; that it involves the state of being preoccupied with adornment for one who wears it;
and that it involves a state of great desire for one who goes about carrying it—and instead wear a garment of bark-fiber (*vākacīra*).
"Bark-fiber" (*vākacīra*) refers to a garment made of *muñja* grass, which has been processed by removing the outer sheaths and weaving them together.
The meaning is that they take it for the purpose of wearing as an undergarment and an upper robe. "Endowed with twelve qualities" means possessed of twelve benefits (*ānisamsa*).
Here, the word *guṇa* signifies "benefit," as in such passages as "a gift is to be expected to have a hundredfold quality.
The letter *m* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction of words. Regarding the bark garment, the twelve benefits are: its low cost, its independence from others, and so forth.
The fact that it can be made with one's own hands; the fact that even when worn out it need not be sewn; the absence of fear of thieves for one who seeks it;
its suitability for the ascetic life of renunciation; the absence of ornamentation for one who uses it; the state of having few desires regarding the requisite of robes;
the quality of comfort in its use; the ease with which it is obtained for the production of speech; [and these qualities] in the bark-garment (*vākacīra*).
He was endowed with these twelve qualities, including being indifferent even toward what has been lost.
Then, while dwelling there in the leaf-hut, the wise Sumedha rose at dawn and, reflecting upon the reason for his departure, thought as follows:
"I have indeed lived in a home delightful to its inhabitants, filled with the sounds of their sweet laughter, conversation, and the jingling of new golden bracelets and anklets."

“Having abandoned my home—which was adorned with magnificent splendor and resembled the palace of the chief of the gods—like a globule of spittle, I have entered the forest of asceticism (tapovana), which delights in seclusion and carries away all the evils of people.
Yet here, dwelling in this leaf-hut, it is like a second household life for me;
well then, I shall dwell at the foot of a tree. Thus it was said:
“I abandoned the leaf-hut, which was beset by eight faults.
In this context, “beset by eight faults” means crowded or connected with eight defects. Which eight?
The necessity of being produced with great effort; the necessity of constant maintenance with grass, leaves, clay, and so forth; and the lodging...
The state of being subject to being awakened at an improper time—thinking, "It reaches even an elderly man"—is such that one-pointedness of mind does not arise;

the state of making the body delicate by warding off cold and heat; the state of concealing blame, thinking that whatever evil might be done is possible once one has entered a house; and the state of having possessions, thinking, "This is mine."

Having seen these eight disadvantages— namely, that a house implies living with another, and that it is a state of great commonality due to being shared with bedbugs, ants, house-lizards, and so forth— the Great Being abandoned the leaf-hut.
Regarding the phrase "approached the ten virtues," this means that having rejected the covered dwelling, he approached the foot of a tree, which is endowed with ten virtues.
The purpose. By which ten [qualities]? (1) Minimal effort; (2) the fact that it is easy to avoid blame, as there is merely the act of approaching;
(3) the arousal of the perception of impermanence by frequently observing the changes in the leaves and foliage; (4) the absence of stinginess regarding the lodging;
for one who commits evil there feels shame in such a place, thus there is an absence of being fit to commit evil; (5) the absence of making it one's own possession; (6) [the presence of] deities...

"Seeing these ten advantages—dwelling together, the rejection of roofs, the ease of enjoyment, and the state of being free from concern due to the availability of tree-root dwellings wherever one goes—he says, 'I have approached the foot of a tree. And it is said:
'The support praised by the Best of Buddhas, and described as a reliance...'"
Where could there be a dwelling as secluded as the foot of a tree?
For one who dwells at the foot of a tree— secluded, protected by deities, and free from the stinginess regarding dwellings— that person of noble vows truly lives in seclusion.
“Beholding the leaves of trees— some still green, some yellowed, and some fallen—
one dispels the perception of permanence.
Therefore, one should take up the inheritance of the Buddha, which is the abode of those who delight in meditation.”
“A wise person should not despise a secluded place at the foot of a tree.
Then, having seen the faults in the leaf-hut and dwelling in the lodging at the foot of a tree after obtaining its benefits, the wise Sumedha reflected further:
“My going to the village for the sake of food and the hardship of seeking food—”
“I have not gone forth out of any loss; I did not renounce the world for the sake of food, for there is no limit to the suffering rooted in the search for food.
What if I were to subsist on fallen fruit? And illustrating this specific point:
32–33. “I abandoned entirely all grain that is sown and planted.”
“He took the fruit that had grown spontaneously, which was endowed with manifold virtues”—thus he spoke.
Therein, “planted” (*vāpita*) means produced after being sown. “Grafted” (*ropita*) means produced after being planted.

The production of crops is twofold, according to the methods of sowing and planting; having abandoned both of these types through his own fewness of desires, [he lived] on fruit that had grown spontaneously.
I sustained myself. "Falling fruit" means fruit that has fallen of its own accord.
"Taking" means consuming. "Content with falling fruit, living independent of others, having abandoned craving for food—such is the four-quadrant sage."
“He abandons craving for flavors, and his livelihood becomes pure;
therefore, one should not despise those who subsist on fallen fruit.
Living in this manner, the wise Sumedha, before long, within seven days, attained the eight meditative absorptions (samāpatti) and the five higher knowledges (abhiññā).
And he attained it. To clarify this meaning, it was said: “There he applied himself to striving,” and so forth.

In that context, “there” means in that hermitage. “Striving” (*padhāna*) refers to energy (*vīriya*); for energy is called “striving” because it must be exerted, or because it brings about the state of striving.
“He applied himself” means he initiated energy. “In the walking-place for sitting” means in the place for sitting... [in the walking-place].
and by standing and by walking.
But the wise man Sumedha, having rejected lying down, spent his days and nights only in sitting, standing, and walking;
and within seven days, he attained the power of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). Having thus attained the power of the higher knowledges, the ascetic Sumedha—

While they were thus passing their time in the bliss of meditative attainment, there arose in the world a Teacher named Dīpaṅkara—one who gathered all people to himself, who struck terror into the power of Māra, and who kindled the lamp of knowledge.
This is his account in brief: it is said that this Great Being named Dīpaṅkara [was among] the thirty-two...
Having fulfilled the perfections and remaining in an existence similar to that of Vessantara, he gave great gifts such as the shaking of the earth.
At the end of his lifespan, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven; having remained there for the duration of his life, the deities of ten thousand world-systems assembled and said:
"It is now the time for you, O Great Hero, to descend into a mother’s womb."
"Delivering the world together with its gods, awaken to the deathless state. When this was said,
having heard the words of the deities and having performed the five great observations (*pañca mahāvilokanāni*), he passed away from that life and, by means of his own glory and majesty,
appeared in the city of Rammavatī before King Sudeva— also known as Vijita-Vāsudeva— the god among men.
Having taken conception in the womb of Queen Sumedhā of the king’s family on the full moon day of Āsāḷha under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha,
he dwelt for ten months in the queen’s womb— attended by a great retinue and unsullied by any impurity like a cluster of jewels—
and then emerged from her belly like the autumn moon appearing from a rift in a rain cloud.
The Thirty-two Omens:
At the moment of the conception and at the moment of the birth of that Prince Dīpaṅkara, thirty-two omens and miracles appeared.
These same omens appear whenever any omniscient Bodhisatta descends into his mother’s womb or emerges from it.
"In these four instances—when [beings] awaken and when the Wheel of Dhamma is set in motion—the thirty-two miracles indeed manifest.
Therefore, because they were well-known to me, I have shown them in the birth story of Prince Dīpaṅkara:
"When the beautiful-making Prince Dīpaṅkara was born, the auspicious-making and peace-bringing one;..."
Then the ten thousand world-systems, numbering a thousand, trembled and shook on all sides.
“In those ten thousand world-systems, there were ten thousand deities;
at that time, they all gathered together within a single world-system.”
“As soon as the Bodhisatta, the Great Being, was born,
the deities received him first, and only afterwards did human beings do so.
Even though they had not been struck by anyone, the drums with their leather heads and the lutes with their beautiful sound-holes resounded.”
At that moment, ornaments that had not even been struck rang out sweetly on all sides:
"The bonds everywhere were severed, and all diseases vanished of their own accord;
those blind from birth saw forms, and the deaf heard sounds on every side."
“Through recollection, people slow-witted by birth obtained vehicles, and the lame traveled on foot;
those traveling abroad reached their own ships quickly, together with the port.
All that was situated in the sky and all that was on the earth shone forth of its own accord from every side like jewels.”
The fire in the dreadful hells was extinguished, and even the water in the rivers ceased to flow.
"Even in the world-intervals, which are filled with incessant suffering, a sublime and vast radiance arose;
likewise at that time, this great ocean, with its waves in peaceful succession, became sweet-watered."
“Neither did the wind blow harshly or fiercely, nor were the trees with their blossoms in full bloom;
the moon shone all the more brightly along with the stars, and the sun was not even hot.
The birds, joyful both from the sky and from the trees, descended to the earth below.”
And a great cloud, having reached the four continents, rained sweet water everywhere. Yet,
remaining in their own celestial abodes with hearts full of faith,
the deities danced, sang, played instruments, clapped their hands, and made merry.
“It is said that the gates and great door-panels opened instantly of their own accord;
hunger and thirst did not afflict the great multitude, nor did they afflict anyone in the world.
Furthermore, those groups of living beings who were constant enemies attained the supreme state of a mind of loving-kindness.”
Crows wandered together with owls, and mongooses played with wild boars.
Even the fierce and venomous snakes sported at will with mongooses;
lice infested the heads of cats, and even the house mice felt secure in their hearts.
“Even in the interval between Buddhas, when water was not found, the world of the *pisācas* was freed from thirst;
the hunchbacked became beautiful with symmetrical bodies, and the mute spoke sweet words.
With hearts full of faith, the throngs of beings then addressed one another with endearing speech.”
The horses were indeed joyful in heart, and even the noble elephants trumpeted in rut.
"Filled with the dust of fragrant sandalwood, scented with flowers, saffron, and incense, and adorned with garlands of various beautiful great banners—
the ten-thousandfold world-system was thus on every side."
In that regard, the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system was the omen for his attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
The gathering of the deities in a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) at the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma was the omen for their gathering simultaneously to receive the Dhamma.
The first reception [of the teaching] by the deities was [the omen] for the four fine-material-sphere jhānas.
The subsequent acceptance by humans is a premonitory sign of the attainment of the four formless-sphere jhānas;
the spontaneous sounding of leather-bound drums is a premonitory sign of the proclamation by the great Dhamma drum;
and the spontaneous sounding of lutes and musical instruments is a premonitory sign of the attainment of the successive meditative abidings.
The spontaneous severing of bonds is a precursor to the eradication of the conceit "I am";

the removal of all diseases from the great multitude is a precursor to the attainment of the fruit of the Four Noble Truths; the sight of forms by those born blind is a precursor to the attainment of the divine eye;
and the hearing of sounds by the deaf is a precursor to the attainment of the divine ear-element.
The arising of mindfulness in those who are born blind is a precursor to the attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness;
the walking on foot by those who are lame is a precursor to the attainment of the four bases of psychic power;

the arrival at port of ships that have gone abroad is a precursor to the acquisition of the four analytical knowledges; and the self-radiance of jewels is a precursor to the attainment of the light of the Dhamma.

The extinguishing of fire in hell is a simile for the extinguishing of the eleven fires; the non-flowing of water in rivers is a simile for the attainment of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*);

light in the intervals between worlds is a simile for the vision of the light of knowledge after dispelling the darkness of ignorance; the sweetness of the water in the great ocean is a simile for the state of having a single flavor through the taste of *nibbāna*;
and the non-blowing of the wind is a simile for the shattering of the sixty-two types of views. Regarding trees...
The state of flowering is a precursor to the state of flowering with the flowers of liberation (*vimuttipuppha*).
The moon’s extreme radiance is a precursor to being beloved by many people; the sun’s lack of excessive heat and its stainless nature is a precursor to the arising of physical and mental happiness;
and the birds’ movement across the earth from mountains and other places is a precursor to the great multitude hearing the instruction.
The taking of refuge by living beings is like the raining down of a great cloud that has reached the four continents;
the sporting of the deities with dance and other performances while remaining in their respective abodes is like the uttering of inspired exclamations (*udāna*) upon attaining Buddhahood;
the self-opening of the door-panels is like the opening of the door to the Eightfold Path; [and the removal] of the affliction of hunger...

The absence [of enemies] is a premonitory sign of being happy through the bliss of liberation; the acquisition of a mind of loving-kindness toward one's enemies is a premonitory sign of acquiring the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*);
the fact that the ten-thousandfold world system was adorned with a single banner is a premonitory sign of being adorned with the banner of the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
Furthermore, the remaining distinctions should be understood as premonitory signs of acquiring the remaining qualities of a Buddha.
Then Prince Dīpaṅkara, being entertained with great prosperity, gradually reached auspicious youth and,
enjoying the glory of sovereignty like the splendor of the deva-worlds in three palaces suited to the three seasons,
saw in due course the three divine messengers known as the old man, the sick man, and the dead man at the time of going for a pleasure excursion in the park.
Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, he turned back and entered the city named Rammavatī, which possessed a splendor and wealth like that of the city of Sudassana.
Having entered the city, on the fourth occasion, he summoned the elephant trainer and said to him:
"Dear son, I shall go out for the purpose of seeing the gardens; prepare the elephant vehicles. He replied, "Very well."
Having assented with the words, “So be it, O gods,” he prepared eighty-four thousand elephants.

Then the divine son named Vissakamma adorned the Bodhisatta, who was clothed in garments of various colors, wearing pearl necklaces, armlets, beautiful rings of fresh gold, a crown, and earrings, and whose hair was decorated with garlands of most fragrant flowers. Then Prince Dīpaṅkara—
Surrounded by eighty-four thousand elephants like a divine youth, seated upon the back of a noble elephant and accompanied by a vast army,
he entered a pleasure garden that aroused delight. Alighting from the elephant's back and wandering through that garden,
he sat down upon a stone slab as cool as his own heart— a sight of supreme beauty— and conceived the thought of going forth into homelessness.
At that very moment, a Great Brahmā from the Pure Abodes, whose taints were exhausted, appeared within the range of vision of the Great Man, carrying the eight requisites of a recluse.
Upon seeing him, the Great Man asked, "What is this? and having heard it was "the requisites of a recluse," he [discarded] his ornaments.
Having removed [the hair] and placed it in the hands of the treasurer of ornaments, he took the auspicious sword and, together with the crown,
cut off his hair and cast it into the sky, into the atmosphere. Then Sakka, the king of the gods,
took that hair and crown with a golden casket and, upon the summit of Sineru, constructed a three-league-wide Shrine of the Crown made of sapphire.
...gave him that name. Then the Great Being, having donned the saffron robe—the banner of Arahatship belonging to Devadatta—threw his pair of garments into the air.
Brahmā received them and, in the Brahma-world, constructed a cetiya twelve yojanas in size, made entirely of all kinds of jewels.
Furthermore, when Prince Dīpaṅkara went forth into homelessness, ten million men followed him into the religious life. And by her...
Surrounded by his retinue, the Bodhisatta practiced the life of striving for ten months.
Then, on the full moon day of Visākha, he entered a certain city for alms.
It is said that in that city, on that very day, they had cooked rice gruel without water for the purpose of making offerings to the deities.
When that Great Being had entered for alms together with his retinue, people gave to them;
it is said that this was sufficient for all those monks numbering in the tens of millions. However, deities placed divine food into the bowl of the Great Man.
Having consumed that and spent the day’s rest right there in the Sāla grove, he...
In the evening, having emerged from seclusion and dismissed his followers,
he took eight handfuls of grass given by the Ājīvaka named Sunanda; going to the foot of the Pipphalī-bodhi tree, he spread out a layer of grass,
placed the ninety-cubit trunk of the Bodhi tree behind him, sat down cross-legged, and applied the fourfold energy.
Having made his resolve, he sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then, having shattered the army of Māra, he recollected his past lives during the first watch of the night;
in the middle watch, he purified his divine eye; and in the last watch, he comprehended the nature of conditions by way of direct and reverse order.
Having attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing and emerged from it, he focused his attention upon the five aggregates;
having seen the fifty characteristics by way of their arising and passing away, he developed insight up to the stage of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa).
At the rising of the dawn, having penetrated all the qualities of a Buddha through the Noble Path and uttered the Lion’s Roar of a Buddha, [he remained] for seven weeks.
Having spent the time in the vicinity of Bodhi itself and having accepted Brahmā’s request for a teaching on the Dhamma,
he set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma at the Sunanda Monastery. Having caused hundreds of millions of gods and humans to drink the nectar of the Dhamma,
raining down the rain of the Dhamma like a great cloud over the four continents, he wandered through the countryside, effecting the release from bonds for the great multitude of people.
At that time, it is said, the wise Sumedha, while spending his time in the bliss of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), perceived neither the earthquake nor those signs. Therefore it was said:
“Thus, when I had attained accomplishment and mastery in the Teaching, the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, appeared.”
“While phenomena were arising, being born, and awakening through the teaching of the Dhamma, I did not perceive the four signs, being fully absorbed in the delight of jhāna.
In this context, *evaṃ* indicates what is now to be stated. *Me* means “my. *Siddhippattassa* means “of one who has attained the accomplishment of the five higher knowledges (*pañcābhiññā*).”

"Of one who has become masterful" (*vasībhūtassa*) means one who has become a master of what has come to be; the meaning is "one who has attained mastery. "In the Dispensation" (*sāsane*) refers to the Dispensation of those whose minds are inclined toward seclusion;
it should be understood as a genitive case used in the sense of disregard. "The Victor" (*jino*) is so called because of his victory over the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*).

"Arising" (*uppajjante*) refers to the taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); "being born" (*jāyante*) refers to emerging from the mother’s womb; "awakening" (*bujjhante*) refers to [attaining] the unsurpassed...
While he was awakening to perfect enlightenment. "The teaching of the Dhamma" refers to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.

"Four signs" means four portents. The meaning is that at the four occasions of the conception, birth, enlightenment, and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma of the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara, there were signs such as the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system. Here it is asked: those...
"But there are many signs; why then is it said, 'four signs'? Is this not improper? It is not improper.
Although these are many signs, they are called "four signs" because they occur in four places.
"I did not see, I did not see. Now, pointing out the reason for not seeing those four signs:
“He was absorbed in the delight of jhāna,” it is said. “Delight of jhāna” is a designation for the bliss of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Because he was absorbed in—that is, possessed of—the delight of jhāna, they did not see those signs; this is the meaning.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers, surrounded by four hundred thousand *khīṇāsavas*, gradually [proceeded].
While wandering on his journey, having reached the most delightful city named Ramma, he resided in the Sudassana Great Monastery.

The inhabitants of the city of Ramma heard: "It is said that Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers, having attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, has been wandering on his journey in due course and has now arrived at the city of Ramma, residing in the Sudassana Great Monastery."

Having heard this, they took medicinal requisites such as clarified butter and other items; having eaten their morning meal and adjusted their upper robes so they were clean, they went with flowers, incense, and perfumes in their hands to where the Buddha was.
Having approached and paid homage to the Teacher, and having honored him with the flowers and other offerings, they sat down to one side.
After hearing the exceedingly sweet discourse on the Dhamma, they invited the Blessed One for the following day’s meal.
Rising from their seats and circumambulating the One of Ten Powers, they departed.
On the following day, they prepared an incomparable great almsgiving;

they had pavilions constructed, covered them with spotless, delicate blue lotuses, adorned the surroundings with the four kinds of fragrant incense, and scattered flowers—scented and with parched grain as the fifth—about.
Having placed jars filled with cool, sweet water at the four corners of the pavilion and covered them with plantain leaves,
and having tied a most beautiful and lovely cloth canopy over the pavilion— resembling *jayasumana* flowers and adorned with stars of gold,
gems, and silver— he hung there garlands of perfumes, flowers, leaves, and jewels, making it cloudy with incense.
Having made that entire delightful city of Ramma well-swept, having set up plantain trees laden with fruit and adorned with flowers,
having placed full water-jars, and having hoisted banners and flags of various colors,
they surrounded both sides of the great highway with cloth fences while decorating the path for the arrival of the Great Seer Dīpaṅkara.
In places where the ground was eroded by water, they threw soil and leveled the muddy earth;
they scattered sand resembling pearls and flowers with parched grain as the fifth ingredient, and they set up plantain trees with their trunks and leaves intact.
Then, at that time, the ascetic Sumedha, having risen from his own hermitage, [appeared] before those inhabitants of the city of Ramma.
Traveling through the air above the people, he saw them clearing and decorating the road with great joy;

thinking, "What could be the reason for this?", he descended from the sky while everyone was looking on, stood to one side, and asked those people: "Ho there! For whose sake are you clearing this road? Thus it was said.
“In a border region, having invited the Tathāgata,
they cleanse the path for his arrival with joyful minds.
At that time, I departed from my own Sakka realm.”
Shaking off my bark garments, I then traveled through the sky.
Seeing the people born of the Vedas— joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness—
I descended from the heavens and immediately questioned the men.
“The great multitude, thrilled, joyful, delighted, and filled with rapture—whose path is being cleared?
The straight way, the path for traveling.
Therein, “in a border region” refers to a district designated as a border region situated on one side of the Middle Country itself.
“His path of arrival” means the path by which he should come. “At that time” (*tena samayena*) means “at that moment”;
here, the instrumental case should be understood as having the sense of the locative. “From my own hermitage” (*sakassamā*) means having departed from one’s own hermitage.
“Shaking” (*dhunanto*) means shaking off. Regarding these two terms, “at that time” (*tena samayena*) and “then” (*tadā*):
Because the words have a single meaning, the connection should be understood between the action of "departing" for the former and the action of "going" for the latter;
otherwise, one does not escape the fault of redundancy (*punarutta-dosa*). *Tadā* means "at that time.
*Vedajātaṃ* means "one in whom joy has arisen. These three terms—*tuṭṭha*, *haṭṭha*, and *pamodita*—are synonyms for one another.
These are explanations of their mutual meanings. Alternatively, he was satisfied with happiness (*sukha*), gladdened by rapture (*pīti*), and delighted by joy (*pāmojja*).
"Having descended" (*orohitvāna*) means having gone down. "He questioned the men" (*manusse pucchi*) means he questioned human beings; this is indeed the reading.
"At that time" (*tāvade*) means then, at that very moment—this is the meaning. Now, in order to show the matter being questioned, [the text says] "satisfied, gladdened, and delighted," and so forth.
It has been said. In that context, this great multitude, being joyful, elated, and delighted in heart, clears the path.
For what reason do they clear it, or for whose sake do they clear it? Thus, the meaning should be understood by bringing forward the word "clears" (*sodheti*);

otherwise, it would not be logical. "Is cleared" (*sodhīyati*) means that the state of purity (*suddhabhāva*) is brought about. The path is the direct way (*añjasam*), the course of travel (*vaṭumāyam*).
These are synonyms for the Path.
Thus questioned by that ascetic Sumedha, those people said:

"Venerable Sumedha, do you not know that the Buddha named Dīpaṅkara, having attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, is wandering through the countryside?"
“Traveling by stages, he will reach our city and reside at the Sudassana Great Monastery;
we shall invite that Blessed One and clear the path for the arrival of that very Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having heard this, the wise Sumedha reflected: “Even the mere sound of the word ‘Buddha’ is rare to hear, let alone [meeting him].”
“The Buddha has appeared; therefore, it is fitting that I too should clear the path for the One of Ten Powers along with these men.
He said to those men: “Sirs, if you are clearing this path for the Buddha, give me a share as well; I too shall clear the path for the Buddha together with you.”

Then, having accepted with the words “Very well,” and knowing that “this wise Sumedha is of great psychic power and great majesty,” they observed a certain spot that was difficult to clean, mixed with water, and exceedingly uneven;
they gave it to him, saying, “Clean this spot and adorn it. Then the wise Sumedha, taking the Buddha as his object—
Having conceived a sense of joy, he thought: "I am indeed capable of making this place most beautiful by means of my psychic power (iddhi), but once that is done, it will not satisfy me.
Today, however, it is fitting for me to perform physical service.
Thinking thus, he brought earth and filled that spot.
But while that place remained unswept and unfinished, the people dwelling in Ramma City announced the time to the Blessed One, saying, "The meal, venerable sir, is ready.
When they had thus announced the time, the Ten-Powered One covered himself with his double-layered robe, which was the color of a *jayasumana* flower;
he arranged it so as to conceal the three circles of his body, and over it he fastened a cluster of *jayasumana* flowers with a golden cord.
Having fastened his waistband, which possessed the splendor of a flash of lightning as if encircling him,
he appeared like a golden cetiya being drenched with lacquer juice atop the peak of Mount Meru,
or like a golden pitcher being wrapped in a net of coral, or like the autumnal moon being veiled by crimson clouds.

Having put on a superior rag-robe (*paṃsukūlacīvara*) of excellent red color, resembling lac juice or the blossoms of the *tintaka* and *kiṃsuka* trees, he emerged from the door of the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*)—like a lion from a golden cave—and stood at the entrance of the Fragrant Chamber.
Then all the monks, each taking his own bowl and robe, surrounded the Blessed One. They...
Furthermore, the monks who stood surrounding him were such as these:
"They were few in desires and contented, admonishers yet patient with correction;
secluded and unattached, disciplined and reproving of evil."
“All were endowed with virtue, skilled in concentration and jhāna;
endowed with wisdom and liberation, possessed of the three and fivefold bases.
They had destroyed the taints, attained mastery, were powerful and renowned.”
“With peaceful faculties, tamed, pure, and with further existence exhausted.

Thus the Blessed One, himself free from lust, surrounded by those free from lust; free from hatred, surrounded by those free from hatred; free from delusion, surrounded by those free from delusion—shone forth exceedingly.
Then the Teacher [honored] the great-souled ones, the Arahants whose taints were destroyed and who possessed the six direct knowledges, with four...
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands, like the ten-headed Indra surrounded by the hosts of Maruts, or like the Great Brahmā Hārita surrounded by the hosts of Brahmas,

he proceeded along that path— which was beautifully adorned and prepared— with the incomparable grace of a Buddha born from the power of merit accumulated over immeasurable eons, like the moon of the autumn season surrounded by the host of stars.
“With a golden radiance, the Wise One, it is said, proceeded along the path toward the golden-hued tree, scattering golden-hued flowers; he of golden hue set out upon the road.
And as the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was approaching along that path, which had been thus adorned and prepared, the ascetic Sumedha [beheld him].
Having opened his eyes and gazed upon that physical form which had reached the pinnacle of beauty— adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, embellished by the eighty minor characteristics,
encircled by a fathom-wide aura, radiant, resembling a sapphire, emitting six-colored rays of Buddha-light like various streaks of lightning in the sky— he thought: "Today, by me..."
“It is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for the One Possessing the Ten Powers. “Do not tread upon the mud, Blessed One!
May you walk upon my back together with the four hundred thousand who have exhausted the taints, as if walking upon a bridge made of jeweled planks;
that shall be for my benefit and happiness for a long time. Having thus loosened his hair and cast off his deerskin, matted locks, and bark garments, he said:
Having spread out upon the black-colored mud, he lay down right there on the surface of that mud. Therefore it was said:
“When they were questioned by me, they replied: ‘The Buddha, the unsurpassed in the world, the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, has appeared.’”
His path was cleared, the straight way, the path to travel.
Having heard the word "Buddha," joy arose at that very moment;
saying "Buddha, Buddha," I experienced great gladness.
Standing there, I reflected, my mind joyful and moved by awe:
"I shall plant seeds here; let not the opportune moment pass me by.
If you would clear a space for the Buddha, grant me a single spot."
“I too shall clear the straight path, the way to travel.
“They gave me leave then to clear the straight path;
thinking ‘Buddha, Buddha,’ I then cleared the road.”
"While my place was not yet finished, the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara,
the Conqueror, set out upon the straight path together with four hundred thousand Tathāgatas who possessed the six supernormal powers, whose taints were destroyed, and who were stainless."
“Processions went forth to meet him, and many drums were sounded;
humans and gods were filled with joy and raised shouts of ‘Excellent!
Gods beheld men, and men also beheld the gods.”
Both of them, with palms joined in reverence, follow the Tathāgata.
Both gods with celestial instruments and humans with human ones—
both of them, playing their music, follow the Tathāgata.
“Celestial Mandārava flowers, Paduma, and Pārichattaka— these the Maruts,
having gone into the sky, scatter in every direction.
And celestial sandalwood powder, and pure, excellent fragrance— ”
The gods, having ascended into the sky, scatter [flowers] in every direction.
Men standing upon the surface of the earth raise aloft campaka,
sarala, nīpa, nāga, punnāga, and ketaka flowers in every direction.
“Having loosened my hair there, and having spread out my bark garment and hide upon the mud,
I lay down face downwards. ‘Treading over me,
may the Buddha go forth together with his disciples.’”
"Do not step upon this mire; it will be for my welfare.
Therein, "they proclaimed" (*viyākaṃsu*) means they announced. There is also a reading: "The Victor named Dīpaṅkara—his path is being cleared.
"They manifested joy" (*somanassaṃ pavedayinsu*) means they experienced joy. "Standing there" (*tattha ṭhatvā*) refers to the place where...
He descended from the sky and stood right there. "With a heart full of agitation" means with a mind struck by joy and wonder.

"Here" refers to this field of merit, Dīpaṅkara. "Seeds" refers to the seeds of wholesome kamma. "I shall plant" means I will plant them. "The moment" refers to the ninth conjunction of conditions, which is free from the eight unfavorable moments;
that is exceedingly rare, yet it has been obtained by me. "Vā" is merely a particle. "Do not let [this moment] pass you by."
"So let it not pass; let it not elapse"—this is the meaning. "Give" means "grant. "Those who" refers to those people whom I questioned;
"those" is the meaning. "I shall then purify that" means "I shall then purify it. "While it is unfinished" means while it is incomplete or unaccomplished.

Regarding "by those whose taints are destroyed," there are four taints here: the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*), and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).

These are the four taints (*āsava*) which, being exhausted, abandoned, uprooted, stilled, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge—those are the ones whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*);
[the phrase] "by those whose taints are exhausted" refers to them. Because their taints are exhausted, they are "stainless.
Regarding the statement "gods see humans," there is nothing further to be said concerning the gods' vision of humans, as it occurs according to their natural mode of seeing.
But the meaning is that just as humans here, standing on this earth, see, so too do the gods see humans.
"Devas" means gods. "Both" refers to both gods and humans. "With palms joined" means having made the añjali gesture; the meaning is that they have placed both hands upon their heads.
"Follow the Tathāgata" means they go behind the Tathāgata; [it is used] in the sense of following in pursuit.
The characteristic is that when the sense of "possessor" (sāmī-attha) is present, there is the case of the instrumental (upayoga-vacana). Therefore it is said: "They follow the Tathāgata.
"Vajjayantā" means speaking.
"Mandārava" means the mandārava flower. "Disodisaṃ" means from every direction. "Okiranti" means they scatter.
“Gone to the region of space” means gone into the sky, which is designated as space. Alternatively, “gone to space” means simply gone to heaven;
for “nabha” is said to mean heaven. “Marū” means immortals (gods). “Sarala” refers to the flower of the *sarala* tree. “Nīpa” refers to the *kadamba* flower.
“Nāga, punnāga, and ketaka” refers to the flowers of the *nāga*, *punnāga*, and *ketaka*. “Gone to the surface of the earth” means gone to the ground.
"Having loosened my hair"—this means having loosened and scattered the mass of my matted locks that were tied up.
"Therein" means in the space granted to me. "A piece of leather" means a fragment of hide. "In the mire" means in the mud and slime.
"Upside down" means with my face turned downwards. "I lay down" means I lay myself down. Regarding the word "mā" here, it has the sense of prohibition.
"nipāto. The word "na" is a particle used for the purpose of completing the meter; the meaning is: "O Buddha, do not step on the mud.
"It will be for my welfare" means that his not stepping on the mud will be for the sake of my long-term welfare.
There is also a reading: "It will be for my happiness."
Then, while still lying on the surface of the mud, the wise Sumedha thought thus:

"If I were to wish to enter the city of Ramma as a junior member of the Saṅgha after burning away all defilements, there would be no need for me to burn away my defilements in an unknown guise to attain Nibbāna.
What if I were to attain supreme perfect enlightenment, just like the Ten-Powered One, Dīpaṅkara?"

"It would be fitting for me," he thought, "to attain the Dhamma-ship, embark upon it with the great multitude of people, ferry them across the ocean of saṃsāra, and only afterwards enter final Nibbāna.
Thereupon, having brought together the eight qualities and made the resolution for Buddhahood, he lay down. Thus it was said:
“As I lay upon the ground, such was the thought in my mind:
‘If I so desired, I could today burn away my defilements.
What need have I for this disguise? I have realized the Dhamma right here.’”
“Having attained omniscience, I shall become a Buddha in the world with its devas.
“What is the use of my being a man of power and insight who has crossed over alone?
Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world with its devas.”
“By this service rendered to the Supreme Person,
having attained omniscience, may I deliver the vast multitude of beings.
Having cut the stream of saṃsāra and shattered the three realms of existence...”
“Having boarded the ship of the Dhamma, I shall ferry across the world with its devas.

In this context, “lying on the earth” means lying upon the ground; *pathaviyaṃ* is the same as *puthaviyā*. Or rather, this very reading (*pathaviyaṃ*) is the correct one. “Of the mind” means that there was a reflection of the mind;
the meaning is that such a thought occurred to him. There is also the reading “thus was my intention. “Wishing” means desiring.
*Kilesā* means "defilements" because they defile and afflict; they are the ten [types] beginning with lust (*rāga*). *Jhāpaye* means "I would burn away";
the sense is, "May I burn away my own defilements.
*Kiṃ* is a word of negation. *Aññātavesena* means by way of an unmanifested appearance, that is, by being unrecognized and concealed.

Furthermore, the intention is as follows: "Having achieved the destruction of the taints just like the monks here, and having fulfilled the qualities that make one a Buddha, and having caused the great earth to tremble at the moments of conception, birth, enlightenment, and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, may I become a Buddha, an awakener; one who has crossed over, a deliverer; one who is liberated, a liberator.
"Sadevake" means in the world together with its devas.
"Thāmadassinā" means by one who perceives his own strength and power. "Santāressanti" means I shall cause them to cross over.
"Sadevakaṃ" means the host of beings together with the devas, or the world together with the devas. "Adhikārena" means by a distinguished manner;
the meaning is: by the manner of my having sacrificed my life for the Buddha and lying upon a bed of mud.

The "stream of saṃsāra" refers to the wandering hither and thither among the various modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, by way of kamma and defilements.
As it is said: "The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as they proceed is called 'saṃsāra'."

It is "the stream of saṃsāra" (*saṃsārasota*) because it is both *saṃsāra* and a *sota*. Alternatively, it is the stream of *saṃsāra*, meaning that one has cut off the stream of craving (*taṇhāsota*), which is the cause of *saṃsāra*.
"The three existences" (*tayo bhavā*) refers to the existences of sense-desire (*kāma*), form (*rūpa*), and formlessness (*arūpa*).
What is intended by "the three existences" are the kamma and defilements that produce those three existences. "The ship of Dhamma" (*dhammanāva*) refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
The path. For that [path] is called the "Dhamma-ship" in the sense of crossing over the four floods. *Samāruhya* means having ascended.
*Santāressanti* means "I shall cause them to cross over. Furthermore, for one aspiring to Buddhahood, it is said:
"Human birth, the perfection of gender, the cause, and the sight of the Teacher;..."
“Going forth, the perfection of qualities, the requisite capacity, and zeal—through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.

In this context, “human state” means that the aspiration of one who, remaining in the human form itself, aspires to Buddhahood, succeeds; it does not succeed for those remaining in the birth of a nāga or other such states. Why? Because of the absence of the necessary causal conditions.
"Endowment with the male sex organ (*liṅgasampatti*)" means that even for one existing in a human body, the aspiration succeeds only if they abide in the male sex organ;
it does not succeed for a woman, nor for a *paṇḍaka*, a neuter (*napuṃsaka*), or a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*). Why?
Because of the absence of the perfection of the [required] characteristics. For this has been said: "It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that a woman should be an *arhat*..."
“The Perfectly Enlightened One,” and so on in detail. Therefore, even for one of human birth who exists in the female gender, the aspiration does not succeed.
As for the cause: even for a male, the aspiration succeeds only if he is endowed with the causes for attaining Arahantship in that very life, and not otherwise.
Regarding "seeing the Teacher": if one makes the aspiration in the presence of a living Buddha, the aspiration succeeds.

When the Blessed One has attained *parinibbāna*, an aspiration does not succeed near a *cetiya*, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, before a statue, or in the presence of *paccekabuddhas* or disciples of the Buddha.

Why? Because [the Buddhas] are unable to predict [the outcome] after discerning who is capable and who is incapable, having delimited it through the knowledge that delimits the ripening of kamma. Therefore, an aspiration succeeds only in the presence of a Buddha.

Regarding "going forth" (*pabbajjā*): even for one making a resolution in the presence of the Buddha, the Blessed One, the aspiration succeeds only if they have gone forth among the ascetics who profess the efficacy of action or among the monks, and not while remaining in the garb of a householder. Why?
Because it is only those who have gone forth that Bodhisattvas attain full enlightenment, not those who remain as householders. Therefore, at the very beginning, at the time of making the vow—

One must indeed be one who has gone forth. As for "perfection of qualities": this succeeds only for one who has gone forth and attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) and the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhiññā*), but not for one devoid of these perfections of qualities.

Why? Because those qualities are absent in one who lacks them. As for "qualification": even for one endowed with qualities, this succeeds only for one who has sacrificed his own life for the Buddhas through this qualification, and not for another.

"Zeal" (*chanda*): Even for one who has perfected the aspiration (*abhinīhāra*), success belongs only to him who possesses great zeal, effort, exertion, and search for the sake of the qualities that make a Buddha, and not to another. Herein is an illustration of the greatness of zeal:
Suppose it were thus: "Whoever, having filled the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) with water and, by means of his own..."
One who is capable of crossing over and reaching the further shore by means of the strength of his own arms attains Buddhahood.

However, for one who does not consider this task difficult for himself, thinking, "I shall cross this over and go to the further shore," and who is thus endowed with great desire and exertion, his aspiration succeeds; it does not succeed for the other.
The wise Sumedha, however, having combined these eight qualities and made his aspiration for Buddhahood, lay down.
The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara also arrived and, standing at the head of the wise Sumedha, saw the ascetic Sumedha lying on the surface of the mud and said:
"This ascetic has lain down after making an aspiration for Buddhahood."
Sending forth his knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) and investigating, "Will this aspiration of his succeed, or will it not? he knew:
"After four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) and one hundred thousand aeons have passed from now, one named Gotama will become a Buddha.
Knowing this, while remaining standing right there in the midst of the assembly, he declared: "Behold, monks!"
“This ascetic of fierce penance is lying on a bed of mud. “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied.
“This one has lain down after making a resolution for Buddhahood; this aspiration of the ascetic will succeed.
For at the end of four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand additional kappas from now, a Buddha named Gotama will appear in the world. And regarding him...”
"In his final existence, his residence will be the city named Kapilavatthu; Queen Mahāmāyā will be his mother, King Suddhodana his father;
Upatissa and Kolita will be his two chief disciples; Ānanda will be his attendant;
and Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā will be his two chief female disciples. Having reached the maturity of wisdom, he will undertake the Great Renunciation."
"Having gone forth and exerted himself in the Great Struggle, he will receive the milk-rice offered by the maiden named Sujātā at the foot of the Nigrodha tree;
having eaten it on the bank of the Nerañjarā, he will ascend the seat of enlightenment and attain full awakening at the foot of the Assattha tree. Thus it was said.
“Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
standing at my head, spoke these words:
‘Behold this ascetic, the matted-hair ascetic who practices fierce austerities.’”
“In immeasurable eons, a Buddha will appear in the world.
Having gone forth from the delightful city called Kapila, the Tathāgata,
after exerting himself in striving and performing difficult austerities...”
“Having sat at the foot of the Ajapāla tree, the Tathāgata will take his milk-rice there and proceed to the Nerañjarā River.
On the bank of the Nerañjarā, that Conqueror will eat the milk-rice.”
By the prepared supreme path, he will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then, having circumambulated the seat of enlightenment from the right,
the unsurpassed one of great renown will awaken at the foot of the Assattha tree.
“His mother who gave him birth shall be named Māyā;
his father shall be named Suddhodana, and he himself shall be Gotama.
Free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and composed, [they shall serve him].”
Kolita and Upatissa shall be the foremost disciples;
he named Ānanda shall be the attendant who will serve this Conqueror.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples.
Taintless, free from passion, with peaceful minds and composed, they said:
“The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Assattha;
Citta and Hatthāḷavaka shall be the foremost attendants.”
"And Uttarā, Nandamātā, shall be the foremost among those who serve.
In this context, "knower of the world" (*lokavidū*) means one who has known the world in every respect.

For the Blessed One has known, understood, and penetrated the world in its entirety—by way of its intrinsic nature, its origin, its cessation, and the means to its cessation. Therefore, he is called "knower of the world. As it is said:

“Therefore, indeed, the wise one who knows the world, having reached the end of the world and lived the holy life—having known the end of the world as a tranquilizer, he shall desire neither this world nor the next.

Furthermore, there are three worlds: the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*), the world of beings (*satta-loka*), and the world of space (*okāsa-loka*). Among these, the world of formations is as follows:

The elements such as earth and so forth are dependently arisen phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppanna*). What is called the "world of beings" (*sattaloka*) consists of sentient beings who possess perception, those without perception, and those with neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is called the "world of space" (*okāsaloka*) is the dwelling place of sentient beings. These three worlds, moreover, were known by the Blessed One according to their true nature;
therefore, he is called the "Knower of the World" (*lokavidū*). He is the "recipient of offerings" (*āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho*) because he is worthy of receiving gifts.
"Because of being worthy of offerings, he is the recipient of oblations. "Standing at my head" means standing near my head;
the meaning is that he spoke these words which were now to be said. "Jaṭila" means one who has matted hair (*jaṭā*); thus, he is a *jaṭila*.
"Uggatāpana" means one of fierce asceticism (*tāpasa*). "Ahū" means on the day; the sense is "then. Or else, this very reading [is preferred].
"Named Kapila" means having the designation *Kapila*. "Delightful" means because it is charming. "Exertion" means energy (*vīriya*).
"He will come" means he will go. The remaining verses are self-evident.
Then the wise Sumedha, thinking, "It seems my aspiration will be fulfilled," was filled with joy.
Having heard the words of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the great multitude was thrilled and delighted, thinking, "The ascetic Sumedha is indeed the sprout from which the seed of a Buddha shall grow.

And this thought occurred to them: "Just as a man crossing a river, being unable to cross by a straight ford, might instead cross at a lower ford, even so we [have missed] the teaching of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara..."
"May we, failing to attain the fruits of the path now, be capable of realizing those fruits in your presence when you become a Buddha in the future," they made this aspiration.
The Ten-Powered One, Dīpaṅkara, having praised the Bodhisatta Mahāsatta, worshipped him with eight handfuls of flowers, circumambulated him, and departed. They too—
Four hundred thousand *khīṇāsavas*, having honored the Bodhisatta with flowers and perfumes and having circumambulated him, departed.
Gods and humans likewise, having honored and paid homage to him, departed.
Then the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the lamp that illuminates the entire world, was surrounded by four hundred thousand *khīṇāsavas*.
Being honored by the inhabitants of Ramma City and saluted by the deities, like the peak of the excellent Golden Mountain colored by the radiance of twilight as he moved along,
while many miracles were occurring, he proceeded by that road which was adorned and prepared,

scented with the fragrance of various fragrant flowers and the blended scent of aromatic powders, strewn with raised banners and flags, and where the hearts of the people were bound to him by the scent.
Having entered the delightful city of Ramma— which, with its incense-smoke darkening the air and humming with swarms of bees,
possessed a splendor like that of the city of the immortals— the One Endowed with the Ten Powers sat upon the magnificent, well-prepared Buddha-throne at the summit of Mount Yugandhara,
like the sun, the maker of day, which at the end of autumn possesses beautiful rays, destroys the mass of darkness, and causes the lotus groves to bloom.
He sat down. The community of monks also sat down in order, each upon his own seat.

The lay followers residing in the city of Ramma, endowed with virtues such as faith, gave to the community of monks headed by the Buddha an incomparable gift that was the cause of happiness—a gift adorned with various kinds of hard foods and other offerings, possessing excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.

Then the Bodhisatta, having heard the prophecy of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers and considering his own future Buddhahood as if it were already held in the palm of his hand, sat up from his bed with a heart full of joy after everyone had departed. Thinking, "I shall now seek out the perfections," he sat cross-legged upon a heap of flowers.
While the Great Being was thus seated, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world system...

Having given his approval, he said: "Venerable ascetic Sumedha, all those signs known as 'omens' that appeared when the ancient Bodhisattvas sat cross-legged, thinking, 'I shall investigate the perfections,' have manifested today.
Without doubt you will become a Buddha; we know this."
—“He in whom these signs are perceived will certainly become a Buddha.
Therefore, exerting and strengthening your own energy, they praised the Bodhisatta with various kinds of hymns. Thus it is said:
“Having heard these words of the Peerless Great Seer...”
Men and gods were filled with joy, for this one is indeed the seed of a Buddha.
Shouts of exultation arise; they clap their hands and laugh.
With palms joined in reverence, the ten thousand worlds, including the devas, pay homage.
“If we should fail in the teaching of this Lord of the World,
in a future time we shall stand face-to-face with him.
Just as people crossing a river, having missed a ford, [struggle on]...”
"Having taken hold at a shallow ford, they cross the great river.
'In just this way, if we all release this Conqueror,
in a future time we shall stand face to face with him.'"
“Dīpaṅkara, the knower of the world, the recipient of offerings,
having proclaimed my deed, lifted up his right foot.
Those sons of the Conqueror who were there circumambulated me.”
The devas, humans, and asuras, having paid homage, departed.
"When the Leader of the World, together with his Saṅgha, had passed beyond my sight,
I rose from my bed and then sat cross-legged."
“Happy through happiness, delighted by joy,
and suffused with rapture, I then sat cross-legged.
Having sat down cross-legged, I then reflected thus:”
I have attained mastery in meditation and reached perfection in the higher knowledges.
In this world-system of a thousand worlds, there are no seers equal to me;
peerless in the powers of psychic transformation, I have obtained such happiness as this.
“As I sat cross-legged upon my excellent throne, the ten thousand world-systems resounded with a great roar: ‘Surely you will become a Buddha.
This was the very same sound that arose in the past when Bodhisattvas sat upon their supreme thrones.”
The signs appear; they appear today.
"The cold has departed and the heat is subsiding;
these signs appear today—surely you will become a Buddha."
“The ten-thousandfold world system has become silent and undisturbed;
these signs are visible today, so surely you will become a Buddha.
The great winds do not blow, and the rivers do not flow.”
“Those [trees] are visible today; surely you will become a Buddha.
‘The flowers born on land and those born in water—all of them bloom only at that time;
today they have all blossomed; surely you will become a Buddha.’”
“Just as the creepers or the trees are now laden with fruit, so too have they all borne fruit today; surely you will become a Buddha.
And just as the jewels situated in the sky and on the earth shine forth today,”
"These three jewels shine forth; surely you will become a Buddha.
Human and divine musical instruments resound all at once;
they resound together from both sides; surely you will become a Buddha."
“Variegated flowers rain down from the sky at that time;
they are raining down even today. Surely you will become a Buddha.
The great ocean surges and the ten-thousandfold world system trembles.”
“Today all the fires are blazing; you will surely become a Buddha.
“Even in the ten thousandfold world-systems of hell, the fires were extinguished at that moment;
today those fires have been extinguished—you will surely become a Buddha.”
“The sun has become clear, and all the stars are visible;
yet even they are shining today—surely you will become a Buddha.
Even without rain, water has burst forth from the earth at this very moment.”
The earth trembles and bursts open; surely you will become a Buddha.
The hosts of stars shine forth, the constellations in the circle of the sky;
the moon is joined with the constellation Viśākhā; surely you will become a Buddha.
“From their own dwellings, they emerge from their lairs and caves;
today they have abandoned those abodes. Surely you will become a Buddha.
No discontent arises in these beings; for now, they are filled with satisfaction.”
"Today all are content; surely you will become a Buddha.
Today the diseases are pacified and hunger has vanished;
those [signs] are visible today—surely you will become a Buddha."
“Then your illness was slight, and your hatred and delusion were destroyed;
now all these have vanished, so you will surely become a Buddha.
That fear no longer exists, yet even today it is seen.”
“By this sign we know: you will certainly become a Buddha.
Dust rising upward is seen even today;
by this sign we know: you will certainly become a Buddha.”
“The unpleasant odor departs, and a divine fragrance wafts forth;
this fragrance blows today—surely you will become a Buddha.
All the gods appear, with the exception of those who are formless.”
All these are seen today; surely you will become a Buddha.
“As many as there are places called hells, all of them are seen today;
all these are seen today; surely you will become a Buddha.”
“Walls, doors, and rocks will not be obstacles then;
they will become like space. Today you are surely destined to become a Buddha.
At that moment, neither death nor rebirth exists.”
"These signs are now appearing; you will surely become a Buddha.
Exert firm energy; do not turn back, but press forward!
We too recognize this: you will surely become a Buddha."

In this context, "having heard these words" means having heard these words of the prophecy from the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara regarding the Bodhisatta. "Peerless" (*asama*) is because there is no one equal (*sama*) to him. As it is said:
"I have no teacher; no one equal to me is found.
In the world with its devas, there is no rival to me."
"Mahesī" means one who seeks or searches for the great aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom; thus he is "Mahesī," and [the phrase] refers to that Mahesī.

"Naramarū" means humans and immortals (gods); this is an expression used in its highest sense, for even all the nāgas, supaṇṇas, yakkhas, and so forth within the ten-thousandfold world system were filled with joy.
"Ayanti kira buddhabījam" means that they are indeed the seed of a Buddha; "ayaṃ kira buddhaṅkuro" means that this is indeed the sprout of a Buddha.
"Arisen" means "rejoiced.
