"Sounds of exultation" refers to sounds of loud shouting. "Clapping their hands" means they strike their arms with their hands.

"The ten-thousandfold world system" refers to the ten thousand world-systems. "Together with the devas" means together with the gods; thus, the ten-thousandfold world system, together with the devas, pays homage.
The meaning [of the passage] is as follows: *yadimassa* means "if for this one"; alternatively, *ayameva* is the reading. *Virajjhissāma* means "if we do not attain.
*Anāgatamhi addhāne* means "in the future time. *Hessāma* means "we shall become. *Sammukhā* means "having appeared before [us]. *Imaṃ* means "for this one";
it is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmi-attha*).
“Crossing the river” (*nadiṃ tarantā*) means those crossing the river; there is also a reading as *naditarantā*. “Against the current” (*paṭititthaṃ*) means against the flow of the ford.

“Having missed” (*virajjhiya*) means having missed [the opportunity]. “If we should let go” (*yadi muñcāma*) means if we should depart without having completed our task after letting go of this Blessed One.
“Having proclaimed my deed” (*mama kammaṃ pakittetvā*) means having explained the matter developed by me. “The offering” (*dakkhiṇaṃ*)...
"He lifts his foot" means he raised his right foot; there is also a reading, "having performed a circumambulation.
"Sons of the Conqueror" refers to the disciples of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.

"Gods, humans, and asuras, having paid homage, departed"—all these beings, beginning with the gods, having circumambulated me three times and worshipped me with flowers and other offerings, stood with their five limbs well-placed.
Having paid homage, turned back, and gazed upon him again and again, they departed while praising him with various kinds of hymns of praise consisting of sweet meanings and phrasing.
There is also a reading: “Men, nāgas, and gandhabbas, having bowed down, departed.
“My sight has passed beyond” means that the Blessed One had passed beyond the range of my vision. There is also the reading: “When the range of sight was abandoned.”

The reading is *sasaṅgho*. "Together with the Saṅgha" means accompanied by the Saṅgha; [the phrase] "in that [assembly] together with the Saṅgha" (*sasaṅghe*) refers to that. "Having risen from his seat" means having risen from the place where he was lying down, from the couch.
"Folding his legs crosswise" (*pallaṅkaṃ ābhujim*) means having assumed the cross-legged posture, he sat upon a heap of flowers—this is the meaning.
There is also the reading: "Joyful, with a joyful mind, I then rose from my seat"; its meaning is self-evident.
“Saturated with rapture” means permeated by rapture (*pīti*). “Mastery attained” means having reached the state of mastery (*vasībhāva*).

“In jhāna” refers to the fine-material and immaterial-sphere jhānas. “In the thousandfold” means in the ten-thousandfold world system. “In the world” means in the world-system (*lokadhātu*). “Equal to me” means like me.
Having stated generally, “There is none equal to me,” he now specifies that very point by saying, “Peerless in the powers of psychic potency (*iddhidhamma*). In this regard:
"In the phenomena of psychic power" means in the five kinds of psychic powers. "Obtained" means acquired. "Such happiness" means such joy.

Then, having heard the declaration of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, the ascetic Sumedha, considering his future Buddhahood as if it were already held in the palm of his hand, with a heart full of rapture, [addressed] the Great Brahmas of the Suddhāvāsa realm throughout the ten thousand world-systems who had seen past Buddhas.

Showing that they spoke these verses in order to satisfy me by demonstrating the infallibility of the Tathāgata’s word through the display of miracles occurring at the time of the prophecy for those bodhisattvas who were destined for enlightenment, the Blessed One said, “While I was sitting cross-legged,” and so forth.

Therein, “while I was sitting cross-legged” (*pallaṅkābhujane mayhaṃ*) means while I was sitting cross-legged; this is indeed the reading. “The inhabitants of the ten thousand [world-systems]” (*dasasahassādhivāsino*).
The Great Brahmās dwelling in the ten-thousandfold world-system. "Those which were before" (*yā pubbe*) should be understood as having been stated by eliding the case-ending (*vibhattilopa*).
"He sat upon the excellent couch" (*pallaṅkavaramābhujeti*) means: in the act of sitting upon the excellent couch. "Signs will be seen" (*nimittāni padissantīti*) means: signs were seen;
although the past tense should have been used, the present tense was employed. Even though it was so stated...

The meaning should be understood by way of the past. "Those [signs] appear today" means that those very signs which previously arose when the Bodhisattvas destined for enlightenment sat cross-legged, those same signs appear today. Therefore, the meaning is: "Consequently, you will certainly become a Buddha.
However, it is not that those exact same signs arose; rather, because they are similar to them, it is said, "those [same signs] appear today."
It should be understood that this is what is meant by "they appear.
"Cold" means coldness. "Departed" means gone or vanished. "Those" refers to the departure of cold and the subsiding of heat;
such is the meaning. "Soundless" means without sound or without noise. "Untroubled" means undisturbed; or rather, this is the reading itself. "They do not flow" means—
They do not flow; they do not move. "Rivers" means streams. "Those" refers to the non-flowing and non-dripping [flowers].

"Land-born" means those produced on the surface of the earth, on mountains, and on trees. "Water-born" means aquatic flowers. Regarding "they are blooming": previously they bloomed for the Bodhisattas;
this present tense should be understood in the sense of the past, according to the method explained below. "Today they have blossomed."
The meaning is that those flowers have bloomed today.
"Phalabhārā" means bearing fruit. "Tepajjā" means even they today; it is stated as "tepi" in the masculine gender because of the mention of "creepers or trees.
"Phalitā" means having produced fruit. "Ākāsaṭṭhā ca bhūmaṭṭhā ca" means situated in the sky and situated on the ground. "Ākāsagatā" [is the same].
"And gems found on the earth" refers to gems such as pearls and the like. "Shining" means radiating light. "Human" means belonging to humans;

"divine" means belonging to the devas. "Musical instruments" refers to the five types of instruments: the stretched (*ātata*), the loose-stretched (*vitata*), the stretched-and-loose-stretched (*ātatavitata*), the hollow (*susira*), and the solid (*ghana*). Among these, the "stretched" refers to drums and the like covered with leather.

"Single-surfaced" (*ekatala*) refers to [instruments] with one surface. "Stretched" (*vitata*) means those with two surfaces. "Covered and stretched" (*ātatavitata*) refers to large lutes (*vallakī*) and the like, which are covered on all sides.
"Hollow" (*susira*) refers to flutes and the like. "Solid" (*ghana*) refers to cymbals (*sammatāḷa*) and the like. "They resounded" (*vajjanti*):
this should be understood as a present tense verb used in the sense of the past, according to the method explained below. This same method applies to what follows.

In such statements as these: "They resound" means that here and there they resound like being well-released, well-beaten, and well-played by skilled musicians; the meaning is that they resound or ring out.
"Variegated flowers" means flowers of various scents and colors. "They rained down" means they have rained down.
"Fall down" is the meaning. "Those too" means those various flowers were seen raining down; the intention is that they were being strewn by hosts of devas and brahmas.
"He folds" means he withdraws. "Both these today" refers to both great oceans of ten thousand [world-systems].
"Resounding" means crying out. "In hell" means in the hells. "Ten thousand" means many tens of thousands. "Are extinguished" means...
"They settle" means they attain peace. "Stars" refers to the constellations.
"Even these shall be seen today" means that even these stars will be visible today by day due to the sun's stainless state.
"Anovaṭṭhena" means "in the absence of rain"; the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. Alternatively, "anovaṭṭhe" means "even when it has not rained."
*Na* is merely a particle, as in such expressions as *sutvā na dūtavacanaṃ*. *Tampajjubbhijjate*: that water also wells up today;
the meaning is that having welled up, it rises forth. *Mahiyā*: from the earth; this is an ablative expression. *Tārāgaṇā*:
all the hosts of stars, including the planets, lunar mansions (*nakkhatta*), and so forth. *Nakkhattā*: the lunar mansions and the stars. *Gaganamaṇḍale*: in the circle of the sky.
The meaning is that they shine throughout the entire circle of the sky. "Hole-dwellers" refers to snakes, mongooses, monitor lizards, iguanas, and so forth.
"Cave-dwellers" refers to those who dwell in waterfalls; this is the same reading as well. "Emerging" means they emerged.
"From their own abodes" means from their respective dwelling places. There is also the reading "tadāsayā"; its meaning is: "then," at that time, "from their abode," that is, from the hole.
"Pure" means perfectly pure, well-understood; the meaning is "emerged. "Discontent" (*arati*) means longing.
"Contented" means contented with the highest form of contentment. "Perishes" means it disappears. "Lust" (*rāga*) means sensual lust.
"Then it becomes thin" means it becomes slight; by this, he indicates the absence of its active manifestation (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
"Vihatā" means ruined. "Tadā" means previously; the sense is: "at the time when Bodhisattas sit cross-legged. "Na bhavati" means it does not exist.
"Ajjapetaṃ" means even today, even while you sit cross-legged, this fear does not exist at all—this is the meaning.
"Tena liṅgena jānāma" means for that reason we all know: that you will become a Buddha—this is the meaning.
*Anuddhaṃsati* means it does not rise up. *Aniṭṭhagandho* means having a foul odor. *Pakkamati* means it departed; *vigacchi* means it vanished.
*Pavāyati* means it blew forth. *Sopajja* means even that divine fragrance today.
*Padissanti* means they appeared. *Tepajja* means all those gods today. *Yāvatā* is a particle used in the sense of a limit, meaning "as many as. *Kuṭṭā* means walls.

"Non-obstructive" means they did not act as obstructions. "Then" refers to previously. "Become like space" means that those walls, doors, and mountains were unable to act as an obstruction or a screen;
the meaning is that they became like unobstructed space. "Death" means passing away. "Rebirth" means the taking up of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"At the moment" refers to the previous moment when the Bodhisattvas folded their legs in the cross-legged posture. "Is not found" means...
"It was not so. "Those births" means those very births of today, characterized by passing away and arising. "Do not turn back" means do not retreat.
"Advance" means exert yourself. The rest here is self-evident.
Then the wise Sumedha [heard] the words of Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers, and of the deities of the ten thousand world-systems.
Having heard this, his courage increased all the more, and he thought: "The Buddhas are indeed those whose words are never in vain;

there is no deviation from the speech of the Buddhas. For as the falling of a clod thrown into the air is certain, as is death for one who is born, the rising of the sun when dawn has broken, and the emergence of a lion from its lair—"
Just as the delivery of the burden by a woman heavy with child is certain and inevitable, even so the word of the Buddhas is certainly not in vain;
"Surely I shall become a Buddha. Therefore it was said:
"Having heard the word of the Buddha, the ten-thousandfold world-system on both sides..."
With a joyful heart, thrilled and delighted, I then thought thus:
“The Buddhas speak words free from duplicity; the Conquerors’ words are never in vain.
There is nothing false in the Buddhas; surely I shall become a Buddha.”
"Just as a clod of earth thrown into the sky will certainly fall to the ground, so too the word of the Best of Buddhas is certain and eternal.
There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; I shall certainly become a Buddha."
“Just as death is certain and constant for all beings, so too is the word of the Best of Buddhas certain and constant.
There is nothing false in the Buddhas; ‘I shall become a Buddha’ is a certainty.”
"Just as the rising of the sun is certain when the night has ended, so too the word of the Best of Buddhas is certain and eternal.
There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; it is certain that I shall become a Buddha."
“Just as the roar of a lion who has emerged from his lair is certain, so too the word of the Best of Buddhas is certain and eternal.
There is nothing false in the Buddhas; it is certain that I shall become a Buddha.”
“Just as the laying down of the burden by those who have conceived a fetus is certain, so too the word of the Supreme Buddhas is certain and eternal.
There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; we shall certainly become Buddhas.”

Therein, "having heard the word of the Buddha" means having heard the words of the Perfectly Enlightened One Dīpaṅkara and the deities of the ten thousand world-systems (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*). "Ubhayaṃ" means "of both";
it is the nominative case used in the sense of the genitive, or it is the dual form. "Evaṃ cintesahaṃ" means "I thought thus."
“Unambiguous words” means words that do not function in two ways; the meaning is that they are categorical words (*ekaṃsava-cana*).
There is also the reading “unbroken words,” which means faultless words. “Not in vain” means not false words.
The meaning is that there is no such thing as a false word [for him]. “I shall certainly become a Buddha” means by way of certainty: “I alone shall certainly become a Buddha.”
And it should be understood that the present tense is used here by way of its inevitable occurrence.
"The rising of the sun" means the appearance of the sun; this is the reading itself.

"Permanent and eternal" means both certain to happen and everlasting. "Of one who has emerged from bed" means of one who has come out from his bed. "Of those who have conceived a being" means of those pregnant with a heavy fetus.
The meaning is "of pregnant women. "Bhāramoropanaṃ" means the laying down of the burden; the meaning is "the laying down of the fetus.
The letter *ma* is used for metrical conjunction (*padasandhi*). The rest here is also self-evident.
Having thus made the resolution, "I shall certainly become a Buddha," [he proceeded] to examine the qualities that constitute a Buddha.

—“Where, indeed, are the qualities that make a Buddha? Thus, searching through the entire element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) in succession—upward, downward, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions—he first beheld the perfection of giving (dānapāramī), which had been practiced and cultivated by previous Bodhisattvas of old.
Then he exhorted himself thus: “O wise Sumedha, from this moment forth, you must first [practice]…”

"You shall fulfill the perfection of giving. For just as an overturned water-jar pours out its water entirely and does not draw it back again, even so, without looking back at wealth or fame, children or wife, or even your own limbs and members, you shall give everything desired by supplicants in every instance until nothing remains; and having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree,"
“‘You shall become a Buddha!’—thus, first making firm the perfection of giving, he made this resolution. Therefore it is said:
‘Come now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that make a Buddha, upwards and downwards throughout the ten directions, as far as the realm of phenomena extends.’”
“Then, while searching, I beheld the first perfection of giving,
that great path practiced by the great seers of old.
First of all, you must undertake this with firm resolve.”
Go to the perfection of giving if you wish to attain awakening.
Just as a full jar, when turned upside down, vomits out its water entirely without retaining any of it; so too must one give.
“Likewise, seeing beggars—whether low, high, or middling—give them gifts without remainder, like a jar turned upside down.

In this context, *handā* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation (*vavassagga*). *Buddhakare dhamme* means the qualities that make one a Buddha. [These are] the qualities that produce Buddhahood.
“Dhammas” refers to the ten qualities beginning with the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). “I shall investigate” (*vicināmi*) means that I will search for, examine, and scrutinize them.
“Hither and thither” (*ito cito*)—or this reading may simply be *ito ito*—means that I shall investigate here and there.

“Above” (*uddhaṃ*) refers to the world of the devas. “Below” (*adho*) refers to the world of humans. “In the ten directions” (*dasasu disāsu*) means throughout the ten quarters: where indeed are those qualities that constitute a Buddha?
"Upward, downward, across, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions"—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "as far as the element of phenomena" (*dhammadhātu*), here *yāvatā* is a term of delimitation. *Dhammadhātuyā* refers to the phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*); it should be understood that the word *pavattinī* ("that which proceeds") is to be supplied.
What is meant? As far as the occurrence of all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature—namely, phenomena of the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms—extends, so far [does this reach].
"I shall investigate"—this is what is meant.
"Investigating" means examining and scrutinizing. "By the predecessors" means by the ancient Bodhisattvas.
"Practiced" means habitually practiced and cultivated. "Take it up" means perform the act of undertaking; from this day forward, this is the first [precept].

"The meaning of 'I must fulfill the perfection of giving' (dānapāramī) is that one undertakes it in this way. 'Go to the perfection of giving' (dānapāramitaṃ gaccha) means go to the perfection of giving; the meaning is 'fulfill it.

'If you wish to attain enlightenment' (yadi bodhiṃ pattum icchasi) means if you wish to attain unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment (anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ) after approaching the foot of the Bodhi tree.
'Of whatever' (yassa kassaci) refers to water, milk, or whatever else."
"Complete. When the word *sampuṇṇa* (complete) is used in conjunction [with another], grammarians maintain that the genitive case is required.
Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "by means of whatever [is complete]. "Turned downward" means made to face downwards.
"He does not protect there" means he does not protect against that vomiting; the meaning is that he vomits the water without remainder. "Inferior, superior, and middling."
"Inferior, middling, and superior. The letter *m* is used here for metrical conjunction (*padasaṃdhikara*). "Like a jar turned downward" means like a jar whose opening has been turned downwards.
Upon seeing supplicants approach, [he said]: "O Sumedha, fulfill the perfection of giving by relinquishing all your wealth without remainder;
fulfill the near-perfection by relinquishing your limbs; and fulfill the ultimate perfection by relinquishing even your life."
Thus he exhorted himself by means of himself.

Then, thinking to himself, "The qualities that produce a Buddha must be more than just these," as he reflected further, he beheld the second perfection, that of virtue (sīla-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him:
"O Wise Sumedha, from this time forth, you must practice the perfection of virtue."

“You shall fulfill it. Just as the animal known as the yak (camarī-miga) protects its own tail even at the cost of its life, so too, from this moment forth, by protecting your virtue alone even at the cost of your life, you will become a Buddha.
Thus he made a firm resolve, strengthening the second perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī). Therefore it is said:
“It will not be only these that constitute the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall search for others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the second perfection: that of virtue.
“Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old:
‘First, you must firmly undertake this second one;
go forth to the perfection of virtue if you wish to attain enlightenment.’”
“Just as a yak, when her tail becomes entangled anywhere,
meets her death there rather than wrenching the tail free;
even so, you should fulfill the precepts throughout all four stages.”
"Always protect your virtue, as the yak protects its tail.
In this context, "not only these" means that it is not merely these [perfections]. "Ripening for enlightenment" means ripening for the path or ripening for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
The second is the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*); virtue is the foundation for all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), and one who is established in virtue...
One does not fall away from wholesome states and acquires all mundane and supramundane qualities.
Therefore, "the perfection of virtue must be fulfilled" means that they perceived the second perfection of virtue.
*Āsevitam nisevitam* means both cultivated and practiced frequently. *Camarī* refers to the yak deer. *Kismiñci* means in whatever [place].
"In some place" means among trees, creepers, thorns, or any such thing. "Entangled" means clinging fast.
"Right there" means that having died while remaining right where it became entangled, it does not move away. "Does not shake off" means it does not cut [the entanglement].
"The tail-hair" means that having cut its hair, it does not go; the meaning is that it meets death right there.

"Virtues in the four planes" means the virtues analyzed into four places; the meaning is: by way of restraint of the Pātimokkha, restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and dependence on the [proper] requisites.
However, according to the division of planes, that which is included in only two planes is likewise these same four virtues.
"Fulfill" means to fulfill by being free from brokenness, gaps, and weakness. "At all times" means at every moment. "Like a yak-cow" means like a *camarī*.
Like a deer. The rest here is also of plain meaning.

Then, as he reflected further, thinking, "The qualities that constitute a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone," and having seen the third perfection, renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*), this thought occurred to him:
"O wise Sumedha, from this time forth, you must also [fulfill] the perfection of renunciation."

You should fulfill it. Just as a man who has lived for a very long time in a prison does not feel attachment to it, but rather becomes weary of it and desires to leave, even so you too, regarding all states of existence as similar to a prison, see them with weariness;
becoming desirous of liberation from all states of existence, you should turn toward renunciation alone.
“Thus you shall become a Buddha”—thus he made firm his resolve, strengthening the third perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*). Therefore it is said:
“These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely these many;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.”
“Then, searching, I beheld the third perfection of renunciation,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. ‘Therefore, you too,
having firmly undertaken this third [perfection],’”
Go to the perfection of renunciation, if you desire to attain enlightenment.
Just as a man who has long been imprisoned in a dungeon and is afflicted by suffering does not conceive passion for it, but seeks only liberation.
“In that very way, you should view all states of existence as if they were a prison-house;
turn toward renunciation for the sake of liberation from existence.
In this context, “prison-house” means a place of confinement. “Long-imprisoned” means having been confined for a long time. “Afflicted by suffering” means oppressed by pain.
"He does not generate passion for that" means he does not generate or produce passion—that is, affection—for that prison house.

The intention is that he does not generate passion there by thinking, "Having left this prison house, I will not go anywhere else," but rather seeks only liberation, only release. "Facing toward renunciation" means facing toward going forth.
“...there is. ‘From existence’ means from all states of becoming (*bhava*). ‘For the sake of complete liberation’ means for the purpose of total release.
There is also a reading: ‘Having turned toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*), you shall attain full enlightenment (*sambodhi*)’. The rest here is of plain meaning.
Then, as he reflected further, thinking, “It cannot be that there are only these qualities that make one a Buddha,” [he continued].
Having seen the fourth perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī), he thought: "O wise Sumedha, from this time forth you should fulfill the perfection of wisdom as well.
Without excluding anyone among those who are inferior, middling, or superior, you should approach all wise men and ask them questions.
Just as an alms-collecting monk, without avoiding any household among the various classes of families—whether lowly or otherwise—"
"Just as one who wanders for alms in regular succession obtains enough quickly to sustain life, even so you too, by approaching and questioning all the wise, will become a Buddha.
Having thus made firm his resolve upon the fourth perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī), he established it.
Therefore it is said:
“It will not be only these that constitute the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the fourth perfection: wisdom.”
“Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old:
‘First, having firmly undertaken this fourth perfection of wisdom,
proceed toward the perfection of wisdom if you desire to attain enlightenment.’”
“Just as a monk, while wandering for alms,
does not avoid families— whether low, high, or middling— and thus obtains his sustenance;
even so, you too, at all times, should question wise people.”
"Having reached perfection in wisdom, you will attain full enlightenment.
In this context, "begging" means wandering for alms. "Low, high, and middle" means low, high, and middle families;
the gender has been changed [from neuter to masculine]. "Not avoiding" means not bypassing, following the sequence of houses.

"Moving about having abandoned" means he avoids [unwholesome things]; the meaning is that he does not do so. "Sustenance" (yāpana) means he obtains food sufficient for sustenance, enough to maintain life.

"Inquiring" means approaching wise people well-known in various places and asking in such a manner as: "Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? and so forth.
The meaning is "one who asks thoroughly. "Budhaṃ" means wise people. There is also a reading as "budhe jane" (among wise people).
"Paññāya pāramiṃ" means the further shore of wisdom. There is also a reading as "paññāpāramitaṃ gantvā" (having gone to the perfection of wisdom). The rest here is also quite clear.
Then, thinking to himself, "There must be more qualities that make one a Buddha than just these," he investigated further.
Having seen the fifth perfection, that of energy, he thought: "O wise Sumedha, from this time forth you must fulfill the perfection of energy as well.
Just as Sīha, the king of beasts, possesses firm energy in all postures, so too, by maintaining firm and unflagging energy in all states of existence and in all postures, you shall become a Buddha."
Having made the fifth perfection, energy, firm, he resolved. Therefore it was said:
“These alone shall not be the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen enlightenment.”
“Then, searching, I beheld the fifth perfection of energy,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. ‘Therefore,
first of all, having taken up this fifth perfection and made it firm,’”
Go to the perfection of energy if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as the lion, the king of beasts, whether sitting,
standing, or walking, is always unflagging in energy and ever resolute in mind.
“In the same way, exert firm energy in all states of existence;
having reached the perfection of energy, you will attain full enlightenment.

Herein, “unflagging energy” means energy that does not shrink back. “In all states of existence” means in every birth as it occurs, or in all forms of existence—this is the meaning. There is also a reading: “Having become one who has initiated energy, you will attain full enlightenment. The rest here is also self-evident.

Then, thinking to himself, "The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone," as he investigated further, he saw the sixth perfection, patience (*khantipāramī*), and this thought occurred to him:
"O wise Sumedha, from this time forth you should fulfill the perfection of patience;
whether treated with honor or with contempt, you should remain patient. For just as, for example, upon the earth..."
“They throw both pure things and impure things [upon it], yet the earth feels neither affection nor aversion toward them;
it endures, bears, and simply tolerates them. In the same way, you too, being patient under all honors and insults, will become a Buddha.
Thus he made a firm resolve, strengthening the sixth perfection of patience (*khantipāramitā*). Therefore it is said:
“It will not be merely these that constitute the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the sixth perfection, patience.
“Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old—
first undertake this sixth [perfection], making it firm;
with a mind free from doubt therein, you shall attain full enlightenment.”
“Just as the earth, indeed, whether it be pure or impure,
endures all that is cast upon it and does not harbor resentment because of you;
even so, may you also be patient with both honor and dishonor from everyone.”
“Having reached the perfection of patience, you will attain full enlightenment.
In that context, “therein, therein” means in that perfection of patience. “With a mind free from duplicity” means with a single-minded intent.

“Even what is pure” refers to the purity of sandalwood, saffron, perfumes, garlands, and so forth. “Even what is impure” refers to the impurity of snakes, dogs, human corpses, excrement, urine, saliva, mucus, and so forth.
"He endures" means he forgives; he patiently accepts. "Laying down" means that which has been laid down. "Resistance" means anger.

"By that" means by that conduct, or by that state of having laid it down. There is also a reading, "He gives up resistance," the meaning of which is: by that laying down, he does not comply with resistance.
"Patient toward honor and dishonor" means one who endures the honoring and dishonoring of all.

“*Tvampi bhava*” means “you too shall exist. Some also read: “*Tatheva tvampi sabbabhavesu sammānanavimānakkhamo*,” meaning “in the same way, you too are patient toward both honor and dishonor in all states of existence.
There is also the reading “*Khantiyā pāramiṃ gantvā*,” which means “having gone to the perfection of patience by way of fulfilling that patience.
The rest here is also self-evident. Beyond this, without saying even so much more, wherever there is a specific distinction:
"Having stated each of those and shown the alternative readings, we shall proceed.

Then, as he reflected further, thinking, "The qualities that constitute a Buddha cannot be limited to just these many," he beheld the seventh perfection, Truth (sacca-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him:
"O wise Sumedha, from this point forward, you must also [fulfill] the perfection of truth."
Even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon your head, do not speak a conscious lie for the sake of wealth and such things under the influence of desire and the like.

Just as the medicinal star (osadhītārakā) never abandons its own path of movement throughout all seasons and does not travel by another path but only by its own, even so you too [must not abandon the truth].
"Even while not speaking, you shall become a Buddha"—thus he made firm his resolve, establishing the seventh perfection of truth (sacca-pāramī).
Therefore it is said:
"These alone will not be the qualities of a Buddha;"
“I shall search for other qualities as well that ripen enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the seventh perfection of truth,
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this seventh [precept],
you should be free from duplicity in speech regarding it, and you will attain full enlightenment.
Just as the plant called Osadhi is the standard of measure for all that exists, including the gods,”
“In the dry season or during the rains, it does not deviate from its path.
In the same way, you too must not deviate from the path of the truths;
having reached the perfection of truth, you will attain full enlightenment.”
“In each and every instance” refers to the perfection of truth (*saccapāramī*). “One whose speech is not double” means one whose speech is not false. “The herb-star” means the *osadhī* constellation;
for when taking herbs, people take them upon seeing the *osadhī* star risen, and therefore it is called the “herb-star.
“Become a scale” means become a measure. “In the world with its devas” means in the world together with its devas. “At the time” means at the time of the rains.
“Utuvassa” means during the winter and summer seasons. There is also a reading: “samaye utuvaṭṭe. For that, the meaning is: “samaye” (at the time) refers to the summer;

“utuvaṭṭe” (when the season has turned) refers to the winter and the rainy season. “It does not deviate from its path” means that in each respective season it does not deviate from its own course of movement, nor does it depart from it;
for six months it goes toward the western direction, and for six months toward the eastern direction.
"It goes. Alternatively, "herbs" refers to medicinal herbs such as ginger, long pepper, black pepper, and so forth.
"It does not turn back" means that whichever herb is capable of yielding its fruit, it does not turn back from approaching the giving of that fruit without having bestowed its own result.
"From the path" means from the path of movement; a bile-curing [herb] simply carries away the bile, and a wind-curing [herb] [carries away] the wind.
"Harateva": "Semhaharo" means he carries away phlegm; the rest here is also self-evident.

Then, as he reflected further, thinking, "The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone," and having seen the eighth foundation, the perfection of determination (*adhiṭṭhānapāramī*), this thought occurred to him:
"O wise Sumedha, from this point forward, you must also [fulfill] the perfection of determination."
“Fill it! In that resolve which you have made, you must remain unshakable;

just as a mountain, even when winds blow from all directions, does not tremble or waver but stands firm in its own place, even so, by remaining unshakable in your own resolve, you shall become a Buddha.
Thus he spoke regarding the eighth perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*).
"Having made a firm resolve," it is said:
"These alone shall not be the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall search for others as well, those qualities that bring enlightenment to fruition."
“Then, while searching, I saw the eighth perfection of resolve,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. ‘Therefore,
you too should first undertake this eighth one, making it firm.’”
Remaining unshakable therein, you shall attain full enlightenment.
"Just as a rocky mountain, immovable and well-established,
does not tremble before violent winds but remains in its own place."
“Right there, in that very resolve, remain forever unshakable;
having reached the perfection of resolve, you shall attain full enlightenment.
In this context, *sela* means made of stone. *Acala* means immovable and well-established; it is because of being unshakable that it is well-established.
“Just as a mountain is immovable, dug deep and well-established”—this is also a reading.
“By violent winds” means by powerful winds. “In their own place” means in their very own place; the meaning is, “exactly where they were situated. The rest here is also plain.
Then, thinking to himself, “It cannot be that there are only these qualities that make one a Buddha,” he investigated further.
Having seen the ninth perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*), this thought occurred to him: "O Wise Sumedha, from this time forth you should fulfill the perfection of loving-kindness;
you should remain with a single mind toward both those who wish you well and those who do not.
Just as water, for instance, pervades all people—both the wicked and the virtuous—making its coolness exactly the same for all, even so should you also [behave] toward all beings."
“With a mind of loving-kindness, becoming one-pointed in thought, you will become a Buddha. Thus, having made firm the ninth perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*), he resolved.
Therefore it was said:
“These alone shall not be all the qualities of a Buddha;”
“I shall search for other qualities as well that ripen enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the ninth perfection, loving-kindness (*mettā*),
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this ninth [precept],
be peerless in loving-kindness if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as water, indeed, toward both good and evil people...”
“It pervades equally with coolness and blows away dust and dirt.
In the same way, you should cultivate loving-kindness equally toward the beneficial and the harmful;
having reached the perfection of loving-kindness, you will attain full enlightenment.”
In that context, "be peerless" means be without equal through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*).

There is also the reading, "you shall be equal to the equals," which has the same obvious meaning. "Equal" (*sama*) means similar. "Pervades" (*pharati*) means touches. "Washes away" (*pavāheti*) means purifies. "Dust" (*raja*) refers to adventitious dust.
"Filth" (*mala*) refers to the sweat, grime, and so forth arising on the body. There is also the reading, "dust and filth" (*rajamala*).
“Soyevattho”: regarding “hita-ahite,” the meaning is both the beneficial and the harmful, and likewise friends and enemies.
“Mettāya bhāvaya” means cultivate and increase loving-kindness (*mettā*). The rest here is also self-evident.
Then, as he reflected further, thinking, “The qualities that constitute a Buddha cannot be limited to just these many,” he considered even more.
Having seen the tenth perfection, equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*), he thought: "O wise Sumedha, from this time forward you should fulfill the perfection of equanimity;

whether in pleasure or in pain, you should remain exactly neutral. Just as the earth remains neutral when both pure and impure things are thrown upon it, even so you too should remain neutral amidst pleasure and pain."
“Truly, you shall become a Buddha! Thus he made a firm resolve, strengthening the tenth perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*). Therefore it is said:
“These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely these many;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.”
“Then, searching, I beheld the tenth perfection, equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī),
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. ‘Therefore, you too,
having firmly undertaken this tenth perfection, [should practice it].’”
Becoming firm like a scale, you will attain full enlightenment.
Just as the earth, indeed, remains equanimous toward both the impure and the pure that are cast upon it, free from both anger and attachment.
“In the very same way, you should always remain like a balance scale toward pleasure and pain;
having reached the perfection of equanimity, you will attain full enlightenment.
In this context, “like a balance scale” means being established in a state of neutrality, just as the beam of a scale remains level when things are weighed equally.
It does not bend nor does it rise; even so, you too, by becoming like a scale amidst pleasure and pain, will attain full enlightenment.
"Free from anger and attachment" means free from aversion and compliance. There is also a reading, "free from compassion and anger," which has the same meaning.
The rest should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Khantipāramī* (Perfection of Forbearance).
Then, having investigated these ten perfections (pāramī-dhamma), the wise Sumedha thought further:
"In this world, these alone are the qualities that must be fulfilled by Bodhisattvas to ripen for enlightenment and to bring about Buddhahood;
there are no more than these. Furthermore, these perfections do not exist above in the sky, nor below in the earth, nor in the eastern or other directions."
“They exist in all directions, yet they are established only within the flesh of my own heart.
Having thus seen that they were established in his own heart, he resolved firmly upon them all;

repeatedly contemplating them, he contemplated them in direct and reverse order, taking them from the end and bringing them to the beginning, and taking them from the beginning and [bringing them to] the end.
He placed it [in the center], took hold of both ends and drew them out; he took hold of both ends and drew them out toward the center.
The relinquishing of external possessions is called the *pāramīs*; the relinquishing of limbs is called the *upapāramīs*; and the relinquishing of life is called the *paramatthapāramīs*.
Thus, there are ten *pāramīs*, ten *upapāramīs*, and ten *paramatthapāramīs*, making thirty *pāramīs* in total.
He contemplated [the Dhamma] as if unwinding a *yamaka* oil-wick. As he contemplated the ten perfections (*pāramī*),
through the spiritual power (*dhammateja*) of that contemplation, this vast great earth— though it is two hundred and forty thousand *yojanas* in thickness—
trembled and shook violently, emitting a great roar like a bundle of reeds trampled by an elephant or like a field of sugarcane being crushed.
I trembled violently. Like a potter’s wheel or an oil-press wheel, I whirled around. Therefore it was said:
“Only so many things in the world are those factors that ripen enlightenment;
beyond these there is nothing else—therein establish yourself firmly.”
“As he comprehends these phenomena— those characterized by their intrinsic nature, essence,
and defining marks— the earth of the ten-thousandfold world system trembles through the power of the Dhamma.
The earth shakes and roars like a sugar-cane press being crushed.”
“As the wheel turns upon its axle, so does the earth tremble.
In this context, the phrase “only so many” is stated for the purpose of showing that there are neither fewer nor more than the ten perfections (pāramitās) thus specified.
“Beyond that” means there is nothing above those ten perfections. “Other than” means something else; [the term] *lakkhaṇa* is derived from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
It should be grasped. The meaning is that there is no quality other than the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) that brings about Buddhahood.
"Therein" means among those ten perfections. "He stands firm" (*patiṭṭhahāti*) means he stands while fulfilling them. "These qualities" refers to the qualities of the perfections.
"Of one who reflects" (*sammasato*) means of one who examines; the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (i.e., it is not the agent of the action).

It should be seen. "By the characteristic of its own inherent nature" means by means of the characteristic of its own inherent nature, which is designated as its "own-nature" (*sabhāva*), while one is contemplating it.
"By the splendor of the Dhamma" means by the splendor of the knowledge that investigates the perfections (*pāramī*). "Vasudhā": *vasu* is said to mean a treasure;
that which holds (*dhāreti*) or in which things are held (*dhīyati*) is *vasudhā*. What is it? It is the earth (*medanī*). "Pakampatha" means it shook (*pakampittha*).

The meaning is that while the wise Sumedha was investigating the perfections (*pāramī*), the ten-thousandfold world system shook due to the power of his knowledge. "It shakes" means it trembled in six ways.
"It roars" means it cries out and makes a tumultuous sound. "Like a sugar-cane press being crushed" means like a sugar-cane press that has been thoroughly squeezed.
There is also a reading, "like a jaggery-press being crushed," which has the same meaning. "In an oil-press" means in an oil-milling machine.
"Like a wheel" means like the great wheel-machine of those who work with wheels.
"Thus" means that just as an oil-pressing wheel-machine revolves and shakes, so too does this earth shake; such is the meaning. The rest here is self-evident.
Thus, while the great earth was shaking, the people living in the city of Ramma were serving the Blessed One.
Unable to remain steady, they fell down in a swoon like great *sāla* trees struck by the winds from Mount Yugandhara.
The pottery vessels, such as jars and the like, being tossed about and clashing against one another, were reduced to powder and dust.
The great multitude, terrified and trembling, approached the Teacher and asked: "What is this, Blessed One? Is this a whirlpool of *nāgas*, or of spirits, *yakṣas*, and deities?"
"Or is it some other portent? "No, indeed, we do not know this. However, this entire great multitude is afflicted by fear;
what evil will befall this world, or what good?
Tell us the reason for this," they asked.
Then the Teacher, having heard their words, said: "Do not be afraid; do not worry.

You have no cause for fear on this account. That wise Sumedha whom I prophesied today, saying, 'In the future he will become a Buddha named Gotama,' is now contemplating the perfections (pāramīs). By the power of his Dhamma as he contemplates them—"
“The entire ten-thousandfold world system shook and resounded all at once,” he said. Therefore it was stated:
“As far as the assembly gathered for the Buddha’s meal distribution, they were so shaken there that they lay unconscious upon the ground.”
“Thousands of jars and many hundreds of pots were there,
crushed and ground together, clashing against one another.
Agitated, thirsty, and terrified, they were distraught with troubled minds.”
The great multitude, having gathered together, approached Dīpaṅkara:
"What will happen for the world—will it be auspicious or evil?
The entire world is distressed; dispel that, O Visionary One."
“Then Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, reassured them:
‘Be confident, do not fear this trembling of the earth.
Regarding him whom I have prophesied today—that he will become a Buddha in the world—’”
“He contemplates the Dhamma, the ancient one practiced by the Conquerors.
As he contemplates the Dhamma, the ground of Buddhahood in its entirety,
because of that this earth, together with its ten thousand worlds and its devas, has trembled.”
In that context, *yāvatā* means "as many as. *Āsi* means "was. There is also the reading *“yā tadā parisā āsi,”* the meaning of which is "the assembly that was standing there at that time.
*Pavedhamānā* means "trembling. *Sā* refers to that assembly. *Tattha* means "in that place of distribution.
*Seti* means "she lay down" (past tense).
*Ghaṭāti ghaṭānaṃ*: this is the nominative case used in the sense of the genitive; the meaning is "of many thousands of jars. *Sañcuṇṇamathitā*: both crushed and churned;
the meaning is "churned and crushed. *Aññamaññaṃ paghaṭṭitā*: struck against one another. *Ubbiggā*: with hearts full of terror. *Tasitā*:
having become thirsty (or distressed). *Bhītā*: terrified by fear. *Bhantā*: bewildered.
"Phandanamānasā" means having a wandering mind; that is, having a distracted heart. All these terms are synonyms for one another.
"Samāgammā" means having come together;
or rather, this is simply the reading [of the word]. "Upadduto" means afflicted. "Taṃ vinodehī" means dispel that affliction of fear; the sense is: destroy it.
"Cakkhumā" means one who possesses eyes by way of the five kinds of vision. "Tesaṃ tadā" means "to those people at that time"; here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
"Saññāpesi" means he made known, he informed, he awakened. "Vissatthā" means with confident minds. "Mā bhātha" means do not fear.
"Yamahaṃ" means "him whom I," namely the wise Sumedha. "Dhammaṃ" means the dhamma of the perfections (pāramitā). "Pubbakaṃ" means ancient. "Jinasevitaṃ" means practiced by the Conquerors.

The meaning is that it was practiced by the Conquerors during their time as Bodhisattvas. "The stage of Buddhahood" refers to the dharma of the perfections (*pāramī*). "By that" means by that cause of thorough reflection.
"Trembled" means they shook. "In the world with its devas" means in the world including the devas.
Then, having heard the words of the Tathāgata, the great multitude, joyful and elated, took up garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth.

Having departed from the city of Ramma, he approached the Bodhisatta, honored him with garlands, perfumes, and other offerings, paid homage, and circumambulated him before re-entering the city of Ramma.
Then the Bodhisatta, having reflected upon the ten perfections (pāramīs) and exerted firm energy, rose from his seat with a resolute determination. Thus it is said:
“Having heard the Buddha’s word, my mind was immediately extinguished;
all of them approached me and once again paid homage to me.
Having undertaken the qualities of a Buddha and having made my mind firm,”
“Having paid homage to Dīpaṅkara, I then rose from my seat.

In this context, *mano nibbāyi* means that when the great multitude, their hearts alarmed by the earthquake, heard the reason for it, their minds were extinguished—that is, they attained peace (*santi*). There is also a reading, *jano nibbāyi*, which has the same meaning.
“Having undertaken” means having properly undertaken; the sense is “having taken up. “The qualities of a Buddha” refers to the perfections (*pāramīs*). The rest is self-evident.

Then, as the Bodhisatta—the one who cherishes all beings—was rising from his seat, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*) assembled, honored him with divine garlands, perfumes, and so forth, and said:
“Noble Sumedha ascetic, today by you [the offering was made] to the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara...”
A great aspiration was made at the soles of your feet; may it be fulfilled for you without obstacle, and may there be no fear or trepidation in that regard.
May not even the slightest ailment arise in your body; quickly fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*), may you realize perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
Just as trees that bear flowers and fruits blossom in their proper season...
“...and they indeed bear fruit; even so, you too, without transgressing that time, shall quickly touch supreme enlightenment.
Having thus recited these verses of praise and auspiciousness, and having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, each deity departed for his own celestial abode.
The Bodhisatta, being extolled by the deities, thought: “Having fulfilled the ten perfections...”

“Having made firm my effort and resolved, ‘I shall become a Buddha at the conclusion of four incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand kappas,’ I rose up into the air and went to the Himālaya mountains, where the company of seers dwelt. Thus it is said:
“Divine and human flowers—both gods and humans alike;”
They scatter flowers as he rises from his seat.
Both gods and humans alike proclaim his well-being:
"A great aspiration you have cherished—may you obtain it just as you wish."
“May all calamities be avoided; may sorrow and disease perish.
May no obstacles arise for you; may you quickly touch supreme enlightenment.
Just as when the proper season arrives, flowering trees burst into bloom;”
In that same way, O Great Hero, cause yourself to blossom with the wisdoms of a Buddha.
Just as all those Perfectly Awakened Ones fulfilled the ten perfections,
so too, O Great Hero, fulfill the ten perfections.
“Just as all those who were perfectly awakened ones awakened at the seat of enlightenment,
so too may you, O Great Hero, awaken to the enlightenment of the Conqueror.
Just as all those who were perfectly awakened ones set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma...”
In that same way, O Great Hero, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
Just as the moon on the full-moon day shines forth perfectly pure,
so too, you with a fulfilled mind, shine throughout the ten thousandfold world-system.
“Just as the sun, freed from Rāhu, outshines all with its heat, even so,
having been liberated from the worlds, you shine forth with glory.
Just as whatever rivers there may be flow toward the great ocean...”
“Thus may the worlds, including the devas, come into your presence.
Praised and extolled by them, he undertook ten qualities;
fulfilling those qualities, he then entered the forest.
In this context, "they scattered" means that the gods and humans took celestial flowers—such as *māndārava*, *pāricchattaka*, *santānaka*, *kusa*, and so forth—and human flowers;

such is the meaning. "They scattered over me" means they scattered [them] upon me; such is the meaning. "As he was emerging" means while he was emerging. "They made known" means they informed him and made him aware.
"Safety" means the state of being safe. Now, for the purpose of showing the manner in which it was made known:
“‘A great aspiration has been made by you,’ and so forth, was said. The meaning is: ‘O wise Sumedha, you have aspired to a great state;
may you obtain it exactly as you have aspired. ‘Sabbītiyo’ means ‘all calamities’ (*ītiyo*); they are called *ītiyo* because they come (*enti*). ‘Vivajjantu’ means ‘may they not occur.’”
"May sorrow and disease perish": may that which is termed sorrow (*soka*) and that which is termed disease (*roga*) be destroyed.
"Thine" (*te*): belonging to you. "Let there be no obstacles": let there be no hindrances. "Attain" (*phusa*): reach, obtain. "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*):
this refers both to the knowledge of the path of Arhatship and to omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). "Supreme" (*uttama*): most excellent, because it bestows all the qualities of a Buddha.
The knowledge of the path to arahantship is called "supreme.
"At the time" means when the flowering season of each respective tree has arrived. "Flowering" means those that are in bloom.
"By the Buddha-knowledges" means by the eighteen Buddha-knowledges. "In flowers" means in the flowers. "They filled" means they have filled.
"Pūrayāti" means "he fulfills. "Bujjhareti" means "they awakened. "Jinabodhiyanti" means "of the awakening of the Jinas, the Buddhas";

the meaning is "at the root of the omniscient awakening. "Puṇṇamāyeti" means "on the full-moon day. "Puṇṇamanoti" means "one whose desires are fulfilled. "Rāhumuttoti" means "released from Rāhu," that is, from the sun and moon.
"Tāpenāti" means "by the heat," that is, by the light. "Lokā muccitvāti" means "the world having been released."
The meaning is: having become unsullied by the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*). "Virocāti" means he shines forth (*virāja*). "Siriyā" means by the glory of a Buddha.
"Osarantī" means they enter the great ocean. "Osarantu" means may they approach. "Tavantike" means in your presence. "Tehī" means by those gods.
"Thutappasattho" means both praised and extolled, or extolled by those who have themselves been praised, such as Dīpaṅkara and others.
*Thutappasattho*. "The ten qualities" (*dasa dhamme*) refers to the ten perfections (*pāramitā-dhamma*). "The forest" (*pavanaṃ*) means the great forest;
the meaning is that he entered the great forest on Mount Dhammika. The remaining verses are quite clear.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Madhuratthavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*.
The commentary on the narrative of Sumedha’s aspiration is finished.
3. Commentary on the lineage of Buddha Dīpaṅkara:
Those lay followers residing in the city of Ramma, having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, ...

Again, when the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, they honored him with garlands, perfumes, and other offerings, and having paid homage, they sat down close by, desiring to hear the expression of appreciation for their gift.
Then the Teacher offered them an expression of appreciation for the gift that was most sweet and heart-stirring:
“Giving is considered the supreme cause Of happiness and all other blessings.”
But Nibbāna is said to be the staircase and the firm foundation.
"Generosity is the refuge of humans; generosity is their kinsman and their ultimate resort.
For beings who have fallen into suffering, generosity is the supreme goal."
“Giving is illustrated as a ship in the sense of carrying one across suffering;
giving is praised as a city in the sense of protection from fear.
Giving is said to be like a venomous snake in the sense of being difficult to approach.”
Generosity is unstained by the impurities of greed and the like, just as a lotus is unstained [by water].
"In this world, there is no support for a person equal to generosity;
therefore, practice it with both action and intention."
“The wise person here gives gifts that are the cause for rebirth in the heavenly world;
for what man in this world, delighting in his own welfare, would not give?
Having heard of the prosperity among the gods that arises from giving, what man would not give?”
One should give a gift that bestows happiness,
a gift that gladdens the mind. By practicing generosity,
one is surrounded by celestial nymphs and delights for a very long time in the Nandana Grove, the delight of the gods.
“The donor experiences the excellence of joy; he gains respect in this world.
The donor attains infinite fame, and the donor becomes trustworthy.
Having given a gift, that person goes forth with abundant wealth and long life.”
One finds a form of beautiful voice and sports with the gods in heaven,
staying in various celestial mansions resounding with the cries of intoxicated peacocks.
"Theft, enemies, kings, water, and fire— giving is wealth that cannot be shared with these."
“He gives [the fruit of] that level of the disciple’s knowledge, as well as the level of the Paccekabuddha and the level of the Buddha.

Having expressed appreciation for the gift in this manner and having thus proclaimed the benefits of giving, he immediately thereafter delivered a discourse on virtue (*sīla*). This virtue is indeed the root of prosperity in both this world and the next:
“Virtue is the supreme cause of happiness; by virtue, the virtuous one goes to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.”
For one who has entered the cycle of existence, virtue is indeed a refuge, a shelter, and a final resort.
"Where else in this world or the next can there be for people a support equal to virtue?
Virtue is the supreme foundation of all qualities, just as the earth is the foundation for all things stable and moving."
“Virtue alone is indeed beautiful; virtue is unsurpassed in the world.
It is the conduct and practice of the Noble Ones, by which one is called ‘virtuous.
There is no ornament equal to the ornament of virtue; there is no fragrance equal to the fragrance of virtue; there is no purifier of the stains of defilements equal to virtue.”
There is nothing equal to virtue for the quelling of fever; there is nothing equal to virtue for generating renown;
there is no stairway for ascending to heaven equal to virtue; and for entering the city of Nibbāna, there is no door equal to virtue. As it has been said:
"Kings adorned with pearls and gems do not shine so brightly as those who are adorned with the jewel of virtue."
Just as those who strive shine, adorned with the ornament of virtue—
where indeed could there be a fragrance equal to the fragrance of virtue,
which wafts equally both with the wind and against the wind?
“The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine;
but the fragrance of the virtuous goes against the wind—the person of integrity wafts in all directions.
Whether it be sandalwood or tagara, or even the blue lotus or the vassikī flower...”
Of all these kinds of fragrances, the fragrance of virtue is unsurpassed:
“Neither the Gaṅgā nor the Yamunā, nor the Sarabhū or the Sarasvatī;
nor the river Aciravatī, nor even the Mahī, the great river.”
“Living beings here are able to cleanse that defilement;
indeed, it is the water of virtue that cleanses the defilement of sentient beings.
Neither the winds accompanied by rain-clouds nor even yellow sandalwood can do so.”
Neither necklaces nor jewels, nor the rays of the moon,
can soothe the burning fever of beings here in this world as effectively as this noble virtue, which is supremely cool and brings peace.
“Virtue always destroys for the virtuous the fear of self-reproach and the like, and it constantly generates fame and laughter.
Where else is there a staircase for ascending to heaven equal to virtue?”
Or rather, Nibbāna is like a gateway for entering the city.
Thus, you should know the unsurpassed benefit of virtue, which is the root of all good qualities and the destroyer of the strength of faults.
Having thus shown the benefits of virtue, the Blessed One then spoke on the subject of heaven in order to demonstrate: "Relying upon this very virtue, one attains this heaven.
This so-called heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing;
it is exclusively blissful, where play is eternal and prosperity is ever-present. The gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings [dwell there] for nine million years.
They obtain divine happiness and divine prosperity. He spoke such discourse connected with the qualities of heaven as: "The Thirty-three [gods] remain for thirty-six million years," and so forth.
Having thus enticed them with talk of heaven, he then spoke of the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, saying:
"Even this heaven is impermanent and unstable; one should not form desire or lust for it."
Having proclaimed the benefits of renunciation, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma that culminates in the Deathless.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to that great multitude, some took refuge [in the Triple Gem], some undertook the five precepts, some attained the fruit of stream-entry,
some the fruit of once-returning, some the fruit of non-returning, some all four fruits, and some three.

Having established some in the true knowledges (*vijjā*), some in the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and some in the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), he rose from his seat, departed from the city of Ramma, and entered the Sudassana Great Monastery. Thus it is said:
“Then, having fed the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha...”
They went for refuge to that Teacher, Dīpaṅkara.
“The Tathāgata establishes some in the going for refuge;
he establishes others in the five precepts, and still others in the tenfold morality.”
“To some he gives the state of recluseship, the four supreme fruits;
to some he gives the peerless states, the analytical knowledges.
To some the Bull among Men gives the eight excellent attainments.”
He bestowed upon someone the three true knowledges and the six direct knowledges.
By that means, the Great Sage exhorted the multitude of people;
by that means, the teaching of the Lord of the World became widespread.
“Mahāhanu, Sabhakkhandha, and Dīpaṅkara by name—
these deliver many people and liberate them from miserable rebirths.
Having seen people capable of being awakened, even at a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas,”
"Having approached in an instant, the Great Sage awakened him.
In this context, "them" refers to the lay followers residing in the city of Ramma. Regarding "refuge": here, refuge, the act of going for refuge, and the one who goes for refuge should be understood.
It is called *saraṇa* because it "remembers," "harms," or "destroys" [the defilements]. What is that? It is the Triple Gem. That—
However, for those who have gone for refuge, that very act of going for refuge destroys, harms, and annihilates fear, terror, suffering, states of woe, and defilement;
thus it is called "refuge" (*saraṇa*). For this has been said:
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, they shall not go to the plane of misery."
Having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas.
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, they shall not go to the plane of misery;
having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas.”
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha will not go to the plane of misery;
having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas.

Going for refuge (saraṇagamana) is a mental state that arises in the manner of taking the Three Jewels as one’s ultimate resort. One who goes for refuge is the person who possesses that state. Thus, these three—refuge, going for refuge, and the one who goes for refuge—should be understood.

*Tassa* means "to him," namely Dīpaṅkara; it should be understood as a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. There is also a reading: *“Upagacchuṃ saraṇaṃ tatthā”* (they went there for refuge). *Satthuno* means "the Teacher.
Regarding the phrase *kañci saraṇāgamane*, the meaning is that he established some person in the going for refuge.
Although this was stated by way of the present tense, the meaning should be understood by way of the past tense. This...
The same method applies to the others as well. There is also a reading, "In the taking of refuge by someone," and its meaning is the very same.

"To someone in the five precepts" means he established a certain person in the five precepts of abstinence (*virati*). There is also a reading, "In the five precepts for someone," and its meaning is the same.
"In the tenfold precepts for another" means he established another person in the tenfold precepts.
The meaning is as follows. There is also a reading, “To someone, ten wholesome [states],” the meaning of which is that he exhorted a certain person in the ten wholesome qualities.

Regarding the phrase, “He gives to someone the state of recluseship” (*sāmañña*): here, in the ultimate sense, “the state of recluseship” refers to the Path. As it is said: “And what, monks, is the state of recluseship?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say: right view... right concentration. This, monks, is called the state of recluseship.”
"Four supreme fruits" means four supreme fruits; the letter *ma* is used for metrical conjunction. It is stated with a change of gender.
The meaning is that, according to his specific support (*upanissaya*), he gave to someone the four paths and the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
"To someone incomparable dharmas" means he gave to someone the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), which are without equal.
"To some, the excellent attainments" means that he gave to some the eight principal attainments through the removal of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

"To some, the three types of clear knowledge" means that, depending on the specific individual's underlying support (*upanissaya*), he gave to some the three types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) by way of the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*). "He bestows the six direct knowledges" means that he gave the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) to some.
"By that method" means by that principle and by that sequence. "The multitude of people" (*janakāya*) means a collection of people. "He exhorted" (*ovadati*) means he exhorted (*ovadi*).
It should be understood that this is stated using a shift in tense; in similar expressions hereafter, the meaning should be taken according to the past tense alone.
"By that it became widespread" means by that exhortation and instruction of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara.
The Dispensation became widespread, extensive, and vast.
Regarding "Mahāhanu": it is said that great men possess two full jaws which, like the moon on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight, have a shape resembling the moon;
he whose jaws were thus large was Mahāhanu, meaning he had "lion-like jaws. Regarding "Usabhakkhandho":

He whose shoulder is like that of a bull is "Usabhakkhandha" (Bull-shouldered). The meaning is: one with a beautiful, well-rounded shoulder resembling a well-fashioned golden pillar, possessing a symmetrical and lovely shoulder.
"Named Dīpaṅkara" means he whose name was Dīpaṅkara. "He ferried many people across" means he caused many people who were to be guided by a Buddha to cross over.
"He liberated" means he caused them to be fully released. "From a miserable state" (*duggati*); this is the accusative case used in the sense of the ablative.
Now, in order to show the manner of performing the act of ferrying across and liberating, the verse beginning with “the people who are to be awakened” was spoken.

Therein, “the people who are to be awakened” means the generation of those to be awakened; this is indeed the reading. “Having seen” means having seen either with the Buddha-eye or with the universal eye.
“Even at a hundred thousand yojanas” means even though they are situated at many hundreds of thousands of yojanas away.
However, it should be understood that this was said specifically with reference to the ten-thousandfold world system.
It is said that after the Teacher Dīpaṅkara had attained Buddhahood and spent seven weeks at the foot of the Bodhi tree, on the eighth week,
having accepted the invitation of Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma, he set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma in the Sunanda Garden.
He caused hundreds of millions of gods and humans to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. This was the first realization.

Then the Teacher, knowing that his own son—whose shoulders were well-rounded like those of a bull and who was named Usabhakkhandha—had reached maturity in wisdom, made that son his foremost and taught him the Dhamma similar to the "Exhortation to Rāhula," for the sake of gods and humans.
He caused ninety million beings to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. This was the second great realization (abhisamaya).

Then, at the gate of the city of Amaravatī, at the foot of the Mahāsiri tree, the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle, liberated the great multitude from their bonds, and, surrounded by a host of deities, dwelt in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven—a palace radiating a splendor exceeding that of the sun.
Seated at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree upon the supremely cool Paṇḍukambala stone slab,
the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara— the God of Gods, whose purity is known by the entire world— placed Queen Sumedhā, the mother who brings joy to the entire host of deities,
at his head, and [taught] the Seven Treatises (*sattappakaraṇa*), which bring benefit to all beings and are supremely, exceedingly profound, subtle, and clarifying to the intellect.
Having taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, he caused ninety thousand koṭis of devas to drink the nectar of the Dhamma.
This was the third great realization (abhisamaya). Thus it is said:
"At the first great realization, the Buddha awakened a hundred koṭis."
At the second realization, the Protector awakened ninety koṭis.
And when the Buddha taught the Dhamma in the abode of the gods,
there was a third realization for ninety thousand koṭis.
The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara had three assemblies of disciples. Among them, the first assembly took place in Sunandārāma, consisting of one hundred thousand koṭis. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara;
The first gathering was of one hundred thousand koṭis.”
Then, on another occasion, the One of Ten Powers, surrounded by four hundred thousand bhikkhus,
wandering on tour through villages, market towns, and cities while bestowing favor upon the great masses of people, eventually arrived at a certain place. There,

he encountered a mountain peak that was renowned throughout the world for the honors paid to it by the great multitude, protected by non-human beings, exceedingly terrifying, and kissed by hanging clouds.
He reached the mountain named Nāradakūṭa, which was most delightful, its peaks scented by the flowers of various fragrant trees and frequented by many herds of wild beasts.
It is said that this mountain was possessed by a yakṣa named Nārada;
there, every year, the great multitude of people would bring a human sacrifice for that yakṣa.

Then, it is said, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, having perceived the excellence of that great multitude’s spiritual potential (*upanissaya-sampatti*), dispatched the Saṅgha of monks to the four quarters.
Then, alone and without a companion, his heart moved by the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he ascended Mount Nārada in order to convert that *yakkha*.
Now, that one who subsisted on human flesh was indifferent to his own welfare and intent on the slaughter of others.
Unable to endure the Buddha’s reproach, the yakkha, his mind overcome by anger, shook that mountain, desiring to terrify and drive away the One of Ten Powers.
As that mountain was being shaken by him, it seemed as though it were falling right upon the Blessed One’s own head through the power of the Blessed One’s majesty.
Then, terrified, he thought, “Well now, I shall consume him with fire,” and he conjured up a great mass of flames of most terrifying appearance.
That mass of flames, like a fire cast against a headwind, produced suffering for himself alone;
it was not even capable of burning a single thread of the Blessed One’s robe. But the yakkha [thought], “The ascetic has been consumed!”

Looking about and thinking, "He is not burned," he saw the One of Ten Powers—the Blessed One—seated like the cool center of a lotus upon the surface of cool water, resembling the moon that brings delight to all people with its mass of stainless rays during the autumn season;
and seeing him, he thought: "Oh, how great is the power of this ascetic! Whatever harm I do to him, each and every one of those..."
"It falls right back upon me; yet, having abandoned this ascetic, I have no other refuge or resort.
Just as those who stumble on the earth rise up relying on the very earth, let me go for refuge to this very ascetic."

But having thought thus, he prostrated his head at the Blessed One’s feet, which were marked with wheels, and said, “Venerable Sir, transgression has overcome me,” and thus he went for refuge to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One spoke to him in gradual discourse.
At the conclusion of that teaching, together with ten thousand *yakkhas*, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
It is said that on that day, all the people dwelling throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa brought one man from each village for the purpose of making an offering to him.
They also brought vast quantities of sesame, rice, horse-gram, mung beans, black gram, and so forth, as well as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and other such items.
Then, on that day, that yakṣa gave all the rice and other provisions brought to them back to those very people.
He presented the men brought back for the sake of the ritual to the One Possessing the Ten Powers.
Then the Teacher, having ordained those men through the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-pabbajjā*), established them all in Arahatship within seven days.
On the full moon day of Māgha, in the midst of an assembly of one hundred million monks endowed with the four factors, he [preached].

He recited the Pātimokkha. The four factors are as follows: all were "come-hither" monks (ehibhikkhus), all possessed the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā), all had arrived without being invited, and it was the fifteenth day of the Uposatha.
This was the second assembly. Thus it is said:
“Furthermore, when the Conqueror had gone to seclusion at Nāradakūṭa, one hundred million [monks] whose taints were destroyed and who were free from stain assembled there.
In this context, “gone to seclusion” means having departed from the group. “Assembled” means they gathered together.
When Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, entered the rainy-season retreat on the mountain named Sudassana,
it is said that the people dwelling in Jambudīpa held an annual festival at the foot of a hill.
At that festival, the people who had gathered there, having seen the One of Ten Powers and heard his discourse on the Dhamma, gained confidence in him and went forth into homelessness.
On the day of the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā), the Teacher gave a discourse on insight (vipassanā) suited to their inclinations.
Having heard it, they all contemplated all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) and, through the successive stages of insight and the successive stages of the path, attained Arahatship.
Then the Teacher invited [alms] together with ninety billion followers. This was the third great assembly. Thus it is said:
“At the time when the Great Hero, the Great Sage,
was offering alms to ninety thousand koṭis on the Sudassana mountain of stone,
I at that time was a matted-hair ascetic, practicing fierce austerities.”
“Wandering through the air, he reached the further shore of the five supernormal powers.
This verse is recorded in the *Dīpaṅkara-buddhavaṃsa* within the *Nidāna-vaṇṇanā* (Introduction) of the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
However, it does not appear in this [present] *Buddhavaṃsa*. Its absence alone is more appropriate. Why?
Why? Because it was already explained below in the discourse on Sumedha.
Indeed, while the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was teaching the Dhamma, there was an attainment of the Dhamma by ten thousand and twenty thousand beings.
However, regarding those who attained it one by one, two by two, three by three, four by four, and so forth—the end of such attainments—[is as follows].
There was none. Therefore, the teaching of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara became widespread and well-known among many people. Thus it is said:
“For ten thousand and twenty thousand, there was the realization of the Dhamma;
The realizations of those who attained it singly or in pairs were beyond counting.”
In this context, "ten or twenty thousand" means ten thousand and twenty thousand.
"The realization of the Dhamma" (*dhammābhisamaya*) is the penetration of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "One or two" means one and two;
by way of the sequence beginning with "three, four... ten," the meaning is that they are incalculable (*asaṅkhyeyya*). And because there is such an incalculable realization, it is widespread.
It had reached greatness; it was to be known as "widely recognized" (bāhujañña) by many wise gods and humans because it was leading to liberation.
It was "prosperous" (iddha) through the training in higher virtue and so forth, and "flourishing" (phīta) through concentration and so forth. Therefore it is said:
"It was widespread, widely recognized, prosperous, and flourishing at that time."
“The dispensation of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was well-purified.
