In this context, “well-purified” means it was thoroughly purified and made pure by the Blessed One.
It is said that during the time of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara, there were four hundred thousand bhikkhus who possessed the six supernormal knowledges and great psychic power at all times.
They surrounded him. At that time, those who were still in training (sekkha) who passed away were subject to criticism;
the intention is that all [who passed away] attained final nibbāna only after becoming those whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava).
Therefore, the teaching of that Blessed One was truly in full bloom and highly prosperous, being exceedingly resplendent with bhikkhus whose taints were destroyed. Thus it was said:
“Four hundred thousand [beings], possessing the six higher knowledges and great psychic power,
always surrounded Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World.
Whosoever at that time abandoned their human existence,”
“Those trainees who have not yet attained the goal are subject to reproach.
But the well-flowered dispensation, by means of such Arhats—
those stainless ones whose taints are destroyed— is ever resplendent.”
In this context, the number "four hundred thousand" is shown by way of enumeration;
however, the phrase "sixfold-versed and of great psychic power" is stated for the purpose of identifying these bhikkhus. Thus the meaning should be understood.

Alternatively, "sixfold-versed and of great psychic power" should be seen as a nominative plural used in the sense of a genitive (possessive), meaning "of those who are sixfold-versed and of great psychic power."
"Parivārenti sabbadā" means they attend upon the One of Ten Powers at all times; the intention is that, having left the Blessed One, they do not go anywhere else.
"Tena samayena" means at that time. Furthermore, this word *samaya* is seen in nine senses, such as "assemblage" (*samavāya*) and so forth. As it has been said:
“*Samavāya* is seen in the sense of conjunction, moment, time, collection, cause, view, acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.
Here, it should be understood as “time”; the meaning is “in that time. *Mānusaṃ bhavaṃ* means the human state. *Appattamānasā* means...
Those by whom the mind (*mānasa*) has not been reached or attained are "those who have not reached the mind. *Mānasa* is a designation for passion (*rāga*), consciousness (*citta*), and Arahantship.
For in the passage, "The snare that moves through the air is this which moves as the mind," passion is called "the mind.
In the passage, "Consciousness, mind, the mental, the heart, the pure," it refers to consciousness.
Regarding the phrase, “A trainee who has not yet attained his heart’s ideal might pass away, O hearer of men,” it refers here to *arahatta* (Arahatship).
In this context as well, only Arahatship is intended. Therefore, the meaning is: those who have not yet attained the fruit of Arahatship. In what sense are they called “trainees” (*sekha*)?
They are trainees in the sense of having acquired the qualities of a trainee. For this has been said: “In what way, venerable sir, is one a trainee? Here, monks, a monk...”
“He is possessed of the right view of one in training... he is possessed of the right concentration of one in training.
To this extent, monks, a monk is one in training. Furthermore, they train, thus they are called *sekhā*.
For it has been said: “He trains, he trains, monk; therefore he is called ‘one in training. And what does he train in? He trains in higher virtue...”
“Because he trains in higher mind and also trains in higher wisdom, monk, for that reason he is called a ‘trainee’ (sekha).
“Well-flowered” means fully blossomed. “Pāvacana” means praised speech; alternatively, speech that has reached growth is *pavacana*, and *pāvacana* is simply *pavacana*;
the meaning is “the teaching” (*sāsana*). “It shines forth” means it is resplendent, it glows intensely.
"Sabbadā" means at all times. There is also a reading:
"It shines forth in the world with its gods. That Blessed One Dīpaṅkara had a city named Rammavatī;
his father was the kṣatriya Sudeva, his mother was Queen Sumedhā, his two chief disciples were Sumaṅgala and Tissa, and his attendant was named Sāgata.
Nandā and Sunandā were his two chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One was a *pipphali* tree, eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of showing these [details] such as the birth city and so forth?
It is said: if neither the birth city, nor the father, nor the mother of a person were known, [the lineage would remain obscure].
Furthermore, neither his birthplace, nor his father, nor his mother is known; he is thought to be either a god, Sakka, a yakkha, Māra, or Brahmā.

Thinking that such a miracle is not extraordinary even for the gods, they would consider it unworthy of being heard or believed, and consequently, there would be no realization (*abhisamaya*). In the absence of realization...

The arising of a Buddha would be purposeless, and the Teaching would not lead to liberation. Therefore, the specific details regarding the birthplace and other particulars of all Buddhas must be shown. Thus it was said:
“The city was named Rammavatī, and the kshatriya king was named Sudeva;”
The mother of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Sumedhā.
Sumaṅgala and Tissa were his two chief disciples,
and the attendant of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Sāgata.
“Nandā and Sunandā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Pipphalī.
Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, was eighty cubits in height.”
He shines like a lamp-tree, like a king of sal trees in full bloom.
For a hundred thousand years was the lifespan of that Great Sage;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
“Having kindled the True Dharma and having brought many people across, he—
like a blazing mass of fire— has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.
That psychic power, that glory, and those wheel-treasures upon his feet [have all vanished].”
"All that has vanished; are not all conditioned things empty?
In this context, "the kṣatriya named Sudeva" means that Sudeva was the name of his father, the kṣatriya. "Janikā" means mother.
"Pipphalī" refers to the Bodhi tree, which was a *pilakkha* (ficus religiosa) or *kapitana* tree. "Eighty cubits high" means eighty *hattha*s in height.

"Exalted in height. "Like a lamp-tree": just as a lamp-tree crowded with blazing garlands of lamps shines, so too the Blessed One, during his lifetime, shone—endowed with the perfection of height, circumference, and shape;
his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the secondary characteristics;

and like the vault of the sky made brilliant by a multitude of stars, he was radiant with the spreading web of his rays—and thus he "shone" (*sobhittha*). "Like a king of *sāla* trees in full bloom": he was "in bloom" (*phullita*) [like that tree].
Like a king of sal trees in full bloom, and like a *pāricchattaka* tree a hundred yojanas high in full bloom, the Blessed One, eighty cubits tall, shone exceedingly.
"For a hundred thousand years" means his lifespan was one hundred thousand years; "remaining for that long" means for that duration of time.

“Remaining for a time”: for a duration. “The multitude of people” (*janataṃ*): a collection of persons. “Having ferried across the great multitude” (*mahājanaṃ*): having caused the great mass of people to cross over.
There is also a reading, “having ferried across including the world of devas” (*santāretvā sadevakaṃ*); its meaning is “the world together with the devas.
“And that psychic power” (*iddhi*): that excellence, that majesty. “And that glory” (*yaso*): that retinue. “All that has vanished” (*sabbaṃ tamantarahitaṃ*): all of that [has disappeared].
The meaning is that the kind of excellence already described has disappeared and vanished.
"Are not all formations empty?"—indeed, are not all conditioned phenomena empty and hollow? The meaning is that they are devoid of such things as permanence and essence.
Here, however, the description of the city and so forth has indeed come down in the Pāḷi; but the section on the multitude of people has not, and that should be brought in.

It should be illustrated. Namely: the delimitation of sons, the delimitation of wife, the delimitation of the palace, the delimitation of household life, the delimitation of female dancers, the delimitation of the Great Departure, the delimitation of striving, the delimitation of the monastery, and the delimitation of attendants.
The reason for illustrating these has already been stated above. Now, as for that Dīpaṅkara...
He had three hundred thousand wives. His chief queen was named Padumā, and his son was named Usabhakkhandha. Thus it is said:
“His wife was named Padumā, with a face like a full-blown lotus;
His biological son was Usabhakkhandha, of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.”
“Hamsa, Koñca, and the one called Mayūra—these three are considered palaces;
it is said that he lived in the household for ten thousand years.
Departing on an elephant vehicle, the Victor resided in the Nanda Garden.”
"Nanda was indeed his attendant, who brought joy to the world.
Furthermore, there are five differences among all Buddhas: difference in lifespan, difference in physical stature, difference in lineage, difference in exertion, and difference in rays of light.
Among these, "difference in lifespan" means that some have long lifespans while others do not.
They have short lifespans. For instance, the lifespan of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was one hundred thousand years, whereas that of our Blessed One is one hundred years.
This difference in measure means that some are long and some are short. Thus, Dīpaṅkara was eighty cubits in height, while our Blessed One is eighteen cubits in height.

"Variety of family" means that some are reborn in a kṣatriya family and some in a brāhmaṇa family; for instance, Dīpaṅkara and others were reborn in kṣatriya families, while Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and others were reborn in brāhmaṇa families.
"Variety of exertion" means that for some the exertion is merely brief, as in the case of the Blessed One Kassapa, while for others it is enduring, as in the case of our own Blessed One.
"Variety of rays" means that from the body of the Blessed One Maṅgala, rays spread throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.
It stood at a distance of one fathom from our Blessed One. In that regard, the extent of the rays is dependent upon one's intention (*ajjhāsaya*).
Whosoever desires as much as they wish, to that person that much radiance of the body spreads forth. However, Maṅgala’s intention was, "May it spread throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system.
Yet, regarding the qualities already penetrated, there is no such thing as a difference between any [of them].
Likewise, there are four places that all Buddhas never abandon. The Bodhi throne is never abandoned; it remains in one and the same place.
The site for turning the Wheel of Dhamma is likewise never abandoned; it is at Isipatana in the Deer Park.
At the time of descending from the deva realm, the first step taken at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa is likewise never abandoned. [And so too] in Jeta’s Grove.
The four feet of the bed in the Fragrant Chamber remain fixed in place; the vihāra itself also remains fixed.
It may be either small or large.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between our own Blessed One’s simultaneous boundary (*sahajāta-pariccheda*) and the lunar mansion boundary (*nakkhatta-pariccheda*).
It is said that these were our co-natal companions with the Omniscient Bodhisatta:
Rāhulamātā, the Elder Ānanda, Channa, Kaṇḍaka the king of horses, the treasure jars, the Great Bodhi Tree, and Kāḷudāyī.
It is said that the Great Man descended into his mother’s womb under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha, and likewise departed on the Great Renunciation and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
He set the wheel of Dhamma in motion and performed the Twin Miracle. He was born under the constellation Viśākhā, attained full enlightenment under Viśākhā, and passed into parinirvāṇa under Viśākhā.
Under the constellation Māgha, there occurred both the assembly of his disciples and his relinquishing of the life-faculty. Under the constellation Assayuja, he descended from the deva realm.
Having brought these points forward, it should be explained. This is the section defining the numerous instances. The remaining verses are indeed with their respective origins (sauttānā).
Thus the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, having remained for the full span of his life and performed all the duties of a Buddha, eventually attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
In the same eon in which the Ten-Powered One Dīpaṅkara appeared, there were three other Buddhas as well: Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and Saraṇaṅkara.
However, there was no formal prophecy concerning the Bodhisatta in their presence.
Therefore, they have not been shown here. However, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), in order to show all the Buddhas who appeared from the beginning of that *kappa* onwards, this was said:
“Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and also Saraṇaṅkara;”
The Fully Enlightened One Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, the supreme among bipeds;
Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, the Sage Sobhita;
Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, and Padumuttara.
“Sumedha and Sujāta, Piyadassi of great renown;
Atthadassi and Dhammadassi, Siddhattha, the Leader of the World.
Tissa and Phussa, the Sambuddhas; Vipassi, Sikhi, and Vessabhu.”
Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa the Leader—
these were the Fully Enlightened Ones, free from passion and composed in mind;
they arose like suns of a hundred rays, dispelling the great darkness.
“Having blazed like masses of fire, they have gone out together with their disciples.
Thus concludes the *Madhuratthavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*,
composed in a manner that is neither too concise nor too prolix.
The commentary on the lineage of Buddha Dīpaṅkara is finished.
The first lineage of Buddhas is completed.
4. Commentary on the lineage of Buddha Koṇḍañña.
It is said that when the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara had attained final Nibbāna, his dispensation continued for one hundred thousand years.
Then, with the disappearance of the disciples who had awakened after the Buddha, his dispensation also vanished.
After that, once an incalculable eon had passed, in a certain kappa a teacher named Koṇḍañña appeared.
Thus, the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections for sixteen incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, having brought the knowledge of enlightenment (*bodhiñāṇa*) to maturity,
and having remained in an existence similar to that of Vessantara, passed away from there and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Having lived there for the full span of his lifespan and given his promise to the deities, he passed away from the Tusita heaven and [was conceived] in the city of Rammavatī.
He took rebirth in the womb of Queen Sujātā in the family of King Sunanda.
At the moment of his conception, thirty-two miracles occurred, of the same nature as those described in the lineage of Buddha Dīpaṅkara.
Protected by the deities who had made arrangements for his defense, at the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb.
Having emerged, the one who surpasses all beings walked seven steps facing north;
then, having surveyed all directions, he uttered this lion’s roar: “I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world;
this is my final birth; now there is no more renewed existence.”
Then, on the day of the prince’s naming ceremony, those performing the naming gave him the name Koṇḍañña. For that Blessed One was of the Koṇḍañña clan.
It is said that he had three palaces—named Rāma, Surāma, and Subha—which were exceedingly delightful.
Within them, three hundred thousand female dancers, skilled in dancing, singing, and instrumental music, were constantly present at his service.
...existed. His chief queen was named Rucidevī. He had a son named Vijitasena.
He lived as a householder for ten thousand years.
Then, having seen those who were aged, sick, dying, and those who had gone forth, he departed in a noble chariot, went forth, and [attained] the ten...

He practiced the life of striving for ten months. When Prince Koṇḍañña went forth, ten koṭis of people followed him into the homeless life. Surrounded by them, he practiced the life of striving for ten months;

then, on the full moon day of the month of Visākha, at Sunandagāma, after consuming the most delicious honey-milk-rice offered by the merchant’s daughter named Yasodharā, whose breasts were firm, even, and closely set, [he sat] beneath a tree adorned with fruits, shoots, and sprouts.
Having spent the day’s rest in the Sāla grove, at the time of evening,
leaving his retinue behind and taking the eight handfuls of grass given by the Ājīvaka Sunandaka, he circumambulated the Sālakalyāṇī tree three times,
looked toward the eastern direction, placed the Bodhi tree behind him, and spread out a layer of grass eighty-eight cubits wide.
Having sat cross-legged and resolved upon the fourfold energy, he shattered the army of Māra;
having purified the knowledge of recollecting past lives during the first watch of the night, purified the divine eye during the middle watch,
and comprehended the principle of conditionality during the last watch, he emerged from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing and applied his attention to the five aggregates.
Having seen the fifty characteristics by way of their arising and passing away, and having developed insight up to the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa),

he penetrated the four knowledges of the path, the four knowledges of the fruition, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth, the knowledge that delimits the five destinations,
the six uncommon knowledges, and all the qualities of a Buddha.
With his purpose fulfilled, even as he sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he thought:
“Through many births in saṃsāra I have wandered without finding, seeking the builder of the house; for birth again and again is suffering.”
“House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered.
The mind has reached the unconditioned; it has attained the destruction of craving.”
“Just as the course of a fire, kindled by a blow from an iron bar,
is not known when it has gradually subsided,
so too for those who are rightly liberated, who have crossed over the flood of the bonds of sense-desire.”
“There is no way to describe it; for those who have attained it, there is unshakable happiness.

Having thus uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), and having spent seven weeks right at the foot of the Bodhi tree in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), on the eighth week, in response to the entreaty of Brahmā, [the Blessed One reflected]: “To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?”
While reflecting, "Whom shall I teach? he saw ten billion monks who had gone forth together with him.
[He thought: "These sons of noble family, having accumulated roots of merit, followed me when I went forth; they practiced striving along with me and attended upon me.
Therefore, let me teach the Dhamma to them first of all. Thus...

Having reflected thus, and looking to see where they were dwelling now, he saw that they were staying in the Devavana grove at the city of Aruṇḍhavatī, eighteen yojanas from there. Thinking, "I shall go to teach them the Dhamma," he took his bowl and robe;
and just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, [he vanished from that place].
or might bend his arm; even so, having vanished from the foot of the Bodhi tree, he appeared in the Devavana grove.
At that time, those ten koṭis of bhikkhus were dwelling in the Devavana grove near the city of Aruṇavatī.
When those bhikkhus saw the One of Ten Powers approaching from afar, they went out to meet him with hearts full of faith.
Having received the Blessed One’s bowl and robe, having prepared the Buddha’s seat, and having shown reverence to the Teacher, they paid homage to the Blessed One and,
surrounding him, sat down to one side. There, the Ten-Powered Koṇḍañña, the Sage,

seated upon the Buddha’s throne and surrounded by a host of sages, shone like the thousand-eyed Indra surrounded by the hosts of the Thirty-three, or like the moon at the autumn season risen in the stainless vault of the sky.
He shone like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars.

Then the Teacher, having preached to them the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta—the unsurpassed discourse on the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, which has three revolutions and twelve aspects, and which is frequented by all Buddhas—he caused ten million bhikkhus, headed by the ten crores, as well as ten million deities and humans, to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. Thus it was said:
"After Dīpaṅkara, there was a leader named Koṇḍañña,
of infinite splendor and immeasurable fame, unfathomable and difficult to approach.
He was like the earth in patience and like the ocean in virtue."
In concentration he is like Mount Meru; in wisdom he is like the sky.
The Buddha, for the benefit of all living beings, constantly proclaimed the exposition of the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, and the truths.
“When Koṇḍañña, the Leader of the World, was setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, there was the first realization for one hundred thousand times ten million [beings].
In this context, “after the time of Dīpaṅkara” means after the period of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara. Koṇḍañña...
"By name" means one who has acquired a name according to his own clan. "Leader" means a guide.

"Of infinite splendor" means one whose splendor—consisting of his own virtue, qualities, knowledge, and merit—is infinite. From the Avīci hell below to the peak of existence above, and throughout the infinite world-systems across the intermediate directions, not even a single person is capable of standing before him while gazing upon his face.
There was no limit to it; therefore, he is called "of infinite splendor" (anantatejo). "Of immeasurable fame" (amitayaso) means having an infinite retinue.
For during that Blessed One’s time, from the hundred thousand years until the moment of his final nibbāna, there was no measurable limit to the number of the assembly of monks.
Therefore, he is called "of immeasurable fame. Furthermore, the praise of his immeasurable virtues is also called "immeasurable fame."
"Immeasurable" means that he is immeasurable by way of the measure of his multitude of qualities. As it is said:

"Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of a Buddha for an eon, without speaking of anything else, the eon might be exhausted in its long duration, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted."

Therefore, because he possesses an immeasurable multitude of virtues, he is called "immeasurable" (*appameyyo*). "Difficult to approach" (*durāsado*) means difficult to draw near; he is "difficult to approach" because it is impossible to approach him by attacking or provoking him—the meaning is that he is difficult to overcome.

"Like the earth" (*dharaṇūpamo*) means equal to the earth. By "forbearance" (*khamanena*), that is, by patience, he is "like the earth" because, like the great earth which is four hundred and twenty thousand yojanas thick, he remains unshaken by natural winds or by gain and loss, the desirable and the undesirable, and so forth.
It is said: "By virtue, he is like the ocean" means that through the restraint of virtue, by way of not transgressing its boundary, he is equal to the ocean.
For it is said: "The great ocean, bhikkhus, is stable in nature; it does not overstep its shore.
"By concentration, he is like Mount Meru" means that because he is free from the shaking produced by states opposed to concentration, he is like Meru, the king of mountains.
"Equal" means "similar. Alternatively, it means his body is more steadfast than even the excellent Mount Meru.

Regarding the phrase "like the sky by way of knowledge," here a comparison is made with the infinite space because of the infinite nature of the Blessed One’s knowledge. Four infinities were taught by the Blessed One, as he said:
“The body of beings and space, the world-systems and their infinity,
the Buddha’s knowledge is immeasurable— it is not possible to fully comprehend these.
Therefore, a comparison is made between infinite knowledge and infinite space.
"Proclamation of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path, and truths":
by the inclusion of these faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, paths, and truths, the foundations of mindfulness, right exertions, and bases of psychic power are also included.

Therefore, the meaning is that he proclaimed—that is, taught—the Dhamma which makes manifest the thirty-seven states conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) by way of these four groups beginning with the faculties.
"For the welfare" means for the sake of benefit. "While setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma" refers to when the knowledge of teaching was being set in motion.
Subsequently, at the great assembly of auspiciousness, deities from ten thousand world-systems, having manifested subtle bodies, gathered together in this very world-system.
It is said that there, a certain son of the gods [addressed] Koṇḍañña, the One of Ten Powers.
He asked about the question of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). The Blessed One explained the auspicious factors to him. Therein, ninety thousand koṭis attained *arahantship*.
As for those who had attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotāpanna*) and so forth, there was no limit to their number. Therefore it is said:
“After that, as he continued teaching in the assembly of humans and gods...”
“There was a second realization for ninety thousand koṭis.
Regarding that, “after that” means at a later time. “While he was teaching” means while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma. “Of men and gods” means of both humans and immortals (gods).
Furthermore, when the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle, which crushes the pride of the heretics, in the vault of the sky—
While teaching the Dhamma, eighty thousand times ten million attained arahantship.
Those established in the three fruits were beyond counting. Therefore it was said:
“When he taught the Dhamma, crushing the heretics;”
“There was a third realization for eighty thousand crores.
In this context, the meaning should be understood by supplying the word *tadā* (then): when the Blessed One taught the Dhamma, then there was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty thousand crores.
It is said that after the Teacher had attained full enlightenment, during his first rainy season retreat, he stayed near the city of Candavatī.
He dwelt in the Candāra Park. There, Bhadda Māṇava— the son of the brahmin mahāsāla Sucindharo—
and Subhadda Māṇava— the son of the brahmin Yasodhara— having heard the teaching of the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha Koṇḍañña,
with minds full of faith, [approached] him together with ten thousand young brahmins.
Having gone forth, they attained arahantship.
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Jeṭṭha, the Teacher Koṇḍañña—surrounded by one hundred thousand crores led by the Elder Subhadda—proclaimed the Pātimokkha;
that was the first great assembly. After that, during the time of the Teacher Koṇḍañña...
When his son named Vijitasena had attained *arahantship*, the Blessed One recited the *Pātimokkha* in the midst of a gathering headed by him, consisting of one thousand million followers;

that was the second great assembly. Then, at another time, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, the Ten-Powered One ordained King Udena—who was accompanied by a retinue of nine hundred million people—along with that entire assembly.
When he had attained Arahantship, the Blessed One, surrounded by ninety million Arahants headed by him, recited the Pātimokkha;
that was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies, O Koṇḍañña, of the Great Sage.”
“Of those whose taints were exhausted, stainless, with peaceful minds and poised—
there was a first assembly of one hundred thousand times ten million,
a second of ten thousand times ten million, and a third of ninety times ten million.”
At that time, it is said, our Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch named Vijitāvī, was residing in the city of Candavatī.

Surrounded by many eminent men, he protected the earth—which dwells upon the ocean, is bounded by Mount Meru and Mount Yugandhara, and possesses immeasurable wealth—by means of righteousness alone, without the rod or the sword.
At that same time, the Buddha Koṇḍañña was also surrounded by a hundred thousand koṭis of those whose taints were exhausted.
While wandering on a tour of the countryside, he eventually arrived at the city of Candavatī. King Vijitāvī,
having heard that the Perfectly Enlightened One had arrived in his city, went out to meet him,
prepared a dwelling place for the Blessed One, and invited him together with the community of monks for the following day’s meal.

On the following day, having prepared the meal arrangements very well, he gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, numbering one hundred thousand crores. After the Bodhisatta had fed the Blessed One, at the conclusion of the expression of thanks, he requested:
"Venerable Sir, please dwell right here for the three months, gathering the great multitude. For those three months, [the Buddha] stayed continuously...
He gave an incomparable great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Then the Teacher, having prophesied of the Bodhisatta, "In the future he will become a Buddha named Gotama," taught him the Dhamma.
Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he handed over his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and mastered the Three Piṭakas.
Having developed the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges, he was reborn in the Brahma-world without falling away from his jhāna. Therefore it was said:
“At that time, I was a noble named Vijitāvī;
I exercised sovereign power over the ocean to its very limits.”
“I satisfied one hundred thousand times ten million stainless Great Seers,
together with the Lord of the World, with the finest rice-milk.
That Buddha Koṇḍañña, the Leader of the World, also gave me this prediction:”
"In immeasurable eons, a Buddha will appear in the world.
Having exerted himself in striving and performed ascetic practices,
the Greatly Renowned One, a Perfectly Awakened One, will awaken at the foot of an assattha tree."
“His mother who gave him birth shall be named Māyā;
his father shall be named Suddhodana, and he himself shall be Gotama.
Kolita and Upatissa shall be his foremost disciples.”
“Ānanda shall be his attendant, serving that Conqueror.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is said to be the Assattha.”
“Citta and Hatthāḷavaka shall be the foremost attendants;
Nandamātā and Uttarā shall be the foremost female attendants;
the lifespan of that illustrious Gotama shall be one hundred years.”
“Having heard these words of the peerless Great Sage, humans and gods were filled with joy, thinking: ‘This, they say, is the seed of the Buddha.
Shouts of exultation arose, and they clapped their hands and laughed.”
With palms joined in reverence, ten thousand deities pay homage,
saying: "If we fail to fulfill the teaching of this Lord of the World,
in a future time we shall stand face-to-face with him."
"Just as people crossing a river, having missed a convenient ford,
take hold at a lower ford and cross over the great river—
so too, if we all release this Conqueror, [we shall likewise cross over]."
“In a future time, we shall stand face-to-face with him.
Having heard his words, my heart became even more serene;
fulfilling that very purpose, I gave the Great Kingdom to the Victor.
Having bestowed upon me the status of a great king, I went forth into homelessness in his presence.
Having mastered the entire teaching of the Teacher— the Suttantas, the Vinaya,
and the ninefold division— I brought glory to the dispensation of the Conqueror.
“Dwelling there with diligence, whether sitting, standing, or walking, you reached the perfection of direct knowledge and went to the Brahma-world.
Therein, “at that time, I” means at that moment, I. “Named Vijitāvī” refers to the universal monarch (cakkavatti-rāja) who bore that name.

"I existed. Regarding the phrase "having made the ocean my boundary," the meaning is: having established the Cakkavāḷa mountain as the limit and the boundary, I exercised sovereignty making the ocean my end. Up to this point, it was not yet clear.
It is said that the Cakkavatti king, by the power of the Wheel-treasure, took Sineru on his left side and [traversed] across the upper surface of the ocean.
It travels to Pubbavideha, which measures eight thousand yojanas. There, the Wheel-turning Monarch gives this exhortation:
"Living beings must not be killed; what is not given must not be taken; one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehoods; intoxicants must not be drunk;
and you should eat only as much as is required. When this exhortation has been given, that Wheel-treasure—
Having ascended into the air, it plunges into the eastern ocean.
And in proportion as it plunges therein, the waters of the great ocean, having their surging waves contracted, descend a league deep;
and within the ocean, on both sides, they become exceedingly beautiful, like walls of beryl gems.
It remains there; having thus traveled as far as the eastern ocean, that Wheel-Treasure turns back.
As it turns back, the assembly is in front, the Wheel-turning King is in the middle, and the Wheel-Treasure is at the rear.
That water, as if unable to bear separation from the blazing [wheel], approaches the shore while striking right up to the limit of the rim’s circumference.
Thus, having completely conquered Pubbavideha as far as the eastern ocean, the Wheel-turning Monarch,
desiring to conquer Jambudīpa as far as the southern ocean, proceeds toward the southern ocean by the path indicated by the Wheel-treasure.
Having completely conquered that Jambudīpa measuring ten thousand yojanas and having emerged from the southern ocean, he...
Having gone by the same method described below in order to conquer Aparagoyāna, which measures seven thousand yojanas,
and having completely conquered that as well up to the edge of the ocean, he crossed over from the western sea and went in the same manner to conquer Uttarakuru,
which measures eight thousand yojanas; having reached the edge of that sea, he likewise completely conquered it.
He even crosses back from the northern ocean. To this extent, the sovereignty over the earth bounded by the ocean has been attained by the Wheel-turning Monarch.
Therefore it is said: "We exercise sovereignty as far as the very edge of the ocean.
"Hundreds of thousands of millions" means hundreds of thousands of millions; or rather, this is the reading itself. "Pure ones" means those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
"Together with the Lord of the World" means together with the One Possessing the Ten Powers (*dasabala*). "With a hundred thousand crores" is the meaning.

"With supreme food" means with excellent food. "He satisfied them" means he gratified them. "From immeasurable eons" means from this point forward, after passing three incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus a hundred thousand eons, in one auspicious eon (*bhaddakappa*); such is the meaning.

"Exertion" (*padhāna*) means energy (*vīriya*). "Accomplishing that very purpose" means accomplishing, fulfilling, and bringing to completion that very purpose which constitutes the qualities of a Buddha, while fulfilling the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*);
such is the meaning. "Great sovereignty" (*mahārajja*) refers to the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rājja*).

Regarding "to the Victor" (*jine*), it should be understood as either referring to the Blessed One (*bhagavati*) or as a locative case used in the sense of the dative. "Aḍa" means he gave. This is to be connected with the phrase "thus accomplishing the purpose."
It should be seen. Some read, “He gave the great kingdom to the Victor. Having given means having relinquished.
*Suttanta* refers to the Sutta Piṭaka. *Vinaya* refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka. *Navaṅga* refers to the ninefold division beginning with the Sutta and Geyya.
“I adorned the teaching of the Victor” means I embellished it with both mundane *āgama* (scriptural learning) and *adhigama* (realization). *Tattha* means in that teaching of the Blessed One.
"Appamatto" means endowed with mindfulness. "Brahmalokamaganchaham" means "I went to the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, this Buddha Koṇḍañña had a city named Rammavatī;
his father was King Sunanda, his mother was Queen Sujātā, his two chief disciples were Bhadda and Subhadda, and his attendant was named Anuruddha.
Tissā and Upatissā were her two chief female disciples; the Sāla-kalyāṇi tree was her Bodhi tree; her body was eighty-eight cubits in height;
the measure of her lifespan was one hundred thousand years; Rucidevī was the name of his chief queen; Vijitasena was the name of his son;
and Canda was the name of the king who served as his attendant. It is said that he dwelt in the Candārāma. Therefore it was said:
“The city was named Rammavatī; the kṣatriya was named Sunanda;
and Sujātā was the mother of Koṇḍañña, the Great Seer.
Bhadda and Subhadda were his two chief disciples.”
Anuruddha was the attendant of Koṇḍañña, the Great Sage.
Tissa and Upatissa were his chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree of Koṇḍañña, the Great Sage, was the Salakalyāṇika.
“Thus the Great Sage stands eight cubits tall;
he shines like the lord of stars or like the sun at midday.
His lifespan lasts for as long as one hundred thousand years.”
Remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
With those whose taints were exhausted and who were stainless, the earth became variegated;
indeed, it shone just as the sky does with owls.
“Even those nāgas, immeasurable, unshakeable, and difficult to approach,
having displayed a flash of lightning as it were, have been extinguished, they of great renown.
And that incomparable supernormal power of the Victor, and his concentration perfumed by wisdom— ”
"All that has vanished; are not all conditioned things empty?
In this context, "sālakalyāṇika" refers to the *sālakalyāṇi* tree. It is said to grow only at the time of a Buddha or a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), and never at other times.
It is said to sprout in a single day. "The earth was variegated by those stainless ones whose taints were destroyed"—this...

The earth became variegated and most beautiful, illuminated by the single saffron robes of those whose taints were destroyed. The word *hi* is a particle used in the sense of an illustration (*opamma*).
Just as the vault of heaven is variegated by the constellations and clusters of stars, so too was this earth adorned and made beautiful by those whose taints were destroyed; such is the meaning.
“Unshakable” means unshakeable and changeless by the eight worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*). “Having shown a flash of lightning” means having displayed it like a flash of lightning;

there is also a reading, “or like a flash of lightning. It is said that at the time of the Buddha Koṇḍañña’s parinibbāna, the monks, while passing away, rose up into the sky to the height of seventy palm trees and appeared like streaks of lightning entering the gaps between dark clouds.
Shining forth on all sides, they entered the element of fire and, being without fuel, attained final nibbāna like a blazing fire.
Therefore it is said: "having displayed a flash of lightning. "Incomparable" (atuliyā) means peerless or matchless.
"Cultivated by wisdom" (ñāṇaparibhāvito) means increased by wisdom. The remaining verses are clear, as their method has already been explained below.
“The Sambuddha named Koṇḍañña passed away at the delightful Candārāma.
A seven-yojana stupa was built for him.
Yet, the relics of that Teacher did not scatter; they remained intact.”
"Standing firm as a single solid mass, like a golden statue.

All the people dwelling throughout Jambudīpa gathered together and completed [the image], seven yojanas in height and made of the seven precious gems; they performed the function of clay with yellow orpiment and realgar, and the function of water with oil and ghee.
The *Vaṇṇanā* (Commentary) on the lineage of Buddha Koṇḍañña is finished.
The second lineage of Buddhas is finished.
5. The Commentary on the Lineage of Buddha Maṅgala:
When the Teacher Koṇḍañña had attained final Nibbāna, his dispensation continued for one hundred thousand years. [There were] those who awakened following the Buddha...
With the disappearance of his disciples, his Dispensation vanished.
But after the time of Koṇḍañña, once an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya*) had passed, four Buddhas were born in a single eon: Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita.
Among them, Maṅgala, the Leader of the World, fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*) for sixteen incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand eons.
Having fulfilled [the perfections] and been reborn in the Tusita heaven, he remained there for the full span of his lifespan;

then, when the five portents appeared, that which is called the "Buddha-proclamation" arose. At that time, the deities from ten thousand world-systems gathered in a single world-system and made this supplication:
“O Great Hero, the time has come for you to arise in a mother’s womb;
crossing over the world including the devas, awaken to the deathless state.
Thus entreated by the devas, he performed the fivefold observations and, passing away from the Tusita realm, [descended] into the supreme city of all cities, the northern city.
He took rebirth in the womb of Queen Uttarā, in the family of King Uttara, who was unsurpassed and supreme.
At that time, many miracles appeared; these are to be understood in the same manner as described in the lineage of Dīpaṅkara Buddha.
It is said that while he was in the womb of the great queen Uttarā, [he was] the auspiciousness of all auspicious things in the world...
From the moment of the Great Being’s conception, the radiance of his body remained, pervading an area eighty cubits in extent day and night; it stood unassailable by the light of the moon or the sun.
And that radiance, dispelling darkness through the manifestation of its own bodily glow without the need for any other light, [surrounded him] with sixty-eight nurses.
She wanders about being attended by her retinue.
It is said that she, protected by the deities, after the lapse of ten months,

[resided] in a place where the branches and boughs bore most fragrant flowers and fruits, which was adorned with lotuses and water-lilies, and frequented by various herds of deer such as the ruru, lion, tiger, elephant, gavaya, and buffalo.
In the most delightful northern garden known as Maṅgala Garden, she gave birth to the Auspicious Great Being.
Immediately upon his birth, the Great Being looked toward all directions, walked seven steps facing north, and uttered a lion’s roar.
At that very moment, throughout the entire ten-thousandfold world-system, the deities appeared with their bodies visible.
With their limbs adorned with celestial garlands and other ornaments, they stood here and there and uttered words of praise for victory and auspiciousness.

The miracles occurred exactly as previously described. On the day of his naming, however, the readers of signs, seeing that he was born endowed with every kind of auspicious excellence, gave him the name Maṅgalakumāra (Auspicious Prince).
It is said that he had three palaces named Yasavā, Rucimā, and Sirimā. He had thirty thousand female dancers, headed by Queen Yasavatī.

Therein, the Great Being, having experienced happiness like celestial bliss for nine thousand years, obtained a son named Sīlavant in the womb of his chief queen Yasavatī, and [beheld] the four signs.
Having seen this, he mounted his beautiful, preeminent steed named Paṇḍara, made a Great Renunciation, and went forth.
As he was going forth, thirty million people followed him into the homeless life.
Surrounded by them, the Great Being practiced the life of striving for eight months.

Then, on the full moon day of the month of Visākha, having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice mixed with divine nutrients (dibboja) offered by Uttarā, the daughter of the merchant Uttara in the village of Uttaragāma,
and having spent the day in meditation in a delightful Sāla grove that was fragrant with flowers,
blue in hue, and enchanting, he took eight handfuls of grass given by an Ājīvika named Uttara— [grass] resembling the Asitañjana mountain— and [proceeded].
Having approached the Nāgabodhi tree— which possessed a cool shade like a peak covered by a net of excellent gold, which was devoid of the gathering of various herds of deer,
which was adorned with thick branches swayed by gentle breezes, and which shone as if dancing with joy— he, who walked with the gait of a noble elephant in rut,
circumambulated the Nāgabodhi tree from left to right, stood on its north-eastern side, [and beheld] that which was eighty-eight cubits in extent.
Having spread out a grass mat and sat down cross-legged upon it,
he resolved upon energy endowed with four factors; having shattered the powerful host of Māra, acquired the knowledge of past lives and the divine eye,
and performed a synthesis of the conditions of dependent origination, he focused his attention on the aggregates as impermanent and so forth, and gradually attained the unsurpassed state.
Having attained supreme perfect enlightenment,
[he said]: "Through many births in saṃsāra I have wandered without finding rest,
seeking the builder of the house, for birth again and again is suffering.
“House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered.
The mind has reached the unconditioned; it has attained the destruction of craving.”
He uttered an inspired utterance (udāna).
However, the bodily radiance of the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala was greater than that of other Buddhas.
Whereas for other Perfectly Enlightened Ones it extended a distance of eighty cubits or one fathom on all sides, [for Maṅgala it was even greater].
The radiance of his body was not like that [of others]. Indeed, the bodily radiance of that Blessed One stood pervading the ten-thousandfold world system at all times.
Trees, mountains, houses, walls, jars, door-bolts, and so forth, became as if covered with plates of gold.
His lifespan was nine million years. For such a length of time, [the light] of the moon, sun, stars, and so on—

There was no light. The distinction between night and day was not perceived. During the day, as if by the light of the sun, beings went about performing all their activities solely by the light of the Buddha.
By means of flowers that bloom at evening and birds and other creatures that cry out at dawn, the world discerned the distinction between night and day.
But is it that other Buddhas do not possess this power? No, they do not.
For if they so desired, they too could pervade a ten-thousandfold world-system, or even more, with their radiance.
However, due to the Blessed One Maṅgala’s previous aspiration, his bodily radiance—unlike the fathom-wide aura of others—is constantly present throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system.

Having pervaded [the area], he stood there. It is said that in his time as a Bodhisatta, while in an existence similar to that of Vessantara, he dwelt with his wife and children on a mountain resembling Vaṅka-pabbata.
Then, a powerful yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, a man-eater who harassed all people, having heard of the Great Being’s inclination toward generosity, approached him in the guise of a brahmin.

The Great Being asked for the two children. "I give the two little sons to the brahmin," said the Great Being, joyful and exceedingly glad, as he gave the two children while making the earth, bounded by the waters, tremble.

Then, even as the Great Man looked on, that yakkha cast off his brahmin disguise and revealed his true form, with eyes tawny like a mass of fire, hideous in appearance, and with uneven, deformed, crooked, and terrifying tusks.
Having become one with a flat and deformed nose, hair that was tawny, coarse, and long, and a body resembling the trunk of a freshly burnt palm tree,
he seized those children like a bundle of lotus stalks and devoured them. When the Great Being looked at the yakkha, even upon seeing his mouth— which, as soon as it was opened,
was vomiting forth streams of blood like a mass of flames— he did not tremble even by the measure of a hair’s breadth.
No mental distress arose. However, as he thought, "Truly, my gift was well-bestowed," a great surge of rapture and joy arose within his body.
He made this aspiration: "By the result of this, may rays of light issue forth from my body in this manner in the future.
Based on that aspiration, when he became a Buddha, rays of light issued forth from his body.
They pervaded that much space.

Furthermore, there is another account of his former conduct. It is said that in the time of his existence as a Bodhisatta, upon seeing the stupa of a certain Buddha, he thought, "It is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for this Buddha," and according to the method of wrapping a torch-wick...
Having wrapped his entire body [in fragrant cloth], filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces]—
which was adorned with a crest-jewel the size of a gem— with fragrant ghee, lit a thousand wicks therein, and taking it upon his head,
he spent the whole night performing circumambulations around the Jina’s cetiya while setting his entire body ablaze. Thus, he exerted himself until the rising of the dawn.
Not even a breath of warmth reached the pores of his skin; it was as if he had entered the interior of a lotus.
For indeed, this Dhamma protects him who protects himself. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Truly, Dhamma protects the one who lives by Dhamma; Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.”
“This is the benefit when the Dhamma is well-practiced: one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to an evil destination.
Through the outflow of this very deed, the radiance of his body remained pervading the ten-thousandfold world system. Therefore it was said:
“After Koṇḍañña, the Leader named Maṅgala appeared.”
Having destroyed the darkness in the world, he upheld the vehicle of the Dhamma.
"His splendor was incomparable, surpassing that of other Conquerors;
having eclipsed the light of the moon and sun, he shines throughout the ten-thousandfold world system."
In this context, "that" refers to both the darkness of the world and the darkness of the heart. "Having destroyed" means having overcome. Regarding the term *dhammokkā*:
here, this word *ukkā* is seen in many senses, such as a goldsmith’s crucible and so forth.
For instance, in the passage, "Having taken the gold with tongs, one should place it in the mouth of the crucible," the word *ukkā* refers to the goldsmiths' crucible.
It should be understood as follows: In the passage, “One should fasten a torch; having fastened the torch, one should kindle the mouth of the torch,” it refers to the charcoal pan of smiths.
In the passage, “Just as the torch of smiths glows within but not without,” it refers to the smith’s forge.
In the passage, “A meteor shower of such a ripening will occur,” the term “torch” (*ukkā*) refers to the force of the wind.
It is said: "While torches were being carried. In the places where this occurs, a lamp is called a "torch" (*ukkā*).
Here too, a lamp is intended by the word "torch. Therefore, the meaning here is: "He held aloft the torch made of Dhamma";
that is, he bore the torch made of Dhamma for the world that was shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and overcome by the darkness of ignorance.
*Atulāsī* means she was incomparable (*atulyā*). Or rather, this is the reading: the meaning is that she was unlike any other Buddhas.
*Jinehaññehīti* means "by other Conquerors" (*jinehi aññehi*). *Candasūriyappabhaṃ hantvā* means having overcome the radiance of the moon and the sun.
*Dasasahassī virocatīti* means that even without the light of the moon and the sun, the ten-thousandfold world-system shines by the light of the Buddha alone; such is the meaning.
But the Maṅgala Sammasambuddha, having attained the knowledge of enlightenment, spent seven weeks right there at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then, accepting the invitation of Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom indeed should I teach this Dhamma?
While thus considering, he perceived that three crores of bhikkhus who had gone forth together with him were endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*).
He saw them. Then this thought occurred to him: “These sons of good family have followed me into the going-forth;

they are endowed with the necessary support. Having been dismissed by me on the full moon of Visākha while I was seeking seclusion, they are dwelling near the city of Sirivaḍḍhana, having gone to the Sirīvaṇa grove.
Well then, let me go there and teach the Dhamma to them.”
Taking his own bowl and robe, he rose up into the expanse of the sky like a king of swans and alighted in the Sirīvanagahana grove.
Those monks, having paid homage to the Blessed One and performed the duties of a resident pupil, sat surrounding the Blessed One.
To them, the Blessed One preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is frequented by all the Buddhas.
He preached it. Thereupon, thirty million bhikkhus attained arahantship. One hundred and ten million gods and humans realized the Dhamma. Therefore it is said:
“That Buddha also proclaimed the four most excellent truths.”
Having drunk that essence of truth, they dispel the great darkness.
Having attained the incomparable Bodhi at the first teaching of the Dhamma,
there was the realization of the Dhamma for one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
In that context, *caturo* means four. Regarding *saccavaruttama*: they are both truths (*sacca*) and excellent (*vara*), thus "excellent truths" (*saccavara*);
the meaning is "supreme truths. There is also a reading, *cattāro saccavaruttame*, for which the meaning is "the four excellent truths are supreme.
*Te te* refers to those various gods and humans who were disciplined by the Buddha, the Blessed One. *Saccarasaṃ* means the flavor of the nectar of the penetration of the Four Truths.
"Having drunk. "They dispel the great darkness": they dispel the darkness of delusion that is to be abandoned by each respective path;
the meaning is that they shatter it. "Having reached": having penetrated. Regarding the word *bodhi* here:
"In the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, the tree, and likewise in designation;..."
"And the word 'Bodhi' has come to mean omniscient knowledge.
For indeed, this term occurs in reference to the Path in such passages as, "Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths," and so forth.

It occurs in reference to the Fruit in the passage, "It leads to peace, to direct knowledge, and to full enlightenment (sambodha). And it occurs in reference to Nibbāna in the passage, "Having attained Bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned."
In this context, it refers to Nibbāna. In the phrase "between Gayā and the Bodhi tree," it refers to the Assattha tree.
In the phrase "Prince Bodhi pays homage at the feet of Master Gotama with his head," it refers to a designation (a person).
In the phrase "the one of vast wisdom attains Bodhi," it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). Here too, it should be understood as referring to omniscient knowledge.
It is also appropriate [to apply this] to the knowledge of the path of arahantship. "Incomparable" (*atulam*) means devoid of comparison, exceeding all measure; the meaning is "immeasurable.
The meaning should be understood as the first teaching of the Dhamma by that Blessed One after he had attained full enlightenment while teaching the Dhamma.
Furthermore, when he was dwelling near the city named Citta, at the foot of a *campaka* tree and at the foot of a *kaṇḍamba* tree...
Just as our Blessed One did for us, having performed the Twin Miracle that crushed the pride of the heretics,

he sat upon the yellow sandalwood stone slab at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven— the magnificent, new palace made of gold and silver, produced by the delight of the young women of the Suras and Asuras—
and there he preached the Abhidhamma; at that time, there was a realization of the Dhamma by one hundred thousand times ten million deities.
This was the second clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Furthermore, when the wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) named Sunanda,

having fulfilled the duties of a wheel-turner in the city of Surabhi, obtained the precious wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), King Sunanda— seeing that the wheel-treasure had receded from its place since the appearance of the Blessed One Maṅgaladasabala in the world— became dejected and questioned the brahmins.
—“This Wheel-Treasure has arisen through my wholesome merit; why has it receded from its place?

Then they explained to the king the reason for its recession: “The Wheel-Treasure recedes from its place due to the exhaustion of the life-span of a Wheel-turning Monarch, or his departure into homelessness, or the appearance of a Buddha; but as for you, Great King—”
"There is no end to your lifespan; you are exceedingly long-lived. However, because the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala has appeared in the world, your Wheel-Treasure has withdrawn.
Upon hearing this, King Sunanda, the wheel-turning monarch, together with his retinue, paid homage to that Wheel-Treasure with his head and entreated it:
"As long as I shall honor the Ten-Powered One, Maṅgala, through your power, so long..."
"Do not vanish from my sight. Then the Wheel-Treasure stood back in its very place.

Thereupon, King Sunanda the Wheel-turning Monarch, accompanied by his joyful retinue and surrounded by an assembly thirty-six *yojanas* in circumference, approached the Blessed One—the Auspicious One for all the world, the One Endowed with the Ten Powers of Auspiciousness—together with his community of disciples.
Having satisfied one hundred thousand times ten million arahants with a great gift, having given them Kāsī garments, and having offered all requisites to the Tathāgata,
he performed a worship of the Blessed One that caused wonder throughout the entire world. Then, approaching the Auspicious One, the Lord of All Worlds,
he placed his hands together in a mudrā at his head— hands as radiant as ten nails joined, like a stainless lotus bud.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. His son, Prince Anurāja by name, likewise sat down there.
Then the Blessed One spoke a gradual discourse to them, headed by the universal monarch Sunanda. Sunanda—
The Wheel-turning Monarch, together with his retinue, attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

Then the Teacher, surveying their past conduct and perceiving the necessary support for supernaturally produced bowls and robes, extended his right hand adorned with a web-like network and said, "Come, monks.
At that very moment, the hair on all of them was two finger-breadths long.
Wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power, they surrounded the Blessed One with perfected deportment like elder monks of sixty years' standing.
This was the third realization. Therefore it is said:
"In the celestial palace of Surindadeva, the Buddha taught the Dhamma."
There was a second realization for one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
When the wheel-turning monarch Sunanda approached the Fully Enlightened One,
then the Fully Enlightened One struck the supreme, excellent drum of the Dhamma.
“The people who were followers of Sunanda numbered ninety koṭis;
all of them, without exception, became those for whom the ‘Come, monk’ formula was used.
In that context, “in the abode of the Lord of Gods” (surindadevabhavana) means again “in the abode of the Lord of Devas” (devindabhavana). “The Dhamma” means the Abhidhamma. “He struck” means...
*Abhihani*: "Varuttamam" means the Blessed One, the supreme one, [beat] the most excellent drum of the Dhamma; such is the meaning. *Anucārā*: attendants who follow constantly;
servants. *Āsuṃ*: they were. There is also a reading: "Then there were ninety crores. Regarding that, it says "there was a multitude";
if one asks how great that multitude was, the meaning is "ninety crores."
Now, while the Maṅgala Lokanātha was dwelling in the city of Mekhala, two young brahmins named Sudeva and Dhammasena,
accompanied by a retinue of a thousand young brahmins, went forth in the presence of that Blessed One through the "Come,
monk" (ehibhikkhu) ordination. On the full moon day of the month of Māgha, when his two chief disciples together with their retinues had attained arahantship, the Teacher—
In the midst of a community of one hundred thousand million bhikkhus, he recited the Pātimokkha; this was the first assembly.
Again, in the unsurpassed gathering of kinsmen at the place called Uttarārāma, where there was an assembly of one hundred thousand million who had gone forth, he recited the Pātimokkha;
this was the second assembly. [And] in the assembly of the community of bhikkhus headed by the Wheel-turning Monarch Sunanda...
In the midst of ninety thousand koṭis of bhikkhus, he recited the Pātimokkha; this was the third assembly.
Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies of Maṅgala, the Great Sage;”
“The first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand times ten million;
the second was of one hundred thousand times ten million, and the third was of ninety million—
this was the gathering of those stainless ones whose taints were exhausted.”
At that time, our Bodhisatta was born in the village of Surucibrāhmaṇa as a brahmin named Suruci.
He had mastered the three Vedas, including the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha vocabularies, the Sakkharappabheda phonology, and the Itihāsa as the fifth;

he was an expert in grammar and etymology, and was thoroughly proficient in Lokāyata philosophy and the marks of a Great Man. Having approached the Teacher, [he spoke] to the One Possessed of Ten Powers...

Having heard the sweet discourse on the Dhamma, he gained confidence in the Blessed One, went for refuge, and invited the Blessed One together with his community of disciples, saying, "Please accept my alms tomorrow.
When the Blessed One asked him, "Brāhmaṇa, how many monks do you require? he replied, "But how large, venerable sir, is your retinue of monks?"

At that time, it was indeed the first assembly; therefore, when he said, "A hundred thousand koṭis," [the brahmin] invited him, saying, "If that is so, venerable sir, please accept alms from me together with all of them. The Teacher consented.
Having invited the Blessed One for the following day's meal, the brahmin, while returning to his own home, thought: "I..."
"I am able to provide such a number of monks with rice gruel, food, clothing, and so forth, but how will there be a place for them to sit?
It is said that this thought of his produced a sense of heat upon the ivory-white stone throne of the ten-eyed King of Devas,
who was seated on the summit of Mount Meru, eighty-four thousand yojanas in extent.
Then Sakka, the king of the gods, perceiving the heat of his seat, thought to himself, "Who indeed desires to displace me from this position?
With his divine eye, he surveyed the world of humans;
seeing the Great Being, he reflected, "This Great Being, having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, has been thinking [of something] for the purpose of providing a seat for him."
"It would be fitting for me also to go there and take a portion of merit," he thought;
so, assuming the guise of a carpenter with an axe and adze in hand, he appeared before the Great Being.
He asked, "Is there any work to be done for wages?"
The Great Being saw him and asked, "What work are you able to do? He replied, "There is no craft unknown to me;
whatever anyone desires—whether a pavilion, a palace, or any other dwelling—I am capable of making it for them.
"In that case, I have some work for you," he said. "Of what kind, noble sir? he asked.
“I have invited one hundred thousand million bhikkhus for my own sake; will you construct a pavilion for them to sit in?
“I would indeed do so, if you could provide me with wages. “I shall be able to do so, dear son,” he replied.
“If that is the case, very well, I shall do it,” he said, and looking toward a certain spot, [he saw] that place measuring twelve yojanas.

That area became as level as a *kasiṇa* disk and exceedingly beautiful. Again, he thought, "In this much space, let a pavilion arise made of the seven precious gems and adorned with the finest essences," and he looked.
Immediately, a pavilion like that [he had envisioned] burst forth from the surface of the earth. Upon its pillars made of gold were [roofs] made of silver...
There were golden vases on silver pillars, coral vases on gemstone pillars, gemstone vases on coral pillars,
and vases made of the seven precious gems on pillars made of the seven precious gems. Then he looked, thinking,
"Let nets of tinkling bells hang here and there within the pavilion," and as soon as he looked, the nets of tinkling bells appeared.
Hanging down were [garlands], from which, stirred by a gentle breeze, a most enchanting and sweet sound issued forth, like the time when celestial music is being performed.

He thought, "Let garlands of divine perfumes, flower garlands, leaf garlands, and garlands of the seven jewels hang down at intervals," and as soon as he thought it, the garlands hung down. [He provided for] one hundred thousand times ten million monks...
He thought, "Let worthy and costly rugs for the seats and their supporting stands emerge by splitting the earth," and at that very moment they emerged.
He thought, "Let a water-jar arise in each corner," and at that instant water-jars appeared,
filled with most cool, sweet, perfectly pure, and fragrant, allowable water, their mouths covered with plantain leaves.
They rose up. Having created all this, the Ten-Thousand-Eyed One went into the presence of the brahmin and said, “Come, sir;
having seen your pavilion, give me my wages. The Great Being went and looked at that pavilion.
As he was looking, his entire body became suffused without interruption by five-colored rapture.
Then, as he was looking at the pavilion, this thought occurred to him: "This pavilion was not made by a human being;

surely because of my intention and my virtue, the abode of Sakka, the king of the gods, became hot, and therefore this pavilion was created by Sakka, the lord of the devas. "But it is not fitting for me [to enter] such a pavilion..."
He thought, "I shall give a gift for only a single day; I will not give for seven days.
Indeed, even such an amount of external giving is unable to bring satisfaction to the hearts of Bodhisattvas.

Rather, it is at the time when they have cut off their own head while it is adorned, plucked out their eyes while they are anointed, or torn out the flesh of their heart, that the Bodhisattvas [experience true joy].
Indeed, satisfaction arises by depending upon generosity.

For instance, when our Bodhisatta was in the *Sivi Jātaka*, even though he bestowed five hundred thousand kahāpaṇas daily and gave alms at five locations—the four city gates and the center of the city—that giving was unable to produce the satisfaction of renunciation (*cāgatuṭṭhi*).
However, when Sakka came to him in the guise of a brahmin...
The king of the gods requested his eyes; at that time, having gouged out those eyes, he gave them away.
Even as he was giving them, joy arose within him, and there was not even a hair’s breadth of change in his mind.
Thus, for the omniscient Bodhisattvas, there is no satiety based on external giving. Therefore, that Great Being also—[thinking], "By me, [a gift] numbering one hundred thousand crores..."
Thinking, "It is fitting to give alms to the bhikkhus," he had them seated in that pavilion and for seven days gave the gift known as *gavapāna*.
Here, *gavapāna* refers to a prepared food made by filling large jars with milk, placing them on hearths, and when the milk has been thickened by intense cooking,
adding small amounts of rice, along with honey, sugar-candy powder, and clarified butter.
It is so called. It is also called "the food of the four sweets. However, humans alone were unable to serve it;
even the devas served it only at intervals. Those bhikkhus were not even able to occupy that area, which measured twelve yojanas in extent;
yet those bhikkhus sat down by means of their own respective spiritual power. On the final day—
Having had the alms-bowls of all the bhikkhus washed and having filled them for the sake of medicine with ghee,
fresh butter, honey, molasses, and so forth, he gave them together with the three robes. Among those,
the robes and cloths received by the most junior bhikkhu of the Saṅgha were worth one hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Then the Teacher, offering words of appreciation, reflected: “This Great Being has given such a great gift;

who indeed will he become? As he investigated, he saw: “In the future, at the conclusion of two incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand kalpas, there will be a Buddha named Gotama. Having seen this, he then addressed the Great Being: “You—”
“After such a length of time has passed, you will become a Buddha named Gotama,” he prophesied.
Then, having heard the Blessed One’s prophecy, the Great Man, with a heart full of joy, thought: “I shall indeed become a Buddha; I have no need for the life of a householder;
I shall go forth. Having thus abandoned such magnificent prosperity as if it were a globule of spittle, he [approached] the Teacher.
Having gone forth in his presence and mastered the word of the Buddha, he attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Without falling away from those jhānas, he remained for the full span of his life and, at the end of his life, was reborn in the Brahma-world. Therefore it was said:
"At that time, I was a brahmin named Suruci..."
A reciter of the scriptures, a bearer of the mantras, one who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas—
having approached him and gone for refuge to the Teacher,
I honored the Saṅgha headed by the Perfectly Enlightened One with perfumes and garlands.
Having worshipped him with perfumes and garlands, I satisfied him with a drink of cow's milk.
That Buddha Maṅgala, the supreme among bipeds, also prophesied for me:
"In an incalculable aeon, this one shall become a Buddha."
“Having exerted the effort... [and so on] ...we shall stand face to face with him.”—These eight verses are to be recited in full.
“Having heard his words as well, my mind became even more serene.”
I resolved upon a further vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
Then, cultivating joy for the sake of attaining supreme enlightenment,
I gave my house to the Buddha and went forth into homelessness in his presence.
“Having mastered the Suttanta and the Vinaya— the ninefold teaching of the Teacher—
I have brought glory to the Conqueror’s dispensation.
Dwell there with diligence, cultivating the sublime meditation.”
"Having reached the perfection of direct knowledge, you went to the Brahma-world.
In this context, "with perfumes and garlands" means with both perfumes and garlands. "With cow's milk" has already been explained.
Some read it as "with ghee-milk. "I satisfied" means I caused them to be satisfied. "I resolved upon a further vow" means I undertook an even greater vow.
"For the fulfillment of the ten perfections" means for the sake of completing the ten perfections (*pāramī*). "Joy" means satisfaction of the heart. "Increasing" means making it grow.
"For the attainment of the excellence of perfect enlightenment" means for the attainment of Buddhahood. "Having given to the Buddha" means having relinquished [it] to the Buddha.
"My house" means my home; [the phrase] "having relinquished all my possessions for the sake of the four requisites to the Blessed One, the Buddha," [is implied].
The meaning [is as follows]. "Therein" means in that teaching of the Buddha. "Brahmā" means having cultivated the meditation on the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Furthermore, the city of the Blessed One Maṅgala was named Uttara;
his father was a Kṣatriya king named Uttara, and his mother was also named Uttarā. Sudeva and Dhammasena were his two chief disciples, and Pālita was...
His attendant was [Uttara], and his two chief female disciples were Sīvalā and Asokā. His Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree;
his body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and the measure of his lifespan was ninety thousand years. His wife was named Yasavatī, and his son was named Sīvala.
He went forth on horseback and resided at Uttarārāma. His attendant there was named Uttara. However, in that...
When the Blessed One had remained for ninety thousand years and attained final Nibbāna, ten thousand world-systems simultaneously became one vast darkness.
In all those world-systems, there was great weeping and lamentation among the people. Thus it is said:
“The city named Uttara, the kshatriya named Uttara;”
The mother of the Great Sage Maṅgala was named Uttarā.
Sudeva and Dhammasena were his chief disciples,
and the attendant of the Great Sage Maṅgala was named Pālita.
“Sīvalā and Asokā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Nāga-tree.
The Great Sage rose up eighty cubits in height.”
Then a radiance issued forth, numbering many hundreds of thousands.
"The lifespan exists for ninety thousand years;
remaining for that long, he delivered a vast multitude of people."
“Just as the waves in the ocean cannot be counted,
so too his disciples cannot be counted.
As long as the Sambuddha Maṅgala, the Leader of the World, remained [in this world],”
At that time, there was no death with defilements remaining in his teaching.
Having upheld the Dhamma-standard and delivered the great multitude,
he— like a flaming meteor— extinguished himself, he of great renown.
“Having displayed the true nature of conditioned phenomena to the world including the devas, he has passed away like a mass of fire that has burned out, or like the sun that has set.
In this context, *tato* means from the body of that Maṅgala. *Niddhāvati* means they run out; it is a grammatical variation of the verb.
It should be seen. *Raṃsī* means rays. *Aneka-sata-sahassiyā* means many hundreds of thousands. *Ūmī* means waves or billows.

*Gaṇetuye* means to count or to calculate. Just as it is impossible to count how many waves there are in the ocean, even so the disciples of that Blessed One cannot be counted; rather, the meaning is that they have transcended the path of calculation.

"For as long as" means for however much time. "Death with defilements" (*sakilesamaraṇa*): together with defilements is "with defilements" (*sakileso*); the death of one who has defilements is "death with defilements.
That [death] did not exist. It is said that at that time, in the teaching of that Blessed One, all disciples attained *arahantship* and then alone passed away into *parinibbāna*.
Neither worldlings nor those who were stream-enterers and so forth died [without having attained the goal].
The meaning [is as follows]. Some read, "Then there was a deluding death.
*Dhammokkam* means that which illuminates the Dhamma. *Dhūmaketu* refers to fire; however, here it should be understood as a lamp.
Therefore, the meaning is: having blazed like a lamp, it has gone out. *Mahāyaso* means having a great retinue. Some read, "Nibbuto..."
They recite, "He together with his disciples. "Of conditioned phenomena" (*saṅkhārānaṃ*) means of those things that have been reckoned, namely, of things possessing causes.
"The common characteristic" (*sabhāvattaṃ*) refers to the general characteristics such as impermanence and so forth. "Just as the sun has set" (*sūriyo atthaṅgato yathā*):
just as the thousand-rayed maker of day, having dispelled the entire mass of darkness and illuminated the whole world, goes to its setting, even so does the maker of the day of auspiciousness.

The meaning is that he has set, having blazed with the radiance of his own body after dispelling all darkness of the internal and external world, acting as the cause for the blossoming of the lotus-forest of those capable of being trained (*veneyya*). The remaining verses are clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Maṅgala-Buddhavaṃsa* is finished.
The third lineage of Buddhas is finished.
6. The Exposition of the Lineage of Buddha Sumanas:
Thus, having simultaneously plunged the ten-thousandfold world system into total darkness upon the Parinibbāna of that Blessed One,
In the subsequent period, when the lifespan of human beings had gradually decreased from ninety thousand years until they were born with a ten-year lifespan,
and then increased again until their lifespan reached incalculable aeons, and subsequently decreased once more until they were born with a lifespan of ninety thousand years,
the Bodhisatta named Sumana fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*), was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and passed away from there.
He took rebirth in the womb of Queen Sirimā in the family of King Sudatta in the city of Mekhala.
The miracles occurred in the same manner as previously described.
Having gradually reached maturity, he was given three names: Sirivaḍḍhana, Somavaḍḍhana, and Iddhivaḍḍhana.
While being entertained by three million six hundred thousand female dancers in his palaces,
and attended by celestial maidens like a young god, he experienced sense-pleasures similar to divine bliss for nine thousand years; then,
having fathered a son named Anupama (Incomparable) with his queen named Vaṭaṃsikā, and having seen the four omens, [he departed] on an elephant mount.
Having gone forth, he renounced the world. As he was renouncing, thirty koṭis followed him into the religious life.

Surrounded by them, after practicing the course of striving for ten months, on the full moon day of Visākha, he partook of the milk-rice—into which divine nutrients had been infused—which was offered by Anupamā, the daughter of the merchant Anoma in the town of Anoma. He then spent the day in meditation in a grove of Sāla trees.
Having passed the night, he took the eight handfuls of grass given by Anupama-jīvaka,
approached the Nāga-bodhi tree, circumambulated it, and having spread a grass mat thirty cubits wide with those eight handfuls of grass,
sat down there cross-legged. Then, having shattered the army of Māra and penetrated the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), [he attained enlightenment].
He uttered this inspired utterance: “Through many births in saṃsāra… [and so on] … he has attained the destruction of craving. Therefore it was said:
“After Maṅgala, there was a Leader named Sumana, peerless in all qualities, supreme among all beings.”
