In that context, "after Maṅgala" means after the Blessed One Maṅgala. "Peerless among all phenomena" means he was unequaled and without equal in all phenomena such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
It is said that the Blessed One, having spent seven weeks right near the Bodhi tree, accepted the invitation of Brahmā for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma;
then, while reflecting, "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?"—
Seeing that thirty koṭis of those who had gone forth with him, as well as his own younger half-brother Prince Saraṇa and the young Brahmin Bhāvitatta—
the son of the family priest— were endowed with the necessary spiritual qualities (upanissaya),
he thought, “I shall teach the Dhamma to them first. Then, like a king of swans, he descended through the path of the sky into the Mekhalu Garden and [addressed] the park-keeper.
Having sent for his younger brother, Prince Saraṇa, and the chaplain’s son, Prince Bhāvitatta,
he caused them to go forth along with seventy-three million followers, thirty million who had gone forth with him, and many other millions of gods and humans; thus,
by means of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, one hundred thousand million beings [were established].
He caused them to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. Thus it is said:
"Then, in the city of Mekhala, he struck the drum of the Deathless, joined with the conch of the Dhamma—the ninefold teaching of the Victor."
In this context, "the drum of the Deathless" means the drum for the attainment of the Deathless, the attainment of Nibbāna.

"He struck it" means he sounded it; the meaning is that he taught the Dhamma. This so-called "drum of the Deathless" is the ninefold word of the Buddha, which culminates in the Deathless. For this very reason it is said:
"The ninefold teaching of the Conqueror, joined with the conch of the Dhamma. In that phrase, "joined with the conch of the Dhamma" means:
It was joined with the excellent conch of discourses on the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
Then the Leader of the World, Sumana, having attained full enlightenment and practicing the path in accordance with his promise,
[taught] for the sake of releasing the great multitude from the bonds of existence, [the jewel of wholesome states] which is being plundered by the thieves of the defilements.

For the sake of protecting beings, he constructed the excellent city of the Deathless, which had morality as its lofty ramparts, was surrounded by the moat of concentration, possessed the gate of insight-knowledge, had the strong doors of mindfulness and clear comprehension, was adorned with pavilions such as the meditative attainments, and was crowded with the people who are the factors of enlightenment. Thus it is said:
"Having conquered the defilements and attained supreme enlightenment..."
“The Teacher built the city, the supreme, foremost town of the True Dhamma.

Therein, *nijjinitvā* means having conquered, having overcome; the meaning is, having destroyed the Māras of the defilements (*kilesa*), the formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the son of the gods (*devaputta*).

*So* refers to that Blessed One, Sumana. There is also a reading: *“vijinitvā kilese hi”* (having conquered the defilements indeed). In that case, the particle *hi* serves merely to fill out the meter.
*Nipāto* (is) a particle. *Patvā* means having attained (*adhigantvā*). There is also a reading: *patto*. *Nagaraṃ* refers to the city of Nibbāna.
*Saddhammapuravaruttamaṃ* means the most excellent, the best, the preeminent among the foremost cities known as the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*).

Alternatively, it means the most excellent among the foremost cities composed of the True Dhamma; thus, *saddhammapuravaruttamaṃ*. In the first interpretation of the meaning, [the word] is "city" (*nagaraṃ*).

This should be understood as a synonym for that very [Nibbāna]. For the noble individuals—both those in training (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha)—who have penetrated the true nature of phenomena, Nibbāna is called a "city" in the sense of being their foundation and dwelling place.

In that city of the excellent Dhamma, the Teacher [established] a great street consisting of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), which is uninterrupted, straight, upright, broad, and expansive.
He had it measured out. Therefore it was said:
"He laid out that great street, continuous, straight, not crooked, vast and wide—the most excellent and supreme foundation of mindfulness."
In this context, "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*) means uninterrupted because it occurs immediately after the transition of the wholesome impulsion (*kusalajavana*).

"Not crooked" (*akuṭila*) means not crooked because it is free from faults that produce crookedness. "Straight" (*uju*) means straight precisely because it is not crooked; this term is merely an explanatory gloss for the meaning of the preceding word.

"Vast and extensive" (*vipulavitthata*) means broad and wide both in length and in breadth; its state of being broad and wide is by way of the mundane and supramundane foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

It should be seen. "The great thoroughfare" (*mahāvīthi*) means the great road. "The supreme excellence of the foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānavaruttama*) means that it is both the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and the most excellent among the excellences;
or alternatively, the meaning is that it is the supreme thoroughfare consisting of the excellent foundations of mindfulness.
Now, within that thoroughfare of the foundations of mindfulness leading to that great city of Nibbāna, there are the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
The four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the eight meditative attainments—these precious gems he displayed on both sides in the Dhamma market. Therefore it was said:
“The four fruits of recluseship, The four analytical knowledges...”
"The six direct knowledges and the eight attainments—he displayed them there upon the path.

Now, the Blessed One, showing the means for seizing those treasures—namely, that those who are diligent, mindful, wise, and endowed with moral shame (*hiri*), fortitude (*vīriya*), and so forth, take possession of them—said:
"Those who are diligent, free from blemish, and possessed of moral shame and fortitude..."
“Those excellent qualities they take up at their own pleasure,” he said.

In this context, *ye* (those) is an indefinite designation. *Appamattā* means endowed with heedfulness (*appamāda*), which has the characteristic of non-separation from mindfulness as the antidote to negligence. *Akhilā* means free from the five mental barrennesses (*cetokhila*).
*Hirivīriyehupāgatā* [means those who have approached] through moral shame (*hiri*) and energy (*viriya*) regarding bodily misconduct and so forth.
*Hirī* means one who is ashamed; it is a designation for modesty (*lajjā*). *Vīriya* is the state of a hero (*vīra*); its characteristic is exertion.

By means of those two—modesty and energy—the individuals who have approached [the teaching] are endowed with them; they are persons capable [of realization]. The word "those" (*te*) here serves as a specific definition following the previous general reference.
Again, "those" refers to those sons of noble family who take up—that is, obtain—these aforementioned specific jewels of virtue.
The meaning is "they attain. But the Blessed One, being well-disposed and having a mind that had accomplished its task, struck the drum of the Dhamma and established the city of the Dhamma;
by this method, he first awakened one hundred thousand koṭis [of beings]. Therefore it is said:
"Thus, by this means, lifting up the great multitude..."
"The Teacher first attained enlightenment, [delivering] hundreds of thousands of millions.

In this context, "delivering" means rescuing by means of the ship of the Noble Path from the ocean of *saṃsāra*. "Hundreds of thousands of millions" means one hundred thousand times ten million; it is expressed here in reverse order.
Furthermore, when the Joyful One, the Leader of the World, was at the foot of an *amba* tree in the city of Sunandavatī, he crushed the pride and arrogance of the heretics.
Having performed the Twin Miracle, he caused thousands of millions of beings to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. This was the second realization.
Thus it is said:
“At the time when the Great Hero exhorted the hosts of heretics;”
“Thousands of koṭis attained [realization] during the second teaching of the Dhamma.

In this context, regarding the phrase *titthiye gaṇeti*, some read it as “crushing the heretics (*titthiye*), the Buddha taught the Dhamma,” meaning he crushed those who had become heretics (*titthiyabhūte*), or the groups of heretics (*titthiyānaṃ gaṇe*).
However, when the deities from ten thousand world-systems had assembled here in this world-system, and the humans—
And they raised a discussion on cessation: “How do they enter cessation? How do they become attained to cessation?

How do they emerge from cessation? Being unable to provide a definitive explanation regarding such matters as the manner of entry, the resolution, and the emergence, [they consulted] both the humans and the gods in the six sense-sphere heavens, as well as the gods in the nine Brahma-worlds.
The Brahmās, having become full of doubt, were split into two factions.
Then, at the time of evening, they approached the Blessed One, the Lord of All Worlds, the Ten-Powered One named Sumanadāsa, together with King Arindama, known as Narasundara.
Having approached, King Arindama asked the Blessed One a question concerning cessation (*nirodha*). Thereupon, when the Blessed One had answered the question on cessation,
There was a realization of the Dhamma by ninety thousand koṭis of beings. This was the third realization. Therefore it is said:
“When gods and humans, united and of one mind, asked about cessation and their mental doubt.”
“Even then, during the teaching of the Dhamma that elucidated cessation, there was a third realization for ninety thousand times ten million.
Now, that Blessed One Sumanas had three assemblies of disciples. Therein, at the first assembly—

Having spent the rains retreat in dependence on Mekhalanagara, at the first Pavāraṇā ceremony, the Blessed One performed the Pavāraṇā together with one thousand koṭis of Arahants who had gone forth by the "Come, monk" (ehi-bhikkhu) ordination; this was the first great assembly.
Then, at a later time, not far from the city of Saṅkassanagara, [a place] produced by the power of King Arindama’s merit...
Seated upon a golden mountain a yojana in height, like the sun— the mass of whose rays is beautiful in the autumn season—
upon Mount Yugandhara, the Sun of the Best of Sages subdued ninety thousand koṭis of men who had come surrounding King Arindama;
having ordained them all through the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula, on that very day...
Surrounded by monks who had attained Arahatship, he recited the Pātimokkha at an assembly endowed with four factors;

this was the second assembly. But when Sakka, the king of the gods, approached for the sake of seeing the Sugata, then the Blessed One, surrounded by eighty thousand koṭis of arahants, recited the Pātimokkha; this—
The third assembly took place. Thus it was said:
“There were three assemblies of the Great Sage Sumanas, of those whose taints were destroyed, who were stainless, whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.”
“When the Blessed One had completed the rains retreat and the invitation ceremony was proclaimed,
the Tathāgata invited [the Sangha] with hundreds of thousands of koṭis.
Following that, in the assembly on the stainless Mountain of Gold,”
The second assembly consisted of ninety thousand koṭis.
When Sakka, the king of the gods, approached to see the Buddha,
the third assembly consisted of eighty thousand koṭis.
In that context, "the invitation was proclaimed" (*abhighuṭṭhe pavāraṇe*) should be understood as a change of gender;

the meaning is "when the invitation had been proclaimed. "From there onwards" (*tato paraṃ*) means in the period subsequent to that. "On the Golden Mountain" (*kañcanapabbate*) means on a mountain made of gold.
"He approached to see the Buddha" (*buddhadassanupāgamī*) means he went for the purpose of seeing the Buddha. At that time, it is said, our Bodhisatta was a king of nāgas named Atula.
He was of great psychic power and great majesty. Hearing that "a Buddha has arisen in the world," he departed from his own abode surrounded by his circle of kinsmen.

Having caused offerings to be made with divine musical instruments for the Blessed One Sumanas, who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand times ten million bhikkhus, he distributed a great almsgiving, presented pairs of fine cloths to each [monk], and established himself in the refuges.
The Teacher also prophesied of him, "In the future he will become a Buddha. Thus it was said:
"At that time I was a Naga king of great psychic power, Known by the name Atula, a vast accumulation of wholesome merit."
“Then, having emerged from the abode of the nāgas together with my kinsmen,
I served the Jina and his Saṅgha with divine musical instruments for the nāgas.
I satisfied one hundred thousand koṭis [of beings] with food and drink.”
Having offered a pair of robes for a paccekabuddha, I went to him for refuge.
That Buddha, the joyful leader of the world, also prophesied concerning me:
"In an immeasurable aeon, this one shall become a Buddha."
“Having exerted the effort... [as before] ...we shall stand face-to-face with him.
Just as in the *Koṇḍañña-buddhavaṃsa*, these eight verses are to be expanded in detail.
“Having heard his words as well, my mind became even more serene.”
“I resolved upon a further vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
Now, that Blessed One Sumanas had a city named Mekhalā;
his father was King Sudatta, his mother was Queen Sirimā, his two chief disciples were Saraṇa and Bhāvitatta, and his attendant was named Udena.
Soṇā and Upasoṇā were his two chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree; his body was ninety cubits in height;
the measure of his lifespan was ninety thousand years; Vaṭaṃsikā was his chief queen; his son was named Anūpama;
he went forth on an elephant vehicle; the King of Aṅga was his attendant; and he dwelt in the Aṅga Monastery. Therefore it is said:
“In the city named Mekhala, there was a kṣatriya named Sudatta;
the mother of the Great Seer Sumanas was named Sirimā.
He dwelt in the household for nine thousand years.”
Canda, Sucanda, and Vaṭaṃsa—these were his three supreme palaces.
There were three million six hundred thousand women beautifully adorned;
the woman named Vaṭaṃsikā was his peerless offspring.
“Having seen the four signs, he departed on an elephant vehicle;
for ten full months, the Victor exerted himself in striving.
Being entreated by Brahmā, the Leader of the World was well-pleased.”
The Great Hero turned the wheel in Mekhalā, the supreme city.
Saraṇa and Bhāvitatta were his chief disciples;
the attendant of the Great Seer Sumanas was named Udena.
“Sona and Upasona were his chief female disciples;
that Buddha of immeasurable fame also attained enlightenment at the foot of a naga tree.
Varuṇa and Saraṇa were his chief attendants.”
Cālā and Upacālā were his chief attendants.
In height that Buddha was ninety cubits tall;
resembling a golden pillar, he shone throughout the ten thousandfold world system.
“For ninety thousand years, his lifespan lasted for that long;
remaining for that duration, he delivered many people.
Having delivered those who were to be delivered, he awakened those who were to be awakened.”
The Fully Awakened One attained final Nibbāna like the moon on the eighth day.
"Those bhikkhus whose taints were destroyed and that peerless Buddha,
having displayed their incomparable radiance, have entered Nibbāna, they of great renown."
“That knowledge was incomparable, and those treasures were beyond measure;
all that has vanished—surely all conditioned things are empty.
The Buddha Sumana, the bearer of glory, has attained final nirvana in Aṅgārāma.”
“Right there his Jina-stūpa rises four yojanas high.
In this context, “resembling a golden *agghiya*” means its beautiful form is like a golden *agghiya* ornament variegated with various gems.
“The ten-thousandfold world-system shines” means that by its radiance, even the ten-thousandfold world-system shines. “Tāraṇīye” (in the one who brings across).
"Those to be delivered"—when it is said "to deliver," the meaning is "all those who are to be guided by a Buddha.
"Like the king of stars" means like the moon. "Set" (*atthaṃ*) means gone to its setting; some read it as "gone to its goal" (*atthaṃ gato*). "Peerless" (*asādiso*) means without equal.
"Of great fame" means possessing great renown and a great retinue. "And that knowledge" refers to that omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). "Incomparable" (*atuliyaṃ*).
"Incomparable" means peerless. The remainder is entirely clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Sumanabuddhavaṃsa* is finished.
The fourth lineage of Buddhas is completed.
7. The Exposition of the Lineage of the Buddha Revata:

After the Blessed One Sumanas, when his dispensation had disappeared, human beings whose lifespan was ninety thousand years gradually declined until it reached ten years; then, increasing again by degrees, their lifespan became incalculable.
Having increased [in lifespan] and then decreased again, they came to have a life span of sixty thousand years. At that time, a teacher named Revata appeared.
He too, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was reborn in the Tusita heaven in a palace resplendent with many jewels;
then, passing away from there, he was born in the city of Sudhaññavatī—which abounded in all wealth and grain—surrounded by an immeasurable and beautiful retinue adorned with every ornament.
Having taken conception in the womb of the chief queen named Vipulā—whose lineage belonged to King Vipula, who was agitated by the accumulation of glorious wealth and possessed of vast prosperity;
and who, like a lotus-pond, shone with the beauty of a face as radiant as blossoming blue water-lilies and eyes that captivated the rows of eyelashes of all people;
and who was endowed with a vast abundance of most beautiful and charming qualities—at the end of ten months.
Like a king of golden swans emerging from Cittakūṭa Mountain, he emerged from his mother’s womb.
The miracles surrounding his conception and birth were exactly as described previously.
He possessed three palaces named Sudassana, Ratanaghara, and Veḷuna. Thirty-three thousand women, headed by Queen Sudassanā, attended upon him.
He dwelt at home for six thousand years, experiencing the pleasures of the senses like a young god surrounded by celestial maidens.
When his queen named Sudassanā gave birth to a son named Varuṇa, he beheld four omens;
then, dressed in garments of fine cloth of various colors and adorned with pearl necklaces and jeweled earrings, he [departed].
Wearing bracelets, armlets, a crown, and anklets, adorned with most fragrant flowers,
and possessing a mass of most beautiful rays like the moon at the time of autumn surrounded by a host of stars, he was like the thousand-eyed Indra surrounded by the hosts of the Thirty-three,
and like the Great Brahmā Hārita surrounded by a host of Brahmas; thus he was surrounded by a great fourfold army.
Having set out on the Great Renunciation in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses, he removed all his ornaments and placed them in the hands of the treasurer.
Then, with a sword as sharp and keen as the petal of a blue water-lily (*nīlakuvalaya*) free from dust, he cut off his own hair and topknot and threw it into the air.
Sakka, the king of the gods, caught it with a golden casket and took it to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Having led him to the summit of Sineru, he constructed a cetiya made of the seven precious gems.
The Great Man, having donned the saffron robes of Devadatta, went forth into homelessness, and one crore of men followed him into the religious life.
Surrounded by them, after practicing the life of striving for seven months, on the full moon day of Visākha, [he was attended] by a certain noble lady...
Having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice given by the daughter of the treasurer Nāma, and having spent the day’s rest in the Sāla grove,
at the time of evening he took eight handfuls of grass given by a certain Ājīvaka; then, proceeding like a noble elephant in rut,
he circumambulated the Bodhi tree of the Elephant and spread out a mat of grass fifty-three cubits wide, applying the fourfold energy.
Having made his resolve and sat down, having shattered the army of Māra and penetrated the knowledge of omniscience, he uttered this inspired utterance: “Through many a birth in saṃsāra...
[etc. ...he has attained the destruction of craving. Therefore it was said:
“After Sumanā, there was a leader named Revata;”
“Matchless, peerless, incomparable, supreme is the Jina.
It is said that after the Teacher Revata had spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, he accepted the Brahmā’s entreaty for a teaching;
then, reflecting on whom he should teach first, he [considered] himself...

Seeing many other gods and humans endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), including ten million monks who had gone forth together with him, he traveled through the air and descended at Varuṇārāma.

Surrounded by them, he set in motion the profound, subtle, threefold-revolving, and irreversible Wheel of Dhamma, unsurpassed by any other; he established ten million monks in Arhatship. In the three...
There is no numerical limit to those established in the fruits of the path. Therefore it was said:
“At the request of Brahmā, he too proclaimed the Dhamma:
the determination of the aggregates and elements, and the non-occurrence in this or that state of existence.”

In this context, "the determination of the aggregates and elements" (*khandhadhātuvavatthāna*) refers to the analysis of the five aggregates and the eighteen elements by way of the determination of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth.

The discernment of material and immaterial phenomena by way of their specific characteristics (*sabhāvalakkhaṇa*), general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), and so on, is called the determination of the aggregates and elements.
Alternatively, matter is like a lump of foam because it cannot withstand being crushed and because it possesses a nature of being perforated here and there.
"Feeling is like a water bubble because it lasts only a moment; perception is like a mirage because it deceives;
mental formations are like the trunk of a plantain tree because they lack core substance;

consciousness is like an illusion because it is deceptive"—in such ways, the definition of the aggregates and elements should also be understood by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth. "The non-occurrence in various states of existence..."

In this context, "existence" (bhava) means increase, and "non-existence" (abhava) means decrease. "Existence" refers to the view of eternalism, and "non-existence" refers to the view of annihilationism.

"Existence" refers to a minor existence, and "non-existence" refers to a major existence. "Existence" refers to the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), and "non-existence" refers to the fine-material and immaterial existences (rūpārūpabhava).
In such ways, the meaning of existence and non-existence should be understood. [It is that which serves as the cause for the non-occurrence of those states of existence and non-existence.]

The meaning is that he proclaimed the Dhamma. Alternatively, *bhava* is that by which one comes into being; it refers to karma and so forth, which are the causes for arising within the three realms of existence (*bhava*).

Non-arising (*abhava*) refers to the state of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*). The meaning is that he taught the Dhamma which brings about the abandonment of attachment to both [realms] and which is characterized by non-occurrence.
Furthermore, for that Buddha Revata, there were only three clear realizations (*abhisamaya*). First:
It transcends the path of calculation. Therefore it was said:
“Through his realization, there were three [realizations] during the teaching of the Dhamma;
The first realization cannot be expressed by number.”
In that context, "three" means three; a change of gender has been made [in the original]. This was the first clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Then, at another time, in the city of Uttarā, to the north of the city, there was a king named Arindama, the Subduer of All Enemies.
It is said that having heard that the Blessed One had arrived in his own city, he, surrounded by thirty million people, [set out for] the Blessed One...
Having gone out to meet him and invited him for the following day, he offered a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having performed a lamp-offering extending over thirty gāvutas, he approached the Blessed One and sat down.
Then the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma in a wonderful manner that was suited to his mind. Therein, among gods and humans—
There was a second realization for a thousand million [beings]. Therefore it is said:
“When the Sage Revata disciplined King Arindama, there was a second realization for a thousand million.”
This was the second clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Then, on another occasion, while the Teacher Revata was dwelling in dependence upon the town of Uttara-nigama, he sat for seven days having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
At that time, it is said, the people living in Uttara-nigama [prepared] rice gruel, cooked rice, hard foods, medicines, drinks, and so forth.
Having brought [the food] and given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the bhikkhus asked:
"Venerable sir, where is the Blessed One? Then the bhikkhus said to them: "Friends, the Blessed One has entered the attainment of cessation.
Then, after those seven days had passed, the Blessed One emerged from the attainment of cessation at the time of autumn, like the sun...
Seeing him shining with his own peerless splendor as a Buddha, they asked about the qualities and benefits of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The Blessed One then explained to them the qualities and benefits of the attainment of cessation. At that time, hundreds of millions of gods and humans were established in Arhatship.
This was the third clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Thus it is said:
“Having emerged from seven days of seclusion,
the Bull among Men disciplined a hundred million humans and devas in the supreme fruit. Thus,
at the first recitation of the Great Pātimokkha in the city of Sudhaññavatī, there were those who had gone forth by the “Come, monk” (ehibhikkhu) ordination and attained arahantship.
The first assembly consisted of those who had transcended the path of calculation.
In the city of Mekhala, there was a second assembly of one hundred thousand times ten million arahants who had gone forth by the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) ordination.
Furthermore, the Blessed One Revata’s chief disciple, Varuṇa, who followed the Wheel of Dharma and was the foremost among the wise, was afflicted with illness.

There, having taught the Dhamma that elucidates the three characteristics to the great multitude who had gathered to inquire after his health, he ordained one hundred thousand times ten million men through the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-pabbajjā*) and established them in arahantship;
then, in an assembly of fourfold forces, he recited the Pātimokkha. This was the third Great Assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies of the great seer Revata—
of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless, well-liberated,
and steadfast. Those who first gathered there exceeded all calculation.”
A second assembly of one hundred thousand times ten million took place.
Even he who was peerless in wisdom, the follower of his wheel,
at that time fell ill and reached a state where his life was in doubt.
“Regarding his inquiry after the illness, those who then approached the Sage—arahants numbering one hundred thousand koṭis—this was the third assembly.
In that context, “one who turns the wheel” means one who turns the Wheel of Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase “having reached a state where life is in doubt,” here, in relation to life...
"Having reached a danger to life" means he has reached a state where there is a doubt regarding life—whether he will reach the end of his life or not.
By virtue of the severity of his illness, there is a doubt as to whether he will die or not; this is the meaning of "having reached a danger to life.

Regarding the phrase "the sages who had then approached": if the long vowel form (*upagatā*) is used, it refers to the monks; if the short vowel form (*upagatā*) is used, it refers to the disciples (*anussava*).
It was above Varuṇa.

At that time, our Bodhisatta, having been born as a brahmin named Atideva in the city of Rammavatī and having reached the further shore of brahminical learning, saw the Perfectly Enlightened One Revata; having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, he established himself in the Refuges.
Having praised the One of Ten Powers with a thousand verses, he honored the Blessed One with an upper robe worth a thousand pieces of gold.
The Buddha also prophesied concerning him: "At the end of two incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand kalpas from now, there will be a Buddha named Gotama. Thus it was said:
“At that time, I was a brahmin named Atideva;
having approached the Buddha Revata, I went to him for refuge.
[I praised] his virtue, his concentration, and his unsurpassed quality of wisdom.”
Having bowed according to my strength, I offered him an upper robe.
That Buddha Revata, the Leader of the World, also prophesied concerning me:
"In an immeasurable aeon, this one shall become a Buddha."
“Having exerted ourselves in striving… [and so on] … we shall stand face to face with him.”—
These eight verses are to be recited in full.
“Having heard his words as well, my mind became even more serene.”
“I resolved upon a further vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
Even then, recollecting that Dhamma of the Buddha, I cultivated it, thinking:
‘I shall bring forth that Dhamma which is my heart’s desire.’”
In that regard, "I went to that refuge" means I went to that refuge; here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.

"The quality of wisdom" (*paññāguṇa*) means the perfection of wisdom. "Unsurpassed" (*anuttama*) means supreme. There is also a reading, "The unsurpassed quality of wisdom and liberation," which is self-evident.
"Having praised" (*thomayitvā*) means having extolled or lauded. "According to one's strength" (*yathāthāma*) means according to one's power. "To cross over" (*uttariya*)...
The *uttarāsaṅga*. "Adāsahan" means "I gave. "Buddhadhammaṃ" means the Dhamma that produces Buddhahood;
the meaning is the Dhamma of the perfections (*pāramī*). "Saritvā" means having recollected. "Anubrūhayin" means I caused it to increase.
"Āharissāmi" means I shall bring forth. "Taṃ dhammaṃ" means that state of Buddhahood. "Yaṃ mayhaṃ abhipatthitaṃ" means that Buddhahood which was aspired for by me.
The meaning is: "I shall fetch him.
Now, that Blessed One Revata’s city was named Sudhaññavatī;
his father was a kṣatriya named Vipula, his mother was named Vipulā, and his two chief disciples were Varuṇa and Brahmadeva; his son was named Sambhava.
His attendant was [Varuṇa], and Bhaddā and Subhaddā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree.
His body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years. Sudassanā was the name of his chief queen, and Varuṇa was the name of his son.
He went forth in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. “The peerless mass of radiance that issued from his body—”
“By day and by night, it constantly pervades a league.
“May all my relics be scattered,” the Victor resolved;
thus the Great Hero, compassionate toward all beings, made his determination.
“In the Mahānāga forest grove, near that great city,
Revata, honored by humans and gods, attained final nibbāna.
Thus it was said.
“The city was named Sudhaññavatī, and the kṣatriya father was named Vipula;
the mother of the Great Seer Revata was named Vipulā.
Varuṇa and Brahmadeva were his two chief disciples.”
Sambhava was the attendant of the great seer Revata.
Bhaddā and Subhaddā were his chief female disciples.
That Buddha, too, who was peerless and equal to the Unequaled, attained enlightenment at the foot of a Nāga tree.
“Paduma and Kuñjara were his chief attendants;
Sirimā and Yasavatī were his chief female attendants.
In height, that Buddha was eighty cubits tall.”
It illuminates all directions like a risen banner of Indra.
An unsurpassed garland of light, born from his body,
pervades a league in every direction, whether by day or by night.
“For sixty thousand years, his lifespan lasted that long;
for that duration, manifesting himself, he delivered many people.
Having displayed the power of a Buddha, he proclaimed the Deathless in the world.”
“Extinguished without clinging, just like the exhaustion of a flame through the cessation of its fuel.
That body was like a jewel, and that Dhamma was peerless;
all that has vanished—surely all conditioned phenomena are empty.”
In this context, "illuminates" means makes manifest. "Exalted" means risen up. "Garland of radiance" means a succession of rays.
"Just like fire" means as fire [is]. "With the exhaustion of fuel" means with the exhaustion of the combustible material.
"And that body is like a jewel" means that the body of that Blessed One is golden-colored. There is also a reading: "And that body, like a jewel," by way of a change in grammatical gender.
This has been stated. This indeed is its meaning. In all the remaining verses, the sense is entirely plain.
The commentary on the *Revata-buddhavaṃsa* is finished.
The fifth *buddhavaṃsa* is completed.
8. The Exposition of the Lineage of the Buddha Sobhita.
Furthermore, after his time, when even his dispensation had vanished, the Bodhisatta named Sobhita fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons;
he was reborn in the Tusita heaven and remained there for the duration of his lifespan.

Having remained there and being entreated by the gods, he passed away from the Tusita heaven and took rebirth in the city of Sudhamma, in the womb of Queen Sudhammā, within the family of King Sudhamma.
At the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Sudhamma Garden like the full moon emerging from a mass of pure, radiant, and dense clouds. Of him—
The miracles at his rebirth and birth were of the kinds previously described.
After living as a householder for ten thousand years,
four signs appeared when a son named Prince Sīha was born from the womb of Queen Makhilā, the chief consort among his thirty-seven thousand female dancers.

Having seen this, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency; he went forth right there in the palace, and developing the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-samādhi*) in that very place, he attained the four meditative absorptions (*jhānas*). For seven days, he practiced the life of striving in that same spot.
Then, having partaken of the most delicious honey-rice porridge offered by Queen Makhila Mahādevī, he resolved his mind upon going forth.
—"May this palace, adorned and prepared, travel through the air while the great multitude looks on, and descend upon the earth with the Bodhi tree at its center;
and may these women, while I am seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, emerge from the palace of their own accord without being told.
Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, the palace rose up from the Sudhamma palace of King Vessavaṇa.
It rose up into the sky, resembling dark blue collyrium. Its palace floor was adorned with clusters of fragrant flowers gathered together;
it seemed to embellish the entire expanse of the heavens.
With a mass of rays as beautiful as streams of molten gold, it shone like the sun and like the moon of the autumn season, while nets of various and variegated tinkling bells hung down from it.
Indeed, its sound— like that of a fivefold musical ensemble stirred by the wind and played by highly skilled people—
was charming, intoxicating, and desirable.
As its sweet resonance was heard from afar, it caused living beings to lend their ears in the courtyards of houses, at crossroads, in streets, and so forth.

While people were standing there engaged in conversation and discourse, he ascended into the sky—not too low and not too high, and not far from the tops of the excellent trees—seemingly beckoning them with his splendor, which was as radiant as the spreading luster of various jewels upon the branches of those noble trees;
drawing the eyes of the people toward him as if proclaiming the power of his merit, he proceeded through the expanse of the heavens. Therein:
Even the female dancers sang and cooed with sweet voices to the accompaniment of excellent five-fold musical instruments.

His fourfold army, radiant with the mass of light from their ornaments and body-gear, adorned with various colors, fragrant flowers, garments, and finery, appeared most beautiful to behold like the host of the chief immortals;
and as if the very earth had become the vault of the sky, it proceeded surrounding the palace.

Then the palace, having gone there, descended and came to rest upon the ground, centered around a *nāga* tree that stood eight hundred cubits high, with a straight, broad, and rounded trunk, adorned with flowers, shoots, and buds. And the female dancers, without being told by anyone, descended from that palace and departed.
Indeed, even the Great Man Sobhita, though endowed with manifold virtues, was accompanied by a retinue of many people.
During the three watches of the night, he attained the three knowledges (*tisso vijjāyo*). However, the army of Māra returned by its own inherent power (*dhammatābala*) just as it had come;
the palace, however, remained right where it was. Having attained full enlightenment, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*):
"Through many births in saṃsāra... [I have sought] the end of craving. Then, having spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, he—Sobhita—[remained there].
Having promised Brahmā’s request for the teaching of the Dhamma, the Buddha,
surveying with his Buddha-eye as to "to whom should I first teach the Dhamma?", saw his two half-brothers from a previous birth,
Prince Asama and Prince Sunetta, and perceived: "These two princes possess the necessary spiritual potential (upanissaya) to penetrate the profound and subtle Dhamma."
“They are capable; come now, I shall teach them the Dhamma.

Having said this, he came through the air, descended into the Sudhamma garden, and after having the two princes summoned by the park-keeper, surrounded by them and their retinues, he set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma in the midst of the great multitude. Thus it was said:
After Revata, there was a leader named Sobhita;
he was concentrated, with a peaceful mind, peerless and without equal.
That Conqueror, within his own home, turned back the mind [from worldly things].
Having attained absolute enlightenment, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
From the Avīci hell below up to the peak of existence above,
there was but a single assembly within this interval during his teaching of the Dhamma.
“In that assembly, the Perfectly Enlightened One set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion;
it cannot be expressed by calculation—such was the first realization.
Therein, “in his own home” means in his very residence, specifically on the floor of the inner palace. “He turned back the mind” means...
"He turned his mind" means that while remaining in his own home, within seven days, he turned his mind away from the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and attained Buddhahood.
"Below" means from below. "From the peak of existence" means from the Akaniṭṭha heaven.
"In that assembly" means in the midst of that assembly. "Incalculable" means beyond the path of calculation.

The meaning is as follows: "The first realization" (*paṭhamābhisamayo*) means the first realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamayo*). "There was" (*ahū*) means that the assembly cannot be defined by number;
the sense is that there was such an assembly. There is also a reading: "In the first [teaching], they indeed realized" (*paṭhame abhisamiṃsuyeva*).
The meaning of this is that those people who realized [the truth] during the first teaching of the Dhamma cannot be defined by number.
Then, at another time, having performed the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Cittapāṭali tree at the gate of the city of Sudassana,
he sat upon the Paṇḍukambala stone slab at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Navanavata-kanakamaṇi palace in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and taught the Abhidhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, ninety thousand koṭis attained penetration of the Dhamma.
This was the second realization. Therefore it is said:
"Furthermore, while he was teaching in the assembly of the gods, there occurred a second realization for ninety thousand koṭis."
Then, at another time, a prince named Jayasena, having caused a monastery one *yojana* in extent to be built in the city of Sudassana,
and having planted a grove densely filled with excellent trees such as the *asoka*, *kaṇṇacampaka*, *nāga*, *punnāga*, *vakula*, fragrant mango,
*panasa*, *sāla*, *kunda*, and *sahakāra* (mango), offered it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Having performed the expression of gratitude for the gift, he—
Having praised the sacrifice, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma. At that time, there was a realization of the Dhamma by a multitude of one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
This was the third realization. Therefore it is said:
"Furthermore, a prince, a kshatriya named Jayasena..."
Having planted a grove, he then offered it to the Buddha.
Praising his sacrifice, the Visionary One taught the Dhamma;
at that time, there was a third realization for thousands of millions.
Furthermore, King Uggata, having caused the Sunanda monastery to be built in the city of Sunandapura, gave it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
At that gift-giving, there was an assembly of one hundred koṭis of arahants who had gone forth by the "Come, bhikkhu" (ehibhikkhu) ordination;
in their midst, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha. This was the first assembly.

It came to pass that in the city of Mekhalā, the Dhamma-gaṇa had a magnificent monastery, a great vihāra named Dhammagaṇārāma, constructed and offered it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha; he gave this gift along with all the requisites.
At that assembly, there was a gathering of ninety koṭis of arahants who had gone forth through the "Come, bhikkhu" formula.
He recited the Pātimokkha. This was the second assembly.

But when the Blessed One, having spent the rains retreat in the city of the Ten Thousand Eyes, descended for the Pavāraṇā ceremony surrounded by the best of gods, he then performed the Pavāraṇā in a fourfold assembly together with eighty koṭis of arahants.
This was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies of the great seer Sobhita—
of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless, whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.
That king named Uggata gave gifts to these supreme among men.”
At that almsgiving, one hundred koṭis of Arahants assembled. Furthermore,
when the multitude of people gave alms to the Supreme among Men,
there was a second assembly of ninety koṭis.
“When the Jina, having dwelt in the world of the gods,
descended [from there], that was the third assembly of eighty koṭis.
At that time, it is said, our Bodhisatta was born on both sides of a noble family in the city of Rammavatī as a brahmin named Sujāta.

Having made the offering and heard the Blessed One Sobhita’s teaching of the Dhamma, he established himself in the refuges and gave a great almsgiving for three months to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. He too prophesied of him: "In the future, you will become a Buddha named Gotama.
Thus it was said:
“At that time, I was a brahmin named Sujāta;
then I satisfied the Buddha and his disciples with food and drink.
That Buddha, Sobhita, the Leader of the World, also gave me this prediction:”
"In immeasurable eons, this one shall become a Buddha.
"Having exerted ourselves in striving... [we] shall stand face-to-face with him.
Having heard those words as well, joyful and with a heart moved by spiritual urgency, [he spoke].
“For the sake of attaining that very state, she displayed fierce fortitude.
In this context, “for the sake of attaining that very state” means for the purpose of attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, having heard the words regarding the Buddha Sobhita—“In the future, this one named Gotama will become a Buddha”—she thought, “For his words are never false...”
"Buddhā" means "for the purpose of attaining Buddhahood"—this is the sense. "Uggaṃ" means intense or formidable. "Dhitiṃ" means energy (vīriya).
"Akāsahaṃ" means "I performed.
Now, that Blessed One Sobhita had a city named Sudhamma, and his father was named Sudhamma.
The king was Sudhamma; the queen was named Mātā; the two chief disciples were Asama and Sunetta; the attendant was named Anoma;
the two chief female disciples were Nakulā and Sujātā; the Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height;
the lifespan was ninety thousand years; his chief queen was named Makhilā; and [his son] was named Sīhakumāra.
At this time, Atraja lived as a householder for ninety-three thousand years with thirty-seven thousand dancing girls. He went forth from home by means of a palace.
His attendant was a king named Jayasena. It is said that he dwelt in the White Park (Setārāma). Therefore it was said:
“Sudhamma was the name of the city, and Sudhamma was the name of the kṣatriya;”
The mother of the Great Sage Sobhita was named Sudhammā.
Asama and Sunetta were the two chief disciples of the Great Sage Sobhita, and his attendant was named Anoma.
“Nakulā and Sujātā were his chief female disciples;
while awakening, that Buddha attained enlightenment at the foot of a Nāga tree.
The Great Sage rose to a height of fifty-eight ratanas.”
He illuminates all directions like the risen sun with its hundred rays.
Just as that forest is in full bloom, perfumed by various fragrances,
so too is his teaching perfumed by the fragrance of virtue.
“Just as the one named Sāgara is never satiated by the sight [of him],
even so his teaching is never satiated by hearing.
For ninety thousand years, such is the lifespan that exists.”
Remaining for that long, he brought many people across.
Having given counsel and instruction to the remaining people,
like a sacrificial fire that has finished its burning, he— along with his disciples— attained final peace.
“And so the Buddha, peerless and equal to none, and those disciples who had attained power—all that has vanished.
Are not all conditioned things empty?
In this context, “like the sun with its rays” means that he illuminates all directions like the sun. “Pavana” means a great forest.
*Dhūpitaṃ* means perfumed, scented, or fragrant. *Atappiyaṃ* means that which does not satisfy, or that which produces dissatisfaction.
*Tāvade* means at that time; the meaning is "for such a length of time. *Tāresi* means he caused to cross over. *Ovādaṃ* refers to advice given once; it is called *ovāda*.
*Anusiṭṭhiṃ* refers to repeated instruction; it is called *anusiṭṭhi*. *Sesake jane* refers to the remaining people who have not yet attained the penetration of truth.
The locative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī-atthe*). "Having heated like the fire of sacrifice" means having scorched like a fire. Or rather, this is the correct reading:
"Through the destruction of clinging, the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna"—this is the meaning. In all the remaining verses, the meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Sobhita-Buddhavaṃsa* is finished.
The sixth lineage of Buddhas is concluded.
9. Explanation of the Lineage of Buddha Anomadassī:
However, after the Parinibbāna of Buddha Sobhita, during the period following his passing, there was one incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya) devoid of the arising of any Buddha.
It was so. Furthermore, in the past, during that same incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeya*), three Buddhas appeared in one eon:

Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada. Therein, the Blessed One Anomadassī, having fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*) for sixteen incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons, was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Being entreated by the devas, he passed away from there and [was conceived] in the womb of Candavatī.
In the royal capital named Nāma, he took conception in the womb of the chief queen named Yasodharā— whose breasts were uplifted and beautiful— in the lineage of King Yasava.
It is said that when Prince Anomadassi had entered the womb of Queen Yasodharā,
by the power of his merit, a radiance spread over an area measuring eighty cubits.
She stood there. She remained entirely unassailable by the radiance of the moon and the sun.
At the end of ten months, she gave birth to the Bodhisatta in the Sucandana Grove. The miracles occurred exactly as described below.
On the day of his naming, however, when they were choosing a name for him, because seven jewels had fallen from the sky at his birth, they named him accordingly.
Therefore, because he was the cause for the arising of peerless jewels, they gave him the name Anomadassī.
Having gradually reached maturity, while being entertained with divine objects of sensual pleasure, he dwelt at home for ten thousand years.
It is said that he had three palaces named Siri, Upasiri, and Sirivaḍḍha, and twenty-three [consorts] headed by Sirimādevī.
Thousands of women were present [in attendance]. When his son Upavaṇa was born to Queen Sirimā, he saw four omens;
having departed on a palanquin for the Great Renunciation, he went forth into homelessness.
Three million people followed him into the religious life.
Surrounded by them, the Great Being practiced the life of striving for ten months.

Then, on the full moon of Visākha, having wandered for alms in the village of Anupama-brāhmaṇa and partaken of the honeyed milk-rice given by the daughter of the merchant Anupama-seṭṭhi, he spent the day’s rest in the Sāla grove.
Having taken eight handfuls of grass offered by the Ājīvaka named Aṇoma, [he went] to the Bodhi tree of the Ajjuṇa wood.

Having performed a circumambulation and spread out a grass mat thirty-eight cubits wide, he resolved upon the fourfold energy, sat down cross-legged, and having shattered Māra and his host, he gave rise to the three knowledges during the three watches of the night.
Then he uttered this inspired utterance: “Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [etc. ...I have attained the destruction of craving. Thus it was said.
“After Sobhita, the Sambuddha, the supreme among bipeds,
was Anomadassī, of immeasurable fame, majestic and invincible.
Having severed all fetters and shattered the three realms of existence, he— ”
He taught the path that leads to non-retrogression for gods and humans:
"Like the ocean, he is unshakeable; like a mountain, he is difficult to assail;
like space, he is infinite; like a flowering king of sāl trees, he is radiant."
“Even by merely seeing that Buddha, living beings are satisfied;
having heard him uttering his speech, they attain the Deathless.
In this context, *Anomadassī* means one of incomparable vision or immeasurable vision. *Amitāyasa* means one with an immeasurable retinue or immeasurable fame.
"Radiant" means endowed with the radiance of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. "Difficult to overcome" means difficult to displace;
the meaning is that he cannot be surpassed by any other deity, by Māra, or by anyone else.
"Having severed every bond" means having cut all ten kinds of fetters. "Having shattered the three states of existence" means [having destroyed] that which leads to the three realms of existence.
"Having shattered karma by means of the knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma; the meaning is 'having rendered it non-existent.
Regarding 'the path leading to non-return' (*anivattigamana*): Nibbāna is called 'non-return' because it is the opposite of both retrogression and worldly occurrence.
That which goes to this non-return is 'leading to non-return' (*anivattigamanā*). He taught that eightfold path which leads to such non-return."

The meaning is as follows. There is also a reading “dasseti,” which has the same meaning. “Devamānuse” means “of gods and humans”; it should be understood as the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive (sāmī-attha).

“Asaṅkhobho” means one who cannot be shaken or moved; thus it is “akkhobhiyo. For just as the ocean—eighty-four thousand yojanas deep and the dwelling place of many thousands of beings—is unshakeable, so too he is unshakeable; this is the meaning. “Ākāsova ananto” means “like space, infinite.”
Just as there is no end to space, but rather it is infinite, immeasurable, and boundless, even so the Blessed One is infinite, immeasurable, and boundless by virtue of his Buddha-qualities.

"He" refers to that Blessed One. "Like a king of sal trees in full bloom" means that because his body is adorned with all the primary marks and secondary characteristics, he shines like a fully blossomed king of sal trees. "Even by the sight of him, [one knows] 'that is a Buddha'"—of that Buddha...
The meaning is "even by seeing. Grammarians well-versed in the science of language employ the genitive case even in such instances.
"Tosita" means satisfied, gladdened. "Byāharantaṃ" means "of one who is speaking"; this is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive.
"Amataṃ" means Nibbāna. "Pāpuṇanti" means they attain. "Te" refers to those who hear his voice, his teaching of the Dhamma; the meaning is that they attain the Deathless.
But the Blessed One, having spent seven weeks at the foot of the Bodhi tree, being entreated by Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye.

Seeing that three million people who had gone forth together with him were endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), he considered, "Where are they dwelling now? and while searching, [beheld them] in the city of Subhavatī, in the Sudassana Garden.
Seeing him dwelling there, he traveled through the air and descended into the Sudassana Garden.
Surrounded by them, in the midst of an assembly of devas and humans, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. There, the first realization occurred for one hundred koṭis of beings. Therefore it is said:
"At that time, his realization of the Dhamma was prosperous and flourishing."
“Hundreds of millions attained realization during the first teaching of the Dhamma.

In this context, *phīta* means flourishing due to its great renown. *Koṭisatāni* means hundreds of millions (*koṭīnaṃ satāni*). There is also a reading, *koṭisatayo*, which has the meaning of “hundreds of millions.
Then, on another occasion, having performed the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Asana tree by the gate of the city of Osadhi, [he was] by the asuras...
While seated upon the Paṇḍukambala stone in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, which is difficult to overcome, he caused the rain of the Abhidhamma to fall for three months.
At that time, eighty koṭis of devas attained realization. Therefore it was said:
“After that, while the rains of Dhamma were falling, there was a realization [of the Truth]...”
“Eighty koṭis attained realization during the second teaching of the Dhamma.
Therein, “while it was raining” means while the great cloud of the Buddha was raining. “Showers of Dhamma” means showers of rain consisting of Dhamma discourses.

Then, on another occasion, during the exposition of the Questions on Auspiciousness (*Maṅgalapañhāniddesa*), seventy-eight koṭis attained realization. That was the third realization. Therefore it was said:
“Even thereafter, as he rained down and refreshed living beings, there occurred the third realization for seventy-eight koṭis.

In this context, “raining down” means raining down the stream of water that is the Dhamma discourse. “Refreshing” means refreshing with the rain of the nectar of the Dhamma; the meaning is that the Blessed One was performing an act of refreshing.
The Blessed One Anomadassi also had three assemblies of disciples.

There, having gained confidence while the Dhamma was being taught by King Isidatta in the city of Soreyya, eight hundred thousand arahants who had gone forth by the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) formula sat in the midst of whom he recited the Pātimokkha.
This was the first assembly. In the city of Rādhavatī, [of King] Sundarindhara...
While the Dhamma was being taught to King Nāma, he recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of seven hundred thousand arahants who had gone forth by the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) ordination.

This was the second great assembly. Again, in the city of Soreyya itself, while the Pātimokkha was recited in the midst of six hundred thousand arahants who had gone forth by the "Come, monk" ordination together with King Soreyya—
He designated [the site]. This was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies of that Great Sage as well, of those who had attained the power of direct knowledge and blossomed in liberation.”
“At that time there was an assembly of one hundred and eighty thousand [monks],
who had abandoned pride and delusion, whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.
A second gathering of one hundred and seventy thousand occurred.”
“For those free from blemish, dustless, peaceful,
and poised— there was a third assembly of six hundred thousand ascetics who had attained the power of direct knowledge and were extinguished.”
In that context, *tassāpi ca mahesino* means "of that Great Sage," [namely] Anomadassi. There is also the reading *tassāpi dvipaduttamo*, which has the meaning "of that supreme among bipeds.
The grammatical analysis (*lakkhaṇa*) should be understood from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).

*Abhiññābalappattānaṃ* means "who have attained the power of the direct knowledges" (*abhiññā*); it refers to those who have reached a state of stability in the direct knowledges through mastery (*ciṇṇavasitāya*), by virtue of being swift and ready in their application.

Meaning: "Of those in full bloom" means of those who have attained the highest excellence of beauty through the blossoming of all their faculties. "By liberation" means by the liberation of the fruit of Arahatship (*arahattaphala-vimutti*).
Regarding the term "of those free from blemish" (*anaṅgaṇānaṃ*):
here, this word *aṅgaṇa* is seen in some instances to refer to the defilements (*kilesa*). As it is said: "In that regard..."
“What are the three stains? Lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, and delusion is a stain.
“Friend, ‘stain’ is a designation for evil, unwholesome states that fall within the domain of craving. In some instances it refers to impurity; as it is said:
“He strives for the abandoning of that very dust or stain. In some instances it refers to such a state [of defilement].
On the ground, there are "the courtyard of the shrine," "the courtyard of the Bodhi tree," and "the royal courtyard. Here, however, it should be understood as referring to the defilements (*kilesa*).
Therefore, the meaning is "of those free from defilement" (*nikkilesānaṃ*). "Dustless" (*virajānaṃ*) is a synonym for that same term. Regarding "those who practice austerity" (*tapasīnaṃ*):

those who possess the austerity (*tapa*) known as the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), which brings about the destruction of the defilements, are "those who practice austerity"; the meaning is "of those ascetics" (*tapasīnaṃ*), that is, of those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsavānaṃ*).
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a powerful and influential general of the yakkhas, possessed of great psychic power and majesty,

the lord of many hundreds of thousands of millions of yakkhas. Hearing that "a Buddha has appeared in the world," he came and [erected] a pavilion made of the seven precious gems, most beautiful to behold, resembling the orb of the moon.
Having fashioned it, he gave a great almsgiving there for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

Then, at the time of the expression of thanks for the meal, the Blessed One prophesied concerning him: “In the future, after one incalculable eon plus one hundred thousand aeons have passed, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. Thus it was said.
“At that time, I was a yakkha of great psychic power;
I was the lord and master over many tens of millions of yakkhas.
Even then, having approached that supreme Buddha, the Great Sage,”
I satisfied with food and drink the Leader of the World together with his Saṅgha.
Then that Sage of pure vision made this prediction to me:
"In immeasurable aeons from now, this one shall become a Buddha."
“Having exerted the supreme effort… we shall stand face to face with this one.
Having heard those words as well, joyful and with a heart moved by spiritual urgency,
I resolved upon further practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
In that regard, "he resolved upon a further vow" means that for the sake of fulfilling the perfections (pāramī), he exerted himself even more firmly.
Now, that Blessed One Anomadassi had a city named Candavatī;
his father was King Yasava, his mother was Yasodharā, his two chief disciples were Nisabha and Anoma, and his attendant was named Varuṇa.
Sundarī and Sumanā were his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the *ajjuna* tree; his body was fifty-eight cubits in height;
his lifespan was one hundred thousand years; his chief queen was named Sirimā; his son was named Upavāṇa;
he dwelt in the household for ten thousand years; he went forth by means of a palanquin. Regarding his departure by palanquin, however, there is an account in the *Sobhita-buddhavaṃsa-vaṇṇanā*.
This should be understood in the same manner as described regarding the journey to the palace. King Dhammaka was his attendant.
It is said that the Blessed One dwelt in the Dhammārāma park. Therefore it was said:
“The city was named Candavatī, and the nobleman was named Yasava;”
The mother of the Teacher Anomadassi was named Yasodharā.
Nisabha and Anoma were his chief disciples,
and he who was named Varuṇa was the attendant of the Teacher Anomadassi.
“Sundarī and Sumanā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Ajjuṇa.
The Great Sage rose to a height of fifty-eight ratanas.”
His radiance streams forth like the risen sun with its hundred rays.
"The lifespan exists for as long as one hundred thousand years;
remaining for that duration, he delivered many people."
“The well-flowered Pāvacana, by such Arahants—
those free from passion and stainless— has shone forth the teaching of the Conqueror.
And that Teacher of immeasurable fame, those peerless pairs [of disciples] as well.”
"All that has vanished; are not all conditioned things (saṅkhārā) empty?"—in this context, "the radiance streams forth" means that light issues from his body.
Moreover, the radiance of his body remains at all times pervading an area measuring twelve yojanas. "Those pairs" refers to the pairs of chief disciples and so forth.
“Pairs. All that has vanished means that everything of the kind described has entered the door of impermanence and is destroyed;
this is the meaning. There is also a reading, “Are not all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) indeed empty? The meaning of this is: “Are not all conditioned phenomena indeed empty and hollow?
The letter *ma* is used here for metrical conjunction. In all the remaining verses, the meaning is entirely obvious.

However, in the presence of this Blessed One Anomadassi, these two chief disciples, Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna, made a formal aspiration for the state of being chief disciples. The story of these two elders should be told here;
however, I have not included it for fear of excessive length in this work.
The commentary on the lineage of Anomadassi Buddha is finished.
The seventh lineage of Buddhas is completed.
10. Commentary on the lineage of Paduma Buddha.
But after the time of the Blessed One Anomadassi, when the human lifespan had gradually decreased from one hundred thousand years until it reached ten years,
and then increased again until it became incalculable, and subsequently decreased once more until it was one hundred thousand years,
a Teacher named Paduma appeared in the world. He too [fulfilled] the perfections...

Having fulfilled his perfections and been reborn in the Tusita heaven, he passed away from there and took conception in the womb of the chief queen named Asamā—who was peerless in beauty and other qualities—within the family of King Asama in the city of Campaka.
At the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Campaka grove. And when the prince was born, [a light shone] from the sky throughout the entire Jambudīpa.

A rain of lotuses fell as far as the edge of the ocean. Therefore, on the day his name was being given, the fortune-tellers and his kinsmen gave him the name Mahāpaduma Kumāra. He lived at home for ten thousand years.
He had three palaces named Nanduttara, Vasuttara, and Yasuttara. There were thirty-three [thousand] women headed by Queen Uttarā.
Thousands of women were present there.
Then, when a son named Rammakumāra was born to the chief queen named Uttarā, the Great Being saw the four omens and went forth on the Great Renunciation in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses.
As he was departing for the homeless life, ten million people followed him into the religious life.
Thus surrounded by them, having practiced the life of striving for eight months, on the full moon day of Visākha in the city of Dhaññavatī,
he partook of the honeyed milk-rice offered by Dhaññavatī, the daughter of the merchant Sudhañña;
after spending the midday rest in the Mahāsāla grove, at the time of evening, he took eight handfuls of grass given by the ascetic Tittiriyaka.

Having approached the Mahāsoṇa Bodhi tree and prepared a grass mat thirty-eight cubits wide, he sat down cross-legged, resolved upon the fourfold energy, and having shattered the host of Māra, realized the three knowledges throughout the three watches of the night.
Then he uttered this inspired utterance: “Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [and so on] ...I have attained the destruction of craving.”
Having uttered this inspired utterance and spent seven days in the very vicinity of the Bodhi tree, he accepted the Brahmā’s entreaty;
then, while examining those individuals who were fit vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma, he saw the bhikkhus numbering in the tens of millions who had gone forth together with himself.
At that very moment, traveling by way of the air, he arrived at the Dhanañjaya Garden near the city of Dhaññavatī.
Having descended, surrounded by them and in their midst, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. At that time, there was the realization of one hundred koṭis.
Therefore it is said:
"After Anomadassi, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds;”
One named Paduma by name, peerless and without equal.
His virtue also was peerless, his concentration infinite;
his excellent knowledge was incalculable, and his liberation was beyond compare.
“For him too, of incomparable majesty, upon the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma, there were three realizations that dispel great darkness.
In this context, “unequaled virtue” means not similar to the virtue of others; the sense is that it is supreme and best. Concentration also...
The concentration (*samādhi*) of infinite millions is immeasurable; its infinity is to be seen in such things as the revelation of the world and the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
"The excellence of knowledge" (*ñāṇavara*) refers either to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) or to the unique, uncommon knowledges.

"Liberation" (*vimutti*) also refers to the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship belonging to the Blessed One. "Incomparable" (*anūpamā*) means devoid of comparison. "Of incomparable splendor" (*atulatejassa*) means of the splendor of incomparable knowledge. It is also [read as] "of incomparable splendor of knowledge" (*atulañāṇatejā*).
This is the reading. Its connection should be understood with the subsequent phrase, “three realizations” (*tayo abhisamayā*).
“Dispellers of great darkness” (*mahātamapavāhanā*) means destroyers of great delusion;
that is, those who shatter the darkness of ignorance. Then, on another occasion, the Blessed One Paduma [addressed] his younger brothers, Prince Sālaka and Prince Upasālaka.
Having ordained them along with their retinue during a gathering of kinsmen, he taught the Dhamma to them and caused ninety million beings to drink the nectar of the Dhamma.
But when he taught the Dhamma to the Elder Ramma, there occurred the third great realization (abhisamaya) for eighty million beings.
Thus it is said:
“At the first realization, the Buddha awakened one hundred koṭis;
at the second realization, the Wise One awakened ninety koṭis.
And when the Buddha Paduma exhorted his own son, [he awakened eighty koṭis].”
"At that time, there was a third realization for eighty koṭis.
Furthermore, when the king named Subhāvitatta, surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand koṭis,
went forth by the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) ordination in the presence of the Buddha Paduma, whose face was like a lotus, the Blessed One [spoke] at that assembly:
He recited the Pātimokkha, and that was the first assembly.
Then, at a later time, Mahāpaduma, the bull among sages, whose gait was like that of a bull and who was a bull among men, entered the rains retreat in dependence upon the city of Usabhavatī.
The people living in that city, desiring to see the Blessed One, approached him. To them—
The Blessed One taught the Dhamma. Thereupon, many people with confident hearts went forth.
Then the Ten-Powered One, together with those and three hundred thousand other bhikkhus, performed the invitation ceremony for purification (*visuddhipavāraṇā*).
This was the second great assembly. However, those who did not go forth there, having heard of the benefits of the Kathina robe, [went forth] on the first day of the fortnight.
After five months, they presented the *kathina* robe-cloth, which bestows five benefits.
Then, having requested the Elder Sāla—the Chief Disciple, the General of the Dhamma, and one of vast intelligence—to perform the *kathina* ceremony, they gave that *kathina* robe-cloth to him.
While the Elder was having the *kathina* robe made, the monks were his assistants in the sewing. But as for Paduma, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
Having threaded the threads through the eye of a needle, he gave them to him. When the robe was finished, the Blessed One set out on a journey with three hundred thousand bhikkhus.

Then, at another time, the Lion of Buddhas—like a lion among men who moves with the stride of a lion—proceeded to the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove, which resembled a forest of sal trees whose branches and boughs were bent down by the weight of most fragrant flowers and fruits, and which was adorned with stainless white and blue lotuses.
Flooded by a stream of cool, sweet water; frequented by various herds of wild animals such as ruru deer, yaks, lions, tigers, goats, horses, gavayas, and wild oxen;
surrounded on all sides by young female bees whose hearts were bound by the fragrance of fragrant flowers and who offered their service with humming sounds;
and filled with cuckoos whose hearts were gladdened by the taste of fruit and who warbled with melodies as sweet as the *kākalī* note.
In a forest grove that was exceedingly beautiful, secluded, solitary, and conducive to yoga, where the female cuckoos were singing, he entered upon the rains retreat.
While he was dwelling there, people saw the Tathāgata, the Ten-Powered One, the King of Dhamma, together with his retinue, shining with the glory of a Buddha;
having heard his Dhamma and gained confidence, they went forth by means of the "Come, monk" ordination. At that time...
Surrounded by two hundred thousand bhikkhus, he partook of the Pavāraṇā ceremony. That was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies for Paduma, the Great Sage;
The first gathering consisted of one hundred thousand koṭis.”
“At the time of the Kathina ceremony, when the Kathina robe-material had arisen,
the monks sewed the robe for the sake of the General of the Dhamma.
Then those stainless monks, possessing the six direct knowledges and great psychic power,”
“Three hundred thousand were assembled there, unconquered.
Furthermore, that bull among men went to dwell in the forest;
at that time, there was a gathering of two hundred thousand.”
Therein, "at the time of the Kathina-robe offering" means at the time of spreading out the Kathina robe.

"For the sake of the General of the Dhamma" means for the sake of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma. "Unconquered" (*aparājita*) means not conquered; the elision of the case-ending (*vibhatti*) is to be understood.
"He" refers to that Mahāpaduma. "In the forest" means in the great forest. "The rainy-season residence" (*vāsa*) means the *vassāvāsa*. "He approached" means he arrived. Of the two...
“Two hundred thousand” (*satasahassinam*) means two times one hundred thousand. There is also a reading, “Then there was a gathering” (*tadā āsi samāgamo*); if it exists, it would be more elegant.

At that time, while the Tathāgata was dwelling in that forest grove, our Bodhisatta, having become a lion, saw him sitting for seven days having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
With a clear mind, having performed a circumambulation, he felt joy and gladness.

Having roared the lion’s roar three times, and for seven days not forsaking the joy inspired by the Buddha, he did not depart from his range of vision even while experiencing that very joy and happiness;
having renounced his life, he remained there in attendance.
Then, at the end of those seven days, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of cessation and, like a lion among men, looked toward the lion and said: “In the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as well...”
"May there be confidence in the mind; let the Saṅgha come," he thought. At that very moment, many millions of bhikkhus arrived.
Sīha also placed his confidence in the Saṅgha. Then the Teacher, observing his mind, prophesied:
"In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama. Thus it was said:
“At that time, I was a lion, the lord of beasts;
in the forest, I saw the Conqueror cultivating solitude.
Having bowed my head at his feet and performed a circumambulation of him,”
Having roared three times, I attended upon the Victor for seven days.
"Having emerged from a sublime meditative attainment after seven days, the Tathāgata,
having reflected with his mind, summoned ten million bhikkhus."
“Then too, that Great Hero, in their midst, prophesied:
‘In an immeasurable aeon, this one shall become a Buddha.
Having exerted himself in striving... [we] shall stand face-to-face with him.”
“Having heard her words as well, my heart became even more serene;
I resolved upon a further ascetic practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
In this context, “cultivating seclusion” means having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). “Skilfully” (padakkhiṇaṃ) —
Having circumambulated three times to the right. *Abhināditvā* means having roared the lion’s roar three times.
*Upaṭṭhahanti* means they waited upon him; or rather, this is the reading: *upaṭṭhahiṃ*. *Varasamāpattiyaṃ* means having emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
*Manasā cintayitvāna* means having thought in his mind, "Let all the bhikkhus come here as well. *Samānayī* means he gathered them together.
Now, for that Blessed One Paduma, the city was named Campaka; his father was King Asama, and his mother was named Asamā;
Sāla and Upasāla were his two chief disciples; Varuṇa was his attendant;
Rādhā and Surādhā were his two chief female disciples; the Mahāsoṇa tree was his Bodhi tree; and he was eighty-eight cubits in height.
His body was [exquisite], his lifespan was one hundred thousand years, and his chief queen was unsurpassed and supreme in qualities such as beauty and so forth.
He had a son named Rammakumāra who was exceedingly delightful. Therefore it is said:
“In the city named Campaka, there was a Khattiya named Asama;”
Asamā was the name of the mother of the Great Seer Paduma.
Sāla and Upasāla were his chief disciples,
and he who was named Varuṇa was the attendant of the Great Seer Paduma.
“Rādhā and Surādhā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Mahāsoṇa.
The Great Sage rose up to fifty-eight ratanas in height.”
His radiance streams forth, incomparable in every direction:
“The radiance of the moon, the radiance of the sun, and the radiance of the crest-jewels of the finest gems—
all these are eclipsed upon reaching the supreme radiance of the Victor.”
“For a hundred thousand years, such was the lifespan that existed;
remaining for that long, he brought many people across.
Having awakened, without exception, those beings whose minds were fully ripened,”
Having instructed his disciples, he, together with his followers, has attained Nibbāna:
"Like a snake casting off its worn-out skin, like a tree shedding its old leaves;
having abandoned all conditioned phenomena, he has attained Nibbāna like a fire that has gone out."
In this context, "the radiance of the crest-jewels" refers to the radiance of gems, the radiance of fire, and the radiance of jewels.
"Overpowered" means overcome. "Having reached the supreme radiance of the Victor" means they were overpowered after reaching the preeminent bodily radiance of the Conqueror.
"With a mature mind" refers to those beings to be trained whose faculties have reached maturity. "Old leaves" means ancient leaves. "Like a tree" means just as a tree [is affected].

"All formations" (*sabbasaṅkhāra*) refers to all formations, both internal and external. There is also a reading, "having abandoned all formations" (*hitvā sabbasaṅkhāra*), which has the same meaning.
Just as one says "the fire has gone out," so the Sugata has gone to Nibbāna without fuel.
The rest here is self-evident, as it follows the method already explained below for the preceding verses.
The commentary on the lineage of Padumabuddha is finished.
The eighth lineage of Buddhas is completed.
11. Commentary on the lineage of Nāradabuddha.

But when Padumabuddha had attained final Nibbāna and his dispensation had disappeared, human beings with a lifespan of one hundred thousand years gradually declined until they reached a lifespan of ten years.
Then, after increasing again and reaching an incalculable lifespan, they declined once more until their lifespan was ninety thousand years.
At that time, there appeared one who possessed the Ten Powers, the Threefold Knowledge, and was confident in the Four Grounds of Self-Assurance.
The Teacher, the supreme among men, named Nārada, who was a hero in liberation, appeared in the world.
