Having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven;

then, passing away from there, he entered the womb of the chief queen of King Sudeva—whose name means "Good God"—in the city called Dhāññavatī, a king who had conquered his own enemies through his own valor.
He took conception in the womb of the queen named Anomā. At the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Dhanañjaya Garden.

On the day of the naming ceremony, when the bestowing of a name was being performed, suitable ornaments fit for human enjoyment throughout the whole of Jambudīpa descended from the sky by means of the wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*) and other such sources.
They fell [at his feet]. Because he gave men ornaments worthy of them, they gave him the name "Nārada.
He lived in the midst of the household for nine thousand years. There were three palaces suitable for the three seasons: Vijita, Vijitāvin, and Vijitābhirāma.
To that Prince Nārada, who was endowed with noble lineage, virtue, conduct, and beauty, there was one who was pleasing to the mind...
They made a very fortunate noble maiden named Vijitasenā the chief queen.
Starting with her, there were one hundred and twenty thousand women. To that Queen Vijitasenā was born a son named Prince Nanduttara, who brought joy to the entire world;
having seen four omens, [the king], with a great fourfold army...
Surrounded [by his retinue], dressed in garments of various colors, with pearl necklaces, jeweled earrings, excellent armlets, a crown, and bracelets fastened upon him,
and adorned with most fragrant perfumes and flowers, he went on foot to the park; there,
having removed all his ornaments and placed them in the hands of the treasurer, he himself, with a sword as sharp as the petal of a stainless blue water-lily, [struck].
Having cut off his hair and the diadem adorned with most beautiful jewels, he threw them into the expanse of the sky. Sakka, the king of the gods, received them with a golden casket,
took them to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and on the summit of Sineru, three yojanas high,
erected a cetiya made of the seven precious gems.
But the Great Man, having donned the saffron robes of Devadatta, went forth right there in the park.

And one hundred thousand men followed him into the religious life. Having practiced the life of striving right there for seven days, on the full moon day of Visākha, he partook of the milk-rice offered by Vijitasenā, the chief queen, and right there—
Having spent the day in the garden and taking eight handfuls of grass given by Sudassana, the keeper of the garden, he circumambulated the Mahāsoṇa Bodhi tree.

He spread out a grass mat eighty-eight cubits wide, sat down upon it, and having shattered the host of Māra, he attained the three types of higher knowledge during the three watches of the night; thus, he penetrated the knowledge of omniscience.
Having uttered the inspired utterance (udāna): “Through many births in saṃsāra...
[pe] ...I have now attained the destruction of craving,” and having spent seven weeks, he gave his consent when requested by Brahmā.

Then, surrounded by one hundred thousand bhikkhus who had gone forth together with him in the Dhanañjaya Park, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion there. At that time, [there were] one hundred thousand times ten million...
There was a penetration of the Dhamma. Therefore it is said:
“After Paduma, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds, named Nārada by name, the peerless one, the matchless one.”
Thus the Buddha, the eldest and most beloved legitimate son of the Wheel-turning Monarch,
having cast off his garlands and ornaments, approached the pleasure grove.
There stood a tree, vast in its glory, beautiful, sublime, and pure.
Having reached its middle, he sat down beneath Mahāsoṇa.
There, a supreme knowledge arose— endless and like a thunderbolt—
with which he scrutinized conditioned phenomena in their various positions, whether upright or overturned.
“Therein he carried away all defilements without remainder;
he attained complete enlightenment and the fourteen types of Buddha-knowledge.
Having attained full awakening, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.”
“The first realization occurred for one hundred thousand koṭis.
In this context, “of the wheel-turning monarch” means of the king who turns the wheel. “The eldest” means born first.

“Beloved legitimate son” means a beloved, dear, legitimate son; a son who is cherished and fondled while held to the breast is called a “beloved legitimate son. “Adorned with garlands and ornaments” means...
Adorned with pearl necklaces, armlets, bracelets, crowns, earrings, and garlands, he went to the pleasure garden—an orchard named Dhanañjaya’s Garden located outside the city.
"There was a tree there" means that in that garden, it is said, there was a single tree named Rattasoṇa.

It is said to have been ninety cubits in height, with a perfectly symmetrical trunk, well-developed various branches and twigs, dense and broad green foliage, and a spreading shade; for it was inhabited by deities.
Devoid of the movement of various flocks of birds, serving as an ornament for the surface of the earth, it acted like a sovereign over the trees;
its appearance was supremely beautiful to behold, all its branches adorned with red flowers, and it became a veritable elixir for the eyes of gods and humans.
"Yasavipulo" means one of vast fame; the sense is that he was renowned throughout the entire world, made manifest everywhere by his own prosperity, and thus celebrated.
Some read, "There stood a vast tree. *Brahā* means great; the meaning is that it was like the Pāricchattaka tree of the devas.
*Tamajjhappatvā* means having reached, having approached, and having come near that soṇa tree.
*Heṭṭhato* means beneath that tree.
"Supreme knowledge arose" means that excellent knowledge (*ñāṇavara*) arose. "Infinite" means immeasurable and boundless.
"Like a thunderbolt" means sharp like a thunderbolt; this is a designation for insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) such as the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
"By that he discerned formations" means that by means of that insight-knowledge he discerned formations such as form (*rūpa*). "Upside-down and upside-up" means...

The meaning is that he investigated the arising and passing away of formations. Therefore, having comprehended the mode of conditions and emerged from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, he focused upon the five aggregates;

by way of their arising and passing away, he saw fifty characteristics, and having developed insight up to the level of change-of-lineage knowledge, he attained all the qualities of a Buddha through the successive stages of the Noble Path—this is the meaning.
*Tattha* means "there," at the *soṇa*-tree. *Sabbakilesāni* means "all the defilements"; this is stated with a change in grammatical gender.
Some read it as "tattha sabbakilesehi. *Aseṣaṃ* means "without remainder.

*Abhivāhayī* means he carried away all the defilements by means of both the cleansing of the path and the cleansing of the defilements; the meaning is that he brought them to destruction. *Bodhi* refers to the knowledge of the path of Arahatship.

"And fourteen in the knowledge of a Buddha" means there are fourteen kinds of a Buddha’s knowledge. What are they? The eight knowledges of the paths and fruits and the six uncommon knowledges—thus these are called the fourteen kinds of a Buddha’s knowledge. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of inclusion;
by it, the other four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*), the four kinds of intrepidity (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*), and the four knowledges that delimit the [four] modes of birth are also included.
The meaning is that he attained the knowledges that delimit the five destinies, the ten powers of knowledge, and all the qualities of a Buddha.

Having thus attained Buddhahood and accepted the Brahmā’s entreaty, he established one hundred thousand bhikkhus—those who had gone forth together with himself—in the Dhanañjaya Garden and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma before them. At that time, [there were] one hundred thousand times ten million...
This was the first realization. At that time, it is said, a dragon king named Doṇa resided on the bank of the Ganges in the city of Mahādoṇa;
he possessed great psychic power and majesty, and was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the populace.
Whenever the people living in a certain district failed to perform offerings to him, he would afflict that district with either drought or excessive rain.
Or he destroys it with a rain of gravel.

Then the Teacher Nārada, who could see the shore, perceiving the underlying potential (upanissaya) for the conversion of many living beings within Doṇa the Nāga King, went to the dwelling place of that Nāga King, surrounded by a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then...
When people saw him, they said: "Lord, a nāga king of terrible venom, fierce power, great psychic might, and great majesty dwells here;
he might harm you, so you must not go. But the Blessed One proceeded as if he did not hear their words.
Having gone there, [he entered] the supremely fragrant scent prepared for the honor of that nāga king.

He sat down upon the flower-strewn seat. It is said that the great multitude gathered together, thinking, "We shall witness the battle between both Nārada, the king of sages, and Doṇa, the king of nāgas.
Then, the serpent-nāga, seeing the sage-nāga seated in such a manner and unable to endure the [sage's] arrogance, made his body visible.
The Naga king emitted smoke; the One Possessed of the Ten Powers also emitted smoke. Again the Naga king blazed up; the King of Sages also blazed up.

Then that Naga king, his body exceedingly exhausted by the masses of smoke issuing from the body of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, unable to endure the suffering, released poison, thinking, "I shall kill him with the force of the poison. By the force of the poison, even the entire [body]...
Jambudīpa might have been destroyed, yet that poison was unable to cause even a single hair on the body of the One Possessing Ten Powers to quiver.
Then that Nāga king, looking to see what the state of the ascetic was,
beheld him shining with the six-colored rays of a Buddha like the sun and the moon in the autumn season, his countenance radiant and serene.
Having seen the Blessed One, he thought, "Aho! This ascetic is indeed possessed of great psychic power;
I have acted wrongly, being unaware of my own strength," and seeking refuge, he approached the Blessed One alone for protection.
Then the sage-king Nārada, having disciplined that king of the nāgas, [spoke] for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the minds of the great multitude assembled there.
He performed the Twin Miracle. At that time, ninety thousand koṭis of living beings were established in Arahatship.
This was the second conversion. Therefore it is said:
“The Great Sage, while converting the Naga King Mahādoṇa;”
He then performed a miracle, displaying it to the world with its gods.
At that time, during that proclamation of the Dhamma,
ninety thousand koṭis of devas and humans crossed over all their doubts.
In that context, "he performed a miracle" (*pāṭihīraṃ tadākāsī*) means he performed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*); this is the meaning. Or rather, this very reading [is preferred].
There is also the reading: "Then the gods and humans" (*tadā devamanussā vā*). In that case, *devamanussānaṃ* is used in the nominative case in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*).
Therefore, the meaning is: "of the gods and humans, ninety thousand koṭis. "They crossed over" (*tariṃsu*) means they transcended [the flood].
But when he exhorted his own son, Prince Nanduttara, at that time there was a third realization for eighty thousand koṭis. Thus it is said:
"At the time when the Great Hero exhorted his own son, there was a third realization for eighty thousand koṭis."

Then, in the city of Thullakoṭṭhita, two brahmin friends, Bhaddasāla and Vijitamitta, while searching for the lake of the Deathless, saw the Fully Enlightened One Nārada sitting in an assembly, exceedingly confident.
Seeing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man upon the Blessed One’s body, they thought: "This is the Fully Enlightened One in the world, whose veil has been lifted."
Having reached the conclusion [of their deliberations], they conceived faith in the Blessed One and, together with their retinue, went forth in the presence of the Blessed One.
When they had gone forth and attained arahantship, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of one hundred thousand times ten million bhikkhus;
that was the first great assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies for the great seer Nārada;
the first gathering was of one hundred thousand koṭis.

At the time when the Perfectly Enlightened One Nārada, in the assembly of his kinsmen, recounted his own lineage of Buddhas beginning from his original aspiration, there occurred the second assembly of ninety thousand koṭis of bhikkhus. Thus it is said:
“When the Buddha proclaimed the qualities of a Buddha together with their basis, ninety thousand koṭis of those free from stain then gathered.
In this context, “free from stain” means devoid of impurity; the meaning is that they were those whose taints were destroyed.
But when Verocana, the Naga king, was inspired with faith upon the conversion of Mahādoṇa, the Naga king,
he constructed on the river Gaṅgā a pavilion made of the seven precious gems measuring three gavutas in size; having seated the Blessed One there together with his retinue,
and having invited him along with his followers and the entire kingdom for the purpose of displaying his own hall of almsgiving, he [prepared] the Naga dancers.
Having assembled various musicians adorned with diverse costumes and ornaments, he offered a great almsgiving to the Blessed One and his retinue with the highest honors.
At the conclusion of the meal, the Blessed One delivered a discourse of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*) as if causing the Great Ganges to flow down.
Then, having heard the Dhamma during that thanksgiving, eighty million bhikkhus who were filled with serene confidence went forth by the "Come, Bhikkhu" (*ehi bhikkhu*) ordination.
He recited the Pātimokkha in their midst; that was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“When the Nāga Verocana gave a gift to the Teacher, then eighty hundred thousand sons of the Conqueror gathered together.”
In that regard, "eighty hundred thousand" means eighty times one hundred thousand.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, established a hermitage on the slopes of the Himalayas;
having attained mastery over the five supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he dwelt there. Then, out of compassion for him—

The Blessed One Nārada, surrounded by eighty koṭis of arahants, ten thousand lay followers who had attained the fruit of non-returning, and thousands of other disciples, went to that hermitage. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic’s heart was filled with joy;
he prepared the hermitage for the Blessed One and his retinue to dwell in, and throughout the entire night, he extolled the virtues of the Teacher. To the Blessed One...
Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, he went to Uttarakuru on the following day;

bringing food from there, he gave a great almsgiving to the Buddha and his retinue. Having thus given a great almsgiving for seven days, he brought priceless red sandalwood from the Himavat mountains and honored the Blessed One with that red sandalwood.
Then the One of Ten Powers, surrounded by gods and men, [spoke to him].
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he prophesied: "In the future, there will be a Buddha named Gotama. Therefore it was said:
"At that time, I was a matted-hair ascetic, practicing intense austerities;
I was a wanderer through the air, one who had reached the further shore of the five supernormal powers."
“Then I satisfied that Peerless One, together with his Saṅgha and his retinue,
with food and drink, and honored him with sandalwood.
At that time, Nārada, the Leader of the World, gave me this prediction:”
“In immeasurable eons, a Buddha will appear in the world.
“Having exerted ourselves in striving... [we shall] stand face-to-face with him.
Having heard those words as well, his mind was filled with even greater joy.
“They indeed undertook a formidable vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.

In this context, *tadāpāham* means “then indeed I [was there]. *Asamasamaṃ* means equal to those who are unequal; that is, the past Buddhas are called “unequal” (*asama*), and being equal to those unequals is “equal to the unequal” (*asamasama*).
Alternatively, *asama* means uneven, while *sama* means even, uniform, or virtuous; thus, among those who are “equal to the unequal,” [he is the peerless one].
It should be understood that although it ought to be called “asamasamasama,” it is stated with the elision of one instance of the word *sama*;
the meaning is “the unequaled, the peerless equal. “Saparijanaṃ” means “together with the lay followers.
There is also the reading: “Sopi maṃ tadā naramarūnaṃ, majjhe byākāsi cakkhumā,” which has a self-evident meaning. “Bhiyyo hāsetva mānasaṃ” means “having further gladdened the mind.”
Having gladdened and satisfied his heart, he resolved upon a formidable vow; indeed, he resolved upon a formidable vow.
There is also a reading: “I resolved upon a further vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
Now, that Blessed One Nārada had a city named Dhaññavatī, and a kṣatriya named Sudeva.
His father was [named] Pitā, his mother was named Anomā, and his two chief disciples were Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta.
His attendant was named Vāseṭṭha, and his two chief female disciples were Uttarā and Phaggunī. His Bodhi tree was the Mahāsoṇa tree, and his body was eighty-eight cubits in height.
The radiance of his body constantly pervaded one *yojana*, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years. Of him—
Furthermore, his chief queen was named Vijitasenā, and he had a son named Prince Nanduttara.
He possessed three palaces named Vijita, Vijitāvin, and Vijitābhirāma. He lived the household life for nine thousand years.
He went forth on the Great Renunciation on foot. Therefore it is said:
“The city was named Dhaññavatī; the kshatriya king was named Sudeva;
the mother of the great seer Nārada was named Anomā.
Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta were his two chief disciples.”
Vāseṭṭha was the attendant of the great seer Nārada.
Uttarā Phaggunī were his two chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Mahāsoṇa.
“The Great Sage, eighty cubits in height,
shines like a golden crest-jewel, illuminating the ten thousandfold world-system.
From his body, fathom-deep radiance streams forth in every direction.”
Day and night, without interruption, it always extends for a league.
At that time, within a league all around, no people lit torches or lamps,
as they were overwhelmed by the rays of the Buddha.
“Ninety thousand years—such was the lifespan that existed then.
Remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
Just as the sky is adorned and made beautiful by owls,”
In that same way, his teaching shines forth through the Arahants.
Having built a firm bridge of Dhamma for the rest who have entered the path to cross the stream of saṃsāra,
that Bull among Men has attained Nibbāna.
“That Buddha too was peerless and equal to none; those [disciples] too had exhausted their taints and possessed incomparable splendor.
All that has vanished; are not all conditioned phenomena empty?
In this context, “resembling a golden ornament” means having a beauty of form like a golden ornament (*agghikā*) variegated with various jewels.
“The ten-thousandfold world-system shines because of his radiance”: the meaning is that even the ten-thousandfold world-system shines and glitters because of his light.
To clarify this very point, the Blessed One said: “From his body, fathom-wide radiance streams forth in every direction.
In that context, “fathom-wide radiance from the body” means it is like fathom-wide radiance; [it refers to] our Blessed One’s.
The meaning is "like a fathom-wide radiance.
Regarding the phrase "not any," the particle *na* has a prohibitive sense; its connection should be understood with the word *ujjālenti*.
*Ukkā* refers to a torch or staff-lamp. No people at all kindle or inflame either torches or lamps. Why?
Why? Because it is illuminated by the radiance of the Buddha’s body. "By the rays of the Buddha" means by the Buddha’s rays. "Pervaded" means reached. "By the stars" means by the constellations;
just as the vault of the sky is variegated and beautiful with the stars, so too his teaching is variegated and shines forth with the Arahants—this is the meaning.
"For the crossing of the stream of saṃsāra" means for the crossing of the ocean of saṃsāra.

"For the sake of crossing over" means: regarding "those practicing for the remainder," this refers to the remaining persons in training (*sekha*), excluding the Arahants, together with the virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*).

"The bridge of Dhamma" means the bridge of the Path; the meaning is that having established the bridge of Dhamma to carry the remaining persons across from *saṃsāra*, he performed all his duties and attained final Nibbāna (*parinibbāyi*).
As for the rest, since it has been explained below, it is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Nāradabuddhavaṃsa* is finished.
The ninth *buddhavaṃsa* is completed.
12. The commentary on the *Padumuttarabuddhavaṃsa*.
The teaching of Nāradabuddha continued for ninety thousand years and then disappeared. That eon (kappa) was destroyed.
Following that, for an incalculable number of eons, no Buddhas arose in the world. The world became empty of Buddhas, devoid of the light of the Buddhas.
Then, after those incalculable eons had passed, at the end of one hundred thousand eons from now...

In one eon, a Buddha named Padumuttara arose in the world—he who had conquered Māra, laid down the burden, was as solid as Mount Meru, was beyond saṃsāra, was the essence of beings, and was supreme over the entire world.
Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he was reborn in the Tusita heaven;
then, passing away from there, he entered the womb of the chief queen of King Ānanda, who brought joy to all people, in the city of Haṃsavatī.
He took conception in the womb of Queen Sujātā, who was born of a most exalted lineage.
Protected by the deities, she gave birth to Prince Padumuttara in the Haṃsavatī Park at the end of ten months.
At both his conception and his birth, there were miracles of the kind described below.
It is said that at his birth, a rain of lotuses fell. Therefore, on the day of his naming, his kinsmen gave him the name Padumuttara Kumāra.

He lived as a householder for ten thousand years. He possessed three palaces named Naravāhana, Yasavāhana, and Vasavatti, each suited to one of the three seasons. [He was attended by] women headed by Queen Vasudattā.

Two hundred and twenty thousand [beings] were present. When his son, named Prince Uttara—the most excellent of all virtues—was born to Queen Vasudattā, he saw four omens and thought, "I shall go forth on the Great Renunciation.
As soon as he had this thought, a palace named Vasavatti appeared like a potter’s wheel.
Having ascended as if into the sky, traveling through the vault of heaven like a celestial mansion or like the full moon,
he descended to the earth, making the Bodhi tree stand in the center, like the palace described in the *Sobhita-buddhavaṃsa-vaṇṇanā*.
It is said that the Great Man, having descended from that palace, [donned] the saffron robes belonging to the gods, which serve as the banner of Arahatship.
Having donned [the robes], he went forth right there. As for the palace, it returned and stood in its own place.
Of the assembly that had accompanied the Great Being, all went forth except for the women.
Having practiced the life of striving together with them for seven days, on the full moon of Visākha, in the city of Ujjeni, he accepted the milk-rice given by the daughter of the merchant Rucānanda.
Having partaken of the honey-porridge and spent the day’s rest in the Sāla grove,
at the time of evening he took eight handfuls of grass given by the physician Sumitta. Approaching the Salala Bodhi tree and circumambulating it,
he spread out a grass mat thirty-eight cubits wide, sat down cross-legged, and resolved upon the fourfold energy against Māra.
Having shattered the army of Māra, he recollects his past lives during the first watch; having purified the divine eye during the second watch;

and having comprehended the nature of conditions during the third watch, he emerges from the fourth jhāna based on mindfulness of breathing, fixes his attention upon the five aggregates, and perceives fifty characteristics by way of their arising and passing away, up to the stage of the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa).

Having increased his insight (vipassanā) and penetrated all the qualities of a Buddha through the Noble Path, he uttered the inspired utterance (udāna) practiced by all Buddhas: “Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [etc. ...I have attained the destruction of craving.
At that time, it is said, a rain of lotuses fell as if adorning the entire interior of the ten-thousandfold world-system (dasasahassacakkavāḷa). Therefore it was said:
“After Nārada, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds,
the Victor named Padumuttara, was born— unshakeable like the ocean.
That was either a Maṇḍa-kappa (an intermediate aeon) in which the Buddha was born.”
"In that kappa, people were abundant in wholesome qualities.
In this context, "of ocean-like depth" means having a profundity similar to that of the ocean. Or, "that was a *maṇḍa*-kappa":
here, a kappa in which two Fully Enlightened Buddhas arise is called a *maṇḍa*-kappa. For a kappa is of two kinds: the empty kappa (*suñña-kappa*)...
"And an 'empty aeon' (asuññakappa). In this context, during an empty aeon, Buddhas, Pacceka-buddhas, and Wheel-turning Monarchs do not arise.
Therefore, it is called an "empty aeon" because it is devoid of persons possessing such qualities.

An "unempty aeon" (asuññakappa) is of five kinds: the core aeon (sārakappa), the cream aeon (maṇḍakappa), the excellent aeon (varakappa), the core-cream aeon (sāramaṇḍakappa), and the auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa).

In that regard, a kappa devoid of the essence of virtue is called a "Sārakappa" (Essential Kappa) due to the manifestation of a single Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), who produces the essence of virtue and brings about qualities in accordance with that essence.
However, the kappa in which two leaders of the world arise is called a "Maṇḍakappa" (Mundane Kappa).
In the kappa in which three Buddhas arise, the first [of them]—[regarding] the second...
He grants a boon, saying "the second," "the third," and so on; there, people with joyful hearts choose boons according to their own aspirations and vows.

Therefore, it is called a "boon-age" (*varakappa*). However, that age in which four Buddhas arise is called a "pith-essence-age" (*sāramaṇḍakappa*) because it is more distinguished and more essential than a previous age. In whichever age...
When five Buddhas arise, that eon is called a "Blessed Eon" (*bhaddakappa*).
Furthermore, such an eon is extremely rare. In that eon, for the most part, sentient beings abound in noble happiness;

for the most part, those with three roots bring about the destruction of the defilements, those with two roots go to a happy destination, and those without roots obtain the [wholesome] roots. Therefore, that eon—
It is called a "fortunate aeon" (*bhaddakappa*). Therefore it was said: "The non-empty aeon is fivefold," and so forth. For this was stated by the ancients:
"In an *sārakappa*, there is one Buddha; in a *maṇḍakappa*, two Conquerors; in a *varakappa*, three Buddhas; and in a *sāramaṇḍa*, four Buddhas."
“In this auspicious aeon there were five Buddhas; beyond that, no further Conquerors arose.

Now, the aeon in which the Ten-Powered One Padumuttara appeared was, although it was a *sārakappa* (a core aeon), called a *maṇḍakappa* (an ornamented aeon) because of its excellence of qualities, resembling an ornamented aeon.
The word "or" (*vā*) should be understood in the sense of a simile. [The phrase] "with wholesome states increased" means...
They had accumulated merit. "The people" means a multitude of people.

But the Blessed One Padumuttara, the supreme among assemblies, having spent seven days on the seat of enlightenment, thought, "I shall set my foot upon the earth," and extended his right foot. Then, having split the earth, [there appeared] lotuses with stainless, tender filaments and pericarps.
Land-born and water-born lotuses with pure, flawless, and vast petals sprang up—both those growing on land and those growing in water.
It is said that the stalk-leaves of these were ninety cubits long, their filaments thirty cubits, their pericarps twelve cubits, and the pollen of each was the size of nine jars.
The Teacher, however, was fifty-eight cubits in height. The distance between his two arms was...
His forehead was eighteen cubits long; his hands and feet were five cubits each; and his [other] limbs were eleven cubits.

When he merely stepped with his eleven-cubit foot upon the twelve-cubit lotus pedestal (*kaṇṇikā*), dust the size of nine water-jars rose up, ascended to a height of fifty-eight cubits above his body, and settled back down as if scattered with powdered *manosilā* (emerald).
The reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya say that because of this, the Teacher became known in the world as Padumuttara.
Then the Blessed One Padumuttara, who transcends the entire world, having accepted the Brahmā’s request, surveyed those beings who were fit vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma;
he saw two princes in the city of Mithilā, Devala and Sujāta, who were endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*).
Having seen this, he traveled by way of the air at that very moment, descended into the Mithilā garden, and had the two princes summoned by the park-keeper.
They too thought, "Our paternal aunt’s son, Prince Padumuttara, having gone forth and attained supreme enlightenment, has arrived at our city; come now, let us go to see him."
Together with their retinues, they approached the Blessed One Padumuttara and sat down surrounding him.
Then the Ten-Powered One, surrounded by them like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars, shone brilliantly as he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion there;
at that time, there was the first realization of the Dhamma for one hundred thousand times ten million beings. Thus it is said:
“At the first teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One Padumuttara,
there was a realization of the Dhamma for one hundred thousand times ten million beings. Then,
on another occasion, at a gathering of the Sarada ascetics, [the Buddha] taught the Dhamma after having tormented the great multitude with the heat of hell.
While raining down upon the sevenfold assembly numbering three million seven hundred thousand, he caused them to drink the nectar of the Dhamma; that was the second penetration of the Dhamma.
Therefore it is said:
“Then, as he continued raining down, satisfying living beings;”
“There was a second realization for seven million seven hundred thousand [beings].

Now, when the great king Ānanda appeared in the city of Mithilā in the presence of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Perfectly Enlightened One, together with twenty thousand men and twenty ministers, the Blessed One Padumuttara [addressed] them all...
Having ordained them by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-pabbajjā*), he went forth surrounded by them and, while providing for his father's welfare, resided in the capital city of Haṃsavatī.
There, just as our Blessed One did at Kapilavatthu, he walked upon a jeweled walkway in the sky and preached the *Buddhavaṃsa*;
at that time, there was a third great realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*) among five hundred thousand beings.
It happened thus. Therefore it was said:
“At the time when the Great Hero approached Ānanda, having gone into the presence of his father, he beat the drum of the Deathless.”
“When the drum of the Deathless was struck and the rain of Dhamma poured down, there was a third realization for fifty hundred thousand [beings].
Therein, “he approached Ānanda” is said with reference to King Ānanda, his father. “Was struck” means it was beaten.
“Struck” means having been struck. “Of the deathless drum” means by the deathless drum; the change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa) should be understood here.
There is also a reading “cultivated” (āsevite), the meaning of which is “by that which has been cultivated. “While raining down the rain of Dhamma” means while it is raining the rain of Dhamma.
Now, showing the means for effecting clear realization (abhisamaya):
“He is the advisor, the communicator, the savior of all living beings;
the Buddha, skilled in teaching, has delivered the multitude of people”—thus he said. In this context:

“The advisor” (*ovādaka*) means he advises by means of praising the benefits of the qualities of taking refuge, morality, the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and the undertaking of vows; thus he is the advisor. “The communicator” (*viññāpaka*) means he makes known the Four Truths; thus he is the communicator, the awakener. “The savior” (*tāraka*) means the savior from the four floods (*oghā*).

But when the Teacher, in the city of Mithilā, in the Mithilā Garden, amidst a community of one hundred thousand times ten million bhikkhus, recited the Pātimokkha on the full-moon day of the month of Māgha—his face like the full moon—that was the first assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies for the Teacher Padumuttara;
The first gathering was of one hundred thousand times ten million.”

But when the Blessed One, having spent the rains retreat on the peak of Mount Vebhāra, taught the Dhamma to the great multitude who had come for the purpose of seeing the mountain, and having ordained ninety thousand koṭis by the formula “Come, monk,” he recited the Pātimokkha surrounded by them;
that was the second assembly. Thus it is said:
“When the Buddha, the peerless one, was dwelling on Vebhāra Mountain, there was a second assembly of ninety thousand times ten million [beings].

Furthermore, while the Blessed One—the virtuous Lord of the Three Worlds—was wandering through the countryside performing the liberation from bonds for the great multitude, there occurred a gathering of eighty thousand times ten million bhikkhus. Therefore it is said:
“When he had set out on his wandering from villages, market towns, and kingdoms, there was a third assembly of eighty thousand koṭis.

Regarding that, “from villages, market towns, and kingdoms” means from the villages, market towns, and kingdoms. Or rather, this is the reading: “having gone forth after departing from villages, market towns, and kingdoms”; such is the meaning.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having been a great landowner named Jaṭila possessing many tens of millions of coins, gave a choice gift including robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
At the conclusion of the expression of gratitude for the meal, he also prophesied: "In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, there will be a Buddha named Gotama. Thus it is said:
“At that time, I was a royal counselor named Jaṭila;
I provided food and robes for the Saṅgha headed by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then the Buddha, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, gave me this prediction:”
"In a hundred thousand aeons from now, this one will become a Buddha.
"Having exerted myself in striving... [and so forth] ...we shall stand face to face with him.
Having heard his words as well, I further resolved upon the practice.
“I exercised exceedingly firm fortitude for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
In this context, “to the Saṅgha headed by the Sambuddha” means to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head; the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
“I gave food together with robes” means that I gave food along with the monastic robes. “Uggadaḷhaṃ” means extremely firm.
“Dhitim” means he exerted energy; this is the meaning.
However, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no so-called *titthiyas* (heretics). All gods and humans went for refuge to the Buddha alone. Therefore it was said:
“All the *titthiyas* were then defeated, dejected and dispirited.”
No one attends to them; they are banished from the kingdom.
"All of them, having gathered together there, approached the presence of the Buddha:
'You are our protector, O Great Hero; be our refuge, O Seer of Truth.'"
“Compassionate, merciful, and seeking the welfare of all living beings,
he established all the heretics who arrived there in the five precepts.
Thus it became free from turmoil and empty of those heretics.”
“Varied by the Arahants, those who have attained mastery, the Tādi ones.

Regarding that, “crushed” means their pride and conceit have been destroyed. “Titthiyas”: here one should understand the *tittha* (ford), the founder of the *tittha* (*titthakara*), and the followers of the *tittha* (*titthiya*).
In this context, it is called a *tittha* because they cross over by means of views such as eternalism and so forth.
*Laḍḍhi*. The founder of that doctrine is a *titthakara*; those who exist in a *tittha* (a sect) are called *titthiyas*.

It should be understood that it was said, "The *titthiyas* were defeated," etc., in order to show that although there were no *titthiyas* during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, those who did exist were likewise of such a nature.
*Vimānā* means those with deformed minds; *dummanā* is a synonym for the same.
This is a synonym. "No one attends upon them" means that no men whatsoever perform services for those followers of other sects;

they do not give alms, they do not honor them, they do not revere them, they do not esteem them, they do not worship them, they do not rise from their seats for them, and they do not perform the gesture of joining palms—this is the meaning. "From the entire kingdom" means even from the whole country.
"They drive out" means they expel; the meaning is that they cast them out and do not allow them to dwell there. "They"—that is, the followers of other sects (*titthiya*).

"They approached the presence of the Buddha": while being thus driven out by those people living in the kingdom, all the followers of other sects gathered together and went for refuge to the Blessed One Padumuttara alone, saying: "You are our Teacher."
The meaning is that having said, “He is the Lord, the refuge, the ultimate resort, the shelter,” they went for refuge.
“Anukampako” means one who feels compassion. “Kāruṇiko” means one who acts out of compassion. “Sampatte” means those who had arrived, who had come for refuge—namely, the heretics.
“Paṭiṭṭhahi” means he established them; the meaning is that he established them in the five precepts. “Nirākulaṃ” means undisturbed.
The meaning is: "unmixed with other seekers. "Empty" means it was void and deserted of those non-Buddhist sectarians (*tīrthika*).

"That" should be understood as a remainder of the sentence, referring to "that teaching of the Blessed One. "Variegated" means variegated beyond measure. "By those who have attained mastery" means by those who have reached the state of mastery (*vasībhāva*).
Now, that Blessed One Padumuttara had a city named Haṃsavatī. His father, however, was Ānanda.
His name was the Kṣatriya [Sujāta]; his mother was the queen named Sujātā; Devala and Sujāta were his two chief disciples; his attendant was named Sumana;
Amitā and Asamā were his two chief female disciples; the Salala tree was his Bodhi tree;
his body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and its radiance extended twelve yojanas all around; his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
His chief queen was named Vasudattā, and his son was named Uttara.
It is said that the Blessed One Padumuttara attained final nibbāna in the Nandārāma, which was supremely delightful. His relics did not scatter;
rather, people dwelling throughout the entire Jambudīpa gathered together and constructed a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, twelve yojanas in height. Therefore it is said:
“The city was named Haṃsavatī; the kṣatriya was named Ānanda;
Sujātā was the name of the mother of the Teacher Padumuttara.
Devala and Sujāta were his chief disciples.”
The attendant of the Great Seer Padumuttara was named Sumana.
Amitā and Asamā were his chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Salala.
“The Great Sage, risen fifty-eight ratanas high,
resembles a priceless golden image and possesses the thirty-two excellent marks.
Walls, door-panels, and ramparts, as well as trees, mountains, and rocky peaks— ”
There was no obstruction for him within twelve yojanas all around.
For a hundred thousand years his lifespan lasted;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
“Having ferried across many people, having cut through all doubt, like a blazing mass of fire, he has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.
In this context, *nagasiluccayā* means mountain-peaks known as *naga*. *Āvaraṇa* means concealment or screening.
"Twelve yojanas" means that the radiance of the Blessed One’s body pervades an area twelve yojanas all around and remains there day and night.
In the remaining verses, the meaning is clear in every respect.

From this point forward, we shall proceed by summarizing the matter already repeatedly addressed during the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramī*) and stating only the specific points. For if we were to state again and again what has already been said, when would this commentary ever reach its conclusion?
The commentary on the lineage of Buddha Padumuttara is finished.
The tenth lineage of Buddhas is completed.
13. Commentary on the lineage of Buddha Sumedha.
When the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara had attained final Nibbāna and his Dispensation had also disappeared, for seventy thousand aeons no Buddhas arose;

the worlds were empty of Buddhas. From that point onward, at the end of thirty thousand aeons, in one particular aeon, two Perfectly Enlightened Ones, Sumedha and Sujāta, appeared. Among them, the one who had acquired wisdom...
The Bodhisatta named Sumedha, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was reborn in the Tusita heaven;
passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Sudattā, the chief consort of King Sudatta, in the city of Sudassana.
At the end of ten months, he emerged from her womb in the Sudassana Garden like the young sun appearing through a rift in the clouds.
He emerged from his mother’s womb. He dwelt in the household for nine thousand years.
It is said that he had three palaces named Sucandana, Kañcana, and Sirivaḍḍhana. Forty-eight thousand women, headed by Queen Sumanā Mahādevī, were in attendance upon him.
Having seen the four omens, and after Queen Sumanā had given birth to a son named Punabbasumitta, he [departed] on an elephant mount.
Having gone forth on the Great Renunciation, he went into homelessness. A hundred million people followed him into the religious life.

Surrounded by them, after practicing ascetic discipline for half a month, he partook of the honeyed milk-rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Nakula in the village of Nakula on the full moon of the month of Visākha.
Having spent the day’s rest in the Sāla grove, he was [approached] by Sirivaḍḍha the Ājīvaka.
Having accepted the eight handfuls of grass given to him, he spread a layer of grass twenty cubits wide at the foot of the Nīpa Bodhi tree;
then, having shattered Māra and his host and attained full enlightenment, he uttered this inspired exclamation: “Through many births in saṃsāra...
[I have sought only] the end of craving”; and having spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree itself, he remained there.
In the eighth week, having accepted Brahmā’s request for a teaching on the Dhamma and surveying those individuals capable of liberation,
he saw that his younger brothers, Prince Saraṇa and Prince Sabbakāmin, as well as one hundred million monks who had gone forth with him,
were all capable of penetrating the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; then, traveling through the air, he arrived near the city of Sudassana.
Having descended into the Sudassana Park, he summoned his own brother through the park-keeper and, in the midst of their retinue, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
At that time, there was a realization of the Dhamma by one hundred thousand times ten million beings;
this was the first realization. Thus it is said:
After Padumuttara, there was a leader named Sumedha—
unassailable, of fierce splendor, the Sage supreme over the entire world.
With clear eyes and a beautiful face, tall, upright, and majestic.
A benefactor to all beings, you liberated many from their bonds.
When you had attained supreme, perfect enlightenment, O Buddha,
you set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma in the city of Sudassana.
“Through his realization, there were three [assemblies] during his teaching of the Dhamma;
the first realization was that of one hundred thousand times ten million.
In this context, *uggatejo* means one whose splendor has risen high. *Pasannanetto* means one with very clear eyes, as if they had been washed and cleansed.

His eyes are clear like polished jewel-beads; therefore, he is called "clear-eyed" (*pasannanetta*). The meaning is: one whose eyes are soft, glossy, dark blue, stainless, with fine eyelashes, full, and very clear. It is also appropriate to say "one with five very clear eyes.
"Fair-faced" (*sumukha*) means having a face resembling the full moon of the autumn season. "Noble" (*brahmā*) is because his body measures eighty-eight cubits.
*Brahā* means great; the meaning is that his bodily proportions were not shared by others. *Uju* means straight;

the meaning is that he possessed a straight body, with a stature rising upright like a golden archway erected in a city of the gods. *Patāpavā* means one whose body is radiant. *Hitesī* means one who seeks the welfare [of others].
Regarding *abhisamayā tīṇi*, it means "three realizations"; a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*) has been made.
But when the Blessed One, having at dawn entered the attainment of great compassion and emerged from it, surveyed the world and saw the yakkha named Kumbhakaṇṇa—
who possessed power like that of Kumbhakaṇṇa himself, who was a human-eating spirit with a terrifying body visible at the entrance of the Great Forest,
and who was wandering through the Vattaniya forest— having put an end to his roaming, he looked upon him.
Alone and without a companion, he went to that yakkha’s abode, entered within, and sat down upon the prepared couch of glory.
Then that yakkha, unable to endure the insult, became enraged like a venomous snake struck by a staff;
desiring to terrify the One of Ten Powers, he assumed a more horrific form for himself, with a head resembling a mountain.
Having fashioned eyes resembling the orb of the sun, having made his fangs exceedingly long, broad, sharp, and like the tips of ploughs,
with a large, uneven belly hanging down, arms like palm trunks, a deformed and crooked nose, a wide red mouth like a mountain cave, and coarse, harsh, tawny hair,
he approached the Blessed One Sumedha with an appearance of extreme terror.
Standing before him, emitting smoke and blazing forth, he rained down nine kinds of showers— rocks, mountains, fire-flames,
water, mud, ashes, glowing coals, and sand— and yet, unable to move even a single hair on the Blessed One’s body,
he asked a question, just as Āḷavaka did when thinking, "I will kill the Blessed One after asking him a question. This Blessed One [responded] by answering the question.

He led that *yakkha* to discipline. Then, on the second day, it is said that the people living in his kingdom brought the prince along with food filling a cart and gave him to the *yakkha*. Thereupon, the *yakkha* gave the prince to the Buddha.
People standing at the entrance of the forest approached the Blessed One. At that assembly, the One of Ten Powers—
While teaching the Dhamma that was agreeable to the mind of the yakkha, he caused the Dhamma-eye to arise in ninety thousand koṭis of living beings;
that was the second great realization of the Dhamma. Therefore it is said:
"Furthermore, the Conqueror tamed the yakkha Kumbhakaṇṇa..."
“The second realization of the Dhamma occurred for ninety thousand times ten million.

Furthermore, when he proclaimed the Four Truths in the Sirinanda Garden in the city of Upakāra, then the third realization of the Dhamma occurred for eight hundred thousand times ten million. Thus it is said:
“Again, O one of immeasurable fame, he proclaimed the Four Truths;”
“The third great assembly consisted of eight hundred million [monks].
Thus, the Blessed One Sumedha also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, at the city of Sudassana, there were one hundred billion who had destroyed the taints (*āsava*).
Again, on Mount Devakūṭa, when the *kathina* robe was spread, in the second assembly, there were ninety million.
Again, when the Blessed One was wandering on tour for the third time, there were eighty koṭis [of followers]. Therefore it is said:
“There were three assemblies of the great sage Sumedha, Of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless, Whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.”
“When the Conqueror went to the city named Sudassana,
there were then one hundred million bhikkhus whose taints were exhausted, gathered together.
Furthermore, when the kaṭhina had been spread for the bhikkhus at Devakūṭa— ”
“At that time, there was a second assembly of ninety koṭis.
Furthermore, when the One of Ten Powers was wandering on his journey,
there was a third assembly of eighty koṭis.”
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become a young brahmin named Uttara—the most excellent among all people—distributed eighty million pieces of wealth that had been stored away.

Having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he then heard the Dhamma from the One Possessed of Ten Powers, established himself in the Refuges, went forth, and became a monk. The Teacher, for his part, delivered a discourse of thanksgiving regarding the meal.
While doing so, he prophesied: "In the future, there will be a Buddha named Gotama. Therefore it was said:
"At that time, I was a young brahmin named Uttara;
eighty koṭis of wealth were accumulated in my house."
“Having given everything away, including the Leader of the World together with his Saṅgha,
I went to him for refuge and took delight in the going-forth.
That Buddha also made a prediction concerning me while offering words of appreciation.”
“In thirty thousand eons, this one will become a Buddha.
“Having exerted ourselves in striving... [and so forth] ...we shall stand in the presence of this one.
The verses of the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa-gāthā*) should be recited in full.
Having heard her words as well, my mind became even more serene;
I resolved upon further practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
I [studied] the Suttanta and the Vinaya—the ninefold teaching of the Teacher.
Having mastered everything, I brought glory to the Conqueror’s teaching.
Dwell­ing there with diligence— whether sitting, standing, or walking—
I reached the perfection of direct knowledge and went to the Brahma world.
In this context, *sannicitaṃ* means stored as a hoard. *Kevalaṃ* means entirely; the sense is "whole. *Sabbam* means having given without remainder.
*Sasaṅghaṃ* means together with the Saṅgha. *Tassūpagañchiṃ* means I went to him; here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
*Abhirocayiṃ* means I went forth [into homelessness]. *Tiṃsakappasahassamhi* means when thirty thousand kappas had passed; such is the meaning.
Now, for that Blessed One Sumedha, there was a city named Sudassana; his father was King Sudatta, and his mother was named Sudattā.
His two chief disciples were Saraṇa and Sabbakāma; his attendant was named Sāgara;
his two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Surāmā; his Bodhi tree was the Mahānīpa tree; and his body stood eighty-eight cubits in height.
His lifespan was ninety thousand years; he lived at home for nine thousand years;
his chief queen was named Sumanā; his son was named Punabbasumitta; he went forth on an elephant vehicle. The rest is seen in the verses. Thus it is said:
“The city was named Sudassana, and the kshatriya was named Sudatta;”
The mother of the Great Seer Sumedha was named Sudattā.
Saraṇa and Sabbakāma were the two chief disciples of the Great Seer Sumedha, and his attendant was named Sāgara.
“Rāmā and Surāmā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Mahānīpa.
The Great Sage rose up eighty ratanas in height.”
It illuminates all directions, just as the moon does among the hosts of stars.
Just as the gem known as the Wheel-Turning King’s jewel shines for a league,
even so his jewel radiates its light for a league in every direction.
“For ninety thousand years, his lifespan lasted for that long;
remaining for that duration, he delivered many people.
By means of those who possessed the three knowledges and the six direct knowledges, who had attained power and were composed...”
"This place was crowded with noble Arahants.
They too, all possessed of immeasurable life, were utterly liberated and free from acquisitions;
having shown the light of knowledge, those of great renown have attained final peace."
In that context, "just as the moon among the hosts of stars" means: just as the full moon in the sky illuminates and makes manifest the hosts of stars, even so he illuminates all directions;
this is the meaning. Some read "just as the fifteenth-day moon," which has the same obvious meaning.
"The jewel called the Wheel-turner's gem" means: just as the jewel-treasure of a Wheel-turning Monarch is four cubits in height and equal in circumference to the nave of a chariot wheel.

Accompanied by a retinue of eighty-four thousand gems, like the full autumnal moon surrounded by a host of stars, a jewel of supreme beauty—seemingly summoning the splendor of its gathered majesty—comes forth from Mount Vepulla.
As it approaches, its radiance pervades an area extending for a league in every direction; even so it is with him.
The meaning is that even from the body of the Blessed One Sumedha, a radiance of light extends for a league in every direction.

"By those possessing the three knowledges and the six superknowledges" means by those who possess the three knowledges and by those who possess the six superknowledges. "By those who have attained strength" means by those who have attained the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*). "By those who are such-like" (*tādi*) means by those who have attained the state of being such-like (*tādibhāva*).
"Crowded together" means filled with, shining with the single color of the saffron robe. "This" refers to the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

He spoke with intentional meaning, referring either to the surface of the earth or to one of immeasurable lifespan. "Amitayasa" means having an immeasurable retinue, or having a reputation for incomparable fame.
"Nirūpadhi" means being devoid of the four bases of clinging (*upadhi*). The rest of this [commentary] on all the verses is entirely clear.
The *Sumedhabuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā* is completed.
The eleventh Buddha-chronicle is finished.
14. The Exposition of the Sujāta Buddha-chronicle:
Thereafter, in the subsequent period, during that very same Maṇḍa-kappa, among beings whose lifespan was gradually increasing from immeasurable years, in due course...

After passing away, when beings had been born with a lifespan of ninety thousand years, a Teacher named Sujāta appeared in the world, his body well-born and of pure birth. Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he was reborn in the Tusita heaven;
then, descending from there, he entered the womb of Pabhāvati, the chief queen of King Uggata, in the city of Sumaṅgala.
Having taken rebirth, he emerged from his mother’s womb at the end of ten months.
On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Sujāta, saying, "He was born bringing happiness to all beings throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
He lived the household life for nine thousand years. [His sons were] Sirī, Upasirī, and Sirinanda.
He had three palaces. Twenty-three thousand women, headed by Queen Sirīnandā, attended upon him.

Having seen the four omens and when a son named Upasena was born to Queen Sirīnandā, he mounted his excellent steed named Haṃsavāha, went forth on the Great Renunciation, and became a monk. As he was thus departing for the homeless life—

Ten million people followed him into the homeless life. Then, surrounded by them, after practicing the life of striving for nine months, on the full moon day of the month of Visākha, he partook of the most delicious honey-milk-rice porridge offered by the daughter of the merchant Sirīnandana in the city of Sirīnandana.
Having spent the midday rest in the Sāla grove, at the time of evening, [he was approached] by the physician Sunanda.
Having accepted the eight handfuls of grass given by him, he approached the *velu* tree;
having spread out a layer of grass thirty-three cubits wide, while the sun was still shining, he shattered Māra and his host, realized perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*),
uttered the inspired utterance (*udāna*) practiced by all Buddhas, and spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree.
Being entreated by Brahmā, and seeing that his younger brother Sudassana Kumāra— the son of the family priest— and Devakumāra were capable of penetrating the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths,
he traveled through the air, descended into the Sumaṅgala Garden near the city of Sumaṅgala,
and [introduced] his brother Sudassana Kumāra, the son of the family priest, and Devakumāra to the park keeper.
Having summoned them, he sat in their midst along with their retinues and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
There, eighty koṭis attained realization of the Dhamma; this was the first realization.
Furthermore, when the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Great Sāla tree at the gate of the Sudassana Garden for the devas...
He entered the rains-retreat among the Tāvatiṃsa devas; at that time, there was a realization of the Dhamma by seven million three hundred thousand beings.

This was the second realization. But when Sujāta, the Ten-Powered One, went into the presence of his father, there was a realization of the Dhamma by six million beings. This was the third realization. Thus it is said:
“In that very same Maṇḍakappa, there was a Leader named Sujāta;
with a jaw like a lion’s and shoulders like a bull’s, he was immeasurable and difficult to approach.
Like the stainless moon, the Buddha was radiant like the sun with its hundred rays.”
Thus the Fully Awakened One shines, ever blazing with glory.
Having attained the complete and supreme enlightenment,
the Fully Awakened One set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion in the city of Sumaṅgala.
“When the Well-Born One, the Leader of the World, had descended and proclaimed the sublime Dhamma,
eighty koṭis attained realization during his first teaching of the Dhamma.
When the Well-Born One of immeasurable fame entered upon the rains retreat among the gods,”
There was a second realization for seven million seven hundred thousand [beings].
"When Sujāta, the Peerless One, approached his father’s presence,
there was a third realization for sixty hundred thousand [beings]."
"In that very same aeon of the Maṇḍa" means that in the very same aeon of the Maṇḍa in which the Blessed One Sumedha appeared, the Blessed One Sujāta also appeared;
this is the meaning. "Lion-jawed" (*sīhahanu*) means one whose jaw is like that of a lion.
However, while only the lower jaw of a lion is full and not the upper, the lower jaw of this Great Being was like that of a lion.
Both [his jawbones] are full like the lower jaw, resembling the moon on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight.
Therefore it is said, “lion-jawed. “Ox-shouldered” means having shoulders as even and rounded as an ox’s, with shoulders like a well-rounded golden linga;
this is the meaning. “Like the sun” means like the maker of day. “By glory” means by the glory of a Buddha. “Supreme enlightenment” means the highest perfect awakening.

Having taught the Dhamma to the people who had gathered in the Sudhamma Garden in the city of Sudhammavatī, he ordained sixty hundred thousand [monks] by means of the "Come, monk" formula and recited the Pātimokkha in their midst; that was the first assembly.
Following that, during the descent from the triple heaven, there was a second assembly consisting of fifty hundred thousand [monks].
Again, having heard that "the youth Sudassana, after going forth in the presence of the Blessed One,
attained arahantship," the Elder Sudassana approached Sujāta, the bull among men, taking with him four hundred thousand men who had come saying,
"We too shall go forth. The Blessed One, having taught them the Dhamma and having ordained them by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-pabbajjā*), [established them in the holy life].
When the assembly was endowed with four factors, he recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Therefore it is said:
“There were three assemblies of the Great Sage Sujāta, Of those whose taints were destroyed, who were stainless, Whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.”
“Sixty hundred thousand [beings] who had attained the power of direct knowledge, and those who had not yet reached it across various existences,
first assembled together. Furthermore, at another assembly,
when the Conqueror descended from the three heavens— ”
There was a second assembly of five million [monks].
Sudassana, the foremost disciple, approaching the Bull among Men,
went to the Sambuddha accompanied by four hundred thousand [monks].

In this context, "of those who have not attained" (appattānaṃ) means those who have not reached various states of existence (bhavābhava). There is also a reading, "not wandering in existence and non-existence" (appavattā bhavābhava), which has the same meaning.

In the phrase "in the descent from the three heavens" (tidivorohaṇe), it should be understood as referring to the agent descending from the heavenly world; it is expressed by means of a transposition of the grammatical case (kāraka-vipallāsa).

Alternatively, "in the descent from the three heavens" (tidivorohaṇe) refers to the act of descending from the three heavens. In the word "Jina" (jine), the locative case should be understood in the sense of the genitive (sāmī-atthe), meaning "of the Victor."
At that time, it is said, our Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*), heard that "a Buddha has arisen in the world.

Having approached the Blessed One and listened to his discourse on the Dhamma, he offered the sovereignty of the four great islands along with the seven treasures to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and then went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher. The people dwelling throughout the entire island [then] [appointed him] as the protector of the realm.
Having taken charge and fulfilled the duties of the monastery attendant, they gave a perpetual great almsgiving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher also prophesied concerning him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama. Therefore it was said:
"At that time, I was the lord over the four continents;..."
I was a wheel-turning monarch of great power, traveling through the air.
Having surrendered the great sovereignty over the four continents and the seven supreme treasures to the Buddha,
I went forth into homelessness in his presence.
“Monks from the countryside, having gathered their earnings through labor,
provide the requisites and lodgings for the Saṅgha of monks.
That Buddha too, the Lord of the ten thousandfold world-system, made this prediction concerning me.”
“In thirty thousand eons, this one will become a Buddha.
“Having exerted myself in striving... [I shall] stand face-to-face with him.
“Hearing of his passing away as well, I produced even greater joy.”
They undertook a formidable vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections:
“Having mastered the Suttanta and the Vinaya— the ninefold teaching of the Teacher—
in its entirety, I have brought glory to the Conqueror’s dispensation.”
“Dwelling there with diligence, having cultivated the sublime meditation, and having reached the perfection of direct knowledge, you went to the Brahma-world.
Therein, “in the four continents” means in the four great continents together with their surrounding islands. “Moving through the sky” means...
"Preceded by the wheel-treasure, moving through the air. "Seven treasures" refers to the seven treasures beginning with the elephant-treasure (*hatthiratana*).
"Supreme" means most excellent; alternatively, the meaning should be understood as "in the supreme Buddha. "Having bestowed" means having given.
"Rising" means the prosperity of the kingdom; the meaning is "income. "Having gathered together" means having made into a heap or collected. "Requisite" (*paccaya*).
"Various requisites such as robes" refers to the conditions [for his life]. "Lord over ten thousand" means he is the lord within the ten-thousandfold world system;
it should be understood that this was said with reference to his field of birth (*jātikkhetta*).
The Blessed One is the lord of infinite world systems. "In thirty thousand aeons" means from this point forward, at the culmination of thirty thousand aeons.
Now, for that Blessed One Sujāta, there was a city named Sumaṅgala; his father was King Uggata, and his mother was Pabhāvatī.
His two chief disciples were Sudassana and Sudeva; his attendant was named Nārada;
his two chief female disciples were Nāgā and Nāgasamālā. His Bodhi tree was the Mahāveḷu tree, which, it is said, had few gaps between its leaves.
His dense trunk was supremely beautiful; with its vast branches covered by stainless leaves the color of beryl and gems, it shone like a cluster of peacock feathers.
Furthermore, the body of that Blessed One was fifty cubits in height, his lifespan was ninety thousand years, Sirīnandā was his chief queen, and his son was named Upasena.
He departed by means of an excellent horse-chariot. He, however, attained final nibbāna in the Silārāma at the city of Candavatī. Thus it is said:
“The city named Sumaṅgala, the kṣatriya named Uggata, and the mother named Pabhāvatī belonged to the Great Sage Sujāta.”
“Sudassana and Sudeva were the chief disciples;
the attendant of the Great Seer Sujāta was named Nārada.
Nāga and Nāgasamālā were the chief female disciples.”
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Mahāveḷu.
That tree has a thick trunk, it is without gaps and full of leaves;
it is a straight, tall bamboo, beautiful to behold and delightful.
“Having grown from a single trunk, its branches then spread forth;
like a well-fastened peacock-feather fan, that tree shines resplendent.
It has no thorns, nor was there any flaw in it when it was great.”
With wide-spreading branches and dense foliage, it cast a cool shade and was delightful.
That Victor was fifty ratanas in height;
endowed with the excellence of every form, he possessed every virtuous quality.
“His radiance is unequaled, streaming forth on every side;
immeasurable and incomparable, it is beyond all similes.
For ninety thousand years, such is the lifespan found there.”
Remaining for that long, he brought many people across.
Just as waves in the ocean, or as stars in the sky,
even so was the teaching then adorned by the Arahants.
“And so the Buddha is peerless and equal to none, and those qualities are beyond measure;
all that has vanished—surely all conditioned things are empty.

In this context, *acchiddo* means without flaw (*appacchiddo*). It should be understood in the same way as in expressions such as “a slender-waisted maiden” (*anudarā kaññā*). Some [read] *chiddaṃ*...
They recite: “It becomes small. *Pattiko* means having many leaves; the meaning is that it is covered with leaves the color of crystal-gems (*kācamaṇi*).
*Uju* means straight, not crooked or bent. *Vaṃso* means bamboo. *Brahā* means great all around.
*Ekakkhando* means growing alone on the ground, single and without a second—this is the meaning. *Pavaḍḍhitvā* means having grown. *Tato sākhā pabhijjatīti* means from there a branch breaks forth.
Then, five kinds of branches emerged and split forth from the top of the bamboo. There is also a reading: “Then the branches split forth.
*Subaddha* means well-bound by way of the five types of binding. *Morahattha* refers to a bundle of peacock feathers bound together for the purpose of warding off the heat of the sun.
"Na tassa kaṇṭakā honti" means that on that bamboo there were no thorns, neither from the bamboo itself nor from any thorny trees.
"Aviralo" means covered with dense branches. "Sandacchāyo" means thickly shaded; it is called "sandacchāyo" precisely because of its density.
"Paññāsaratano āsi" means it was fifty cubits long. "Sabbākāravarūpeto" means endowed with excellence in every respect.

"Endowed with the excellence of all modes" (sabbākāravarūpeto) means endowed with all excellent aspects. "Having attained all virtues" (sabbaguṇamupāgato) is merely a synonym for the immediately preceding phrase.
"Immeasurable" (appamāṇo) means devoid of measure; or, he is immeasurable because it is impossible to grasp his measure.

"Incomparable" (atulio) means unequaled; the meaning is that he is peerless by anyone. "By means of similes" (opammehi) means by things that can be compared. "Peerless" (anūpamo) means devoid of comparison. And by this... [text continues]
Because it is impossible to say, “It is like this,” the meaning is that it is “without comparison” (*anūpamo*). “And those qualities” (*guṇāni ca tāni*) means “those qualities” (*guṇā ca te*);
the meaning is the qualities such as omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), etc. This is stated with a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
The *Sujātabuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā* is finished.
The twelfth lineage of Buddhas is concluded.
15. The Exposition of the Lineage of Buddha Piyadassī:
Now, after the time of Sujāta, at the end of one eon, more than one hundred and eight thousand eons ago, in a certain eon—
Three Buddhas were born: Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī.

Among them, the Blessed One named Piyadassī, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) and been reborn in the Tusita heaven, passed away from there and took conception in the womb of Queen Candādevī—whose face was like the moon and who was the chief consort of King Sudatta—in the city of Sudhaññavatī.
Having been conceived, at the end of ten months he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Varuṇa Garden.
On the day of his naming ceremony, because various wonderful miracles pleasing to the world were displayed, they gave him the name Piyadassī (Pleasant-to-Behold).
He lived as a householder for nine thousand years. It is said that he had three palaces named Sunimma, Vimalagiri, and Brahā. With Queen Vimalāmahādevī at their head...
Thirty-three thousand women were presented to him.
Having seen the four omens, and when a son named Kañcanaveḷa had been born to Queen Vimalādevī, he went forth on the Great Renunciation in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses and became a monk.
One million men followed him into the religious life. With them...
Surrounded by his followers, the Great Being, having practiced the course of exertion for six months,
on the full moon day of Visākha partook of the honeyed milk-rice offered by the daughter of the brahmin Vasabha in the village of Varuṇa; after spending the midday rest in the Sāla grove,
he took eight handfuls of grass given by the Ājīvaka Sujāta and approached the Kakudha Bodhi tree.
Having spread out a grass mat fifty-three cubits wide, having sat down cross-legged, and having penetrated the knowledge of omniscience, he uttered the inspired utterance:

“Through many a birth in saṃsāra... Having spent seven times seven days right there, and knowing that those who had gone forth together with him were capable of penetrating the Noble Dhamma, he went there through the air.
Having descended into the Usabhavatī Garden near the city of Usabhavatī, surrounded by ten million bhikkhus, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
At that time, there was a realization of the Dhamma for one hundred thousand times ten million beings. This was the first realization.
Furthermore, not far from the city named Usabhavatī, on Mount Sudassana, there was a king of the gods named Sudassana.
He dwelt there. He was one of wrong view. However, throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa, people brought him an annual offering worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
That divine king Sudassana would sit upon the same seat as the human king and receive the offering. Then the Blessed One Piya-dassī [thought], "Of that Sudassana..."
Thinking, “I shall dispel that wrong view of the king of the gods,” he entered the palace of that king of the gods when he had gone to the assembly of yakkhas;

having ascended his glorious couch, he sat there emitting six-colored rays like the sun upon Mount Yugandhara during the autumn season. His attendant and serving deities [honored him] with garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth.
Having paid homage to the One Possessed of Ten Powers, they stood surrounding him.
Sudassana, the king of the gods, while returning from the assembly of the *yakkhas*, saw six-colored rays of light streaming forth from his own abode and thought:
"On other days, such a splendor, radiant with a web of many rays, has never appeared from my palace."
“Never before have I seen such a sight. Who is this who has entered here—a god or a human?
As he looked about, he saw the Blessed One seated upon the peak of Mount Udaya, blazing with a network of six-colored rays like the sun at the height of autumn;
seeing him, he thought: “This shaven-headed ascetic, surrounded by my own retinue and attendants, sits upon an excellent couch...”
Seated there, his mind overcome by anger, he thought, "Well then,
I shall show him my own power," and he turned that entire mountain into a single mass of flame. Looking at it, thinking, "By this net of fire,

this shaven-headed ascetic has been reduced to ashes," [he beheld the Buddha] with a noble body radiating forth a manifold web of rays, with the splendor of a serene facial complexion and a perfectly clear skin-tint.
Seeing the One Possessed of the Ten Powers blazing with radiance, he thought: "This ascetic endures the heat of fire;
well then, I shall cause this ascetic to be submerged by a flood of water and kill him. He then set a very deep flood of water toward his celestial mansion.
When that mansion was filled by the flood of water, not even a mere thread of the Blessed One’s robe touched him as he sat within it.
Not even so much as a hair on his body was moistened by it. Then Sudassana, the king of the gods, thinking, "By this [water] the ascetic will die, breathless," withdrew the water and looked;
he beheld the Blessed One, like the autumn moon appearing from the rift of a dark cloud, shining with the radiance of a manifold web of rays, surrounded by his own retinue.
Seeing him seated there, unable to endure his own malice, he thought, "Come now, I shall kill him! and out of anger rained down a shower of nine kinds of weapons.
Then, through the power of the Blessed One, all those weapons became various most beautiful and lovely flower garlands and fell at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
Then, having seen that marvel, Sudassana, the king of the devas, with a mind extremely incensed, seized the Blessed One by his feet with both hands;
desiring to drag him out from his own abode, he lifted him up, crossed over the great ocean, and went to the Cakkavāḷa mountain,
where— looking down [thinking], "Is this ascetic still alive, or is he dead?"— he [remained] right there.
Seeing him seated on the seat, he thought: "Oh, how majestic is this ascetic!
I am not able to drive this ascetic out from here. For if anyone were to find out about me, my ill repute would be great.
As long as no one sees him, I shall release him and depart."
Then the One of Ten Powers, having understood the movement of his mind, made such a resolution that all gods and humans could see him.
And on that day, one hundred kings throughout the entire Jambudīpa assembled for the purpose of presenting offerings to him.
Those kings, having grasped the feet of the Blessed One, [beheld] Sudassana, the king of the gods, seated there.
Having seen this, they thought: "Our king of gods is performing service at the feet of the Sage-king, the Teacher Piyadassī;
oh, how wonderful are the Buddhas! Oh, how sublime are the qualities of a Buddha!

With hearts full of faith toward the Blessed One, they all stood bowing to the Blessed One with their hands joined in reverential salutation (añjali) upon their heads. Therein, the Blessed One Piyadassī—
Making the divine king Sudassana the foremost, he taught the Dhamma. At that time, ninety thousand times ten million gods and humans attained arahantship.
That was the second great assembly (abhisamaya).
Furthermore, when the Elder Soṇa was like Devadatta—the adversary of the Buddha—in the city of Kumuda, which measured nine yojanas in extent...
Having consulted with Prince Mahāpaduma and having had his father killed, that King further employed various means to slay the Buddha Piyadassī;
yet being unable to kill him, he summoned the elephant-keeper Doṇamukha, enticed him, and informed him of the matter: "When this ascetic Piyadassī [arrives at] this..."
“When he enters the city for alms, then release the noble elephant named Doṇamukha and kill the ascetic Piyadassī. Then that rider,
a royal favorite who lacked the discernment between what was beneficial and harmful, thinking, “This ascetic might even displace me from my position,” agreed, saying,
“Very well,” and waited for the time on the following day when the One of Ten Powers would enter the city.
Having observed him—whose head, forehead, and temples were well-formed; whose long trunk was like a bow; whose ears were broad and soft; whose eyes were honey-brown;
whose shoulder-seat was beautiful; whose hindquarters were rounded and firm; whose space between the thighs was thick and concealed; whose lovely tusks were like chariot-poles;
who possessed a beautiful tail; who was endowed with all auspicious marks; and who was as lovely to behold as a dark rain-cloud.
Having approached the Sage— the restrainer of hostile folk, who moves with the majestic and graceful gait of a lion, like a walking mountain, established in the sevenfold [steps],
split asunder in seven ways, emitting [the scent] from all sides, and possessing a physical form like Death itself—

he further intoxicated and exhilarated that elephant of the Sage by means of various offerings such as morsels of food, unguents, and incense, just as one might treat Erāvaṇa, the elephant that restrains enemy elephants.
