He sent [the elephant] for the purpose of slaughter. Then that pre-eminent elephant, as soon as it was released, having slain elephants,
buffaloes, horses, men, and women, its tusks and body stained with the blood of those it had killed, its eyes covered by its own webbed eyelids,
shattered the gates, door-panels, upper chambers, and archways, and being pursued by crows, hawks, vultures, and other birds, [it trampled] the slain buffaloes, men, horses, elephants, and the rest.
Tearing off his limbs and devouring them like a *yakkha* that feeds on human flesh, he saw from afar the One of Ten Powers approaching surrounded by a host of disciples;
with a speed like that of the wind or Garuḍa, he rushed impetuously toward the Blessed One.
Meanwhile, the people living in the city, their minds filled with fear and anguish, had taken refuge upon the terraces of palaces, the ramparts, and the tops of trees.
Seeing him rushing toward the Tathāgata, they raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! Some lay followers, however, began to restrain him by various means.
Then that elephant among Buddhas, beholding the approaching elephant among elephants, his heart cooled by the expansion of compassion, suffused him with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Thereupon, the elephant among elephants, his heart and mental continuum softened by that suffusion of loving-kindness—
Recognizing his own fault and transgression, and being unable to stand before the Blessed One out of shame,
he fell with his head at the Blessed One’s feet as if sinking into the earth. Prostrate in this manner, his body, which resembled a mass of darkness,
shone like a bank of dark clouds approaching the peak of the excellent Golden Mountain, which is suffused with the radiance of its pure splendor.
Then, seeing the king of elephants prostrate with his head at the feet of the King of Sages, the people of the city, their hearts filled with supreme joy, raised shouts of "Sādhu!
and lion-like roars, and let out a great clamor of acclamation. They honored him in many ways with fragrant flower garlands, sandalwood paste, scented powders, ornaments, and other offerings.
On all sides, the waving of cloths took place, and in the vault of the sky, the drums of the gods resounded.
They roared. Then the Blessed One, having looked at that noble elephant lying at his feet like the peak of Mount Tamasa,
and having touched the head of the excellent elephant with his palm— which was adorned with the signs of the goad, the banner, the net, the conch, and the wheel—
instructed him with a teaching of the Dhamma suited to the movement of his mind:
“O best of elephants, listen to my words; follow them, for they are beneficial and endowed with meaning.
O one with beautiful tusks, cast away this evil disposition that delights in killing you, and approach a state of peace.
O lord of elephants, whoever harms living beings out of greed, hatred, or delusion—”
Thus, for a very long time, the killer of living beings experiences most terrible suffering in hell.
"O Mātaṅga, do not ever again perform such a deed through negligence or even through intoxication;
one who takes the life of a living being encounters unbearable suffering in Avīci for an eon."
“Having experienced most terrible suffering in hell, if one returns again to the world of men,
one is short-lived, deformed, harmful, and a partaker of manifold miseries.
And just as living beings are supremely dear to you, O elephant, noble tusker among the great folk!”
Likewise, knowing that others are dear to you as well, you should avoid taking life.
"Having understood the fault in one who delights in violence and the virtue in one who refrains from taking life,
you should avoid taking life if you desire happiness in heaven in the future world."
“One who abstains from taking life and is well-tamed becomes dear and pleasing in this world;
and after the breaking up of the body, the Buddhas declare that he dwells in heaven hereafter.
No one in the world desires the arrival of suffering; everyone, once born, seeks only happiness.”
"Therefore, O Great Elephant, abandoning violence, cultivate loving-kindness and compassion at the proper time.

Then, being thus instructed by the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, the noble elephant regained his senses and became exceedingly well-disciplined, like a disciple perfected in the conduct of discipline.
In this way, the Blessed One Piyadassi, like our own Teacher, [instructed] Dhanapāla at Doṇamukha.
Having tamed that excellent elephant in that great assembly of people, he taught the Dhamma. At that time, there was a realization of the Dhamma by eighty thousand crores.
This was the third realization. Therefore it is said:
“After Sujāta, the Self-Existent One, the Leader of the World;”
Difficult to approach, peerless and equal to none, lovely to behold and of great renown—
“That Buddha of immeasurable fame also shines like the sun;
having destroyed all darkness, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.”
“For him too, of incomparable majesty, there were three moments of clear realization.
At the first moment of clear realization, there were one hundred thousand times ten million [beings].
Sudassana, the king of the gods, had previously delighted in wrong view.”
Dispelling his wrong view, the Teacher taught the Dhamma:
"An incomparable gathering of people, a great assembly, took place then;
it was the second occasion of realization for ninety thousand koṭis."
“When the Charioteer of Men trained the elephant Doṇamukha, there occurred the third realization for eighty thousand koṭis.
In the city of Sumaṅgala, there were two sons of royalty: the prince named Pālita and Sabbadassikumāra, the son of the chaplain.

They became his companions. When they heard that the Perfectly Enlightened One Piyadassi was wandering on tour and had arrived at their own city, they went out to meet him with a retinue of one hundred thousand times ten million.

Having heard his Dhamma and given a great almsgiving for seven days, on the seventh day, at the conclusion of the Blessed One’s expression of gratitude for the meal, they went forth into homelessness together with those one hundred thousand times ten million.
They attained arahantship. In their midst, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly.
Then, at a later time, during the gathering with Sudassana, the king of the gods, ninety koṭis attained arahantship.
Surrounded by them, the Teacher recited the Pātimokkha; this was the second assembly. Again, at Doṇamukhavinayana...
Eighty koṭis having gone forth attained arahantship. In their midst the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha;
this was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies for that Piyadassin as well.”
“The first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand koṭis.
After that, ninety koṭis gathered together in the Sage;
in the third assembly, there were eighty koṭis.”
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a young brahmin named Kassapa, who had mastered the three Vedas with Itihāsa as the fifth.

Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he constructed the supreme monastery, Paramārāma, by means of a gift of one hundred thousand koṭis, and he established himself in the refuges and the five precepts. Then the Teacher said to him: “One hundred and eighteen aeons from now...”
“A Buddha named Gotama will appear in the world,” he prophesied. Therefore it was said:
“At that time, I was a brahmin named Kassapa;
I was a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, one who had mastered the three Vedas.”
“Having heard his Dhamma, I conceived faith;
together with a hundred thousand koṭis, I had a monastic park constructed.
Having given that park to him, joyful and with a heart full of spiritual urgency, I—”
In Saraṇa, I firmly undertook the five precepts.
That Buddha also, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, prophesied of me:
"In eighteen hundred kappas, this person shall become a Buddha."
“Having exerted the effort... [we] shall stand face-to-face with him.
Having heard his words as well, my mind became even more serene;
I resolved upon further practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.

In that context, "the three refuges and the five precepts" means the three refuges and the five moral precepts. "In eighteen hundred kappas" means after the passing of one thousand eight hundred kappas from now.

That Blessed One had a city named Sudhañña; his father was King Sudatta, his mother was Queen Sucandā, his two chief disciples were Pālita and Sabbadassī, his attendant was named Sobhita, and [his daughter was] Sujātā.
Dhammadinnā and [Sundarī] were his two chief female disciples; the Kakudha tree was his Bodhi tree; his body was eighty cubits in height;
his lifespan was ninety thousand years; Vimalā was his chief queen; his son was named Kañcanāveḷa, who went forth in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. Thus it is said:
“There was a city named Sudhañña, and a kṣatriya named Sudatta;
the mother of the Teacher Piyadassī was named Candā.
Pālita and Sabbadassī were his chief disciples.”
The attendant of the Teacher Piyadassi was named Sobhita.
Sujātā and Dhammadinnā were his chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Kakudha.
“That Buddha of immeasurable fame, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks,
eighty cubits in height, appears like a king of sal trees.
There is no such radiance as his, even among fire, the moon, or the sun.”
Just as was his radiance, so too was the lifespan of that peerless Great Seer.
That God of Gods also had a lifespan of exactly that much:
the Visionary One remained in the world for ninety thousand years.
“That Buddha too was peerless and unequaled; those ages were likewise incomparable.
All that has vanished; are not all conditioned things empty?
In this context, “like a king of sal trees” means a king of sal trees that is in full bloom, most beautiful to behold, and with a trunk of perfectly even proportions.
It appears as if [they were] so. "Those pairs" refers to the pairs beginning with the pair of chief disciples (*aggasāvaka-yugādi*). In all other verses, the meaning is entirely straightforward.
The *Piyadassī Buddhavaṃsa-vaṇṇanā* is finished.
The thirteenth *Buddhavaṃsa* is completed.
16. The Exposition of the Lineage of Buddhas:

Atthadassī When the Perfectly Enlightened One Piyadassī had attained final Nibbāna and his dispensation had disappeared, after the human lifespan—which had first declined and then increased until it was immeasurable—had gradually decreased again until people were born with a lifespan of one hundred thousand years, there appeared Atthadassī.

A Buddha named Atthadassī arose in the world. Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) and been reborn in the Tusita heaven, he passed away from there and took conception in the womb of Queen Sudassanā, the chief consort of King Sāgara, in the most magnificent city named Sobhana.
After dwelling in the womb for ten months, [he was born] in the Sucindhanu Garden.

He emerged from his mother’s womb. As soon as the Great Man had emerged from his mother’s womb, the owners of the wealth recovered great treasures that had been buried for a very long time and passed down through their family lineages;
thus, on the day of his naming, they gave him the name Atthadassī. He lived the household life for ten thousand years. [There were] those named Amaragiri, Suragiri, and Girivāhana...
His three palaces were of supremely fragrant origin. He had thirty-three thousand women, headed by Queen Visākhā.

Having seen the four omens, and after the birth of a son named Selakumāra to Queen Visākhā, he mounted the noble steed named Sudassana, went forth on the Great Renunciation, and became a monk. Nine crores of people followed him.
They followed him into the religious life. Surrounded by them, that Great Being practiced the life of striving for eight months.

Then, on the full moon of Visākha, having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice brought as an offering by the Nāgī Sucindharā—given together with her in a golden bowl while her entire body was visible to the great multitude—he sat at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, which was adorned by hundreds of young saplings.
Having spent the day’s rest in the young *sāla* grove, at the time of evening,
he took eight handfuls of *kusā* grass offered by the Nāga king named Mahāruccī (Dhammaruci). Approaching the Campaka Bodhi tree,

he spread out a mat of *kusā* grass measuring thirty-five cubits in length and breadth, sat down cross-legged, and having attained full enlightenment, performed that which is practiced by all Buddhas.
Having uttered the inspired utterance (udāna): “Through many births in saṃsāra... [etc.
...I have now attained the destruction of craving,” and having spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, he accepted the Brahmā’s request for a teaching on the Dhamma.
Seeing that the nine koṭis of bhikkhus who had gone forth together with him were capable of penetrating the Noble Dhamma, he traveled through the air and arrived near the city of Anoma.

Having descended at Anoma Grove and being surrounded by them, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion there. At that time, there was the first realization of the Dhamma for one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
Later, while the Blessed One, the Leader of the World, was wandering through the celestial realms and teaching the Dhamma there, for another hundred thousand times ten million beings...

There was a second realization of the Dhamma. But when the Blessed One Atthadassī—just as our own Blessed One did—entered the beautiful city of Kapilavatthu and taught the Dhamma, there was a third realization of the Dhamma for one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
Thus it is said:
“In that very same Maṇḍakappa, the one of great renown, Atthadassī,
having destroyed the great darkness, attained supreme enlightenment.
Being entreated by Brahmā, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.”
He satisfied the world with the Deathless, including the ten-thousandfold world system together with its devas.
For that Lord of the World as well, there were three moments of full realization;
the first realization involved one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
“When the Buddha Atthadassī was wandering on a tour among the gods,
there occurred a second realization for hundreds of thousands of millions.
Furthermore, when the Buddha taught in the presence of his father— ”
“There was a third realization for hundreds of thousands of millions.
Regarding this, the phrase *tattha tattheva* means “in that very same kappa. Here, however, *varakappa* is intended in the sense of a *maṇḍakappa*.
As it was stated below in the *Padumuttara-Buddhavaṃsa-vaṇṇanā*: “The kappa in which three Buddhas are born is a *varakappa*.”
Thus it was said. Therefore, a "supreme aeon" (varakappa) is here called a "maṇḍa-aeon. "Having struck down" means having slain; this is indeed the reading. "Being tranquil" means being composed.
"With the deathless" means with the drinking of the nectar consisting of the attainment of the paths and fruits.

"He satisfied" means he gladdened; the sense is that he refreshed them. "The ten-thousandfold" refers to the ten-thousandfold world-system. "A journey among the gods" means for the purpose of training the gods.
The meaning is "wandering through the world of the gods.
It is said that in the city of Sucandaka, the prince Santa and the son of the chaplain Upasanta, having seen no essence in the three Vedas or in any other systems of thought,
stationed four wise and learned men at the four gates of the city.
—"Furthermore, whenever you see or hear of a wise ascetic or brahmin, come and report it to us.
At that time, the World-Protector Atthadassī arrived at Sucandaka City.
Then those men, having been informed by them, went and reported the arrival of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers there. Thereupon—

Those people, tranquil through contentment, upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s arrival, were delighted in heart; accompanied by a retinue of a thousand, they went out to meet the Incomparable One of Ten Powers, paid homage to him, and invited him.

For seven days, they gave an incomparable great almsgiving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and on the seventh day, together with all the inhabitants of the city, they listened to a discourse on the Dhamma.
They heard [this]. It is said that on that day, ninety-eight thousand [monks], having gone forth by the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula, attained *arahantship*.
In the midst of that assembly, the Blessed One recited the *Pātimokkha*; that was the first great gathering (*sannipāta*).
Furthermore, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to his own son, the Elder Sela, eighty-eight thousand [monks]...
Having inspired them, he ordained them by the "Come, monk" formula, led them to Arahantship, and recited the Pātimokkha; this was the second assembly.

Again, at the great auspicious gathering on the full moon of the month of Māgha, while teaching the Dhamma to gods and humans, he led seventy-eight thousand to Arahantship and recited the Pātimokkha; this was the third assembly.
It came to pass. Therefore it was said:
“There were three assemblies of that Great Seer as well—of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless, whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.”
“The first assembly consisted of ninety-eight thousand;
the second assembly consisted of eighty-eight thousand.
The third assembly consisted of seventy-eight thousand.”
"For those great seers who are stainless and liberated through non-clinging.
At that time, it is said, our Bodhisatta was a wealthy brahmin named Susīma in the city of Campaka, highly esteemed by the world.
Having distributed all his wealth and possessions among the poor, the destitute, the wretched, and the needy, he [went] to the vicinity of the Himalayas.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life and attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*),
he became possessed of great psychic power and majesty. Having demonstrated to the great multitude the blameless and blameworthy nature of wholesome and unwholesome states,
he remained there awaiting the appearance of a Buddha.
Then, at another time, when the Leader of the World, Atthadassi,
had appeared in the world and was raining down the nectar of the Dhamma amidst the eight assemblies in the great city of Sudassana, [the king], having heard his Dhamma and gone to the heavenly realm,
brought from the world of the gods celestial flowers such as mandārava, paduma, and pāricchattaka, and [offered them] to himself.
Displaying his supernatural power, while remaining visible in bodily form, he rained down a shower of flowers like a great cloud over the four continents in the four directions.
Having fashioned a pavilion of flowers all around, with flower-made elephant-arches, golden nets, and so forth, he honored the One of Ten Powers with a parasol of *mandārava* flowers.
The Blessed One, in turn, addressed him: "In the future, there will be one named Gotama..."
“He will become a Buddha,” he prophesied. Therefore it was said:
“At that time, I was a matted-hair ascetic, practicing severe austerities;
known by the name Susīma, I was esteemed as the best on earth.”
“Having brought divine mandārava flowers, a lotus,
and a pāricchattaka tree from the world of the gods, I worshipped the Perfectly Enlightened One.
That Buddha Atthadassī, the Great Sage, also gave me this prediction:”
“In eighteen hundred kappas, this one will become a Buddha.
Having exerted himself in striving... [and so forth] ...we shall be in his presence.
Hearing those words as well, joyful and with a heart moved by spiritual urgency—
“I resolved upon a further vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.

In this context, *jaṭila* means one who has matted hair (*jaṭā*). “Regarded as the best on earth” means he was thus esteemed and honored by the entire world as the most excellent, supreme, and preeminent.
That Blessed One had a city named Sobhana; his father was King Sāgara, and [his mother was] Sudassanā.
His mother was named Nāma; his two chief disciples were Santo and Upasanto; his attendant was named Abhaya; his two chief female disciples were Dhammā and Sudhammā;

his Bodhi tree was the Campaka tree; his body was eighty cubits in height; the radiance of his body remained pervading a full league on all sides at all times; his lifespan was one hundred thousand years; [his chief female lay disciple was] Visākhā.
The chief queen of Nāma was Sela by name, his son; he went forth on a horse-chariot. Therefore it is said:
“In the city named Sobhana, there was a kshatriya named Sāgara;
Sudassanā was the mother of the Teacher Atthadassi.”
“Santo and Upasanto were the chief male disciples;
the attendant of the Teacher Atthadassi was named Abhaya.
Dhammā and Sudhammā were the chief female disciples.”
The bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Campaka.
That Buddha too was peerless among his equals, rising eighty cubits high;
he shone like a king of sal trees, like the full moon.
“His natural rays, numbering many hundreds of millions,
constantly pervade ten directions— above, below, and across— for a distance of a league.
He too is a Buddha, a bull among men, the Sage supreme among all beings.”
"For a hundred thousand years, the One with Vision remained in the world.
Having displayed incomparable radiance and shone forth among the world of gods,
he too has succumbed to impermanence, through the exhaustion of grasping at the aggregates."
In this context, "filled like the king of stars" means like the king of stars (the moon) with its entire orb full and stainless during the autumn season;
that is the meaning. "Ordinary" means arising by way of natural occurrence, not by way of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

When the Blessed One wishes, he could pervade even hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) with light. "Rays" means beams of light. "With the destruction of clinging" (*upādānasaṅkhayā*).
Like a fire through the exhaustion of its fuel, [the Blessed One] was like a fire through the exhaustion of the four kinds of clinging (*upādāna*).

That Blessed One also attained final Nibbāna in the incomparable city of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, within the Anoma Grove. His relics, however, were distributed by his own resolve.
The rest here is self-evident from the verses.
The commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa* of Atthadassī is finished.
The fourteenth *Buddhavaṃsa* is completed.
17. The commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa* of Dhammadassī.

When the Perfectly Enlightened One Atthadassi had attained final Nibbāna and an intermediate aeon had passed, as the lifespan of beings gradually decreased from being immeasurable until they were born with a lifespan of one hundred thousand years, a Teacher named Dhammadassī arose in the world.
He was the illuminator of the world, the remover of the stains of the world such as greed, and the sole leader of the world. That Blessed One [fulfilled] the perfections...

Having fulfilled [his perfections], he was reborn in the Tusita heaven; passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Sunandā, the chief consort of King Saraṇa—himself a refuge for the whole world—in the city of Saraṇa.
At the end of ten months, during the rainy season in the Saraṇa Garden, he emerged from his mother’s womb through the opening of a cloud.

He emerged like the full moon. But as soon as the Great Being had emerged from his mother’s womb, unrighteous legal proceedings (*vohāra*)—as recorded in the books of law and precedent—vanished of their own accord, and only righteous legal proceedings remained.
Therefore, on the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name “Dhammadassī. He lived the household life for eighty-four thousand years. It is said that for him...
There were three palaces named Arāja, Viraja, and Sudassana.
He had one hundred and twenty thousand women, headed by the queen Vicikoḷidevī.
Having seen the four omens, and when a son named Puññavaḍḍhana was born to Queen Vicikoḷidevī, he [resembled] a divine youth.
Extremely delicate as if he were a god, experiencing a splendor like that of the celestial realms, he rose during the middle watch of the night and sat upon his royal couch.
Seeing the disarray of the women who had fallen asleep, a sense of spiritual urgency arose within him, and he conceived the thought of the Great Renunciation.
Immediately upon the arising of that thought, the Sudassana palace soared up into the expanse of the sky.
Surrounded by his fourfold army, like a second sun or a celestial mansion, he proceeded and alighted right near the Bodhi tree of the red *kuravaka* grove, where he stood still.

It is said that the Great Man, having taken the saffron robes brought by Brahmā and gone forth into homelessness, descended from the palace and stood at no great distance. The palace, meanwhile, [remained] in the sky.
Having gone to the Bodhi tree, he stood upon the ground with it as his shelter. The women also, descending from the palace with their retinue, went a distance of half a *gāvuta* and stood there.

There, setting aside the women and their female attendants and maidservants, all the men followed him into the homeless life. There were one hundred thousand times ten million (*koṭisatasahassa*) monks.
Then the Bodhisatta Dhammadassi, having practiced the life of striving for seven days and having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice given by the goddess Vicikolī,
spent the day’s rest in the Badara forest; then, at evening time,
taking eight handfuls of grass given by a barley-herder named Sirivaḍḍhana, he approached the Bimbijāla Bodhi tree, which was fifty-three cubits in extent.
Having spread out a grass mat and there penetrated the knowledge of omniscience, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“Through many births in saṃsāra... [etc. ...I have now attained the destruction of craving.

Having spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree and having received the Brahma-request, he [perceived] the capacity of the one hundred thousand times ten million monks who had gone forth with him to penetrate the true Dhamma.
Knowing this, he traveled the eighteen-yojana road and reached Isipatana in a single day;
surrounded by them, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion there, at which time there was the first realization for one hundred thousand times ten million beings. Thus it is said:
“In that very same auspicious aeon, the highly renowned Dhammadassī;”
Having dispelled that darkness, he shines forth pre-eminently in the world with its devas.
At the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma by that one of incomparable splendor,
there was the first realization for one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
In this context, "that darkness" means the darkness of delusion (moha) known as *tama*.

Now, when King Sañjaya by name, in the city named Tagara, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and renunciation as security, went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isi*), ninety million people followed him in going forth. They all became possessors of the five super-knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*).
They were [there]. Then the Teacher Dhammadassī, seeing their perfection of spiritual potential (*upanissaya-sampatti*), traveled through the air to the hermitage of the ascetic Sañjaya.
Standing in the sky, he taught the Dhamma to those ascetics in accordance with their inclinations and caused the eye of Dhamma (*dhammacakkhu*) to arise;
that was the second clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Thus it is said:
“When the Buddha Dhammadassī disciplined the seer Sañjaya, that was the second great realization for ninety koṭis.
But when Sakka, lord of the devas, desiring to hear the Dhamma from the One of Ten Powers, approached him, that was the third great realization for eighty koṭis. Thus it was said.
“When Sakka approached the Leader together with his retinue,
that was the third occasion of realization for eighty koṭis.
Furthermore, when [the Buddha] was in Saraṇa city, [he ordained] his half-brother Prince Paduma and Prince Phussadeva along with their retinues.

He ordained them; in that same rainy season, in the midst of one hundred thousand times ten million monks who had been ordained, he held the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for purification, and that was the first great assembly (*sannipāta*).
Again, upon the Blessed One’s descent from the deva-world, there was a second assembly of one hundred times ten million.
But when, at the Sudassana Monastery, [the Blessed One] [expounded] the virtues and benefits of the thirteen ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*),...
Having proclaimed [the Dhamma], he placed the great disciple named Hārita at the head of those foremost in this category.
At that time, in the midst of eighty koṭis, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
"Of that God of Gods, there were three assemblies."
Of those whose taints are destroyed, who are stainless, whose minds are peaceful,
and who are steadfast. “When the Buddha Dhammadassī entered the rains retreat at Saraṇa,
that was the first assembly of one hundred thousand times ten million.”
“Furthermore, when the Buddha came from the deva realm to the human world,
there was then also a second assembly of seven hundred million. Furthermore,
when the Buddha proclaimed the virtues of the ascetic practices (dhuta-guṇa),”
“At that time, there was a third assembly of eight hundred million.

At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become Sakka, king of the gods, came surrounded by the devas of two celestial realms and honored the Tathāgata with divine perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as divine musical instruments. And the Teacher [addressed] him: “In the future...”
“Gotama by name will become a Buddha,” he prophesied. Therefore it was said:
“At that time, I was Sakka, Purindada;
With divine garlands of fragrance and with music, I paid him supreme honor.”
“Then he, sitting in the midst of the gods, prophesied to me:
‘In eighteen hundred kappas, this one shall become a Buddha.
Having exerted myself in striving... [we] shall be in his presence.”
“Having heard her words as well, my heart became even more serene;
I resolved upon further vows for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
Now, that Blessed One had a city named Saraṇa, and his father was King Saraṇa, and [his mother] was named Sunandā.
His mother was Padumā; his two chief disciples were Phussadeva and [the other]; his attendant was named Sunetta;
his two chief female disciples were Khemā and Sabbanāmā; his Bodhi tree was the Bimbijāla tree; his body was eighty cubits in height;
his lifespan was one hundred thousand years; Vicikolī was his chief queen; and Puññavaḍḍhana was his son.
He departed from the palace. Therefore it was said:
“The city was named Saraṇa, the kṣatriya king was named Saraṇa, and Sunandā was the mother of the Teacher Dhammadassi.”
“Paduma and Phussadeva were the chief disciples;
he named Sunetta was the attendant of the Teacher Dhammadassi.
Khemā and Sabbanāmā were the chief female disciples.”
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Bimbijāla.
That Buddha too was peerless among the peerless, rising eighty cubits high;
he outshone the ten thousandfold world-system with his splendor.
“Like a king of *sāla* trees in full bloom, like lightning in the sky,
or like the sun at midday— thus did he shine.
Even for him of incomparable splendor, his livelihood was the same as [that of others].”
For one hundred thousand years, the Visionary One remained in the world.
Having displayed his radiance and having purified the Teaching,
he passed away like the moon from the sky— extinguished together with his disciples.
In this context, *bimbijāla* refers to the red *kuravaka* tree. "In the ten-thousandfold" means in the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassi lokadhātu*).

"Like lightning" means like a flash of lightning. "Shone forth" means that just as lightning shines in the sky and the sun shines at midday, so too did that Blessed One shine; such is the meaning. "Equally" means equally with all human beings.
"His lifespan was such"—this is the meaning. "He passed away" (*cavī*) means he fell away (*cuto*). "Like the moon" means he passed away like the moon from the sky; this is the meaning.
It is said that the Blessed One Dhammadassi attained final nibbāna in the Kesārāma monastery at the city of Sālavatī. The rest here is clear from the verses themselves.
The commentary on the lineage of Buddha Dhammadassi is finished.
The fifteenth Buddha-chronicle is finished.
18. The Exposition of the Buddha-chronicle of Siddhattha:
After the Blessed One Dhammadassi had attained final Nibbāna and his Dispensation had disappeared, a thousand aeons having passed in that eon-cycle...

When seven hundred and six aeons had passed, in the ninety-fourth aeon prior to this one, there appeared in the world a Teacher named Siddhattha, a sole wanderer for the welfare of the world who had realized the ultimate truth. Thus it is said:
"After Dhammadassi, the Leader of the World, Siddhattha [appeared];"
"Having destroyed all darkness, he has risen up like the sun.
Thus, the Bodhisatta Siddhattha, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was reborn in the Tusita heaven;
passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Suphassā, the chief consort of King Udena in the city of Vebhāra.
At the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Vīriya Garden.
When the Great Being was born, all undertakings and desired aims reached fulfillment; therefore, his kinsmen gave him the name Siddhattha.
He lived in the midst of the household for ten thousand years. His [sons] were named Kokā, Suppala, and Paduma.
There were three palaces. Forty-eight thousand women, headed by Queen Somanassā, attended upon him.

Having seen the four omens, and when Prince Anupama had been born to Queen Somanassā, he departed on the full moon day of Āsāḷha in a golden palanquin, went to the Vīriya garden, and went forth into homelessness. A hundred thousand million people [followed him].

They followed him into the homeless life. It is said that the Great Being, having practiced the course of striving together with them for ten months, on the full moon of Visākha, partook of the honeyed milk-rice offered by a young Brahmin girl named Sunettā in the village of Asadisa;
he spent the day’s rest in the Badara grove, and in the evening, [he accepted] eight [grains of grass] given by a barley-gatherer named Varuṇa.

Having taken a handful of grass and approached the Kaṇikāra Bodhi tree, he spread out a mat of grass forty cubits wide, sat down cross-legged, and having attained omniscience, uttered this inspired utterance: “Through many births in saṃsāra... [I have wandered]... now I have found the destruction of craving.
Having spent seven times seven days there, [he addressed] those who had gone forth together with him.

Seeing that one hundred thousand times ten million bhikkhus were capable of penetrating the Four Noble Truths, he traveled by way of the air, descended at the Migadāya in Gayā, and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion for them; at that time, there was the first realization (abhisamaya) of one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
Thus it is said:
“He too, having attained full enlightenment, was ferrying across the world including the devas;
he rained down the cloud of Dhamma, extinguishing the world including the devas.
For that one of incomparable splendor, there were also three moments of clear realization.”
“There was the first realization for hundreds of thousands of millions.
In this context, “together with the devas” means the world together with its devas. “By the rain from the cloud of Dhamma” means by the downpour from the cloud of Dhamma-discourse.
Furthermore, having been invited by the king named Bhīmaratha in the city of Bhīmaratha, he sat in the assembly hall constructed in the center of the city.

Filling the ten directions with his Brahma-voice—which was as sweet as the song of the *karavīka* bird, pleasant to hear, supremely melodious, moving the hearts of wise men, and like a consecration with the nectar of immortality—he beat the drum of the nectar of the Dhamma.
At that time, there occurred a second realization for ninety million beings. Thus it is said:
“Furthermore, Bhīmaratha, when he struck the drum, at that time there was a second realization for ninety koṭis.
And when, in the city of Vebhāra, while teaching the lineage of Buddhas to his kinsmen, he caused the eye of Dhamma to arise in ninety koṭis, that was the third realization. Thus it is said:
“When the Buddha taught the Dhamma at Vebhāra,
that most excellent mountain, there occurred the third great realization for ninety koṭis [of beings].
At Amararuciradassana, in the city named Amara, two brothers, Sambala and Sumitta, reigned as kings.
Then the Teacher Siddhattha, perceiving the excellence of the spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) of those kings,

traveled through the expanse of the sky, descended into the midst of the City of the Immortals (*Amaranagara*), and displayed his foot-relics as he pressed the surface of the earth with his feet adorned with wheels.
Having proceeded to the Amaruyyāna garden, he sat upon the supremely delightful stone slab that was cooled by his own compassion.

He sat down. Then the two royal brothers, having seen the footprints of the One of Ten Powers and having followed those footprints, approached the Teacher Siddhattha—the leader of all the world—who had attained the ultimate goal, together with his retinue;
they paid homage to him and sat down surrounding the Blessed One. To them, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in accordance with their inclinations.
He taught them. Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, they all conceived faith, went forth into homelessness, and attained arahantship.
In the midst of those one hundred koṭis of those whose taints were destroyed, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly.
In the city of Vebhāra, during the gathering of kinsmen, he recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of ninety koṭis who had gone forth.
He recited the Pātimokkha in the Sudassana Monastery amidst eighty koṭis of those assembled;
that was the third assembly. Therefore it is said:
"There were three assemblies even during the time of that Best of Bipeds."
Of those whose taints were exhausted, stainless, with peaceful minds and poised in equanimity—
there were nine billion, eight hundred million, and one billion;
these were the three assemblies of the stainless ones.
In that context, "of ninety and also of eighty crores" means that there were gatherings of ninety crores and also of eighty crores;
this is the meaning. "These were the three places" (*ete āsuṃ tayo ṭhānā*) means that these were the three locations for the assemblies; this is the meaning.
There is also a reading: "Those three were the places" (*ṭhānāne tāni tīṇi ahesuṃ*).
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Maṅgala in the city of Surasena, reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Having relinquished a vast accumulation of wealth numbering many koṭis to the poor, the destitute, and others, he became one who delights in solitude.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life and attained the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges, while dwelling therein, [he thought]: “Siddhattha...”
Having heard that "a Buddha has appeared in the world," he approached him, paid homage, and listened to his discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, by means of his supernormal power, he went to the Jambu tree after which this continent is known as Jambudīpa;
having brought a fruit from it, he seated the Teacher Siddhattha—accompanied by a retinue of ninety million bhikkhus—at the Surasena Monastery.
He satisfied and served him with rose-apple fruits. Then the Teacher, having consumed that fruit, prophesied:
"In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, there will be a Buddha named Gotama. Therefore it was said:
"At that time, I was an ascetic named Maṅgala..."
“Of exalted power and difficult to overcome, endowed with the strength of direct knowledge, [the Buddha] said:
‘Having brought a jambu fruit, I gave it to Siddhattha.
Having accepted it, the Sambuddha spoke these words.’”
“Behold this ascetic, the matted-hair practitioner of fierce austerities;
in ninety-four aeons from now, he will become a Buddha.
Having exerted himself in striving... [we shall] be in his presence.”
“Having heard her words as well, my heart became even more serene;
I resolved upon further vows for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
In that context, *duppasaho* means difficult to overcome. Or rather, this is the reading itself. Now, the city of that Blessed One was Vebhāra.
His name was [the Buddha]. King Udena—Jayasena was also his name—was his father;
Suphassā was his mother. Sambala and Sumitta were his two chief disciples; Revata was his attendant; Sīvalā and Surāmā were his two chief female disciples.
His Bodhi tree was the Kaṇikāra tree; his body was sixty cubits in height. [He lived for] one hundred thousand years.
Āyu was the name of his chief queen, Somanassā; Anupama was the name of his son. He went forth in a golden palanquin. Therefore it is said:
“In the city named Vebhāra, there was a kṣatriya named Udena;
Suphassā was the mother of the Great Sage Siddhattha.”
“Sambala and Sumitta were his chief disciples;
the attendant named Revata was the one for Siddhattha, the Great Seer.
Sīvalā and Surāmā were his chief female disciples.”
The enlightenment of that Blessed One is called the Kaṇikāra.
That Buddha, sixty *ratana*s in height, rose up into the sky;
resembling a priceless golden ornament, he illuminated the ten thousandfold world-system.
“That Buddha too was peerless and unequaled, incomparable and without rival;
the Visionary One remained in the world for one hundred thousand years.
Having displayed vast radiance and caused his disciples to blossom like flowers,”
“Having sported through meditative attainment, he has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.
In this context, “sixty ratanas high” means that he rose into the sky to the height of sixty *ratana*s.

“Resembling a golden crown” means that his appearance was like a crown made of gold, variegated with various gems. “The ten-thousandfold world-system shines forth” means within the ten-thousandfold world-system...

It shines. "Vipula" means a sublime radiance. "Having caused to blossom" means having made it blossom with the flowers of the meditative absorptions (jhāna), the direct knowledges (abhiññā), the paths (magga), the fruits (phala), and the attainments (samāpatti), thereby bringing it to the pinnacle of supreme beauty—this is the meaning. "Having sported" means having played or enjoyed oneself.

"By means of attainments" refers to both mundane and supramundane attainments as well as the direct knowledges. "Extinguished" means extinguished through the parinibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna).

It is said that the Teacher Siddhattha attained final Nibbāna in the Anoma Grove at Kañcanaveḷu City. Right there, they constructed for him a jewel-encrusted stupa four yojanas in height. In all the remaining verses, the meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Siddhattha-buddhavaṃsa* is finished.
The sixteenth Buddha-chronicle is completed.
19. The Description of the Lineage of Buddha Tissa.
Following that Blessed One Siddhattha, however, there was one kappa devoid of Buddhas.
Ninety-two kappas ago from this time, two Buddhas named Tissa and Phussa were born in a single kappa. Among them, the Great Being named Tissa—

Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) and been reborn in the Tusita heaven, he passed away from there and took conception in the womb of Queen Padumā—whose eyes resembled lotus petals and who was the chief consort of King Janasandha—in the city of Khemaka.
At the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Anoma Garden. For seven thousand years...
He lived in a palace. He had three palaces named Guhāsela, Nārisaya, and Nisabha.
He had thirty-three thousand women, headed by Queen Subhaddā.
Having seen the four omens, when Prince Ānanda was born as the son of Queen Subhaddā, [he gave him] the name Sonuttara.
Having mounted his unsurpassed, excellent horse and gone forth in the Great Renunciation, he went into homelessness. Ten million people followed him into the religious life.

Surrounded by them, after practicing the conduct of striving for eight months, on the full moon of Visākha, he partook of the honeyed milk-rice offered by the daughter of Vīra-seṭṭhi in the village of Vīra, and spent the day in meditation in the Salala grove.
Having passed the time until evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass brought by a barley-gatherer named Vijitasangāmaka;
approaching the Asana Bodhi tree, he spread out a grass mat forty cubits wide,
sat there cross-legged, and having shattered Māra and his host, attained all-knowing wisdom (sabbaññutaññāṇa).

Having uttered this inspired utterance: “Through many births in saṃsāra... [and so on] ...I have now attained the destruction of craving,” and having spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, he traveled through the air to the city of Yasovatī.
There, finding the two princes, Brahmadeva and Udaya, who were endowed with the necessary spiritual potential, he descended at the Migadāya in Yasovatī.
Having had the park-keeper summon the princes, he [approached] them.
With his retinue, making himself heard throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system with a sweet, pervasive, and non-diffusive Brahma-voice, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion;
at that time, there was the first realization of the Dhamma for one hundred koṭis. Therefore it is said:
"Subsequently to Siddhattha, the peerless one, the matchless one..."
Of infinite splendor and immeasurable fame, Tissa was the leader of the world’s three realms.
Having dispelled that darkness and illuminated the world including the devas,
the compassionate Great Hero, the possessor of vision, arose in the world.
“His supernormal power was incomparable, as were his virtue and concentration;
having reached perfection in every respect, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
That Buddha made his pure voice heard throughout the ten thousandfold world-system.”
“Hundreds of millions attained realization during the first teaching of the Dhamma.
Regarding that, “in all respects” means having gone to the further shore (pāraṃ) in all phenomena.
“In the ten-thousandfold world-system” means that on another occasion, there were ten million monks who had gone forth together with the Teacher Tissa; [this was] for the Great Man.
Having abandoned life in the community, she had gone elsewhere at the time of approaching the foot of the Bodhi tree.

Having heard that the Wheel of Dhamma had been set in motion by the Perfectly Enlightened One, Tissa, she came to the Migadāya at Isipatana, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, and sat down surrounding him.
The Blessed One taught the Dhamma to them; at that time, there was the second great realization (abhisamaya) for ninety crores of beings.
It happened. Furthermore, at the conclusion of the Great Auspicious Assembly, there was a third realization for sixty koṭis.
Therefore it is said:
"The second was for ninety koṭis, the third for sixty koṭis."
"He then liberated beings, both humans and gods, from bondage.
In this context, "the second [assembly] of ninety koṭis" means that the second realization involved ninety koṭis of living beings.
"From bondage" means from bondage; the meaning is that he completely liberated them from the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*). Now, having been liberated...
Showing beings by way of their appearance, he said, "men and gods" (*nara-maru*). "Men and gods" means *narāmare*.
It is said that in the city of Yasavatī, during the rainy season, he partook of alms surrounded by one hundred thousand Arahants who had gone forth;
that was the first great assembly (*sannipāta*). From both sides [of the lineage] came the prince Nārivāhana, the son of King Sujāta, named Sujāta.
When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, arrived at the city of Nārivāhana, the king, together with his retinue, went out to meet him;
having invited the One of Ten Powers along with the community of monks and offered an incomparable gift for seven days, he handed over his own kingdom to his son and, together with his retinue,
received the *ehibhikkhu* ordination in the presence of Tissa Sammāsambuddha, the Sovereign of All the World.
He went forth. Indeed, his renunciation became renowned in all directions; therefore, people came from here and there and followed the youth Nārivāhana into the religious life.
At that time, the Tathāgata, seated in the midst of nine million monks, recited the Pātimokkha;
this was the second great assembly. Later, in the city of Khemavatī, at a gathering of kinsmen...
Having heard the discourse on the lineage of the Buddhas (*buddhavaṃsa*), one hundred and eighty thousand [monks] went forth in his presence and attained *arahantship*.
Surrounded by them, the Sugata recited the *Pātimokkha*; that was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies under Tiṣya, the Leader of the World.”
Of those whose taints are destroyed, who are stainless, whose minds are at peace,
and who are steadfast— there was a first assembly of one hundred thousand who had destroyed their taints;
there was a second assembly of ninety thousand.
“There was a third assembly of one hundred and eighty thousand [monks],
who were stainless, whose taints were destroyed, and who had blossomed through liberation.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become a king named Sujāta in the city of Yasavatī, [ruled over] a prosperous and flourishing realm.
Having renounced a vast accumulation of many millions of coins and his retinue— whose hearts were filled with affection— as if they were blades of grass or reeds,
he went forth with a heart agitated by the realization of birth and other sufferings. Having taken the ascetic’s renunciation and become possessed of great psychic power and majesty,
his body suffused with five-colored rapture upon hearing that "a Buddha has appeared in the world," he set out together with his wife.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he thought: "Come now, I shall worship the Blessed One with celestial flowers such as the *mandārava* and *pāricchattaka*.

Then, having thought thus, he went by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*) to the heavenly realm, entered the *Cittalatāvana* grove, and [took] celestial flowers such as the *paduma*, *pāricchattaka*, and *mandārava* made of jewels.
Having filled and taken up a *caṅkoṭaka* measuring one *gāvuta*, he came through the sky and honored the Blessed One with celestial fragrant flowers.

And holding over the head of the Blessed One in the midst of the fourfold assembly a lotus-umbrella— complete with a jeweled handle, golden sockets, leaves made of *padumarāga* gems, and fragrant filaments like a parasol— he stood there.
He stood there. Then the Blessed One prophesied concerning him: "In ninety-two aeons from now, one named Gotama will become a Buddha.
Therefore it was said:
"At that time, I was a kshatriya named Sujāta..."
Having abandoned great wealth, I went forth into the ascetic life of a seer.
While I was thus gone forth, the Leader of the World appeared.
Upon hearing the word "Buddha," joy arose within me.
“Taking divine mandārava flowers, paduma, and pārichattaka,
I approached him while shaking them with both hands.
Tissa, the leader of the world, was surrounded by the fourfold assembly.”
Taking that flower, I held it over the head of the Jina.
That Buddha, sitting in the midst of the assembly, gave me this prediction:
"In ninety-two aeons from now, this one shall become a Buddha."
“Having exerted the effort... [we] shall stand face to face with him.
Having heard his words as well, my mind became even more serene;
I resolved upon further practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
In that context, *mayi pabbajite* means "when I had entered the homeless life.
The reading found in some manuscripts, *mama pabbajitaṃ santaṃ*, should be understood as a scribal error. *Upapajjatha* means "you were reborn.
*Ubho hatthehi* means "with both hands. *Paggayha* means "having grasped. *Dhunamāno* means "shaking about" or "brandishing" the bark garments.
“Surrounded by the four castes” means surrounded by the four assemblies; the meaning is surrounded by khattiyas, brahmins, householders, and ascetics. Some read it as “surrounded by the four classes.
That Blessed One had a city named Khema. His father was a khattiya named Janasandha, and [his mother was] Padumā...
His mother was named Janikā; his two chief disciples were Brahmadeva and Udaya; his attendant was named Samaṅga; his two chief female disciples were Phussā and Sudattā;
his Bodhi tree was the Asana tree; his body was sixty cubits in height;
his lifespan was one hundred thousand years; his chief queen was named Subhaddā; his son was named Ānanda; and he traveled by means of a horse-drawn carriage.
He went forth. Thus it was said:
“The city named Khemaka, the kshatriya named Janasandha, and the mother named Padumā belonged to Tissa, the Great Seer.”
“Brahmadeva and Udaya were the chief disciples;
the attendant of the Great Seer Tissa was named Samaṅga.
Phussā and Sudattā were the chief female disciples.”
The seat of that Blessed One is called Bodhi.
That Victor, the Buddha, was sixty cubits in height;
peerless and incomparable, he appeared like Mount Himavat.
“For that one of incomparable splendor, there was unsurpassed longevity;
the Visionary One remained in the world for a hundred thousand years.
Having experienced supreme, excellent, and most sublime great glory,”
Having blazed like a mass of fire, he has gone out together with his disciples.
Like a cloud by the wind, like a festival by the sun,
like darkness by a lamp— he has gone out together with his disciples.
In that context, "by height" means by way of lofty stature. "Appears like the Himavat" means he appears just like the Himavat mountain.

Or rather, this is the reading: just as the five-peaked Himavat, rising for hundreds of leagues, appears exceedingly beautiful both through its loftiness and its gentleness even to those standing at a great distance, so too does the Blessed One appear—this is the meaning. "Unsurpassed" (anuttara).
"Neither too tall nor too short. "A lifespan of one hundred thousand years" is the meaning. "Supreme," "excellent," and "best" are synonyms for one another.

"Festival": just as a snowflake, a cloud, or a festival is [transient], so too the Blessed One, together with his disciples, has attained final nibbāna—being afflicted by the winds and fires of impermanence—just as those things are afflicted by the winds and the fires of the sun; this is the meaning.
It is said that the Blessed One, Tissa, attained final Nibbāna in the Sunandārāma at the city of Sunandavatī. The rest here is evident from the verses themselves.
The *Tissabuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā* is finished.
The seventeenth Buddha-chronicle is completed.
20. The Account of the Lineage of Buddha Phussa:
After the time of that Blessed One Tissa, [the lifespan] gradually decreased and then increased again until it became immeasurable;
subsequently, it decreased again until beings were born with a lifespan of ninety thousand years. In that very same kappa, Phussa [appeared].
A Teacher named [Nāma] arose in the world. That Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramī), was reborn in the Tusita heaven;
passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Sirimā, the chief consort of King Jayasena in the city of Kāsika.
At the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Sirima Garden. For nine thousand years...
He lived in a house. It is said that he had three palaces known as Garuḷapakkha, Haṃsa, and Suvaṇṇabhāra.
Thirty thousand women, headed by Kisāgotamī, were in attendance upon him.
Having seen the four omens and when his son named Anupama was born to Kisāgotamī, he mounted the back of a magnificent, adorned elephant.
Having undertaken the Great Renunciation, he went forth. A crore of people followed him into the homeless life once he had gone forth.

Surrounded by them, he practiced the life of striving for six months; then, abandoning that group and cultivating the solitary life for seven days, he dwelt there until, on the full moon day of Visākha, at a certain city, he [encountered] Sirivaḍḍhā, the daughter of a certain merchant.

Having been given that name, and having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice and spent the day’s rest in the Siṃsapā grove, at the time of evening he took eight handfuls of grass offered by the lay follower named Sirivaḍḍha.
Approaching the Āmalaka Bodhi tree, he shattered Māra and his host, attained omniscient knowledge, and [uttered]: “Through many births in saṃsāra... [the craving] for desires.”
Having uttered this inspired utterance, “I have attained the destruction [of the taints],” and having spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree,
he saw that the millions of monks who had gone forth with him were capable of penetrating the Dhamma. Traveling through the air,
he descended at the Deer Park in Isipatana near the city of Sāṅkāśya and set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma in their midst.
At that time, there was the first realization for one hundred thousand times ten million beings. Therefore it is said:
“In that very same Maṇḍa-kappa, there was an unsurpassed Teacher;
peerless, equal to the unequaled, Phussa, the leader of the world.”
"He too, having destroyed all darkness and unraveled the great tangle,
rained down the water of the Deathless, gladdening the world together with its devas.
While the Wheel of Dhamma was being set in motion by Phussa under the auspicious conjunction of the Nakshatras,"
“There was the first realization for one hundred thousand times ten million.
In that context, “in that very same *maṇḍa*-kalpa”: a kalpa in which two Buddhas arise is called a “*maṇḍa*-kalpa,” as stated below.
“Having disentangled” means having unravelled. Regarding “the great tangle”: here, “tangle” is a designation for craving (*taṇhā*).

For it is called "tangle" (*jaṭā*) because, like a tangle of thread, a net, or a mass of cakes, it arises again and again in relation to objects such as visible forms by way of succession from lower to higher levels, and because it binds them together; thus it is said to be "that great tangle.
"Sadevakaṃ" means the world together with its devas. "Abhivassī" means he rained down. "Amatambunā" means with the water of the Dhamma discourse, which is reckoned as the Deathless (*amata*).
The meaning is: "He rained down, causing torment.

Now, when in the city of Bārāṇasī a king named Sirivaḍḍha, having abandoned a vast mass of wealth, went forth into the ascetic life, there were nine million ascetics who had gone forth together with him. To them the Blessed One—
He taught the Dhamma. At that time, there was a second realization for ninety hundred-thousand beings.
But when he taught the Dhamma to his own son, Prince Anupama, at that time there was a third realization for eighty hundred-thousand beings.
Thus it is said:
“There was a second realization for nine million [beings];
there was a third realization for eight million.
Then, at a later time, in the city of Kaṇṇakujja, there were Prince Surakkhita and the son of the family priest, Dhammasena Kumāra.
And when the Sammasambuddha Phussa arrived at his own city, Canda, together with six hundred thousand men, went out to meet him, paid homage, invited him, and for seven days gave a great almsgiving.

Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma from the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, he gained confidence in the Blessed One; then, having gone forth along with his retinue, he and they attained Arahantship. Of those six hundred...
In the midst of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the first great assembly.
Later, in the city of Kāsi, at the gathering of about sixty kinsmen of King Jayasena, he taught the Buddhavaṃsa.
Having heard it, five million people went forth by the "Come, bhikkhu" formula and attained arahantship.
Standing in their midst, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the second assembly.
Again, at the great gathering on the occasion of the Mahāmaṅgala, having heard the discourse on auspiciousness, four million men went forth and attained arahantship.
Standing in their midst, the Sugata recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies, even for the Great Seer Phussa—
of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless, whose minds were at peace,
and who were steadfast. The first gathering consisted of six million.”
The second assembly consisted of five million [monks];
the third assembly consisted of four million [monks]—
those who were liberated through non-clinging and whose rebirth had been severed.
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a kshatriya named Vijitāvin in the city of Arindama.

Having heard his Dhamma and gained confidence in the Blessed One, he gave a great alms-offering to him, renounced his great kingdom, and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having mastered the Three Piṭakas, as a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, he delivered discourses on the Dhamma to the great multitude.
He fulfilled the perfection of virtue. He too prophesied of him, "He will become a Buddha. Therefore it was said:
"At that time, I was a kshatriya named Vijitāvin;
having renounced great sovereignty, I went forth into homelessness in his presence."
“The Buddha Phussa, the leader supreme in the world, also prophesied of me:
‘In ninety-two aeons from now, this one shall become a Buddha.
Having exerted himself in striving... [and so on] ...through the fulfillment of the ten perfections.”
“Having mastered the Suttanta and the Vinaya— the ninefold teaching of the Teacher—
I have brought glory to the dispensation of the Conqueror.
Dwelling there with diligence, having cultivated the sublime meditation,”
"Having reached the perfection of direct knowledge (abhiññā-pāramī), you went to the Brahma-world.
Now, that Blessed One had a city named Kāsika.
His father was King Jayasena, his mother was named Sirimā, his two chief disciples were Surakkhita and Dhammasena, his attendant was named Sabhiya, and [his chief female disciple was] Cālā.
Upacālā and Cālā were his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the Āmalaka tree; his body was fifty-eight cubits in height;
his lifespan was ninety thousand years; Kisāgotamī was his chief queen; his son was named Anupama;
and he went forth on an elephant vehicle. Thus it has been said:
“The city was named Kāsika, and the kshatriya king was named Jayasena;
the mother of the Great Seer Phussa was named Sirimā... [etc.
...The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Āmaṇḍa... [etc. ...”
“That Sage, rising up to eighty-eight *ratana*s in height,
shines like the thousand-rayed sun or like the full moon, the king of stars.
For ninety thousand years, such a lifespan exists.”
Remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
"Having exhorted many beings and having brought many people to peace,
that Teacher of incomparable glory has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples."
In this context, *āmaṇḍa* refers to the *āmalaka* tree. *Ovaditvā* means having given exhortation; the sense is "having instructed.
*Sopi satthā atulayaso* means that teacher also possessed immeasurable fame (*amita-yaso*). There is also a reading, *so jahitvā amitayaso*, for which the meaning is:
"he, having abandoned all those aforementioned distinctions."

It is said that the Sammasambuddha Phussa attained final Nibbāna at the Senārāma in Kusinārā. It is said that his relics were widely distributed. In all the remaining verses, the meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the lineage of Buddha Phussa is finished.
The eighteenth Buddha-lineage is completed.
21. The Exposition of the Lineage of Buddha Vipassī:

Following the period subsequent to Buddha Phussa, after that intermediate aeon had passed and this [present] aeon had reached its ninety-first cycle, there appeared in the world a teacher named Vipassī—a conqueror of all aeons, whose resolve was devoted to the welfare of others—known everywhere as Vipassī.
Having fulfilled the perfections, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven in a palace illuminated by the radiance of many kinds of gems and jewels.

Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of the chief queen named Bandhumatī, of King Bandhumanta—who possessed many kinsmen—in the city of Bandhumatī. At the end of ten months, in Khema...
In the Deer Park, he emerged from his mother’s side like the full moon adorned with a streak of dark clouds.

On the day of his naming, the fortune-tellers and his kinsmen gave him the name “Vipassī,” because they saw him clearly—whether by day or by night—as if there were no intervening darkness caused by the womb, or as if he were seeing with open eyes. [Thinking: “Having discerned...”
“They see by discerning,” they say, thus he is called Vipassī. He lived as a householder for eight thousand years.
He had three palaces named Nanda, Sunanda, and Sirimā.
He had one hundred and twenty thousand women, headed by Queen Sudassanā. Also known as “Sutanū.”

He is called Sudassana. After the passing of eight thousand years, having seen the four signs and seeing that a son named Samavaṭṭakkhandha had been born to Queen Sutanū, he went forth on the Great Renunciation in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses and became a monk.
Eighty-four hundred thousand men followed him into the religious life. Surrounded by them, that Great Man—
Having practiced the course of ascetic striving for eight months, and having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice offered by Visākhā,
the daughter of the merchant Sudassana, he spent the day in meditation in the Sāla grove adorned with flowers; then,
taking eight handfuls of grass given by a barley-gatherer named Sujāta, he beheld the Pāṭalibodhi tree beautifully arrayed.
He approached it from the direction of the southern quarter.
On that day, the trunk of that *pāṭali* tree became perfectly round and rose up fifty *ratana*s;
its branches were fifty *ratana*s [in extent], and in height it reached one hundred *ratana*s. On that very day, that *pāṭali* [tree] was covered with buds bound together like ear-rings.
It became completely covered from the roots upward with flowers of supreme fragrance. A divine scent wafted forth;
not only did this [tree] alone bloom at that time, but all the *pāṭali* trees throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassī cakkavāḷa*) were in full bloom.
Not only the *pāṭali* trees, but all the trees, thickets, and creepers throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system as well—
They scattered flowers. Even the great ocean became covered with five-colored lotuses—blue, red, and white water-lilies—and its waters became cool and sweet.
And the entire interior of the ten-thousandfold world-system was filled with rows of banners.
Here and there, the surface of the earth was strewn with garlands and clusters, adorned with various fragrant flowers, and shrouded in the darkness of incense powder.
He approached that spot, spread out a grass mat fifty-three cubits wide, and sat down, resolving upon energy endowed with four factors, making this vow:
"I shall not rise from here until I have become a Buddha.
Having sat thus, he shattered Māra and his host, and by following the sequence of the paths, he attained the four knowledges of the path.
Immediately following the knowledge of the Path, having placed within the palm of his hand all the Buddha-qualities— the four knowledges of fruition, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā),
the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth, the knowledge that delimits the five destinations, the four kinds of intrepidity, and the six unique knowledges—
he sat upon the seat of enlightenment with his purpose fully accomplished.
“Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [as above] ...he has attained the destruction of craving.
Just as the course of a blazing fire struck by an iron bar, when it has been gradually extinguished, is no longer known;
so too is the destiny of one who has reached the end of existence.
“Thus for those who are rightly liberated, who have crossed the flood of the bond of sensual desire,
there is no destination to point out, for they have attained unshakable bliss.
Having thus uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), and having spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, he accepted the Brahmā’s entreaty.

Having observed the excellence of the supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*) of his own half-brother Prince Khaṇḍa and of Tissa, the son of the royal chaplain, he traveled through the air, descended at Khema Migadāya, and had both of them summoned by the park keeper.
In the midst of their retinues, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). At that time, for immeasurable beings...
There was a penetration of the Dhamma by the deities. Therefore it is said:
"And after Phussa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds, named Vipassī, appeared in the world, possessed of vision."
“Having shattered all ignorance, he attained supreme enlightenment;
to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, he departed for the city of Bandhumatī.
Having set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, the Leader awakened both.”
"He cannot be described by calculation; there was the first realization.
In this context, "having split open" means having broken through; the meaning is "having broken through the darkness of ignorance.
There is also the reading "having turned the wheel in the monastery," where "in the monastery" means in the Khema Deer Park. "He awakened both" refers to his own younger brother.
He awakened both Khaṇḍa, the prince, and Tissa, the son of the chaplain.
"Incalculable" means that there is no limit to the number [of those who attained realization] by way of the devas' clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*).

Then, on another occasion, he caused eighty-four thousand bhikkhus, including Khaṇḍa, the prince, and Tissa, the son of the chaplain, who had followed him into the homeless life, to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. That was the second *abhisamaya*. Thus it is said:
“Furthermore, Amitāyasa proclaimed the Truth there;
there was a second realization for eighty-four thousand [beings].
In that context, “there” means at Khema Migadāya. “Eighty-four thousand [beings] went forth following the Fully Enlightened One.”
In this context, these eighty-four thousand men were indeed the attendants of Prince Vipassi.
Having come to the Prince's quarters early in the morning and not seeing the Prince, they went to eat their breakfast;
having finished their meal, they asked, "Where is the Prince? and hearing from there that he had gone to the park grounds, [they went] right there.

Thinking, "We shall see him," they set out; but seeing his charioteer returning and hearing that "the prince has gone forth," they immediately cast off all their ornaments at the very spot where they had heard the news, had saffron robes brought from the market, shaved off their hair and beards, and went forth.
Having gone forth, they went and surrounded the Great Being.
Then the Bodhisatta Vipassī thought: “While practicing the life of striving, I dwell crowded with company;
yet it is not fitting that these householders who formerly surrounded me should do so now as well—what is the use of this group?
Becoming weary of the socializing of the crowd, he thought, “I shall go this very day,” and further reflected: “Today...”
"It is not the right time; if I were to go today, everyone would find out. I shall go tomorrow," he thought.
On that very day, in a village similar to Uruvelā, the inhabitants invited the Great Man together with his retinue for the following day's meal.
They [prepared food] for those eighty-four thousand and for the Great Man.

They prepared milk-rice alone. Then, on the following day, the full moon of Visākha, the Great Man Vipassī, having performed his meal duties in that village together with those who had gone forth, returned to his dwelling place.
There, those who had gone forth, having shown their service to the Great Man, each entered their own night-quarters and day-quarters.
The Bodhisatta, too, having entered the leaf-hut and sat down, thought: "This is the time to depart.
Having departed and closed the door of the leaf-hut, he set out toward the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
It is said that those renunciants, having gone to attend upon the Bodhisatta in the evening, sat surrounding the leaf-hut, saying: "It has become very late; let us wait."
Having spoken thus, they opened the door of the leaf-hut; yet, not seeing him, they did not pursue him, asking, "Where has the Great Man gone?
Thinking, "The Great Man must be weary of living in a group and wishes to dwell alone;
we shall see him only when he has become a Buddha," they set out on a journey toward the interior of Jambudīpa. Then they heard: "It is said that Vipassī, having attained Buddhahood..."
Having heard, "The Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion," they all gradually went forth and assembled at the Khema Deer Park in the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Then the Blessed One taught them the Dhamma; at that time, there was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand bhikkhus.
That was the third realization. Thus it is said:
“Eighty-four thousand [beings] went forth following the Fully Enlightened One;
to them, having reached the monastery grove, the Visionary One taught the Dhamma.
Having heard it from him as he spoke in every aspect, they sat down close by.”
"Having reached the excellent Dhamma, the third realization occurred.

In this context, regarding the phrase "eighty-four thousand [monks] followed the Sambuddha," it should be understood that the word *sambuddha* is used in the accusative case (*anupabbajunti*) due to its connection with the prefix *anu*.
The meaning is: "They went forth after the Sambuddha. [This concludes the section on] the characteristics.
This should be understood from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). Regarding the reading “*ārāmapattānan*” there, it means “of those who have reached the monastery.
“*Bhāsato*” means “speaking. “*Upanisādino*” means “having gone and relying upon [him], they gave the gift of Dhamma”; this is the meaning.
“*Te pi*” refers to those eighty-four thousand who had gone forth and served as attendants to Vipassī. “*Gantvā*” means “having understood his Dhamma. Thus, for them, this was the third...

There was a realization. Seated in the midst of six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus who had gone forth following the Fully Enlightened One Vipassī and his two chief disciples at the Khema Deer Park, the Blessed One Vipassī said:
"Patience is the highest austerity; the Buddhas declare that nibbāna is supreme."
For one who harms others is not a renunciant, nor is one who oppresses others a śramaṇa.
“To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome,
and to purify one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”
“Refraining from censuring others, refraining from harming others, restraint according to the Pātimokkha,
moderation in food, secluded lodgings,
and devotion to the higher mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”
"I shall recite this Pātimokkha. It should be understood that these, moreover, are the verses for the recitation of the Pātimokkha common to all Buddhas.
That was the first assembly. Then, after seeing the Twin Miracle, there was a second assembly of one hundred thousand monks who had gone forth. But when Vessabhū’s three uterine brothers—
Having pacified the border regions and received permission to attend upon the Blessed One, they led him to their own city and served him;
having heard his Dhamma, they went forth into homelessness.
Seated in the midst of those eight million people, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha in the Khema Migadāya; that was the third great assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies of the Great Seer Vipassī:
of those whose taints were destroyed, who were stainless, whose minds were at peace, and who were steadfast.
The first gathering consisted of six million eight hundred thousand.”
There was a second assembly of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
There was a third assembly of eighty thousand bhikkhus;
there, in the midst of the multitude of bhikkhus, the Fully Enlightened One shone forth.
In that context, “one hundred and sixty-eight thousand” means one hundred thousand plus sixty-eight thousand bhikkhus.
“Therein” (tattha) means there in the Khema Deer Park. “In the midst of the assembly of bhikkhus” (bhikkhugaṇamajjhe) means in the middle of the assembly of bhikkhus.
There is also a reading, “tassa bhikkhugaṇamajjhe,” which means in the midst of that assembly of bhikkhus.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become a Naga king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and great majesty,

and surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of Nagas, had a pavilion constructed— made of the seven precious gems, resembling the orb of the moon, and the very essence of all that is beautiful to behold— in order to pay honor to the One of Ten Powers,
whose virtue was peerless and whose heart was cooled by compassion; and there...

Having had him seated and having given a great almsgiving for seven days befitting his celestial wealth, he presented to the Blessed One a costly golden throne inlaid with the seven gems, resplendent with the radiance streaming from various jewels. At the conclusion of the expression of appreciation for that throne, [the Buddha] prophesied:
"In this very ninety-first aeon from now, he shall become a Buddha. Thus it was said:
“At that time, I was a nāga king of great psychic power,
named Atula by name, possessed of merit and radiance.
Surrounded then by many tens of millions of nāgas,”
Accompanied by celestial musical instruments, I approached the Foremost One in the World.
Having drawn near to the Fully Enlightened Vipassī, the Leader of the World—
who was adorned with all ornaments and bedecked with jewels, pearls, and precious gems—
Having invited the King of Dharma, I offered him a golden throne.
Seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, that Buddha also made this prediction concerning me:
"In the ninety-first aeon, this person shall become a Buddha."
“Having departed from the delightful city called Kapila,
the Tathāgata exerted himself in striving and performed difficult austerities. Then,
sitting at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, the Tathāgata— ”
Taking the milk-rice there, he will go to the Nerañjarā River.
On the bank of the Nerañjarā, that Conqueror will eat the milk-rice;
by the excellent path prepared for him, he will go to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
“Then, having circumambulated it clockwise, the unsurpassed one of great renown will awaken to perfect enlightenment at the foot of the Assattha tree.
His mother, who gives birth to him, shall be named Māyā.”
His father will be named Suddhodana, and he will be Gotama.
Free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated,
Kolita and Upatissa shall be his chief disciples.
“Ānanda shall be my attendant; he will serve me, the Conqueror.
