Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples—free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and composed.”
“The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Assattha...
[as above] ...Having heard his words, my heart became even more serene;
I resolved upon a further practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.”
In this context, "possessing merit" (*puññavā*) means one who has accumulated a store of merit.

"Bearer of radiance" (*jutindhara*) means endowed with light. "Of many tens of millions of *nāgas*" (*nekānaṃ nāgakoṭīnaṃ*): the genitive case here should be understood in the sense of the instrumental; thus, it means "by many tens of millions of *nāgas*.

"Having surrounded" (*parivāretvāna*) means having surrounded the Blessed One. "I" (*ahaṃ*) refers to himself. "Striking" (*vajjanto*) means shouting and beating. "Inlaid with jewels, pearls, and gems" (*maṇimuttaratanakhacitaṃ*).
The meaning is that it was inlaid with various jewels such as gems and pearls.
"Adorned with all ornaments" means decorated with all ornaments made of precious materials, such as the figures of beasts and so forth. "A golden seat" means a seat made of gold.
"Adāsaham" means "I gave."
Now, for that Blessed One Vipassī, the city was named Bandhumatī;
his father was King Bandhumā, and his mother was Bandhumatī; Khaṇḍa and Tissa were the two chief disciples; Asoka was the attendant;
Candā and Candamittā were the two chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree was the Pāṭali tree; and his body was eighty cubits in height.
The radiance of his body remained pervasive for seven *yojanas* at all times; his lifespan was eighty thousand years.
His chief queen was named Sutanu, and his son was named Samavaṭṭakkhandha. He went forth in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. Thus it is said:
“The city was named Bandhumatī, and the noble king was named Bandhuma;”
The mother of the Great Seer Vipassī was named Bandhumatī.
Khaṇḍa and Tissa were his chief disciples,
and the attendant of the Great Seer Vipassī was named Asoka.
“Candā and Candamittā were his two chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Pāṭali.
Vipassī, the Leader of the World, was eighty cubits in height.”
His radiance streamed forth for seven yojanas on all sides.
For eighty thousand years was the lifespan of that Buddha;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
“He has liberated many gods and humans from their bonds;
he has pointed out the path and the non-path to the rest of the worldlings.
Having shown the light and taught the deathless state,”
Having blazed like a mass of fire, he has gone out together with his disciples.
“The excellence of psychic power, the excellence of merit, and the blossoming of the marks—all that has vanished;
are not all conditioned things indeed empty?”
In this context, "bound" means that he released gods and humans from the fetters such as the fetter of sensual lust; the meaning is that he liberated them.

"And he pointed out the path and the non-path" means that he pointed it out to the remaining worldlings, saying: "This is the path for the attainment of the Deathless—the Middle Way free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism; bodily mortification and the like are not the path. "Light..."
"Having shown" means having displayed the light of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) and the light of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).

"And the characteristic is blossomed" means that the Blessed One’s body was fully opened and adorned by the characteristics of the mind (*citta-lakkhaṇa*), and so forth. The rest of the verses is entirely plain in meaning.
The commentary on the *Vipassī-buddhavaṃsa* is finished.
The nineteenth Buddha-chronicle is finished.
22. The Exposition of the Buddha-chronicle of Sikhi:
After the disappearance of Vipassi, and subsequently during the fifty-nine eons that followed in that kappa, [the lineage continued].
Buddhas did not arise in the world; the world was devoid of the light of a Buddha.
It became a realm ruled by the single sovereignty of the defilements and the Māra who is a son of a deva, a place where thorns had been removed.

However, thirty-one aeons ago, two Perfectly Enlightened Ones named Sikhī and Vessabhū arose in the world, like a smokeless flame fed with abundant ghee and composed of smooth, dry, heartwood timber. In that regard:
But the Blessed One Sikhī, having fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven;

then, passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Pabhāvati—whose radiance was as beautiful as a reflection of red gold and who was the chief consort of King Aruṇavata, a monarch possessed of supreme virtues—in the city of Kusalakaraṇavatī.
After spending ten months [there], he [was born] in the Nisabha garden.
He emerged from his mother’s womb. When the fortune-tellers were giving him a name, they named him “Sikhī” because his crest was as prominent as a flame on a turban.
He lived as a householder for seventy thousand years.
He had three palaces named Sucandaka, Sirigiri, and Yasavasa. Twenty-four thousand women, headed by Queen Sabbakāmādevī, attended upon him.

Thus, having seen the four signs, when a son named Atula—equal to whom none could compare—was born to Queen Sabbakāmādevī, he mounted the back of an elephant in an elephant-vehicle and went forth on the Great Renunciation; he then ordained.
Seven hundred thousand men followed him into the religious life. Surrounded by them, he practiced the life of striving for eight months, and on the full moon of Visākha,
Having abandoned the company of the crowd, he partook of the honeyed milk-rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Piyadassī in the town of Sudassana.

After spending the day’s rest in a grove of young khadira trees, he took eight handfuls of *kusaka* grass given by an ascetic named Anomadassi and approached the Puṇḍarīka Bodhi tree. It is said that at that Puṇḍarīka Bodhi tree as well—
The size of the *pāṭali* tree was exactly that [of the previous one].
On that very day, it rose up having become a trunk fifty *ratana*s in girth, and its branches were likewise only fifty *ratana*s long. It was covered with divine fragrances and flowers;
not only with flowers, but also with fruits. From one side of it, there were young fruits.
On one side hung fruits of medium size, on another those not yet fully ripe, and on another those infused with divine essence, as it were;

they were delicious and endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor. And just as that [tree] was, so too throughout the ten-thousandfold world-systems, the flowering trees were adorned with flowers and the fruit-bearing trees with fruits.
So there, having spread out a grass mat twenty-four cubits wide, he sat down cross-legged, having resolved upon the fourfold energy.
Having sat thus, and having shattered the host of Māra extending thirty-six leagues, he attained full enlightenment, [saying]: "Through many births in saṃsāra...
[I have sought] the maker of the house; birth again is not for me, for I have found the end of craving."
Having uttered a solemn utterance (*udāna*) and spent seven days in the very vicinity of the Bodhi tree, and having accepted the Brahmā’s request,
he perceived the excellence of the spiritual potential (*upanissaya-sampatti*) of the seven hundred thousand bhikkhus who had gone forth with him;
then, traveling by way of the path of the gods, he arrived at the Migājina Garden near the royal capital of Aruṇavatī, which was surrounded by various protective walls.

Having descended, surrounded by those hosts of sages, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion in their midst. At that time, there was the first realization for one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
Therefore it is said:
"After Vipassi, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds..."
The Conqueror was named Sikhī, peerless and without equal.
Having crushed the army of Māra, he attained supreme enlightenment;
out of compassion for living beings, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
“When the Conqueror, the Bull among Men, the Śikhin, was setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
there was the first realization for one hundred thousand times ten million [beings].
Furthermore, in the vicinity of the capital city of Aruṇavatī, for the prince Abhibhū and the prince Sambhava...
Having taught the Dhamma to these two along with their retinues, he caused ninety thousand koṭis to drink the nectar of the Dhamma.
This was the second great realization (abhisamaya). Therefore it is said:
"Furthermore, while the Best of the Assembly, the Supreme among Men, was teaching the Dhamma..."
“The second great realization occurred for nine thousand koṭis.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One, at the gate of the city of Sūriyavatī at the foot of a campaka tree, performed the Twin Miracle in order to shatter the pride and conceit of the sectarians and to liberate all beings from their bonds,
and taught the Dhamma, then the third [great realization occurred] for eighty thousand koṭis.
There was a third realization (abhisamaya). Therefore it was said:
“While displaying the Twin Miracle to the world with its devas, there was a third realization for eighty thousand crores.”
Sitting in the midst of one hundred thousand arahants who had gone forth together with the princes Abhibhū and Sambhava, he recited the Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly.
Sitting in the midst of eighty thousand bhikkhus who had gone forth at the gathering of kinsmen in the city of Aruṇavatī, he [recited] the Pātimokkha.

The Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of seventy thousand bhikkhus who had gone forth at the time of subduing the Nāga Dhanapālaka in the city of Dhanañjaya; that was the second assembly.
That was the third assembly. Thus it is said:
“There were three assemblies of the Great Seer Sikhī—
of those whose taints were destroyed, who were stainless, whose minds were peaceful,
and who were steadfast. The first gathering consisted of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.”
There was a second assembly of eighty thousand bhikkhus;
there was a third assembly of seventy thousand bhikkhus—
unsullied like a lotus grown amidst the water.

In this context, "unsoiled like a lotus" means that just as a lotus born in water and grown in water remains unsoiled by water, so too that assembly of monks, though born in the world, remained unsoiled by worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
At that time, it is said, our Bodhisatta was a king named Arindama in the city of Paribhutta, living there without associating with anyone;
when the Teacher Sikhī arrived at the city of Paribhutta, the king, together with his retinue, went out to meet the Blessed One.
With the stream of his heart and eyes increased by serene confidence, he prostrated with his head at the pair of stainless lotus-feet of the One Possessing Ten Powers along with his retinue;
having invited the One Possessing Ten Powers, he gave a great almsgiving for seven days in accordance with his sovereignty,
family, wealth, and faith, and having caused the doors of the storehouses of cloth to be opened, [he offered] highly precious [robes] to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
He gave robes. And having given his own excellent elephant—a restrainer of enemies who was like the elephant Erāvaṇa, endowed with strength, beauty, auspicious marks, and speed;
adorned with a golden net-mesh; resplendent with a pair of chowries from a sheath of beautiful new gold with long handles; possessing vast and soft ears;

and whose face shone with the beauty of a row of moons—he made it the size of an ordinary elephant and gave him requisites as well. Then the Teacher said to him: "In the thirty-first aeon from now..."
“He will become a Buddha,” he prophesied. Therefore it was said:
“At that time I was a noble warrior named Arindama;
I satisfied with food and drink the Saṅgha headed by the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“Having given much excellent cloth, an immense ten million pieces of cloth,
and a decorated elephant-chariot, I gave them to the Sambuddha.
Having fashioned an elephant-chariot myself, I offered it as a permissible gift.”
I fulfilled my mind, which was constantly and firmly established [in this aspiration]:
“That Buddha Sikhī, the leader supreme in the world, prophesied of me:
‘In the thirty-first aeon from now, this one shall become a Buddha.’”
“The delightful city called Kapila... [we shall all] be present before him.
Having heard his words, my heart became even more serene;
I resolved upon further ascetic practices for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
In that context, "having fashioned" means having measured [the object] according to the size of that elephant.
"Suitable" (kappiya) refers to suitable goods; whatever goods are permissible for monks to accept is called "suitable goods.
"I filled my mind" means I filled my heart with the joy of giving; the meaning is that I made it capable of producing gladness within me.
"Constantly and firmly established" means that his mind was firmly established in the practice of giving, thinking, "I shall give gifts at all times.
Furthermore, the city of that Blessed One was named Aruṇavatī;
his father was King Aruṇavā, his mother was named Pabhāvatī, his two chief disciples were Abhibhū and Sambhava, and his attendant was named Khemaṅkara. Sakhilā...
Madumā and Madusārā were his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the Puṇḍarīka tree; his body was seventy cubits in height.
The radiance of his body remained pervading three *yojanas* at all times. His lifespan was seventy thousand years;
Sabbakāmā was his chief queen; his son was named Atula; he went forth on an elephant vehicle. Thus it is said:
“The city was named Aruṇavatī, and the kṣatriya father was named Aruṇa;
the mother of the Great Seer Sikhī was named Pabhāvatī.
Abhibhū and Sambhava were his two chief disciples.”
The attendant of the Great Seer Sikhī was named Khemaṅkara.
Sakhilā and Padumā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Puṇḍarīka.
“Sirivaḍḍha and Nanda were his chief attendants;
Cittā and Suguttā were his chief female attendants.
In height, that Buddha rose to seven cubits.”
Resembling a priceless golden ornament, he possessed the thirty-two excellent marks.
From his body, too, there was a fathom-wide radiance that issued forth continuously day and night in every direction for three yojanas.
“The lifespan of that Great Sage was seventy thousand years;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
Having caused a rain of Dhamma to fall, he moistened the world together with its devas.”
Having brought about the winter season, he, together with his disciples, has attained Nibbāna:
"That which was endowed with perfect minor marks and the thirty-two supreme characteristics—all that has vanished;
are not all conditioned things indeed empty?"
In this context, *puṇḍarīka* means the white mango tree (*setambara*). "Radiating for three leagues" means that its radiance issues forth for three *yojanas*.
*Dhammamegha* means the rain of the Dhamma; it is the Buddha-cloud that rains down the Dhamma. "Having moistened" means having moistened with the water of the Dhamma-discourse;
the meaning is "having sprinkled. *Sadevake* refers to beings together with the devas. *Khemanta* means the state of security, which is Nibbāna.

"Endowed with the secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*)" means that the Blessed One’s body was endowed with the eighty secondary characteristics, such as copper-colored nails, a prominent nose, and rounded fingers; the meaning is that it was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*).
It is said that the Perfectly Enlightened One, Sikhi, attained final *parinibbāna* in the horse-park at the city of Sīlavatī.
“Like a flame blazing with ascetic heat in the world, like a lion roaring at the arrival of the clouds;
having abandoned the great fuel of existence, that Sugata has gone to peace like a flame.
It is said that the relics of the Blessed One Sikhī remained as a single solid mass and did not scatter. All those dwelling in Jambudīpa...
Furthermore, the people constructed a stupa three *yojanas* in height, made of the seven precious gems, with a beauty like that of the Snowy Mountain (Himagiri).
The rest here is evident from the verses themselves.
The commentary on the lineage of Buddha Sikhī is concluded.
The twentieth lineage of Buddhas is finished.
23. The Exposition of the Lineage of Buddha Vessabhū:
After the Perfectly Enlightened One Sikhi had passed away and his dispensation had vanished, there were [beings] with a lifespan of seventy thousand years.
Human beings gradually declined until their lifespan was ten years. Increasing again, they reached an immeasurable lifespan, and then declining once more, their lifespan became sixty thousand years.

At that time, the Teacher named Vessabhū—the self-enlightened one who has conquered the mind and overcomes the entire world—appeared in the world. Having fulfilled the perfections, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Then, passing away from there, he took rebirth in the city of Anoma in the womb of Yasavatī, the virtuous chief queen of King Suppatīta.
At the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb in the incomparable park.
Even as he was being born, he roared a bull-like cry (vasabhanāda), delighting the people; therefore, because of that cause of the bull-like roar—
On the day of his naming, they gave him the name Vessabhū. He lived as a householder for six thousand years.
He possessed three palaces named Ruci, Suruci, and Rativaḍḍhana.
Thirty thousand women, headed by Queen Sucittā, attended upon him.
Thus, having seen the four signs, and after Prince Suppabuddha was born to Queen Sucittā, he went to see the pleasure grove in a golden palanquin;
there, taking the yellow robes of the gods, he went forth.
Then thirty-seven thousand followed him into the homeless life. Surrounded by them, he practiced ascetic exertion for six months.
Having wandered and partaken of the honeyed milk-rice offered by Sirivaḍḍhanā,
whose body was visible in the town of Sucitta on the full moon day of the month of Visākha, and having spent the day’s rest in the Sāla grove,
at the time of evening he took the eight handfuls of grass given by the Nāga king Narinda and approached the Sāla Bodhi tree from the right. Of that Sāla tree as well—
That very [tree] became the standard measure for the *pāṭali* tree. Its splendor of flowers and fruits should be understood in the same way.
Having approached the foot of that *sāla* tree and spread out a grass mat forty cubits wide, he sat cross-legged;
then, having removed the hindrances and the intoxication of all sensual desires, he attained unobstructed knowledge—[reciting]: “Through many births in saṃsāra….”

Having uttered this inspired utterance, “He has attained the destruction of craving,” and having spent seven times seven days right there, he perceived the excellence of the spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) of his younger brothers, Prince Soṇa and Prince Uttara.
Traveling by way of the gods, he descended into the Aruṇa Garden near the city of Anoma; there, through the park keeper, he had the princes summoned and [addressed] them.
In the midst of his retinue, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. At that time, there was the first realization for eighty thousand crores.
Again, while wandering on a tour of the countryside and teaching the Dhamma here and there, there was a realization of the Dhamma for seventy thousand crores;
that was the second realization. It was in the city of Anoma itself that he shattered the net of views.

Causing the banner of pride of the heretics to fall, shattering their intoxication with conceit, and raising high the banner of the Dhamma, he performed the Twin Miracle before an assembly of humans ninety *yojanas* wide and an immeasurable assembly of devas;
having inspired confidence in gods and men, he satisfied sixty *koṭis* with the nectar of the Dhamma. That was the third realization (*abhisamaya*). Thus it is said:
“In that very same Maṇḍakappa, peerless and without rival,
the Leader named Vessabhū appeared in the world.
At that time, the fire of passion was indeed ablaze, yet he had conquered the cravings.”
Like a nāga that has severed its bonds, he attained supreme enlightenment.
While Vessabhū, the Leader of the World, was setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
there occurred the first realization for eighty thousand koṭis.
“When the World-Chief, the Bull among Men, had departed on his wandering tour through the kingdom,
there occurred a second realization for seventy thousand times ten million beings.
Dispelling great views, he performed a miracle.”
“Humans and gods from the ten thousandfold world-system, including the devas, have assembled.
Having seen this great marvel, this wonder that makes the hair stand on end,
sixty million devas and humans have awakened.”
In that context, "blazing" means this entire triple world is set ablaze. "By the fire of lust" means by passion (*rāga*).
"The conquered realm of cravings" means the kingdom of cravings, the sphere of their sovereign power; having understood it thus is the meaning.

"Like an elephant, having severed its bonds" means that, like a tusker who has cut through the bonds of withered creepers, he attained and reached full enlightenment (*sambodhi*). "The ten-thousandfold [world]"...
In the assembly of ten thousand. "Sadevake" means in the world together with its devas. "Bujjhare" means they awakened.

Furthermore, when the two chief disciples, Soṇa and Uttara, had gone forth and gathered together, he recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of eighty thousand arahants on the full moon day of the month of Māgha; that was the first great assembly. But when...

At the time when the thirty-seven thousand monks who had gone forth together with Vessabhu—the Conqueror of All Worlds—had departed from the community, they heard of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma by the Perfectly Enlightened One Vessabhu;
having arrived at the city named Soreyya, they saw the Blessed One. After the Blessed One had taught them the Dhamma,
Having ordained them all through the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula, he recited the *Pātimokkha* before an assembly endowed with the four factors;
that was the second great assembly.
Then, when the prince named Upasanta ruled in the city of Nārivāhana, out of compassion for him—

The Blessed One went there; he too, having heard of the Blessed One’s arrival, went out to meet him with his retinue, invited him, and after giving a great almsgiving, listened to the Dhamma. With a heart full of faith, he went forth.
Sixty thousand men followed him in going forth. Together with them, he attained arahantship. Surrounded by them, Vessabhū...
The Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Therefore it is said:
“There were three assemblies of the Great Seer Vessabhu—of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless, whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.”
“The first assembly consisted of eighty thousand bhikkhus;
the second assembly consisted of seventy thousand bhikkhus;
the third assembly consisted of sixty thousand bhikkhus.”
“Of the heart-born sons of the Great Seer, who have transcended the fear of old age and the like.

At that time, our Bodhisatta, having been King Sudassana—of most lovely appearance—in the city of Sarabhavatī, heard the Dhamma from Vessabhu, the Leader of the World, when he arrived at the city of Sarabha; with a heart full of faith, [he made a gesture] radiant with the joining of his ten fingers...
Placing his palms together in salutation at his head like a cluster of stainless, unblemished lotuses born in water, he gave a great alms-offering including robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha;
right there, he constructed a fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) for the Blessed One’s residence, and having surrounded it, he had a thousand monasteries built.
Having renounced all his wealth for the sake of the Blessed One’s dispensation, [he dedicated it] to him.

Having gone forth in the presence [of the Buddha], he dwelt endowed with virtuous conduct, devoted to the thirteen ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), delighted in seeking the requisites for enlightenment, and rejoiced in the teaching of the Buddha.
The Blessed One also prophesied concerning him: "In a future time, after thirty-one aeons from now, this one shall become a Buddha named Gotama. Therefore it was said:
“At that time, I was a kshatriya named Sudassana;
having invited the Great Hero and given a most costly gift of food,
drink, and clothing, I worshipped the Conqueror together with his Saṅgha.”
“Having heard the sublime Dhamma of that peerless Buddha, who had set in motion the supreme Wheel, I took delight in going forth.
Having bestowed a great gift, untiringly throughout the day and night,”
I went forth in the presence of the Victor, having gone forth endowed with virtue.
Endowed with conduct and virtue, established in the observance of duties and morality,
seeking omniscience, I delight in the teaching of the Victor.
“Having attained the rapture of faith, I pay homage to the Buddha, the Teacher;
rapture arises within me for the very sake of enlightenment.
Knowing that my mind was not turning back, the Perfectly Awakened One said this:”
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, this one will become a Buddha.
“There was a delightful city called Kapila... [and so on] ...we shall stand in his presence.
Having heard his words, my heart became even more serene.
“I resolved upon a further vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
Therein, “the wheel was turned” means the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion. “The sublime Dhamma” means the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma).
“Knowing renunciation to be endowed with virtue” means knowing that one who has gone forth [possesses] virtue. “Concentrated in the duties and moral conduct” refers to the duties...
"And concentrated in the virtues" means being concentrated in fulfilling each and every one of them. "I delighted" (*ramāmi*) means I took pleasure.
"Approaching with faith and joy" means having approached both faith and joy. "I paid homage" (*vandāmi*) means I prostrated; here the present tense should be understood as referring to the past.
"To the Teacher" (*sattharam*) means to the Teacher. "With a mind that does not turn back" means with a mind that does not falter.
That Blessed One had a city named Anoma. His father was the kṣatriya Suppatīta, his mother was named Yasavatī,
his two chief disciples were Soṇa and Uttara, his attendant was named Upasanta,
his two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Samālā, his Bodhi tree was the Sāla tree, and his body was sixty cubits in height.
His lifespan was sixty thousand years; his wife was named Sucittā, and his son was named Suppabuddha.
He went forth in a golden palanquin. Therefore it is said:
“The city was named Anoma, and the kshatriya was named Suppatīta;”
The mother of the great seer Vessabhu was named Yasavatī.
Soṇa and Uttara were his chief disciples,
and the attendant of the great seer Vessabhu was named Upasanta.
“Rāmā and Samālā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Mahāsāla.
Sotthika and Ramma were his chief attendants.”
Gotamī was indeed glorious, and they were her chief attendants.
Sixty ratanas tall, resembling a sacrificial pillar made of gold,
rays of light issued from his body like a fire upon a mountain at night.
“The lifespan of that Great Seer was sixty thousand years;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
Having made the Dhamma widespread and having distinguished it for the great multitude,”
Having set aside the ship of the Dhamma, he has attained Nibbāna along with his disciples.
"The one worthy of being seen by all people—his dwelling, his modes of conduct, everything has vanished.
Are not all conditioned phenomena indeed empty?"
In this context, "resembling a golden sacrificial post" (*hemayūpasamūpamo*) means similar to a pillar of gold. "Emanates" (*niccharati*) means it flows out here and there.
"Ray" (*raṃsi*) means a mass of light. "Like a fire on a mountain at night" (*rattiṃ va pabbate sikhī*) means like a flame on the summit of a mountain at night;

the meaning is that his body is illuminated by rays of light. "Having analyzed" (*vibhajitvā*) means having made a distinction, according to the categories of "concisely stated" (*ugghaṭita*) and so forth.
"And by way of stream-enterers and so forth" is the meaning. "The ship of the Dhamma" means the ship of the Dhamma known as the Eightfold Path;
the meaning is that it was established for the purpose of crossing over the four floods. "Worthy of being seen" means it is beautiful to behold. "All people" means all persons;

the meaning is that the Perfectly Enlightened One together with the community of disciples. "Vihāra" means a dwelling; in every instance, the accusative case should be understood as used in the sense of the nominative.
It is said that the Blessed One Vessabhū attained final Nibbāna at the Khema Deer Park in the city of Usabhavatī. His relics, however, were scattered.
“In the most excellent city of Usabhavatī, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the bull among Conquerors, indeed passed away without remainder in the delightful grove monastery,” so it is said.
The remainder is evident throughout all the verses.
The commentary on the lineage of Buddha Vessabhū is finished.
The twenty-first lineage of Buddhas is completed.
24. The Commentary on the Lineage of Buddha Kakusandha:
When the Self-Existent Vessabhū had attained final Nibbāna and that eon had passed away, for twenty-nine subsequent eons no Conquerors—the suns of the world—arose.
However, in this present Fortunate Eon (Bhaddakappa), four Buddhas were born.
Which four? Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Buddha. Furthermore, the Blessed One Metteyya will arise.
Thus, this eon has been praised by the Blessed One as a "Fortunate Eon" (Bhaddakappa) because it is adorned by the arising of five Buddhas.
In that regard, the Blessed One named Kakusandha, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramī), was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and from there—
Having descended, he took rebirth in the city of Khemavatī in the womb of Visākhā, the chief queen of Aggidatta, the brahmin chaplain who instructed King Khemaṅkara in matters of welfare and Dhamma.
For when kṣatriyas honor, revere, respect, and worship brahmins, it is then that Bodhisattvas [take rebirth].
They are reborn in brahmin families.
But when brahmins honor, respect, esteem, and worship the khattiyas, then they arise in khattiya families.
It is said that at that time the brahmins were honored and respected by the khattiyas; therefore, Saccasandha...

The Bodhisatta Kakusandha was born, making the ten-thousandfold world-system resound and tremble, into an untroubled brahmin family that was agitated by the arising of worldly prosperity. The miracles described below occurred.
Then, at the end of ten months, in the Khemavati garden, he emerged from his mother’s womb like a flame from a golden creeper.
He went forth. He lived as a householder for four thousand years.
It is said that he had three palaces named Kāmakāma, Vaṇṇakāma, and Suddhi. Thirty thousand women, headed by the brahmin lady Rociṇī, attended upon him.
Having seen the four omens, and when the son of the brahmin lady Rociṇī named Anuttara had been born, he [renounced].
Having gone forth on the Great Renunciation in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses yoked with trappings, he went forth. Forty thousand followed him into the religious life.
Surrounded by them, he practiced the life of striving for eight months;
then, on the full moon of Visākha, having partaken of the honey-milk-rice offered by the daughter of the brahmin Vajirindha in the village of Sucirindhana, he [attained enlightenment].
Having spent the day in meditation in the Khadiravana forest, at the time of evening,
he accepted eight handfuls of grass brought by a barley-gatherer named Subhadda; approaching the Sirīsa Bodhi tree— which was the same height as the Pāṭali tree and wafting a divine fragrance—
he spread out a grass mat thirty-four cubits wide and sat down cross-legged.
Having attained full enlightenment, he uttered this inspired utterance: "Through many births in saṃsāra... [I have wandered]... now I have reached the destruction of craving.

After spending seven weeks there, seeing that the forty thousand bhikkhus who had gone forth with him were capable of penetrating the Truth, he went in a single day to Isipatana, which was situated near the city of Makila.
Having entered the Deer Park at Isipatana and standing in their midst, the Blessed One set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
At that time, there was the first great realization of the Dhamma for forty thousand crores.
Then, at the gate of the city of Kaṇṇakujja, at the foot of the Mahāsāla tree, after performing the Twin Miracle, [he brought about the realization] of thirty thousand crores.
He gave rise to the Dhamma-eye; that was the second clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

Then, not far from the city of Khemavatī, at a certain shrine for the gods, a *yakkha* named Naradeva—who had been a beloved king in a previous life—appeared in a visible human body in the middle of the wilderness, [standing] by a pool of water cooled and most sweet with cool waters, adorned with lotuses, water-lilies, and blue lilies.
Standing near the lake known as Sabbajanasaubhīrama, he would lure beings with lotuses, water lilies, white lotuses, and other flowers, and then devour them.
When that path was blocked and devoid of human traffic, he would enter the great wilderness and devour the beings who arrived there.
That route became world-renowned as the Mahākantāra-magga (the Great Wilderness Road). [At] Ubhatokantāra-dvāra (the Gate of the Double Wilderness).
It is said that a great multitude of people had gathered and stood waiting to cross the wilderness.

Then, on one day at dawn, the Teacher Kakusandha, whose bonds to existence were severed, emerged from the attainment of great compassion and, surveying the world, saw within the net of his knowledge that highly influential human deity and that assembly of people. Having seen them, he—
Then, traveling through the expanse of the sky while that multitude of people looked on, the Blessed One performed many kinds of miracles;
descending into the abode of that *naradeva-yakkha*, he sat down upon his auspicious couch.
Then that *yakkha*, who feeds on human flesh, beheld him emitting six-colored rays of light, as if surrounded by a rainbow.
Seeing the Maker of Day, the Sage who is like a sun to the world, approaching through the path of the wind, he thought with a heart full of faith,
"The One of Ten Powers comes here out of compassion for me. Accompanied by his retinue of yakkhas, he went to the Himavat mountain,
which was filled with many herds of wild animals and possessed various colors and fragrances, with water-born and land-born flowers of exquisite beauty and sweet scents.
Having gathered [the flowers], he worshipped the World-Leader Kakusandha—who was seated upon his own throne, free from all blemish—with garlands, perfumes, ointments, and other offerings;
then, uttering hymns of praise and keeping his hands joined in reverent salutation (añjali) at his head, he stood there paying homage.
Then, having witnessed that miracle, the people, with hearts full of faith, assembled together and surrounded the Blessed One, paying him homage.

They stood there. Then the Blessed One Kakusandha, who was without rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandha*), having inspired the humans, gods, and *yakkhas* who had honored him by showing them the connection between kamma and its fruit, and having terrified them with a discourse on hell, delivered a discourse on the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, there was the realization of the Dhamma for immeasurable beings; this was the third realization (*abhisamaya*).
There was. Therefore it was said:
"After Vessabhu, the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, named Kakusandha by name, immeasurable and unassailable."
“Having shattered all existence and reached the perfection of conduct,
he broke through like a lion its cage and attained supreme enlightenment.
While the world-leader Kakusandha was setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion,”
There was a realization of the Dhamma for forty thousand koṭis.
Performing a twin miracle in the sky, in the midst of the atmosphere,
he awakened thirty thousand koṭis of gods and humans.
“For the Yakkha Naradeva, upon the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths, his realization of the Dhamma was beyond counting.
Therein, “having uncovered” means having eradicated. “All existence” refers to all ninefold existence, which is the cause for the arising of existence.
"Kamma" means "action. "He who has reached the perfection of conduct" means he who has gone to the further shore by way of fulfilling all the perfections (*pāramīs*).
"Like a lion breaking through a cage" means that, like a lion, the elephant among sages destroyed the cage of existence (*bhava*).
For Kakusandha, whose bonds of existence were shattered, there was only a single assembly of disciples. [This occurred] in the city of Kaṇṇakujja.

At Isipatana in the Deer Park, surrounded by forty thousand arahants who had gone forth together with him, on the full moon day of the month of Māgha, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha. Therefore it was said:
“For the Blessed One Kakusandha, there was one assembly.”
“There was then a gathering of forty thousand who had destroyed the taints, who were stainless, whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast,
having reached the stage of self-mastery through the destruction of the host of enemies that are the taints.”
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having been King Khema, gave a great alms-offering of bowls and robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and he also gave all kinds of medicines such as collyrium.
Having given other requisites for ascetics and heard his Dhamma teaching, with a heart full of faith, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One. And he...
The Teacher prophesied: "In a future time, in this very same kappa, he will become a Buddha. Therefore it was said:
"At that time, I was a khattiya named Khema;
Having given no small gift to the Tathāgata and his sons, the Jinas."
“Having given a bowl and a robe, as well as ointment and honey-sweetened sugar-cane—
having prepared all these excellent things that I desired,
the Buddha Kakusandha, the Guide, also gave me this prophecy:”
"In this auspicious aeon, he will become a Buddha.
"There was a delightful city called Kapila... [and so on] ...we shall stand face to face with him.
"The city will be named Khemavatī, and I shall then be named Khema."
“Seeking omniscience, I went forth into his presence.
In this context, *añjana* (ointment) is well known. *Madhulaṭṭhika* means *yaṭṭhimadhuka* (the climbing madhuka).
*Imetam* means “this very one. *Patthitam* means desired. *Paṭiyādemī* means I give; the sense is that I gave. *Varam varam* means the best of the best; the sense is the most excellent.
There is also a reading, “yadetaṃ patthitaṃ,” which means: “He gave all this, whatever he desired. This [reading] is more excellent.
Now, for that Blessed One Kakusandha, who was not dull-witted, there was a city named Khema.
His father was a brahmin named Aggidatta, his mother was a brahmin woman named Visākhā, and his two chief disciples were Vidhura and Sañjīva.
His attendant was named Buddhija; his two chief female disciples were Sāmā and Campā; his Bodhi tree was the Mahāsirisarukkha; his body was forty cubits in height;
a bodily radiance issued forth for ten yojanas all around; his lifespan was forty thousand years;
his wife was the brahmin woman named Rociṇī; his son was named Uttara; and he went forth in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. Thus it is said:
The brahmin Aggidatta was the father of that Buddha;
she who was named Visākhā was the mother of the Teacher Kakusandha.
There, in the city of Khema, dwelt the great family of the Sambuddha.
The most excellent and best among men, noble-born and of great renown—
Vidhura and Sañjīva were his chief disciples,
and the attendant of the Teacher Kakusandha was named Buddhija.
Sāmā and Campā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Sirīsa.
The Great Sage rose forty ratanas in height.
A golden radiance issued forth, extending ten yojanas in every direction.
"The lifespan of that Great Seer was forty thousand years;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people."
“Having opened the shop of the Dhamma for men, women, and the world with its gods, he—
having roared a lion’s roar— is now extinguished together with his disciples.
Endowed with speech possessing the eight factors, without gaps and continuous...”
"All that has vanished; are not all conditioned things empty?
Herein, it should be understood that this verse, "He dwelt there in that secure city," was spoken for the purpose of pointing out the birth-city of Kakusandha.
"A great family" refers to the exalted family of the Blessed One’s father. "The most excellent among men."
The meaning is: "the most excellent and best among all human beings by way of birth. "Possessing noble birth" (*jātimanta*) means possessing high lineage (*abhijāti*), being of supreme lineage.
"Of great renown" (*mahāyasa*) means having a great retinue. As for what that great family of the Buddha is:
therein, the connection with the phrase "dwelling in the city of Khema" should be understood as referring to that great family.
"Ten yojanas all around" means that a golden-hued radiance, having issued from his body, constantly pervades ten yojanas in every direction;
this is the meaning. "The marketplace of the Dhamma" refers to the marketplace known as the Dhamma.
"Having set it out" means having displayed the marketplace of the Dhamma, just like a marketplace abundant with various goods for the purpose of selling merchandise; this is the meaning.

"Of men and women" refers to those men and women who are to be trained, for the sake of attaining the specific jewels of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), attainments (*samāpatti*), paths (*magga*), and fruits (*phala*).

"Roars a lion’s roar" means having roared a lion’s roar—that is, a roar of fearlessness. "Endowed with speech possessing eight factors" means the Teacher whose voice is endowed with the eight qualities.
"Unbroken" means that his virtues (*sīla*) are free from defects such as breaches; they are unbroken, untorn, and unblemished.
Alternatively, "unbroken" means without gaps, such as the pair of chief disciples and so forth. "Without interval" means constant, at all times.
"All that has vanished" means that both the Teacher and the pair of chief disciples and so forth—having all attained the state of a sage (munibhāva)—have entered a state of invisibility.
"The Buddha Kakusandha, whose kinsmen have departed, whose wisdom is unclouded, and from whom all bonds have gone away;"
"Tilokasandha was indeed true to his word; he established a dwelling for living beings in safety.
In all the remaining verses, the meaning is quite evident.
The commentary on the lineage of Buddha Kakusandha is concluded.
The twenty-second Buddha-chronicle is finished.
25. Commentary on the Buddha-chronicle of Koṇāgamana:
After the Blessed One Kakusandha had passed away and his teaching had disappeared, when the lifespan of beings was thirty thousand years...

A teacher named Koṇāgamana arose in the world; he was called Koṇāgamana because he approached for the sake of the welfare of others. Alternatively, he was called Koṇāgamana because of his golden approach (*kanakāgamana*).

In that term, by applying the substitution of *ko* for the letter *ka*, the substitution of *ṇa* for the letter *na*, and the elision of one *ka*, according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), [it refers to] gold (*kanaka*)—that is, to ornaments such as necklaces and the like.
The Blessed One during whose time there was the arrival of rain [of the Dhamma] was named Koṇāgamana.
Herein, however, it should be understood that his lifespan was treated as if it had gradually declined, yet it did not decline in that manner; rather, after increasing again, it declined.
How so? In this very eon, the Blessed One Kakusandha was born at a time when the lifespan was forty thousand years.

Furthermore, when that lifespan, having decreased until it reached the period of ten years, increased again to reach an incalculable number of years, and then decreased once more until it was established at a lifespan of thirty thousand years, it should be understood that at that time the Blessed One Koṇāgamana appeared in the world.
Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he was reborn in the Tusita heaven; and passing away from there, in the city of Sobhavatī, [he was born] as the son of Yaññadatta...

Having taken rebirth in the womb of a brahmin woman named Uttarā—who was unsurpassed among the wives of that brahmin in qualities such as beauty—he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Subhavaṇṇa Garden after the lapse of ten months.
At the moment of his birth, rain fell like a shower of gold throughout the entire Jambudīpa. Because this was the cause of his arrival [there] as gold, he was named Kanakagotta.
They gave him the name "Kanakāgama. As that name gradually evolved, it became "Koṇāgamana.
He lived as a householder for three thousand years.
He had three palaces named Tusita, Santusita, and Santuṭṭha. He had sixteen thousand women, headed by the brahmin lady Rucigattā.

Having seen the four signs, while his beloved wife, the Brahmin woman Rucigattā, was giving birth to a son named Satthavāha, he mounted the back of a noble elephant and, departing on the Great Renunciation by means of that elephant-vehicle, went forth into homelessness. Thirty thousand men followed him into the religious life.
Surrounded by them, after practicing the life of striving for six months, on the full moon day of Visākha, at the house of the Brahmin Aggisena—
Having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice given by the Brahmin maiden Aggisoṇā, and having spent the day’s rest in the Khadira forest,
at the time of evening he took eight handfuls of grass given by a barley-herder named Jaṭātinduka,
and approached from the right the Udumbara Bodhi tree, which was as large as the lotus previously described and endowed with the excellence of its fruit.
Having spread out a grass mat twenty cubits wide, having sat down cross-legged, and having shattered the host of Māra, he attained the ten powers of knowledge.
Then, after uttering this inspired exclamation: “Through many births in saṃsāra... [I have wandered on]...
until now I have found the exhaustion of craving,” and after spending seven times seven days, [he addressed] the thirty thousand bhikkhus who had gone forth together with him.
Having seen their excellence of supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*), he traveled through the path of the sky and descended at Isipatana, the Deer Park near the city of Sudassana.
Standing in their midst, he set the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*) in motion; at that time, there was the first realization (*abhisamaya*) for thirty thousand koṭis.
Again, at the gate of the city of Sundara, at the foot of the Mahāsāla tree, he performed the Twin Miracle (*yamaka-pāṭihāriya*) for twenty thousand koṭis.
He caused them to drink the nectar of the Dhamma; that was the second penetration (abhisamaya).

When the Blessed One, placing his own mother Uttara at the forefront, was teaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to the deities who had assembled from ten thousand world-systems, there occurred the third penetration for ten thousand koṭis [of beings]. Thus it is said:
After Kakusandha, there was another Perfectly Enlightened One,
the supreme among bipeds, the Conqueror named Koṇāgamana, the eldest in the world, the bull among men.
Having fulfilled the ten qualities, he crossed over the wilderness.
Having washed away all impurity, he attained supreme enlightenment.
While the Leader named Koṇāgamana was setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion,
there was the first realization for thirty thousand times ten million beings.
"And while performing miracles that crush the arguments of opponents,
there was a second realization for twenty thousand times ten million beings. Then,
having performed his transformations, the Conqueror went to the city of the gods."
The Fully Enlightened One dwelt there upon the pale-white stone slab.
Teaching the *Pakaraṇa* (Treatise) for seven days, that Sage spent the rains retreat;
it was the third occasion when ten thousand times ten million attained realization.
Therein, "having fulfilled ten qualities" means having fulfilled the ten perfections (*pāramī*). "He crossed over the wilderness" means he crossed over the wilderness of birth.
"Having washed away" means having washed it away. "All impurity" refers to the three stains, beginning with lust (*rāga*).
And while performing miracles—[the phrase] "crushing the doctrines of opponents" refers to the crushing of the doctrines of opposing disputants—at the Blessed One’s miraculous display...
"Karonto" means "doing. "Vikubbaṇaṃ" refers to the power of transformation (*vikubbaṇiddhi*);

having performed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*) at the gate of the beautiful city, he went to the city of the gods (*devapura*) and dwelt there upon the pale-white blanket stone (*paṇḍukambalasilā*). How did he dwell? By teaching the seven treatises;
that is, while dwelling there, he taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which consists of the seven treatises for the gods.
The meaning is that while the Blessed One was thus teaching the Abhidhamma there, there was a realization (abhisamaya) for ten thousand times ten million devas.
Koṇāgamana, who had arrived at the fulfillment of the utterly pure perfections, also had one assembly of disciples.
While staying in the city of Surindavatī in the Surindavatī Garden, [he taught] to Prince Bhiyyasa and Prince Uttara.

Having taught the Dhamma to both [assemblies], each with a retinue of thirty thousand, and having ordained them all through the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-pabbajjā*), he recited the Pātimokkha in their midst on the full moon day of the month of Māgha. Thus it is said:
"Of that God of Gods as well, there was one great assembly."
“Of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless, whose minds were peaceful,
and who were steadfast— of thirty thousand bhikkhus who had crossed over the floods and broken through death, there was then a gathering.”

In this context, "of the floods" (*oghānaṃ*) refers to the four floods, such as the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*). Those which exist within someone are called "floods" because they sweep one away and cause one to sink in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); for these "floods," the genitive case should be understood in the sense of the accusative.
The meaning is: "who have transcended the fourfold flood. The same principle applies here to the word "broken" (*bhijjitānaṃ*). "Of death" (*maccuyā*) means of death.
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a king named Pabbata in the city of Mithilā.

Having heard that “Koṇāgamana, to whom all living beings who have come for refuge, has arrived at the city of Mithilā,” the king, together with his retinue, went out to meet him, paid homage, invited the One of Ten Powers, and having given a great almsgiving, requested the Blessed One to reside there for the three-month rains retreat. For those three months...

Having attended upon the Teacher together with his community of disciples, he gave him costly and fine garments—such as those made of wool, Chinese silk, fine linen, silk, and cotton—as well as golden sandals and many other requisites.
The Blessed One then prophesied concerning him: "In this very auspicious eon, he shall become a Buddha. Then...
Having heard that Blessed One’s prophecy, that Great Man renounced his great kingdom and went forth into homelessness in the presence of that very Blessed One. Thus it is said:
“At that time, I was a kshatriya named Pabbata;”
Endowed with friends and ministers, possessing infinite strength and transport,
he went to see the Perfectly Enlightened One and heard the unsurpassed Dhamma.
Having invited the Saṅgha together with the Victorious One, he gave whatever gifts he desired.
“Fine cloth from Pattuṇṇa, silk from China, Koseyya silk,
and even woolen blankets, as well as golden sandals— I gave these to the Teacher’s disciples.
That Buddha too, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, made this prediction concerning me.”
“In this auspicious eon, he will become a Buddha.
“There was a delightful city called Kapila... [and so on] ...we shall stand face to face with him.
Having heard his words as well, my heart became even more serene.
I resolved upon a further vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections:
"Seeking omniscience, having given gifts to the Supreme among Men,
I abandoned my great kingdom and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Victor."
In this context, "possessing infinite power and vehicles" means that my strength is abundant and infinite, as are my vehicles, such as horses and elephants.
"For the sake of seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One" means for the purpose of beholding the Sambuddha.
"As much as desired" means having invited the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, with the four kinds of food, saying "enough, enough," and having had them covered by hand—that is the meaning.
"Of the Teacher’s disciples" means he gave it to both the Teacher and his disciples. "To the supreme among men" means to the one who is supreme among men.
"Having abandoned" means having relinquished and completely renounced.
Now, that Blessed One Koṇāgamana had a city named Sobhavatī, and [his son] was named Yaññadatta.
His father was a brahmin; his mother was a brahmin woman named Uttarā. His two chief disciples were Bhiyyasa and Uttara. His attendant was named Sotthija.
His two chief female disciples were Samuddā and Uttarā. His Bodhi tree was the Udumbara tree.
His body was thirty cubits in height, and his lifespan was thirty thousand years. His wife was Rucigattā.
The mother was named Brāhmaṇī, and the son was named Satthavāha; he set out by means of an elephant-vehicle. Therefore it is said:
“In the city named Sobhavatī, there was a kṣatriya named Sobha;
he lived in that city, a great family of the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
The brahmin Yaññadatta was the father of that Buddha;
the mother of the Teacher Koṇāgamana was named Uttarā;
Bhīyyasa and Uttara were his chief disciples.
The attendant of the Teacher Koṇāgamana was named Sotthija.
Samuddā and Uttarā were his chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is said to be the Udumbara.
“In height that Buddha rose thirty cubits;
like a conch shell at the mouth of a furnace, he was adorned with rays of light.
For as many as thirty thousand years was the lifespan of that Buddha.”
Remaining for that long, he brought many people across.
Having erected a stupa of the Dhamma, adorned with the robes of the Dhamma, and having fashioned a bouquet of Dhamma-flowers,
he has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.
“The people of that Mahāvilāsa, who proclaimed the glorious Dhamma—all of them have vanished;
are not all conditioned things indeed empty?
In this context, *ukkāmukhe* means in the forge of a smith. *Yathā kambū* means like a golden coin. Thus, by means of rays...

"Adorned" means thus embellished and decorated with rays of light. "Having erected a Dhamma-cetiya" means having established a shrine consisting of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*). "Adorned with Dhamma-cloths" means adorned with banners of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

"Having made a bouquet of Dhamma-flowers" means having fashioned a bouquet of flower garlands made of Dhamma. [This was done] for the great multitude standing in the courtyard of the *Vipassanā*-cetiya.
The meaning is that after the Teacher, together with the community of disciples, had established a Dhamma-cetiya for the purpose of veneration, he attained final Nibbāna.
"Possessed of great splendor" means having attained great miraculous power. "Of him" means of that Blessed One. "The people" refers to the community of disciples.
"The manifestation of glorious Dhamma" means that Blessed One was the illuminator of the supramundane Dhamma; and all that has vanished.
“With ease, Koṇāgamana, whose taints were destroyed, the great sage who had reached the state beyond rebirth,
dwelt in the forest solitude named Sirī, having arrived at the lineage of purity.
In all the remaining verses, [the meaning] is quite evident.
The commentary on the lineage of the Buddha Koṇāgamana is finished.
The twenty-third lineage of Buddhas is completed.
26. Commentary on the lineage of the Buddha Kassapa.
But after the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, when his dispensation had disappeared,
beings with a lifespan of thirty thousand years gradually declined until they reached a lifespan of ten years; then, increasing again, they attained an immeasurable lifespan,
only to decline once more until beings were born with a lifespan of twenty thousand years, at which time many human births occurred.
A Teacher named Kassapa arose in the world. Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he was reborn in the Tusita heaven;

passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of the Brahmin woman named Dhanavatī, who possessed great virtues, the wife of the Brahmin named Brahmadatta, in the city of Bārāṇasī. At the end of ten months, at Isipatana—
He emerged from his mother’s womb at Migadāya. By way of his clan, they gave him the name Kassapa Kumāra.
He lived as a householder for two thousand years. He had three palaces named Haṃsavā, Yasavā, and Sirinanda.
Forty-eight thousand women, headed by the brahmin lady named Sunandā, attended upon him.
Thus, having seen the four omens, when a son named Vijitasena was born to the brahmin lady Sunandā,
he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and thought, "I shall go forth on the Great Renunciation.
Immediately upon this reflection, the palace spun like a potter’s wheel, rose up into the expanse of the sky, and became a mass of most radiant light, like the moonlight of the autumn season.
Surrounded as if by a host of stars, accompanied by many hundreds of men, adorning the expanse of the sky as it were, manifesting the power of his merit as it were,
drawing the eyes and hearts of the people toward him as it were, and surpassingly beautifying the tops of the trees as he went,
he arrived and stood firmly upon the ground, making the *nigrodha* Bodhi tree his center. Then the Bodhisatta, the Great Being—
Having established himself on the earth and taking up the banner of Arahatship, Devadatta went forth.
His female dancers descended from the palace, traveled half a *gāvuta* along the road, and having established a camp with their retinue, they sat down.
Then, leaving behind those who were merely attendants to the women, everyone who had come together with them went forth.
It is said that the Great Being, having spent seven days surrounded by them practicing the life of striving,
partook on the full moon day of Visākha of the honeyed milk-rice offered by the brahmin woman named Sunandā; after spending the day in the Khadira grove,
he took eight handfuls of grass brought at evening time by a barley-herder named Soma and approached the Nigrodha Bodhi tree.
Having spread out a grass mat fifteen cubits long and wide, and having sat upon it and attained full enlightenment, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [the verse] ...he has reached the destruction of craving.
After spending seven times seven days there, he perceived the excellence of the spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) in the multitude of monks who had gone forth together with him.
Having traveled through the expanse of the sky and descended at Isipatana, the Deer Park in Bārāṇasī, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion there while surrounded by them.
At that time, there was the first realization of the Dhamma for twenty thousand koṭis. Therefore it is said:
"After Koṇāgamana came the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds."
Known by the clan-name Kassapa, he was a King of Dhamma, a maker of light.
Having cast away his family inheritance— which abounded in food, drink, and provisions—
and having given gifts to beggars, he fulfilled his heart’s desire.
Like a bull breaking through the enclosure, he attained supreme enlightenment.
When Kassapa, the Leader of the World, was setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
there was the first realization for twenty thousand koṭis.
In this context, *sañchaḍḍitaṃ* means abandoned, discarded, relinquished. *Kulamūlaṃ* means the family estate;

the meaning is that he abandoned like grass a family estate consisting of an immeasurable mass of wealth, an accumulation of many thousands of millions of dhanas, a fortune resembling the palace of the Thousand-Eyed One (Indra), which is exceedingly difficult to give away.
*Yācake* means having given to beggars. *Āḷakaṃ* means a cow-pen, just as a bull [enters] a cow-pen.
Just as one who has broken [through] reaches his desired destination according to his pleasure, so too the Great Being, having broken the bonds of the household life,
reached full enlightenment— this is the meaning. Furthermore,
while the Teacher was wandering on tour through the countryside for four months, there occurred a second realization (abhisamaya) for ten billion beings.

It was so. But when he performed the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Aśana tree at the gate of the city of Sūndara and taught the Dhamma, there occurred the third great realization (abhisamaya) for five thousand koṭis.
Again, having performed the Twin Miracle, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven—which is difficult for the enemies of the gods to overcome—there is the divine assembly hall named Sudhammā; therein...

Having sat down and placing his mother, Queen Dhanavatī, at the forefront, he taught the seven treatises of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka for the sake of favoring the deities of the ten-thousandfold world system;
thus, he caused three thousand koṭis of deities to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. Therefore it is said:
“When the Buddha was wandering on tour through the world for four months,
there occurred a second great realization for ten thousand times ten million beings.
Having performed a twin miracle, he proclaimed the element of knowledge.”
There was a third realization for five thousand times ten million [beings].
In the delightful city of the gods, Sudhammā, the Victor proclaimed the Dhamma there;
he awakened three thousand times ten million gods.
“In the Dhamma-teaching of the yakkha Naradeva, those who attained realization through these [teachings] are beyond counting. Therein, *cātumāsaṃ* means for four months;
this is indeed the reading. *Carati* means he practiced (*acari*). *Yamakaṃ vikubbanaṃ* refers to the twin-fold transformation.
"Having performed" means having performed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*). "The element of knowledge" (*ñāṇadhātu*) refers to the nature of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*);

some also call it "the element of all-knowledge" (*sabbañāṇadhātu*). "Proclaimed" means he made it known to the great multitude. "In the Sudhammā" means there is a hall named Sudhammā in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
the meaning is that he sat there. "The Dhamma" refers to the Abhidhamma.
At that time, it seems, there was a powerful and highly influential *yakkha* named Naradeva, who surpassed the king in majesty;
he was a *yakkha* of great psychic power (*mahiddhika*), similar to the *yakkha* Naradeva mentioned below.

Having assumed in a certain city of Jambudīpa a physical form, appearance, and demeanor exactly like those of the king, he killed that king, ate him, and [seized] the kingdom along with the royal harem.
Having set out on his course, he became a consumer of immeasurable amounts of flesh. It is said that he was also a womanizer.
When clever and skillful women recognized him, thinking, "This is not our king;
he is a non-human being," he would become ashamed, devour all of them, and depart for another city. In this very same way, that *naradeva-yakkha*...

When he was devouring humans as he proceeded toward the city of Sundara, the people living in that city, seeing him and being terrified by the fear of death, fled from their own city, scattering in every direction.
Then, seeing those people fleeing, Kassapa Dasabala stood before that yakkha, the god among men.
Having thus seen the God of Gods standing there, Naradeva let out a terrible, piercing cry;
yet, unable to arouse fear in the Blessed One, he went for refuge and asked a question.
After the Blessed One had answered the question and tamed him, while the Dhamma was being taught, those present—humans and gods beyond count—attained realization. By that...
It is said: “Of the yakkha Naradeva,” and so forth. In that context, *aparasmiṃ dhammadesanāya* means “in another teaching of the Dhamma.
*Etesānaṃ* means “of these. Or rather, this is the reading itself.
However, for that Blessed One Kassapa, there was only one assembly of disciples. [In] the city of Bārāṇasī, the son of a chaplain...
His name was Tissa. Having observed the perfection of the marks on the body of the Bodhisatta Kassapa and having heard his father speaking of it, he thought:
"Without doubt, this one will go forth on the Great Renunciation and become a Buddha;
I shall go forth in his presence and be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra. Thinking thus, [he approached] the company of pure sages...
Having gone to the Himavat mountains, he went forth into the ascetic life. He had twenty thousand ascetics as his retinue.
Later, having heard that "the youth Kassapa has gone forth and attained full enlightenment," he came with his retinue;
and in the presence of the Blessed One Kassapa, he and his retinue went forth by means of the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-pabbajjā*).
He attained arahantship. At that assembly, on the full moon of the month of Māgha, the Blessed One Kassapa recited the Pātimokkha. Thus it is said:
“There was also one great assembly of that God of Gods, of those whose taints were destroyed, who were stainless, whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.”
“There was then a gathering of twenty thousand bhikkhus, who had transcended worldly existence, being steadfast through moral shame and virtue.

In this context, “who had transcended worldly existence” means those who have transcended the state of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and so forth; the meaning is that they were all indeed those whose taints (*āsava*) were exhausted. “Steadfast through moral shame and virtue” means those who were equal in both moral shame (*hiri*) and virtue (*sīla*).
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a young brahmin named Jotipāla, a master of the three Vedas, renowned both on earth and in the sky, and a friend of the potter Ghaṭīkāra.
Accompanying him, he approached the Teacher, and having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, he went forth into homelessness in his presence. Being diligent in effort, he mastered the Three Piṭakas.
He beautified the Buddha’s dispensation through his practice of the duties. The Teacher also prophesied concerning him. Thus it was said:
“At that time I was a young brahmin, known as Jotipāla;
a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, one who had mastered the three Vedas.”
“Skilled in the marks and in history, having reached perfection in his own Dhamma;
proficient in the earth and the atmosphere, a knower of all sciences, free from blemish.
He was the attendant named Ghaṭīkāra to the Blessed One Kassapa.”
Reverent and respectful, I attained Nibbāna in the third fruit.
"Taking me with him, Ghaṭīkāra approached the Conqueror Kassapa;
having heard his Dhamma, I went forth into homelessness in his presence."
“Having become one of aroused energy, skilled in what is to be done and what is not to be done,
I did not decline in any respect and fulfilled the teaching of the Conqueror.
As much as has been spoken by the Buddha, the ninefold teaching of the Conqueror— ”
Having mastered everything, I brought splendor to the Conqueror’s teaching.
Seeing my marvel, that Buddha also prophesied:
"In this auspicious aeon, he shall become a Buddha."
“‘The delightful city called Kapila... [we shall be] face to face with him.
Having heard those words as well, my heart became even more serene;
I resolved upon further practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.”
“Thus have I wandered through saṃsāra, avoiding what is improper;
and difficult deeds were performed by me, solely for the sake of enlightenment.
In this context, “skilled in the earth and the sky” means skilled in the training concerning the earth and in the science of light regarding the movement of the celestial spheres in the sky.

And "skilled" (kusala) means one who is proficient. "Attendant" (upaṭṭhaka) means one who waits upon. "Respectful" (sappatissa) means one who possesses deference. "Extinguished" (nibbuta) means disciplined (vinīta) or renowned (vissuta).
In the third [verse], the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-sattamī*);

the meaning is that he is extinguished by reason of attaining the third fruit. "Taking me" (ādāya) means having taken hold of me. "In the minor and major duties" (vattāvattesu) refers to the small and great rules of conduct. "Skilled" (kovidā) means proficient in those.

“Skilled in fulfilling”: he demonstrates, “I do not decline anywhere”—that is, I do not fall away from my virtue, nor from concentration, meditative attainments, and so forth, in any respect or for any reason;
nowhere is there any such thing as my decline. There is also a reading, “na koci parihāyāmi,” which has the same meaning.
“Yāvatā” is a term of delimitation, meaning “as much as. “Buddhabhaṇitaṃ” means the word of the Buddha.

"Sobhayinti" means they beautified or illuminated. "Mama acchariyaṃ" means that the Blessed One Kassapa saw my own marvelous and wonderful right practice, which was not shared by others. "Saṃsaritvā" means having wandered through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
"Anācaraṃ" means improper conduct—that which should not be done; the meaning is "that which ought not to be performed."
Furthermore, the birthplace of that Blessed One Kassapa was the city named Bārāṇasī;
his father was the brahmin named Brahmadatta, and his mother was the brahmin woman named Dhanavatī, who possessed supreme virtue.
His two chief disciples were Tissa and Bhāradvāja; his attendant was named Sabbamitta; his two chief female disciples were Anulā and Uruvelā; and the Bodhi tree was the Nigrodha tree.
Bodhi’s body was twenty cubits in height, his lifespan was twenty thousand years, Sunandā was his chief queen, and Vijitasena was his son;
he went forth by means of a palace-vehicle. Thus it is said:
“The city was named Bārāṇasī, and the kṣatriya was named Kikī.”
In that city dwelt the great family of the Sambuddha.
The Brahmin Brahmadatta was the father of the Buddha;
the mother of the Great Seer Kassapa was named Dhanavatī.
Tissa and Bhāradvāja were the two chief disciples;
Sabbamitta by name was the attendant of the Great Seer Kassapa.
Anulā and Uruvelā were the two chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Nigrodha.
In height, that Buddha was twenty cubits tall,
like a lightning bolt in the sky, or like the moon surrounded by a halo of planets.
“The lifespan of that Great Seer was twenty thousand years;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
Having constructed a Dhamma-tank and given the ointment of virtue, he bestowed it upon the world.”
Having dressed in the robe of the Dhamma and distributed the garland of the Dhamma,
and having set out the stainless mirror of the Dhamma before the great multitude,
some who aspire for Nibbāna may behold my adornment.
“Having given the armor of virtue, armored with the mail of jhāna;
having donned the shield of the Dhamma, and having provided the supreme protection.
Having given the shield of mindfulness and the sharp spear of knowledge;”
Having given the excellent sword of the Dhamma that crushes the contact with immorality;
having given the ornament of the three knowledges, the ear-ornament of the four fruits;
having given the jewelry of the six direct knowledges and the floral wreath of the Dhamma.
“Having bestowed the white parasol of the True Dhamma, which wards off evil,
and having established the flower of fearlessness, he has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.
For this Fully Enlightened One is immeasurable and difficult to approach.”
For this is the treasure of the Dhamma, well-expounded, inviting one to come and see.
For this is the treasure of the Saṅgha, practicing the supreme path;
all that has vanished, for are not all conditioned things empty?
In this context, "like a pillar of lightning" means like a flash of lightning established in a dense mass.

"Like the full moon surrounded by planets" means like the full moon encircled by the planetary hosts. "Having constructed a pond of the Dhamma" means having constructed a pond of the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
"Giving the ointment of virtue" refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), intended for the purpose of adorning the continuum of consciousness.
"Having applied ointment. "Having put on the Dhamma-cloth (*dhammadussa*)" means having put on the pair of garments known as the qualities of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*).

"Having distributed the Dhamma-garland" means having distributed the garland of flowers consisting of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*); that is the meaning of "having prepared.

"The stainless mirror of the Dhamma" refers to the stainless mirror known as the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), for the purpose of discerning wholesome and unwholesome states, as well as those that are blameworthy and blameless.

The meaning is: "having placed the Mirror of Dhamma on the bank of the Dhamma-tank for the sake of the great multitude. Regarding "for the great multitude" (*mahājanassa*): it means for the great multitude. Regarding "whosoever" (*keci*):

it refers to whoever [they may be]. "Aspiring for Nibbāna": they wander about aspiring for Nibbāna—which causes the dissolution of all stains of unwholesomeness, which is deathless, unconditioned, free from calamity, supremely peaceful, and the essence of non-decay. They [aspire] for this ornament of the kind described.
The meaning is: "May they see what has been shown by me. There is also a reading: "Nibbānamabhipatthentā, passantu maṃ alaṅkaraṃ," which has the same meaning.
"Alaṅkaraṃ" is stated with the short vowel.
"Having given the armor of virtue" means having given the armor consisting of the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the fourfold purification of virtue. "Armored with the mail of jhāna"—
Having bound on the armor-binding of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas; "having donned the Dhamma-hide" means having donned the Dhamma-hide known as mindfulness and clear comprehension.
"Having given the supreme armor" means having given the supreme armor of energy endowed with the four factors.

"Having given the shield of mindfulness" means [providing] the protection of the shield of the four foundations of mindfulness for the purpose of warding off the enemies of lust and other defilements.
"Having given": possessing the sharp spear of knowledge—that is, possessing the sharp spear of insight-knowledge capable of penetration;

the meaning is that he possesses the excellent spear sharpened by insight-knowledge. Alternatively, the meaning is "having stationed the excellent warrior among practitioners of yoga who is capable of destroying the power of the defilements.
"Having given the excellent sword of the Dhamma": having given to that practitioner of yoga the edge sharpened on the whetstone of energy.

Having given the noble sword of the wisdom of the path; "the crusher of contact with defilements" refers to the noble supramundane virtue for the purpose of crushing contact with defilements—that is, for the purpose of destroying the defilements.
"Having given the ornament of the three knowledges" means having given the ornament consisting of the three knowledges. "The fourfold garland" refers to the four...
Having made the fruits into a crest-ornament; having given the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiññā*) for the sake of ornaments—that is, for the purpose of decoration—[he gave] them as "ornaments";
having made the flower-garland consisting of the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*), [he gave it];
having given the white parasol of the True Dhamma (*saddhammapaṇḍaracchatta*), which wards off evil—that is, the white parasol of liberation that is utterly pure.
"Having granted protection from all unwholesome torments"—the meaning is that having constructed the Eightfold Path leading to the City of Fearlessness, they have made it into a flower.
It is said that the Blessed One Kassapa attained final Nibbāna in the Setavya Garden in the city of Setavyā in the kingdom of Kāsī. And his relics...

They did not scatter [the relics]. All the people dwelling in Jambudīpa assembled and built a stupa one *yojana* in height, using for its exterior covering one golden tile each worth ten million, adorned with various jewels, and for its interior filling one half-million worth each;
they performed the function of clay with *manosilā* stone and the function of water with oil.
“Lord Kassapa too, having accomplished his task and working solely for the welfare of all beings,
dwelt in the deer park in the city of the King of Kāsi, bringing joy to the world.
In all the remaining verses, the meaning is entirely clear.
Thus ends the commentary on the lineage of the Buddha Kassapa in the Madhuratthavilāsinī, the commentary on the Buddhavaṃsa.
Up to this point, the commentary on the lineages of the twenty-four Buddhas is completed.
Completed in every respect.
27. The Commentary on the Lineage of the Buddha Gotama:
The Discourse on the Remote Past.
“Now, since the commentary on our own Buddhavaṃsa has reached its proper sequence, this is therefore the commentary upon it.
In that regard, our Bodhisatta performed his service in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas, beginning with Dīpaṅkara.
He has come [to this point] after four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus one hundred thousand eons while practicing [the perfections].
However, from the time of the Blessed One Kassapa onwards, there has been no other Buddha except for this Perfectly Enlightened One.
Thus, having received the prophecy (*byākaraṇa*) in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, the Bodhisatta—
“Human birth, possession of the [appropriate] gender, the cause, seeing the Teacher,
going forth, possession of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal—
through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.”

Having combined these eight qualities and having made his resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, saying, "Come now, let me search here and there for the qualities that produce a Buddha," he exerted himself.
As it is said, "While searching, I then beheld the first perfection, that of giving," he perceived the qualities that produce a Buddha, such as the perfection of giving;
