fulfilling them, he proceeded until he reached the Vessantara existence.
And as they were coming, there were those benefits described for Bodhisattvas who have made their resolution:
"Thus, men endowed with all factors are destined for enlightenment,
even after wandering through a long duration of time, for hundreds of millions of eons."
“They are not reborn in the Avīci hell, nor likewise in the Lokantara hells;
they are free from parching thirst and hunger, and they do not become *kāḷakañjika* ghosts.
Nor do they become small creatures that are reborn in states of misery.”
Being born among human beings, they are not born blind.
They have no deficiency in hearing, nor are they mute;
they do not become female, nor are they hermaphrodites or eunuchs.
“Those men destined for enlightenment are not included among the worldly;
they are freed from the deeds of immediate retribution and maintain a pure range of conduct in all respects.
Seeing the efficacy of kamma, they do not cultivate wrong view.”
Even though they dwell in the heavens, they do not take rebirth in the realm of non-perception.
Among the gods of the Pure Abodes, no cause for such rebirth exists;
these true persons are inclined toward renunciation and are detached from existence after existence.
“They practice deeds for the welfare of the world and fulfill all the perfections.
Having attained these benefits, he has come here. While coming in this manner, established in the Vessantara existence, he said:
“This earth is insentient; it does not perceive pleasure or pain.”
“By the power of my gift, even she shook the earth seven times.
Having thus performed such great meritorious deeds as causing the great earth to tremble, at the end of his life-span, he passed away from there and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
This is the proximate introductory narrative.
While the Bodhisatta was still dwelling in the Tusita heaven, that which is called the "Buddha-uproar" arose.
For three kinds of uproars arise in the world: namely, the eon-uproar, the Buddha-uproar, and the wheel-turning monarch uproar.
In this regard, when a hundred thousand years have passed, thinking, "The arising of an eon will occur," the gods of the sense-sphere realm known as the Lokabyūhas—

With their veins showing, their hair disheveled, their faces weeping, wiping away tears with their hands, dressed in red garments and wearing extremely hideous attire, they wandered along the public highways proclaiming: "O sirs, O sirs!
After the passing of one hundred thousand years from now, the end of the eon will come; this world will be destroyed, even the great ocean..."
"It will dry up; this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn away and perish.
There will be a destruction of the world as far as the Brahma-world. Therefore, sirs, cultivate loving-kindness;
sirs, cultivate compassion, gladness, and equanimity. Serve your mother and father; be respectful toward the elders of the family."
This is known as the "clamor for the eon.
Then, after the passing of a thousand years, the world-protecting deities proclaimed, shouting:
"Friends, after the passing of a thousand years from now, a Buddha will arise in the world!"—thinking, "An omniscient Buddha will appear in the world after the passing of a thousand years."
They wander about. This is called the "Buddha-clamor.
After the passing of a hundred years, a wheel-turning monarch will arise—thus the deities wander about, proclaiming:
"From here, sirs, after the passing of a hundred years, a wheel-turning monarch will arise. This is called the "wheel-turning monarch clamor."
Having heard the sound of the Buddha’s proclamation among them, all the deities throughout the ten thousand world-systems assemble together;
knowing that "such-and-such a being will become a Buddha," they approach and make their request.

And while making their request, they do so once the preliminary signs have appeared. At that time, in every single world-system, all those [deities] are accompanied by the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Vasavatti, and Mahābrahmā.
Having assembled together within a single world-system, they went into the presence of the Bodhisatta who had manifested the signs of passing away from the Tusita heaven and said:
"O Noble One, you have fulfilled the ten perfections;
and while fulfilling them, you did not do so aspiring for the attainment of Sakka, Brahmā, or similar states, but rather for the sake of delivering the world, aspiring for omniscience."
He was fulfilled for the state of Buddhahood:
“The time has come for you, O Great Hero, to arise in a mother’s womb;
saving the world with its devas, awaken to the deathless state.”
They made their request.
Then, although the Great Being was thus entreated by the deities, he did not grant them his promise;

instead, he performed the five great observations regarding the time, the continent, the country, the family, and the mother, as well as the limit of the lifespan. Among these, first he observed the time, considering: "Is this the right time, or is it not the right time?"
In that context, the period when the lifespan has increased beyond one hundred thousand years is not called "the time.

Why? Because at that time, birth, aging, and death are not perceived among sentient beings; furthermore, the Dhamma teachings of the Buddhas are never devoid of the three characteristics, yet when they speak of them as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," people ask, "What is it they are talking about?"
They do not consider that it should be heard or believed; consequently, there is no realization (*abhisamaya*).
When that is absent, the teaching becomes non-leading to liberation. Therefore, that is not the right time. Even a time when the lifespan is less than a hundred years is not the right time.
Why? Because at that time, sentient beings have defilements (*kilesa*) in excess; and for those whose defilements are in excess, the instruction given does not remain in its proper place.
It vanishes as quickly as a line drawn with a stick upon water; therefore, that too is not the right time.
From one hundred thousand years down to one hundred years, the period of lifespan is called the "right time. At that time, however, it was the period of a hundred-year lifespan.
Then the Great Being perceived that the time for his rebirth had arrived.

Then, looking toward the continent, he surveyed the four great continents together with their surrounding islands and saw the continent, thinking: "Buddhas are not born on three continents; they are born only on Jambudīpa. Next, thinking:
"Jambudīpa is vast, measuring ten thousand yojanas. In which region, then, are Buddhas born?
and surveying the location, he saw the Middle Country (*majjhima-desa*). [He thought: "There is a city named Kapilavatthu; there—"
“I must be reborn,” he concluded.
Then, surveying the families [suitable for birth], he thought: “Buddhas are not born into merchant families or servant families;
rather, they are born into either a khattiya family or a brahmin family that is esteemed by the world. At present, the khattiya family is esteemed by the world.”
There I shall be reborn; a king named Suddhodana will be my father. Thus he surveyed the family.
Then, looking for a mother, [he reflected]: “The mother of a Buddha is not one who is lustful, addicted to liquor, or a gambler;
rather, she must have fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and maintained the five precepts unbroken from birth onwards. And this woman named Mahāmāyā...”
"The queen is such as this; she will be my mother. But how long is her lifespan? He saw: "It is seven days more than ten months.
Having thus performed these fivefold great observations, he thought: "The time has come for me, dear friends, to attain Buddhahood."
Having given his promise to the gods, saying, "Go, you," he dismissed those deities and, surrounded by the Tusita gods, entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita city.
For indeed, the Nandana Grove exists in all the celestial worlds.
There, the deities wander about, reminding him of the sphere of wholesome kamma performed in the past, saying: "When you pass away from here, go to a happy destination."
Thus, surrounded by those deities who were reminding him of his wholesome deeds, he wandered there;
and having passed away from that state, he took rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha.
At the very moment the Great Being took rebirth in his mother’s womb, the entire ten-thousandfold world system trembled all at once.
The thirty-two auspicious omens appeared.

Thus, to ward off any misfortune for both the Bodhisatta who had taken rebirth and his mother, four sons of gods with swords in hand took up their guard. Any lustful thought toward men in the Bodhisatta’s mother...
She did not experience [the usual difficulties of pregnancy], and having attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame, she was happy and her body was free from fatigue.
She beheld the Bodhisatta within her womb like a yellow thread wound around a clear jewel.
For a womb inhabited by a Bodhisatta is like the interior of a shrine; it is impossible for any other being to dwell in or occupy.
Therefore, seven days after the Bodhisatta was born, the Bodhisatta’s mother passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Furthermore, while other women give birth even before ten months have passed, or after they have elapsed, or while sitting, or while lying down, the Bodhisatta’s mother does not do so.
Rather, the Bodhisatta’s mother carries the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months.
She gives birth while still standing; this is the natural law regarding the mother of a Bodhisatta.
Queen Mahāmāyā, having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months and being fully pregnant, desired to go to her relatives' home and informed King Suddhodana:
"Great King, I wish to go to the city of Devadaha."
"Let him go. The King, accepting with "So be it," had a straight, level road prepared from Kapilavatthu as far as the city of Devadaha;

having had it adorned with plantain trees, full water-jars, umbrellas, banners, flags, and the like, he had [the Prince] seated in a new golden palanquin and dispatched him with great splendor and a vast retinue. However, between the two cities—
There was a grove of auspicious *sāla* trees named Lumbinīvana, worthy of being enjoyed by the inhabitants of both cities;
at that time, from its roots to its topmost branches, it was all in full bloom simultaneously.
Amidst its branches and flowers, five birds—intoxicated with joy and uttering sweet, enchanting, and most delightful songs—were enjoying themselves.
Seeing the forest, which possessed a beauty like that of the Nandana Grove of the gods and was being serenaded by female bees intoxicated with honey,
the Queen’s mind was inclined to enjoy the sport in the Sāla grove.
Adorned with ornaments, wearing a garland, and moving with the grace of a young woman, she appeared like a celestial maiden whose limbs were embellished.
"Lumbinī, garlanding the rows of eyes of people at all times, shines exceedingly as if she were plundering [the world].
Having informed the king, the ministers took the Queen and entered that Lumbinī grove.
She went to the foot of the auspicious *sāla* tree—its trunk straight, symmetrical, and well-rounded, and adorned with flowers, fruits, and young shoots—and [reached] the branch which...
Desiring to grasp it, that branch of the *sāla* tree—weak, swaying with the hearts of men, and hanging down of its own accord—came into the palm of her hand.

Then she seized that *sāla* branch with her right hand, which was most delightful to the touch, adorned with copper-colored, high, and brilliant nails, with fingers as round as lotus petals, and graced by new golden bracelets. She [grasped] that *sāla* branch...

Standing there, she shone like a streak of the young moon entering a rift in a dark cloud, like a flash of light that lasts but a moment, and like a goddess born in the Nandana Grove; yet, at that very instant, the winds of her karma began to blow.
Then the great multitude, having surrounded her with a screen of cloth, withdrew. She took hold of a branch of a *sāla* tree.
While she was still standing, the delivery of the child took place.
At that very moment, four Great Brahmās with purified minds arrived carrying a golden net;
they received the Bodhisatta in that golden net, placed him before his mother, and said: "Rejoice, O Queen!"
"Be of good cheer; a son of great power has been born to you," they said.
However, unlike other beings who emerge from the mother’s womb smeared with loathsome impurities, the Bodhisatta did not do so.
Instead, the Bodhisatta emerged while still standing, with his two hands and two feet outstretched, unsmeared by any impurity arising from the mother’s womb.
Pure and unblemished, he emerged from his mother’s womb shining like a precious gem placed upon fine Kāsī cloth.

Nevertheless, for the sake of honoring both the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta’s mother, two streams of water issued forth from the sky and provided warmth to the bodies of both the Bodhisatta and his mother.
Then, having been received by the Brahmās standing with a golden net, the Four Great Kings took it from their hands upon a deerskin rug that was considered auspicious and pleasant to the touch;
from their hands, men took it upon a cushion of fine linen; and when it was released from the hands of the men, it landed upon the earth in the east.
He surveyed the ten directions, and thousands of world-systems became as one vast open space. There, gods and humans, making offerings with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and the like, said:
"Great Being, there is no one here equal to you; how could there be anyone superior?
Having thus looked across the ten directions and seeing no one equal to himself, he took seven strides toward the northern direction.
He departed. And as he went, he traveled upon the earth itself, not through the air; he went as a naked ascetic, not clothed;
he went as a youth, not one sixteen years of age. Yet to the great multitude, he appeared as if traveling through the air, as if adorned and prepared for festivity, and as if sixteen years of age.
Then, standing on the seventh step, he uttered [the words] beginning with, "I am the foremost in the world."
Uttering a voice like a bull, he roared the lion’s roar.
For the Bodhisatta, in three of his existences, uttered speech as soon as he emerged from his mother’s womb: in the existence as Mahosadha, in the existence as Vessantara, and in this existence.
It is said that in the existence as Mahosadha, as soon as he emerged from his mother’s womb...
Sakka, the king of the gods, came and placed a piece of sandalwood essence in his hand and departed; he emerged having taken it in his very fist.
Then his mother asked him, "Dear son, what have you brought back? "Medicine, mother," he replied.
Because he had returned having obtained medicine, they gave him the name Osadhakumāra (The Medicine Prince).
But in his birth as Vessantara, as soon as he emerged from his mother’s womb, he extended his right hand and went forth saying, “Mother, is there any wealth in the house? I wish to give alms.
Then his mother, saying, “My son, you have been born into a wealthy family,” placed her own palm against her son’s hand.
He set down a thousandfold purse.

"In this very life, I shall utter this lion’s roar"—thus, in three successive existences, the Bodhisatta uttered speech immediately upon emerging from his mother's womb. At the moment of his birth, thirty-two omens appeared.
At the very same time that our Bodhisatta was born in the Lumbinī grove,
Rāhulamātā the queen, Ānanda, the minister Channa, the minister Kāḷudāyī, Kaṇḍaka the king of horses, the Great Bodhi tree, and four jars of treasure were also born;
among them, one measured a gāvuta, one a half-yojana, one three gāvutas, and one...
It was one *yojana* in extent. These seven were known as the co-natives (*sahajāta*).
The inhabitants of both cities took the Great Being and went back to the city of Kapilavatthu. On that very day, it was proclaimed:
"In the city of Kapilavatthu, a son of King Suddhodana, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, will become a Buddha."
In the realm of the Thirty-three, the hosts of devas, joyful and delighted, sported, waving their garments and performing other such acts.
At that time, a forest-dwelling ascetic named Kāḷadevala, a follower of King Suddhodana who had attained the eight meditative attainments,
having finished his meal, went to the realm of the Thirty-three for his midday rest and sat there to dwell during the day.
Seeing those deities playing with delighted minds, he asked, "For what reason do you play with such delighted minds and joyful hearts?
Tell me that reason. Then the deities said, "Venerable sir, a son has been born to King Suddhodana;
having sat at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he will become a Buddha and turn the Wheel of Dhamma. Of him—"
“We are delighted for this reason: ‘We shall be able to behold the Buddha’s peerless grace.

Then, having heard the words of those deities, the ascetic descended from the celestial realm—which was exceedingly beautiful to behold—from there he entered the king’s residence and sat down on the prepared seat. Then, after the customary exchange of greetings had been made...
He said to the king, "O Great King, it is said that a son has been born to you; let us see him.
The king had his son, adorned and prepared, brought forth and led him to pay homage to the ascetic Devala.
As the Great Being’s feet turned around, they rested upon the matted locks of the ascetic like streaks of lightning upon the peaks of dark clouds. By the Bodhisatta...
Indeed, there was no one else worthy of being saluted by him in that state of existence.
Then the ascetic rose from his seat and extended his joined palms in reverence toward the Bodhisatta. Seeing this marvel, the king paid homage to his own son.
Observing the perfection of the Bodhisatta’s marks, the ascetic reflected: "Will he become a Buddha, or will he not? and applied his mind to the matter.
Reflecting thus, and knowing through his knowledge of the future that "he will undoubtedly become a Buddha," he smiled, thinking, "This is a marvelous person.
Then, reflecting, "Shall I or shall I not have the opportunity to see him when he has become a Buddha? he perceived, "I shall not have it."
Seeing that he would die in the very midst of his life and be reborn in the formless realm—a state where even a hundred Buddhas or a thousand Buddhas could not go to awaken him—he wept, thinking:
"I shall not have the opportunity to see such a marvelous person when he has become a Buddha;
alas, a great loss will be mine! But when the people saw this, they said:
“Just now our noble sir laughed, and then he began to weep again. Venerable sir, will there perhaps be some obstacle for our noble son?
they asked. The ascetic replied, “There is no obstacle for him; without doubt, he will become a Buddha. “Then why did you weep? [they asked]. “Because of such a marvelous man,” he said.
“I weep,” he said, “grieving for myself, thinking: ‘I shall not get to see him become a Buddha; alas, a great sorrow will surely befall me.

Then, on the fifth day, having bathed the Bodhisatta’s head, they prepared the royal palace by smearing it with four kinds of fragrant paste, scattering flowers with parched grain as the fifth, and [preparing] unbroken milk-rice.

Having had [the food] cooked, they invited eight hundred brahmins who had mastered the three Vedas, seated them in the royal palace, fed them honeyed milk-rice, and having paid them honor, they had their marks examined, wondering, "What indeed will happen?
Among them, eight brahmin scholars, Rāma and the others, were the examiners of the marks. Of those, seven men [examined] two...
Raising their fingers, they declared in two ways: "One endowed with these marks, if he dwells at home, becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin);
if he goes forth, he becomes a Buddha. Now, among them, the youngest in lineage was a brahmin named Koṇḍañña;
having seen the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the most excellent marks, he thought: "The reason for his staying in the midst of a household..."
“There is no doubt; he will certainly become a Buddha with the veil of ignorance lifted,” he declared, giving a categorical answer while raising a single finger.
Then, those taking his name gave him the name Siddhattha because he would accomplish the welfare of the entire world.
Thereafter, those brahmins went to their own homes, summoned their sons, and spoke thus: “We are old.”
“Whether or not we shall believe that the son of the great king Suddhodana has attained omniscience, you, however, should go forth in his dispensation once he has gone forth and attained omniscience.

Then those seven men, having remained for as long as their lifespan lasted, departed according to their karma. The young man Koṇḍañña remained free from illness. At that time, however, the king [acted] toward them...
Having heard these words, he asked them, "What did my son see that he would go forth?
"The four omens, O King," they replied. "Which ones, and which ones? "An old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a renunciant.
The king said, "From now on, do not allow such persons to come near my son," and [he gave instructions] to the prince.
In order to prevent old men and others from coming within the range of his vision, he stationed guards at intervals of one *gāvuta* in each of the four directions.
On that day, among the eighty thousand kinsmen assembled at the auspicious site, each one pledged a son, saying:
"Whether he becomes a Buddha or a king, we [will give] one son each."
“If he becomes a Buddha, he will wander surrounded only by kshatriya ascetics;
if he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, he will wander surrounded only by kshatriya princes.
Then the king gave the Great Man sixty-four nurses, endowed with supreme beauty and free from all defects. The Bodhisatta, with infinite...
He grew with a great retinue and an abundance of glory.
Then one day, there was a festival for the King’s sowing ceremony.
On that day, as the King was departing from the city with great splendor and a large retinue, he went forth taking his son along as well. At the site of the agricultural work—
There was a single rose-apple tree, most delightful, with dense and thick shade. Having prepared a bed for the prince beneath it,
having fastened above it a canopy of red cloth inlaid with excellent gold stars, having had it enclosed by a screen of reed-matting, and having established a guard, the king—
adorned with all his ornaments and surrounded by a host of ministers— went to the place where the ploughing was to be performed.
There, the king took up the most auspicious golden plough, while the ministers and others took up silver ploughs and the like.
On that day, a thousand ploughs were yoked. The nurses sitting around the Bodhisatta, thinking, "We shall see the king’s prosperity," emerged from within the enclosure.
Then the Bodhisatta, looking here and there and seeing nothing, rose up suddenly, sat cross-legged, and by attending to his breath, attained the first jhāna.
The nurses, who had been wandering among the food and snacks, delayed for a short while.
The shadows of the other trees turned back, but the shadow of that jambu tree remained circular.

Having offered the sacrifice, he remained right there. Meanwhile, because they had heard from the slave-girl that "the noble son is all alone," they hurriedly threw up a screen-wall and searched for him.
Seeing him seated cross-legged on his state couch and witnessing that miracle, they went and reported the matter to the king.
The king came in haste, and having seen that miracle, said: "This one of yours..."
"Dear father, this is the second salutation," he said, and prostrated before his son.

Then, as the Great Being gradually reached the age of sixteen, the King had three palaces built for the Bodhisatta, each suited to one of the three seasons, named Ramaṇa, Suramaṇa, and Subha. One was nine stories high; one...
One [palace] had seven stories and one had five; all three palaces were equal in height, yet there was a difference in their floors.
Then the king thought:
"My son has reached maturity; I shall have the royal parasol raised for him and let him behold the glory of sovereignty."
So he sent a message to the Sakyans, saying: "My son has reached maturity; I shall establish him in the kingdom.
Let all the girls who have reached maturity in their own homes send them here. When they heard the king's message, they thought:
"The prince possesses only physical beauty; he knows no craft at all and will not be able to support a wife."
“We will not give our daughters,” they said. When the king heard this report, he went to his son and explained the matter to him.
The Bodhisatta asked, “What craft should be demonstrated?
“It is fitting, father, to string a bow with a thousand-fold strength. “Then have it brought here,” he said. The king had it brought and gave it to him.
A thousand men could string that bow, and a thousand men could unstring it. The Great Man, having had that bow brought to him, sat cross-legged;
wrapping the bowstring around his big toe and pulling it, he strung the bow with his big toe alone, grasped the handle with his left hand, and drew the string back with his right hand.
He strung it. The entire city was thrown into a state of agitation. When asked, "What is this sound?
they replied, "The rain god is thundering. Then others said, "You do not know; it is not the rain god thundering.
This is the sound of the bowstring snapping as Prince Aṅgīrasa, having strung his thousandfold-strength bow, draws it back."
When the Sākiyas heard this, their hearts were immediately stirred and their minds were filled with joy.
Then the Great Being asked, "What should be done? They replied, "It is fitting to pierce with an arrow an iron plate eight finger-breadths thick.
Having pierced that, he asked, "What else should be done? [They replied,] "An iron plate four finger-breadths thick..."
"It is fitting to pierce a wooden plank. Having pierced that as well, he asked, "What else is it fitting to do?
"It is fitting to pierce a fig-wood plank one span thick. Having pierced that too, he asked, "What else is it fitting to do?
Then they said, "Sand-carts. The Great Being [prepared] both sand-carts and straw-carts.
Having pierced through [the water], he shot an arrow eighteen cubits long into the water and eight cubits long onto the dry land.
Then they said to him, "It is proper to shoot at a hair, using the perception that it is a vātiṅgaṇa fruit. He replied, "In that case, have a vātiṅgaṇa fruit tied at a distance of one league.
Having had a vātiṅgaṇa fruit tied at a distance of one league, in the darkness of night—
While the quarters were covered by masses of clouds, he discharged an arrow; having traveled for about a *yojana*, it split a hair and entered the earth.
Not only this much, but on that day the Great Man displayed every craft existing in the world.
Then the Sākyans sent forth their daughters after adorning them; there were forty thousand dancing women.

Queen Rāhulamātā, however, was the chief consort. Like a divine youth surrounded by celestial maidens, the Great Being was surrounded by human women and entertained by instrumental music performed by men;
enjoying great prosperity, he dwelt in those three palaces according to the changing seasons. Then one day, the Bodhisatta [went] to the pleasure garden.
Desiring to go out, he addressed his charioteer, saying, "Yoke the chariot; I wish to see the pleasure grove.

Having assented with "Very well," the charioteer prepared a magnificent, excellent, beautiful, and sturdy chariot, with firm spokes, naves, and rims, its front pole adorned with choice gold, silver, and precious gems, and its rims and sides inlaid with ninefold patterns of gold, silver, and stars.
Having adorned a magnificent chariot— resplendent with various fragrant flower garlands hanging down from it and as beautiful to behold as the chariot of the sun—
and having yoked to it four noble, auspicious thoroughbreds, white as the moon or the kumuda lily and possessing the speed of the wind or Garuḍa,
he announced it to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta then ascended that excellent chariot, which resembled a celestial palace.
He set out toward the park.
Then a deity, thinking, "The time for Prince Siddhattha’s full awakening is near;
we shall show him a preliminary sign," transformed a certain son of the gods into an old man with a body decrepit with age, broken teeth, grey hair, crooked limbs, and a staff in his hand.
They showed him [the corpse] while it was being shaken about. Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw it.
Then the Bodhisatta, following the method set forth in the Mahāpadāna Sutta, asked: "Charioteer, who is this man? His hair is not like that of others.
Having heard his reply, he said: "Alas, fie upon birth! For when one has been born..."
“Old age will appear,” he thought, and with a heart moved by agitation, he turned back from that very spot and ascended the palace.
The king asked, “For what reason has my son turned back? “Because he saw an old man, Your Majesty.
Thereupon, his mind trembling, the king established a guard for half a *yojana*. On another day, the Bodhisatta went to the park.
As he was going along, he saw a sick man created by those very same deities;
having questioned him in the same manner as before, his heart was filled with agitation, and turning back, he ascended the palace once more. Having been questioned, the king dismissed the dancers.
Thinking, "I shall cause his mind to break away from the desire for renunciation," he increased the guard and established a perimeter extending three *gāvutas* on all sides.
He established a guard over the area.
Again, one day, while going to the pleasure garden, the Bodhisatta saw a person who had passed away, created by the deities in that very same manner;
having questioned him in the same way as before, his heart was filled with agitation, and he turned back and ascended to the palace. The king [asked] the reason for his turning back.
Having asked this, he further increased his protection and established a guard over an area measuring one *yojana*.
Again, one day, while going to the park, the Bodhisatta saw a renunciant who had been created by the deities, well-clad and well-dressed;
seeing him, he asked the charioteer, "Who is this, my friend, O charioteer? The charioteer—

Although he did not know of the appearance of a Buddha, nor of the state of one gone forth, nor the qualities of such a state—because of the power of the deity—he said, "O gods, this man is indeed one who has gone forth," and thus he praised the virtue of the renunciant life to him.
Thereupon, the Bodhisatta conceived a longing for the renunciant life and went to the pleasure grove on that very day. Long-lived ones...
In other cases, Bodhisattas saw one of each—such as the aged and so forth—only after a hundred years had passed.
However, because our Bodhisatta appeared during a time of short lifespan, he saw them one by one in succession as he went to the pleasure grove every four months.
But the Dīgha-bhāṇakas say: "The four signs were seen on a single day."

"Having seen [this], he went there. Therein, having sported for a portion of the day and enjoyed the pleasures of the park, and having bathed in the auspicious lotus pond, when the sun had set, he sat upon the auspicious stone slab, desiring to have himself adorned.
Then, understanding his mental disposition, the divine son named Vissakamma, commanded by Sakka, the lord of the gods, arrived and [proceeded] with respect to him alone.
Having become like a barber, he adorned him with divine ornaments.
Then, while all the musicians displayed their respective skills, and while the brahmins honored him with cries of "Victory, Nandā!

and so forth, and while those skilled in auspicious recitations such as *Sutamaṅgalika* and others raised various kinds of auspicious words and hymns of praise, [he saw] him fully adorned with every ornament.

He ascended the excellent chariot. At that time, having heard that "Rāhula’s mother has given birth to a son," King Suddhodana sent a message saying, "Announce my joy to my son. When the Bodhisatta heard this, he said, "Rāhu is born;
a bond is born. The king asked, "What did my son say? and [received] those words.
Having heard this, he said, "From now on, let my grandson’s name be ‘Prince Rāhula.
The Bodhisattva, having mounted that excellent chariot, entered the city with a vast retinue of most enchanting splendor and majesty.
At that time, there was a woman named Kisāgotamī, who was not thin in physical beauty or in the perfection of her virtues.
A kṣatriya maiden, having gone to the upper terrace of the excellent palace, beheld the splendor of the Bodhisattva’s form as he was entering the city;
filled with joy and gladness, she exclaimed:
“Truly blessed is that mother; truly blessed is that father!”
“Truly extinguished must be that woman, whose husband is such as this!”—he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).
Upon hearing it, the Bodhisatta thought: “He has proclaimed to me words that are most pleasant to hear; for I am [seeking] Nibbāna.”
“Seeking [the goal], I wander; it is fitting that this very day I should abandon the household life, go forth, and seek Nibbāna.

Thinking, “Let this be the teacher’s fee for her,” he untied from his own neck a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces—a pearl necklace that brings supreme delight—and sent it to Kisāgotamī. She thought, “Prince Siddhattha...”
Thinking, "Having set her heart on me, she has sent this gift," she was filled with joy.
The Bodhisatta, too, having ascended a most delightful palace with a great display of splendor, lay down upon a royal couch.
At that very moment, she appeared with a face as beautiful as the full moon and teeth like the fruit of the *bimba* tree.
These excellent young women possess teeth that are white, stainless, even, closely set, and sparse; their eyes and hair are dark, and their eyebrows are well-formed, jet-black, and curved.
Their breasts are well-developed, symmetrical, and closely set like those of a swan. They wear exquisite jeweled girdles fashioned from new gold and silver that provide delight.

Their broad, firm hips are well-proportioned, and their pair of thighs resemble the trunks of elephants. Skilled in dance, song, and instrumental music, they possess a beauty and splendor equal to that of celestial maidens.
Taking up musical instruments that produced sweet sounds, they surrounded the Great Being and, seeking to delight him, employed dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
However, because his mind was detached from the defilements, the Bodhisatta took no pleasure in the dancing, singing, and other performances, and fell asleep for a moment.
Seeing this, they thought: "He for whose sake we employ these dances and other arts has fallen asleep; what is the purpose now?"
Thinking, “I am weary,” they lay down, completely covering the musical instruments they had taken up, while scented oil lamps continued to burn.

The Bodhisatta, having awakened, sat cross-legged upon the back of his couch and saw those women sleeping, covered by their musical instruments, with their cheeks and limbs wet with trickling saliva; some were even gnashing their teeth.
Some were whimpering like crows, some were moaning, some had their mouths agape, and some had their garments and girdles fallen away;
with their private parts exposed in a state of loathsome disorder, some lay there with their hair disheveled and matted, bearing the various forms of the charnel ground.
When the Great Being saw this miserable condition of theirs, his mind became even more utterly detached from sensual pleasures.

It came to pass. However, even that excellent palace terrace, once beautifully adorned and possessing a radiant splendor like the abode of the Thousand-Eyed One, now appeared utterly loathsome—filled with the corpses of discarded dead bodies like a raw charnel ground.
All three realms of existence appeared to him like a house on fire. "Alas, I am truly afflicted! he thought.
"Alas, friend! This is truly an affliction! he exclaimed. His mind was exceedingly inclined toward the life of renunciation.
Thinking, "It is fitting for me to depart on the Great Renunciation this very day," he rose from his royal couch, went near the door, and asked, "Who is there?
Channa, who was lying with his head upon the threshold, replied, "I am here, noble son."
“Channa! Then the Great Man said, “I wish to go forth today on the Great Renunciation;
without informing anyone, prepare quickly a swift, excellent thoroughbred horse.
“Very well, my lord,” he replied, and taking the horse-groom’s gear, he went to the stable where fragrant oil lamps were burning beneath a canopy of jasmine cloth.

Seeing the excellent horse Kaṇḍaka standing on a most delightful stretch of ground, he thought, "Today it is fitting that I prepare this very auspicious steed for the noble son’s departure," and he prepared Kaṇḍaka.
Even as he was being prepared, Kaṇḍaka understood: "This preparation is exceedingly tight; on other days it was for a pleasure excursion to the park."
"It is as if he were making preparations at the very moment of departure. Without a doubt, this very day the noble son will go forth on the Great Renunciation.
Then, with a joyful heart, he broke into a great laugh. That sound would have caused the entire city of Kapilavatthu to resound, but the deities suppressed it and did not allow anyone to hear it.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "First I shall see my son," rose from where he stood, went to the place where Rāhula’s mother was staying, and opened the door of the inner chamber.
At that moment, a lamp of fragrant oil was burning within the room.
Rāhula’s mother was lying on a magnificent couch strewn with a great quantity of jasmine, mallika, and other flowers.
He fell asleep with his hand placed upon the infant's head. The Bodhisatta, standing still with his foot upon the threshold, looked down and thought:
"If I remove the queen's hand and take my son, the queen will wake up;
thus there will be an obstacle to my Great Departure. Only after becoming a Buddha shall I come back and see my son."
Having reflected thus, he descended from the palace roof, approached the horse, and said: "Dear Kaṇḍaka, carry me across this single night;
relying upon you, I shall become a Buddha and carry across the world with its devas.
Then, having leaped up, he mounted the back of Kaṇḍaka. From the neck to the end of his body, Kaṇḍaka was eighteen cubits in length.
He was endowed with a corresponding height, possessed of the excellence of form, speed, and strength, entirely white, and beautiful in appearance like a polished conch shell.
Then the Bodhisatta, seated upon the back of that noble steed and having caused the horse’s tail to be held by Channa,
arrived at the great gate of the city at the hour of midnight.
At that time, however, the king had previously ordered that each of the two gate-leaves be opened by a thousand men,
and he stationed a large guard of men there to prevent the Bodhisatta from departing.

It is said that the Bodhisatta possessed a strength equal to one hundred thousand times ten million men in terms of human force, and one thousand times ten million elephants in terms of elephant force.

Therefore he thought: "If the gate is not opened, then sitting today upon Kaṇḍaka’s back, having Channa seize the tail, I shall press Kaṇḍaka with my thighs and leap over and pass the eighteen-cubit wall.
Channa thought: "If he does not have the gate opened, I [shall help] the noble son..."
“Having made a bundle of my limbs and wrapping Kaṇḍaka with my right hand, I will place him between my armpits, leap up, and cross over the wall. Kaṇḍaka thought:
“If the gate is not opened, I shall take the noble son, who remains seated as he is, along with Channa who holds his tail, leap up and land before the wall.”
In the same way, three men reflected [on this]. The deities dwelling at the gate opened the great gate.
At that moment, Māra the Evil One, thinking, "I shall turn back the Great Being," arrived and stood in the sky, saying:
"Do not go out, O Great Hero; seven days from now, for you, there will be death."
“The divine Wheel-Treasure will surely appear.
You shall rule over the four great continents, surrounded by two thousand minor islands. Turn back, O Noble One! The Great Man asked, “Who are you?
“I am Vasavatti. “I know you, O Great King; I know the origin of my wheel.”
“I have no need for kingship; go away, Māra, do not stay here.
But I shall fill the entire ten-thousandfold world system with my roar and become a Buddha, a leader of the world.”
He said: "He vanished right there.

At the age of twenty-nine, the Great Being, casting aside the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch that had come into his hands as if it were a globule of spittle and without regard for it, departed from the royal palace—the very abode of the glory of a wheel-turner—and on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha, set forth.
While he was thus proceeding, he wished to turn back from the city and look upon it once more.
Immediately after that thought arose, that very spot of ground turned around like a potter’s wheel.

While the Great Being remained standing exactly where he was, having seen the city of Kapilavatthu, he pointed out to him on that spot of ground the site of the Kaṇḍakanivattana Cetiya, and [the horse] turned its face toward the path by which they were to go.
Having made Kaṇḍaka his steed, he set forth with great honor and a magnificent display of splendor.
As the Great Being proceeded, deities held sixty hundred thousand torches before him; likewise, sixty hundred thousand torches were held behind him, and sixty hundred thousand to his right and left.
Other deities [honored him] with fragrant flower garlands, wreaths, sandalwood powder, yak-tail fans, banners, and flags.
Honoring him, they followed, surrounding him on all sides. Celestial songs and many musical instruments resounded.
Proceeding amidst this magnificent display, the Bodhisatta traversed three kingdoms in a single night, covering a journey of thirty yojanas, and arrived at the bank of the Anomā River.
Then, standing on the riverbank, the Bodhisatta questioned Channa.
“What is the name of this river? “It is named Anomā, O King.

“Then our renunciation shall also be ‘Anomā’ (Incomparable),” he said, signaling to the horse by striking it with his heel. The horse leaped over and stood on the far bank of the river, which was eight ox-lengths wide.
The Bodhisatta dismounted from the horse’s back and [stood] upon a sandbank that resembled a heap of excrement.
Standing there, he addressed Channa: "Friend Channa, take my ornaments and Kaṇḍaka and go;
I shall go forth. Channa said, "I too, O Lord, will go forth. The Bodhisatta said, "It is not possible for you to go forth;
you must simply go," and having thus refused him three times, [he gave] the ornaments.
Having entrusted Kaṇḍaka to them, he thought: "These hairs of mine are not suitable for a recluse;
I shall cut them off with a sword. Taking a most excellent, well-sharpened blade in his right hand and grasping his topknot together with the hair-tuft in his left hand, he cut it off.
The hairs, being only two finger-breadths long, curled toward the right.
They were attached to his head. However, the length of those hairs remained exactly that same size for as long as he lived, and his beard was proportionate to them;

furthermore, he had no further need to shave his hair or beard. Taking his topknot together with the *moḷi* (the hair-net), the Bodhisatta said, "If I shall become a Buddha, let it stay suspended in the air;
if not, let it fall to the ground," and he threw it into the sky. That crest-jewel binding...
Having traveled a distance of one *yojana*, he stood in the air.

Then Sakka, the king of the gods, looking down with his divine eye, received it in a jeweled casket one *yojana* in size and established it in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya, three *yojanas* in height and made of the seven precious gems. As it is said:
“Having cut off his topknot, which was scented with excellent perfumes, the Supreme Person tossed it up into the sky.”
“Vāsava, with a thousand eyes, accepted them upon his head with his excellent golden casket.
Again, the Bodhisatta thought: “These Kāsika garments are very costly; they are not suitable for me as an ascetic.
Then, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, his former friend, the Great Brahmā Ghaṭīkāra—who had not met with destruction for an entire interval between Buddhas—[appeared].
With a friendly disposition, he thought: "Today my companion has gone forth on the Great Renunciation;
I shall go after him, taking his requisites for a recluse.
"The three robes and the bowl, the razor, the needle, and the girdle;"
“And these eight water-strainers for a bhikkhu who is devoted to yoga.
Having brought these eight requisites of a recluse, he gave them [to him].

The Great Being, having put on the robe of an arahant and assumed the supreme garb of renunciation, threw his pair of garments into the air. Mahābrahmā received them and [placed them] in the Brahma-world.
Having constructed a stupa twelve yojanas in size made entirely of all kinds of gems, he placed it inside [the chest] and set it down.
Then the Great Being said to him, "Channa, convey my greetings regarding their health to my parents," and dismissed him.
Thereupon Channa, having paid homage to the Great Man and performed a circumambulation, departed. But as for Kaṇḍaka, by Channa—
Standing there, listening to the words of the Bodhisattva as he was consulting with him, and thinking,
"Now I shall never see my master again," he departed from the range of his vision; unable to endure the pain of separation, his heart burst and he passed away,
becoming known as Kaṇḍaka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the abode difficult for the enemies of the gods to overcome.
He was reborn as a son of the gods. His birth story should be taken from the *Vimalatthavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Vimānavatthu*.
For Channa, there had previously been only one sorrow;
now, oppressed by a second sorrow due to the death of Kaṇḍaka, he went along weeping and lamenting in great distress.
The Bodhisatta, too, having gone forth, spent seven days right there in that very place in the bliss of renunciation in a mango grove named Anupiya. After that, during the autumn season,
he— though alone, surrounded by the excellence of his saffron robes like the full moon surrounded by clouds colored by the glow of twilight— appeared as if attended by a multitude of people.
Shining as if with a divine radiance, providing a refreshing draught for the eyes of the forest-dwelling deer and birds,
that lion among men— walking with the graceful gait of an elephant in rut and solitary like a lion— comforting the earth as it were with the soles of his feet,
traversed a road of thirty *yojanas* in a single day and crossed the river Gaṅgā, whose waves break in towering surges and which flows without obstruction.
He entered the city named Rājagaha, which was most beautiful and resplendent with the radiance of many jewels.

Having entered, he wandered for alms from house to house in regular order. Yet the entire city was thrown into a state of agitation at the sight of the Bodhisatta’s form, just as the city of Rājagaha had been when Dhanapālaka entered it, or as the city of the gods is agitated when the lord of the Asuras enters it.

As the Great Being went about for alms, the people living in the city, having conceived joy and gladness at the sight of the Mahāsatta’s form and being struck with wonder, had their hearts captivated by the sight of the Bodhisatta’s form.
Among those people, one said to another: "What is this? Is it that the sun, its web of rays hidden out of fear of Rāhu..."
“The full moon has come to the world of men! Another, having smiled, said to him: “What are you saying, friend?
When have you ever seen the full moon come to the world of men before?
Is this not the flower-bannered God of Love who has come here with his bow, having seen the supreme grace and splendor of our great king and the city-dwellers, to sport?”
Another, having smiled, said this to him: "What, sir? Are you mad?

Is this not Kāma, whose body was scorched by the fire of the wrath of Īśvara, he who has a hundred eyes like those of the Lord of the Gods, and who came here with the perception that this was the city of the immortals?
Another, laughing slightly, said: "What are you saying, sir? Your words are contradictory from beginning to end. Where are his thousand eyes, and where is his thunderbolt?"
“Where is Erāvaṇa? Surely this is Brahmā himself, who, knowing that the brahmin folk are negligent, has come for the purpose of enjoining them to the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having thus disparaged them all, another man of wise nature spoke thus:
“This is neither the full moon, nor Kāmadeva, nor the thousand-eyed Indra, nor even Brahmā; this is the Teacher, the Leader of the whole world, a personage of wondrous character.”
While the citizens were thus conversing, the king’s men went and reported the matter to King Bimbisāra:
“Sire, is it a god, or a gandhabba, or perhaps a nāga king, or a yakkha—what indeed is it that wanders for alms in our city?
Having heard this, the king stood upon the upper terrace of his palace and beheld the Great Being.
Filled with a sense of wonder and amazement, he commanded the king’s men: “Go, my men, and investigate him.
If he is a non-human being, he will depart from the city and vanish;
if he is a deity, he will travel through the air; if he is a nāga-king, he will dive into the earth and depart.”
“He will become a human being and will consume whatever alms-food he receives.
The Great Man, with his senses calmed and his mind at peace, as if drawing the eyes of the great multitude toward him by the splendor of his form, looked ahead only the distance of a yoke;
having gathered enough mixed food for mere sustenance, he departed by the very gate through which he had entered.
Having departed from the city, he sat down facing the east in the shade of Mount Paṇḍava;
after reflecting upon his food, he consumed it without any agitation. Then the king’s men went and reported this occurrence to the king.

Upon hearing the messenger’s words, King Bimbisāra, the lord of Magadha—the essence of Mount Meru, the essence of the Mandāra tree, the essence of the seven [precious] things, who is difficult for foolish people to follow—[acted accordingly].
Upon merely hearing of the Bodhisatta’s virtues, his curiosity to see him arose;
he departed swiftly from the city, proceeded toward Mount Paṇḍava, and alighting from his vehicle, approached the Bodhisatta.
Having been granted permission by him, he sat down upon a stone slab cooled by the affection of his kinsmen. Delighted by the Bodhisatta’s deportment, he exchanged greetings with him.
Having inquired after his name, lineage, and other details, the king handed over all his sovereignty to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta said, “Great King, I have no need for either sensual pleasures of the objects (*vatthukāma*) or sensual pleasures of the defilements (*kilesakāma*).
For I have gone forth aspiring for supreme perfect enlightenment. Although the king entreated him in many ways, he could not win his consent.
—“Surely he will become a Buddha; however, when you have become a Buddha, you must first come to my kingdom,” he said, and then entered the city.
Then, when that best of kings had gone to Rājagaha, the excellent city of Rājagaha...
“The Best of Kings of Mountains, the Best of Kings of Sages, the Well-Gone One has also gone where the King of Beasts goes.
Then the Bodhisatta, wandering on his journey by stages, approached Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta;
having realized the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he concluded: “This is not the path to enlightenment,” and [abandoned] that cultivation of attainment.
Desiring to undertake the Great Struggle without having adorned himself, he went to Uruvelā;
thinking, "How delightful indeed is this spot of ground," he took up residence right there and undertook the Great Struggle.
Koṇḍañña the brahmin and four other sons of the brahmins who had examined his marks—these five persons were the very first to go forth among the villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
While wandering on their alms-round, they arrived there at the place where the Bodhisatta was.

Then, as he was exerting himself in the Great Struggle for six years—thinking, "Now he will become a Buddha, now he will become a Buddha"—they remained in his presence, attending to him with the performance of duties such as sweeping the courtyard.
The Bodhisatta also [thought]: "The limit has been reached..."
Thinking, “I shall perform what is difficult,” he passed his time on a single sesame seed, a grain of rice, and so forth.

He even completely cut off all food intake. Although the deities offered divine nourishment by pouring it into his pores, because of that lack of food, his body—which had reached a state of extreme emaciation—changed from its golden color to a dark hue.
The thirty-two marks of a Great Man had become concealed.

Then, having reached the end of his practice of austerities and realizing, "This is not the path to enlightenment," the Bodhisatta began to take substantial food; he went for alms among the villages and market towns and partook of nourishment.
Thereupon, his thirty-two marks of a Great Man became manifest once again, and his body...
He became golden-hued. Then the five monks, seeing him, said: "Even though he practiced austerities for six years, he was unable to penetrate omniscience;
now that he wanders for alms through villages, market towns, and royal capitals and partakes of substantial food, what will he be able to achieve?
He is a seeker of abundance, fallen away from his exertion."
"What need have we for him? they said, and having abandoned the Great Man, they went to Isipatana in Bārāṇasī.
Then, on the full moon day of Visākha, in the village of Senā at Uruvelā, there was a girl named Sujātā who had been born in the house of the householder Senā;
she offered the Great Man a honeyed milk-rice porridge into which divine essence had been infused, as she was filled with serene confidence.
Having finished his meal, he took the golden bowl and cast it upstream against the current of the Nerañjarā River,
thereby awakening the sleeping Kāḷanāga king. Then, having spent the day’s rest in a delightful Sāla grove on the bank of the Nerañjarā— fragrant with blossoms, blue-hued, and enchanting—
the Bodhisatta set out toward the Bodhi tree at evening along a path adorned by deities.
The gods, nāgas, yakṣas, siddhas, and others honored him with divine garlands, perfumes, and ointments.
At that time, a grass-cutter named Sotthiya, coming along the opposite path carrying grass, recognized the demeanor of the Great Being and offered eight handfuls of grass.
The Bodhisatta took the grass, which was as dark as the mountain of collyrium and appeared as if it were moving.
Having approached the foot of the Assattha Bodhi tree— the King of Trees— which was cool with compassion like the heart of the sun,
possessed cool shade, free from the gathering of various flocks of birds, adorned with dense branches swayed by gentle breezes,
and which shone like a victorious tree dancing and rejoicing in joy among the multitude of trees; having approached the root of the Assattha, the king of trees.
Having circumambulated [the tree] three times clockwise, he stood in the northeastern direction, took those blades of grass by their tips, and shook them.
At that very moment, a couch fourteen cubits long was formed. Those blades of grass appeared as if they had been engraved with lines by a skilled artist.
Thereupon, the Bodhisatta sat upon that fourteen-cubit grass mat, having assumed the cross-legged posture with its three joints.

Resolving upon energy endowed with the four factors, he sat down, having placed the fifty-cubit trunk of the Bodhi tree behind him as if it were a mass of silver set upon a golden throne, and being supported above by the branches of the Bodhi tree like a jeweled canopy.
As the sprouts of the Bodhi tree fell upon his golden-colored robe, they appeared like streaks of gold upon a golden cloth.
They shone as if they were coral set upon it.
While the Bodhisatta was sitting there, the divine son Vasavatti Māra thought: "Prince Siddhattha wishes to transcend my domain;
I shall not allow him to transcend it. And he informed the host of Māra of this matter.
Having announced this, he set out, taking the Māra-force with him. It is said that this army of Māra was twelve yojanas in front of him, and likewise on his right and left sides;

behind him, however, it stood extending as far as the limits of the world-system (cakkavāḷa), and it was nine yojanas in height. And when it roared aloud, its sound reached from nine thousand yojanas away.
It resounded like the sound of the earth-quaking drum. At that time, Sakka, the king of the devas, stood there blowing a conch shell named Vijayuttara;
it is said that this conch was one hundred and twenty cubits long.
Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba devas, stood playing a yellow-bellied lute made of *beḷuva* wood three gavutas in length, singing songs appropriate for an auspicious occasion.
Suyāma, the king of the gods, stood fanning [the Blessed One] very gently with a divine chowrie that was three *gāvutas* long and as radiant as the autumnal moon.
And Sahampati Brahmā stood holding a white parasol above the Blessed One, three *yojanas* in width, like a second full moon. And the Naga king Mahākāla [stood] with eighty...
Surrounded by thousands of nāgas and nāṭakas, he stood offering praise and song while paying homage to the Mahāsatta.
In the ten thousand world-systems, the deities stood offering worship with various kinds of fragrant flower garlands, incense, and powders, while uttering cries of "Well done! (sādhukāra).
Then Māra, the son of a deva, mounted a magnificent, jewel-encrusted noble elephant named Girimekhala— which was a hundred and fifty yojanas high,
resembling a peak of the Snowy Mountains, most beautiful to behold, and capable of warding off the elephants of his enemies— and having manifested a thousand arms,
he caused various weapons to be seized by those who were not yet grasping them. Māra’s retinue also [was equipped] with swords, spears, javelins, lances, and maces.

With upraised maces, pestles, ploughs, spikes, spears, javelins, stones, clubs, bracelets, golden ornaments, cleavers, discs, rings, and the faces of deer, lions, rhinoceroses, elephants, and so forth;
with bodies of various terrifying, deformed, and hideous shapes, resembling humans, *yakṣas*, and *piśācas*; [they approached] the Great Being, the Bodhisattva.
Approaching and covering him who was seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, they stood surrounding him and awaited Māra’s message.
Then, as soon as Māra’s army drew near to the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), not even one among those such as Sakka and the others was able to remain;
they fled from their very positions face-to-face. But Sakka, the king of the gods, [took] that Vijayuttara conch—

Placing [the elephant] on his back and fleeing, he stood upon the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭi*). Mahābrahmā, having placed the white parasol at the edge of the world-system, returned to the Brahma-world itself.
The Naga king Kāḷa, abandoning all the dancers, submerged into the earth and went to his own Naga-abode, Mañjerika, which was five hundred yojanas long; there, with his hand, he covered his mouth.
Having closed them, he lay down. Not even a single deity was able to remain there.
But the Great Being sat all alone in the empty mansion like a Great Brahmā.
Then, thinking, "Now Māra will come," many undesirable and evil omens of various forms appeared even before that.
While the battle was raging between the Friend of the Negligent and the Friend of the Three Worlds,
terrible meteors fell on all sides and the quarters were shrouded in the darkness of smoke.
Even though it was insentient, it was as if possessed of consciousness, like a passionate woman who has gone to separation from her lover.
Struck by the winds, the great earth, together with the oceans and its various mountain ranges, trembled.
The oceans had their waters tossed upward, and the rivers flowed even in reverse.
The peaks, composed of various clusters of trees, shattered and split the earth.
“A harsh wind blew from all sides, and a tumultuous sound of crashing arose.
A terrible darkness accompanied by the roar of thunder pervaded the air, and headless trunks moved about in the sky.
Such were the portents—inauspicious, undesirable, and dreadful—occurring both in the heavens and upon the earth.”
Indeed, many kinds of ill omens appeared on all sides at the time of Māra’s approach.
But upon seeing Kāma, who was desirous of attacking that God of Gods, the hosts of deities, together with the celestial nymphs, uttered cries of "Alas! out of compassion.
“Even later they saw him of beautiful teeth fleeing through the cardinal and intermediate directions;
with his army and many attendants, they struck him down with hands and clubs.
Like a Garuḍa in the midst of birds, like a supreme lion in the midst of beasts;”
“Mahāyasas sat down in the midst of Māra’s army, confident and free from fear.
Then Māra, thinking, “I shall frighten Siddhattha and cause him to flee,” rained down a wind-storm, a weapon-storm, and a stone-storm;
furthermore, with nine Māric powers—rains of glowing embers, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness—he sought to terrify the Bodhisattva.
Unable [to prevail] and with a mind full of rage, he commanded his host of Māra, saying: "Hey! What are you waiting for?
Make this Siddhattha ‘Asiddhattha’ (the Unaccomplished)! Seize him, strike him, cut him down, bind him, do not let him go, drive him away!
Then, sitting upon the shoulder of Girimekhala and twirling an arrow with one hand, he [aimed it] at the Bodhisatta.
Having approached, he said, "O Siddhattha, rise from your cross-legged posture! And Māra’s assembly also inflicted a most terrible affliction upon the Great Being.

Then the Great Man, having spoken such words as, "When, O Māra, were the perfections fulfilled for the sake of this cross-legged posture?", extended his right hand toward the earth. At that very moment, fourteen thousand [beings]...
First, the winds and waters that support the earth, which are a hundred thousand yojanas in thickness, were shaken;
immediately thereafter, this great earth, two hundred and forty-four thousand yojanas in thickness, trembled in six ways.
In the sky above, many thousands of lightning flashes and thunderbolts burst forth. Then, Girimekhala, the mountain-king, with his knee—
Māra fell from his seat upon the peak of Mount Girimekhala onto the ground. Māra’s retinue, too, was scattered in all directions like a handful of dust.

Then the Great Being, having destroyed that Māra and his host through the power of his own perfections—patience, loving-kindness, energy, wisdom, and the rest—recalled his past lives during the first watch of the night and purified his divine eye during the middle watch.
At the time of dawn, having applied his knowledge to the customary mode of conditions practiced by all Buddhas, he attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing;
taking that very state as a basis, he developed insight and, by means of the fourth path realized through the sequence of the paths,
exhausted all defilements, penetrated all the qualities of a Buddha, and [performed] what is customary for all Buddhas—
“Through many births in saṃsāra, I have wandered without finding rest, seeking the builder of the house, for birth again and again is suffering.
‘O builder of the house, you are seen! You shall build no more houses.”
“All your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered;
the mind has reached the unconditioned and attained the destruction of craving.
Thus he uttered this inspired utterance.
The Introduction to the Prologue:
As the Blessed One sat having uttered the *Udāna*, this thought occurred to him:
"For four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, I have run the course for the sake of this cross-legged seat; this is my cross-legged seat, my seat of victory."

"This is my auspicious seat; as long as my resolve is not fulfilled, I shall not rise from here," he said, and entering meditative attainments numbering many hundreds of thousands of koṭis, he sat right there for seven days.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "Then the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation."
Then, a reflection arose in some of the deities: "Surely there must still be some task to be performed for Siddhattha; for he does not yet relinquish his attachment to the seat.
Then the Teacher, knowing the deities' thought, rose up into the air and displayed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*) in order to pacify their thoughts. Thus, by means of this miracle—
Having calmed the thoughts of the deities, he stood slightly to the northeast of his seat and thought:
"In this very seat, indeed, omniscient knowledge was realized by me.
He then gazed upon both the seat and the Bodhi tree—the place where the fruit of the perfections fulfilled over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons was attained.
He spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes; that place became known as the Animisa Cetiya.

Then, having established a walking path between the seat of the cross-legged posture and the standing spot, he spent seven days walking back and forth on the long jeweled walkway extending from east to west; that place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya.
On the fourth week, however, the deities constructed a jeweled house to the northwest of the Bodhi tree.
There, sitting cross-legged, he spent seven days examining the Abhidhamma Piṭaka;
that place subsequently became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya.
Thus, having spent four weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, on the fifth week, from the foot of the Bodhi tree...
He approached the Goatherd’s Banyan tree. There too, investigating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he sat down.
After spending seven days there, the Teacher went to the foot of the Mucalinda tree.
There, when a seven-day storm arose, the Naga King Mucalinda encircled him seven times with his coils to ward off the cold and other discomforts.
Dwelling there as if in his own Gandhakuṭī, experiencing the bliss of liberation, he spent seven days;
then he approached the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. There too, experiencing the bliss of liberation, he sat for seven days.
At this point, the seven weeks were complete. During this interval, neither did the Blessed One—
There was no washing of the face, no grooming of the body, and no need for food; he passed the time solely in the bliss of the fruit [of his meditation].

Then, on the forty-ninth day, at the end of seven weeks, having washed his face with a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* brought by Sakka, lord of the gods, and with water from Lake Anotatta, he sat down right there at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree.
At that time, two merchants named Tapussa and Bhallika, encouraged by a deity who was a blood relative,

approached the Teacher carrying rice-porridge and honey-cakes, and stood before him, saying, “May the Blessed One accept this food out of compassion. On the very day of accepting the milk-rice, the Blessed One—
Because Devadatta’s bowl had disappeared, he thought: “The Tathāgatas do not accept food in their hands; in what, then, should I receive this?
Then, knowing the Blessed One’s intention, the Four Great Kings from the four directions presented him with four bowls made of sapphire. The Blessed One—
He declined them. Again, they offered four stone bowls the color of mung beans.

Out of compassion for those four sons of gods, the Blessed One accepted them, merged them into one, and having accepted the food in that exquisite stone bowl and partaken of it, he gave a blessing of thanksgiving.
Those two brothers, the merchants, [saw] the Buddha...
Having gone for refuge to the Dhamma, they became lay followers by the two-fold formula.
Then the Teacher went again to the Ajapāla Nigrodha tree and sat down at its foot.
As soon as he was seated there, while reflecting upon the profundity of the Dhamma he had attained, it occurred to him—this being the custom of all Buddhas: "The Dhamma has been attained..."
Then, with the thought "This Dhamma is indeed profound," a reflection arose in him characterized by a reluctance to teach the Dhamma to others.
Then Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, "Alas, the world is perishing! Alas, the world is being destroyed!
took with him the Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Nimmānarati, Paranimmitavasavatti, and Mahābrahmās from ten thousand world-systems, and approached the Teacher.
Having approached him, he requested a teaching on the Dhamma in this manner: "May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma, venerable sir," and so forth.
Then the Teacher, having given him his consent, reflected: "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?
Realizing that Āḷāra and Udaka had passed away, he thought: "The bhikkhus of the group of five have been very helpful to me."
Applying his attention to the group of five monks, he directed his mind, wondering, "Where are they living now?
Perceiving that they were at the Deer Park in Isipatana near Bārāṇasī, he thought, "Having gone there, I shall set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
Having stayed for several days in the vicinity of the seat of enlightenment while wandering for alms, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, he went to Bārāṇasī.
“I shall go,” he said, and taking his bowl and robe, he set out on the eighteen-yojana road.
On the way, seeing an Ājīvika named Upaka who was joyful and elated, he declared to him his state as a Buddha and went to Isipatana that very day at the time of evening.
However, when the group of five monks saw the Tathāgata approaching from afar, they said: “Friends, here comes the ascetic Gotama...”
"Because of his abundance of favorable conditions, he will return with a full body, his faculties plump, and possessing a golden complexion;
we shall not perform such acts as saluting him, but we shall merely prepare a seat for him.
Having made this agreement, the Blessed One, knowing their mental disposition, [manifested] a mind of loving-kindness capable of pervading all beings without partiality.
Having condensed [the range], he suffused them with a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) directed toward each individual.

Touched by the Blessed One’s mind of loving-kindness, they were unable to maintain their prior agreement when the Tathāgata approached; they performed all the duties, such as paying homage and so forth.
The detailed account should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Vinaya Mahāvagga* and other texts.
Then the Blessed One, having made his own state as a Buddha known to them, sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared.
While the conjunction of the Uttarāsāḷha constellation was occurring, surrounded by eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, he addressed the five bhikkhus of the group and taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.
Among them, Aññā Koṇḍañña, directing his knowledge according to the course of the teaching, [attained realization] at the conclusion of the sutta, together with eighteen...
Together with ten million Brahmās, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Therefore it was said:
“I am now the Fully Awakened One, Gotama, the scion of the Sakyas;
having exerted the supreme effort, I have attained unsurpassed enlightenment.”
“Being entreated by Brahmā, I set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma;
there was the first realization for eighteen koṭis.
Therein, “I” refers to himself. “At present” means at this time. “Increaser of the Sakyans” means the one who increases the Sakyan clan.
“Sakyapuṅgava” is also a reading. “Padhāna” means energy (*vīriya*). “Having exerted” (*padahitvāna*) means having striven, having endeavored;

the meaning is, having performed difficult austerities. “Of eighteen crores” refers to the eighteen [crores] headed by the Elder Aññā-Koṇḍañña, who were present during the discourse on the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta* at Isipatana in the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī.
The meaning is that it was the first realization for ten million Brahmās.
Now, having spoken of the past, the Blessed One, while speaking of the future realization, said:
"And thereafter, as he taught in the assembly of gods and men..."
"He cannot be described by calculation; there was a second realization"—thus he spoke at the beginning.

Therein, "at the assembly of men and gods" means that on another occasion thereafter, at a great auspicious assembly in the midst of gods and humans from ten thousand world-systems, at the conclusion of the Maṅgala Sutta, among those men and gods who had transcended the path of calculation.

“*Dutiyābhisamayo ahū*” means “there will be a second realization. Although a future tense should have been used, the past tense “*ahū*” was employed because it falls within the scope of the discourse, or by way of a shift in time.
This same method applies to similar expressions that follow.
Furthermore, through the teaching of the *Rāhulovāda Sutta*, beings who have transcended the path of counting [innumerable] have drunk the nectar of realization.
He caused him to drink. This was the third realization. Therefore it was said:
“Even here and now, I have exhorted my own son;
it cannot be expressed by calculation—there was the third realization.”
It is said that there was only one assembly of disciples for the Blessed One.

There was an assembly of these one thousand and two hundred and fifty—the thousand matted-hair ascetics beginning with Uruvelakassapa, and the two chief disciples along with two hundred and fifty each. Therefore it was said:
“There was one assembly of mine, Of disciples, the great seers.”
“There was a gathering of one hundred and twenty-five monks.
In that context, *eko āsi* means there was only one [other besides the Buddha]. *Aḍḍhateḷasasatānaṃ* refers to my disciples numbering one hundred and twenty-five.
*Bhikkhūnāsi* means there were monks. Standing in their midst, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha during this fourfold assembly.
Then the Blessed One, showing his own state,
spoke these verses beginning with: “Radiant and stainless, standing in the midst of the community of monks,
I grant everything desired, like a wish-fulfilling gem.”
In this context, "shining forth" means shining with the infinite glory of a Buddha. "Stainless" means free from the stains of defilements such as lust.
"Like a gem that grants all desires" means that, like a *cintāmaṇi* jewel, I too grant every desired and prayed-for excellence of both mundane and supramundane happiness; this is the meaning.
Now, demonstrating his earnest aspiration, he said:
"To those longing for the fruit, who seek to abandon the desire for existence, I proclaim the Four Truths out of compassion for living beings. And so forth.

In this context, "fruits" refers to the fourfold fruit beginning with the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). "To those who desire to abandon the will for existence" means to those who seek to relinquish craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*), to those desiring to abandon craving for existence.

"Out of compassion" means out of sympathy. Now, demonstrating the realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the exposition of the Four Noble Truths, he spoke the verse beginning with "Ten and twenty thousand.

In this regard, "ten and twenty thousand" means ten thousand and twenty thousand; the sense is according to the method beginning with "one or two," and so forth. The ninth and tenth verses are of plain meaning.

11–12. In the eleventh and twelfth verses, the terms *idāni* and *etarahi* both have the same meaning; they are spoken as if referring to distinct individuals (*purisa-puggala*) according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Alternatively, *idāni* means "when I have appeared," and *etarahi* means "while I am teaching the Dhamma.

*Apattamānasā* means "those who have not attained the mind [of Arahantship]," i.e., those who have not reached the fruit of Arahantship. *Ariya-añjasam* means the noble Eightfold Path. *Thomayanta* means praising.
"They will awaken" means they will penetrate the Dhamma of the Four Truths in the future. "The stream of saṃsāra" refers to the ocean of saṃsāra.
Now, showing his own birthplace and so forth, he says:
"Kapilavatthu is my city; King Suddhodana is my father."
My mother who gave me birth is called Queen Māyā.
For twenty-nine years I dwelt in the household;
there were three most excellent palaces—delightful, very charming, and beautiful.
“Forty thousand women were beautifully adorned;
the woman named Bhaddakaccānā was my wife, and Rāhula was my son.
Having seen the four signs, I went forth on a horse-drawn chariot.”
For six years I practiced the course of striving, performing what is difficult.
At Isipatana in Bārāṇasī, the Wheel was set in motion by me;
I am Gotama the Fully Awakened One, the refuge for all living beings.
“Kolita and Upatissa are the two chief disciples among the monks;
the one named Ānanda is my attendant, who stays close to me;
and Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā are the chief female disciples among the bhikkhunīs.”
“Citta and Hatthāḷavaka are the foremost lay male supporters;
Nandamātā and Uttarā are the foremost lay female supporters.
At the foot of the Assattha tree, I attained supreme enlightenment.”
My body-radiance is always sixteen cubits high.
Although the lifespan found at this present time is but a mere hundred years,
I remain for that duration to deliver the vast multitude of people.
“Having established the pinnacle of the Dhamma for the final awakening of the people,
I too, before long, together with the community of disciples,
shall attain final Nibbāna right here through the exhaustion of fuel, like a fire. Thus he spoke.
I, however, had three palaces named Ramma, Suramma, and Subha—nine-storied, seven-storied, and five-storied respectively;
forty thousand dancing girls; and Yasodharā was my chief queen.
Having seen the four omens, I went forth on a horse-drawn carriage for the Great Renunciation. Then, having exerted myself in striving for six years, I [attained enlightenment].
On the full moon day of Visākha, at Uruvelā in the village of Senā, having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice offered by Sujātā— the daughter of the householder Senā—
who was filled with serene faith, and having spent the day in meditation in a grove of Sāla trees,
he took eight handfuls of grass given by a grass-cutter named Sotthiya in the evening and approached the foot of the Assattha Bodhi tree.
There, having shattered the power of Māra, he explained everything, saying, "I have attained full enlightenment.
In that context, "together with the community of disciples" means together with the assembly of disciples. "Will attain final Nibbāna" means I shall attain final Nibbāna.
