"With the exhaustion of the fuel of fire": just as a fire goes out when its fuel is exhausted, so too—like a fire—when there is no further substrate, it attains extinction.
The meaning is: "I too, being without clinging, shall attain final Nibbāna.
And "those of incomparable splendor" refers to the pair of chief disciples and others, who possess peerless majesty. And "these ten powers" refers to these physical powers of the body;
for "the body that bears qualities" means this body which possesses qualities such as the sixfold uncommon knowledge.
"And they shall pass away": all these things of the aforementioned kind will disappear and perish.

"Are not all conditioned phenomena empty?"—here, *nanu* is a particle used in the sense of seeking agreement (*anumati*). "Empty" (*rittā*) means void because they lack any permanent core, essence, or lasting substance;
indeed, every conditioned thing is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Because they have been sacrificed, they are impermanent; because they are oppressed by arising and so forth, they are suffering; because they lack mastery, they are non-self.
Therefore, having attributed the three characteristics to formations and having increased insight, you should attain Nibbāna—the deathless, the unconditioned, the undecaying.
This is our instruction to you; this is our teaching: [practice] with heedfulness.
"Complete it! At the conclusion of this teaching, it is said that the minds of one hundred thousand koṭis of deities were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Furthermore, those established in the remaining paths and fruits were beyond calculation.
Thus, the Blessed One [recited] the entire *Buddhavaṃsa*, which is fixed according to the names, births, and other details of the [former] Buddhas, upon the jeweled walkway in the sky.
As if walking back and forth, he spoke and had his kinsmen pay their respects; then, descending from the sky, he sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared.
When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, was thus seated, the assembly of kinsmen reached its peak, and they all sat with one-pointed minds.
Then a great cloud rained down a shower of lotuses. At that very moment, the water [fell] below.
He went toward Viravanta. As if wishing to sprinkle him, he sprinkled him; yet not even a single drop fell upon the body of one who did not wish to be sprinkled.
Seeing this, everyone was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement and raised the cry:
"Oh, how marvelous! Oh, how extraordinary! Hearing this, the Teacher said: "It is not only now that, in the assembly of my kinsmen..."
"Rain fell like rain from a lotus; he rained even in the past"—on account of this occasion, he related the Vessantara Jātaka.
That teaching of the Dhamma became fruitful. Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered the monastery.
Thus ends [the section] from the Madhuratthavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Buddhavaṃsa.
The commentary on the *Gotama-buddhavaṃsa* is finished.
The twenty-fifth *buddhavaṃsa* is completed.
28. Miscellaneous Discourse on the Buddhas.

It should be understood that the eighteen verses beginning with “In immeasurable eons, there were four leaders” were placed by the compilers of the Saṅgīti as the concluding verses (*nigamana-gāthā*). In all other verses, [the meaning] is self-evident. Regarding the discussion of differences:
however, in this entire *Buddhavaṃsa*, there are eight differences among the twenty-five Buddhas who have been described.

These should be understood. Which eight? The difference in lifespan, the difference in physical stature, the difference in lineage, the difference in exertion, the difference in rays of light, the difference in vehicles, the difference in the Bodhi tree, and the difference in the cross-legged seat.
Therein, "difference in lifespan" means that some are long-lived while others are short-lived. For instance, Dīpaṅkara and Koṇḍañña...
Anomadassi, Paduma, Padumuttara, Atthadassi, Dhammadassi, Siddhattha, and Tissa—these nine Buddhas had a lifespan of one hundred thousand years.
Maṅgala, Sumana, Sobhita, Nārada, Sumedha, Sujāta, Piyadassi, and Phussa—these eight Buddhas had a lifespan of ninety thousand years. Revata and Vessabhū...
These two Buddhas, Cāru and Dīpaṅkara, had a lifespan of sixty thousand years. The Blessed One Vipassī had a lifespan of eighty thousand years.
These four Buddhas—Sikhī, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa—had lifespans of seventy, forty-eight, thirty, and twenty thousand years, respectively.
However, the measure of the lifespan of our own Blessed One was one hundred years for those who have accumulated a store of merit.
Even for Buddhas who were endowed with kamma conducive to long life, the measure of their lifespan was indefinite according to the particular era [in which they appeared].
This is what is called the "difference in lifespan" among the twenty-five Buddhas.
As for the "difference in size," some were tall and some were short. For instance, among the Buddhas Dīpaṅkara, Revata, Piyadassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, and Vipassī—
The height of his body was eighty cubits. The bodies of Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Nārada, and Sumedha were eighty-eight cubits high. The body of Sumanas was ninety cubits high.
The bodies of the Buddhas Sobhita, Anomadassī, Paduma, Padumuttara, and Phussa were fifty-eight cubits high. Sujāta had a body fifty cubits high.
Siddhattha, Tissa, and Vessabhu were sixty cubits in height. Sikhi was seventy cubits in height.
Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa were forty, thirty, and twenty cubits in height respectively.
Our Blessed One was eighteen cubits in height. This is the [height] of the twenty-five Buddhas.
"Difference in measure" means [the difference in height].
"Difference in lineage" means that some were born into the khattiya clan and some into the brāhmaṇa clan;

for instance, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa were born into brāhmaṇa clans, whereas the twenty-two Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara and ending with Gotama were born only into khattiya clans.
They were thus reborn. This is called the difference in lineage among the twenty-five Buddhas.
Regarding the difference in their practice of striving (*padhāna-vematta*):

for Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, Sumana, Anomadassī, Sujāta, Siddhattha, and Kakusandha, the practice of striving lasted ten months. For Maṅgala, Sumedha, Tissa, and Sikhī, it lasted eight months. For Revata, it lasted seven months.
For Sobhita, it was four months; for Padumuttara, Atthadassī, and Vipassī, it was half a month each;
for Nārada, Padumuttara, Dhammadassī, and Kassapa, it was seven days; for Piyadassī, Phussa, Vessabhū, and Koṇāgamana, it was six months; for our Buddha, the practice of striving lasted six years.
This is what is called the difference in the practice of striving.
It is said that the light of the Blessed One Maṅgala, the Perfectly Enlightened One, stood pervading the ten-thousandfold world system.
That of Buddha Padumuttara was twelve yojanas; that of the Blessed One Vipassī was seven yojanas;
that of Sikhī was three yojanas in measure; and that of Kakusandha was ten yojanas. As for our own...
Around the Blessed One, it was the measure of a fathom (vyāma); for the others, it was indefinite.
This variation in rays is dependent upon one's aspiration (ajjhāsaya): whoever desires it to be so great, his bodily radiance pervades that much.
But regarding the qualities already penetrated, there is no variation whatsoever for anyone. This is what is called the "variation in rays."

Regarding the diversity of vehicles (*yāna-vematta*): some depart by means of an elephant vehicle, some by a horse vehicle, and others by one among various means such as a chariot, a foot-pavilion, or a palanquin.

For instance, Dīpaṅkara, Sumana, Sumedha, Phussa, Sikhī, and Koṇāgamana departed by means of an elephant vehicle; while Koṇḍañña, Revata, Paduma, Piyadassī, Vipassī, and Kakusandha departed by means of a chariot vehicle.
Maṅgala, Sujāta, Atthadassī, Tissa, and Gotama went forth by horse-carriage; Anomadassī, Siddhattha, and Vessabhu went forth by palanquin;
Nārada went forth on foot; Sobhita, Padumuttara, Dhammadassī, and Kassapa went forth by palace.
This is what is called the difference in vehicles.
Regarding the diversity of the Bodhi trees: for the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the Bodhi was the *kapītana* tree; for the Blessed One Koṇḍañña, it was the *sālakalyāṇī* tree;
for Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita, it was the *nāga* tree; for Anomadassi, it was the *ajjuna* tree; for Paduma and Nārada, it was the *mahāsoṇa* tree;
for Padumuttara, it was the *salala* tree; for Sumedha, it was the *nīpa* tree; for Sujāta...
For Veḷu, it was the Piyadassinī; for Kakudha, the Campaka tree; for Atthadassi, the red Kuravaka tree;
for Dhammadassi, the Kaṇikāra tree; for Siddhattha, the Asana tree; for Tissa, the Āmalaka tree; for Phussa, the Pāṭali tree;
for Vipassi, the Puṇḍarīka tree; for Vessabhu, the Sāla tree; and for Kakusandha, the Sirīsa tree.
The *udumbara* tree was for Koṇāgamana, the *nigrodha* for Kassapa, and the *assattha* for Gotama;
this is what is called the diversity of the Bodhi trees. As for the diversity of the seats (*pallaṅka*):
for Dīpaṅkara, Revata, Piyaḍassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, and Vipassī, the seats were fifty-three cubits long; for Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Nārada, and Sumedha, they were fifty-seven cubits.
For Sumanas, the throne was sixty cubits long; for Sobhita, Anomadassī, Paduma, Padumuttara, and Phussa, it was thirty-eight cubits;
for Sujāta, thirty-two cubits; for Siddhattha, Tissa, and Vessabhū, forty cubits;
for Sikhī, thirty-two cubits; for Kakusandha, twenty-six cubits; and for Koṇāgamana, twenty cubits.
For Kassapa, the couch was fifteen cubits long; for Gotama, it was fourteen cubits.
This is what is called the difference regarding the couches. These are the eight differences.
The Discussion on the Unabandoned State.
Furthermore, there are four places that are never forsaken by all Buddhas. For all Buddhas, the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka) is never forsaken;
it remains in one and the same place. The turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakkappavattana) occurs unfailingly at Isipatana in the Deer Park.
At the time of the descent from heaven (devorohaṇa), the spot where the first footprint was set at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa is likewise never forsaken.
In the Jeta Grove, the four locations for the legs of the Perfumed Chamber remain fixed; however, the monastery may be either small or large.
The monastery itself does not shift, but the city may shift.
This concludes the discussion on the delimitation by co-arising and the delimitation by constellations.
Furthermore, they pointed out the simultaneous birth (sahajātapariccheda) and the astrological conjunction (nakkhattapariccheda) of our very own Blessed One.

It is said that these seven were born simultaneously with our Omniscient Bodhisatta: Rāhulamātā, the Elder Ānanda, Channa, Kaṇḍaka the king of horses, the treasure-pot, the Great Bodhi tree, and Kāḷudāyī. This is the section on simultaneous birth.
The Great Being, moreover, entered his mother’s womb under the constellation Uttarāsāḷhā;
he made the Great Renunciation, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and performed the Twin Miracle.

He was born under the constellation Visākha, attained full enlightenment under Visākha, and passed away into Parinibbāna under Visākha. Under the constellation Māgha occurred both the assembly of his disciples and his relinquishing of the life-faculty.
It was so. The descent from the deva-world occurred under the constellation Assayuja.
This is the section on constellations.
Now, we shall explain the common characteristics shared by all Buddhas. There are thirty-two such characteristics for all Buddhas.
This is the natural law (*dhammatā*). Namely: the descent of the Bodhisatta bound for his final existence into his mother’s womb with full awareness;
sitting cross-legged within the mother’s womb and looking outwards; the Bodhisatta’s mother giving birth while standing;
the emergence from the mother’s womb in the forest alone; and [the infant] standing with feet planted upon golden cloths, facing north.
Having taken seven strides toward the four quarters and uttered the lion’s roar, having seen the four omens, the Great Beings who had just been born underwent the Great Renunciation;
taking up the banner of the Arahants, they went forth and practiced asceticism for seven days at the very least;
and on the day of attaining Perfect Enlightenment, they partook of the milk-rice meal.
Sitting upon a grass mat, he attained the knowledge of omniscience; he performed the preparatory exercises for the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing; he shattered the power of Māra;
on the very seat of enlightenment, beginning with the three types of higher knowledge, he acquired qualities such as uncommon wisdom;
he spent seven times seven days in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree; and he received the entreaty from Mahābrahmā for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
The turning of the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana in the Deer Park; the recitation of the Pātimokkha during the fourfold assembly on the full moon of the month of Māgha;
his permanent residence at the Jetavana; the performance of the Twin Miracle at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī; the teaching of the Abhidhamma in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
and his descent from the world of the gods at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa, where he constantly entered the attainment of fruition.
On two occasions there was the surveying of those to be trained; on another, the proclamation of a training rule when a matter had arisen;

on another, the telling of a Jātaka story when a specific occasion had arisen; on another, the recounting of the lineage of Buddhas during a gathering of kinsmen; on another, the performing of hospitality by visiting monks;
on another, the failure to depart without taking leave from those who had invited him after he had completed the rains retreat; and day after day...
The performance of duties before the meal, after the meal, during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch; the consumption of meat broth on the day of the Parinibbāna;
and the attainment of twenty-four hundred thousand koṭis of meditative absorptions (samāpatti) prior to the Parinibbāna—these thirty-two are the natural laws (dhammatā) common to all Buddhas.
The Discourse on the Conditions that are Free from Obstacles:
There are four conditions free from obstacles for all Buddhas. What are the four?
No one can create an obstacle to the four requisites brought specifically for the Buddhas. No one can [create an obstacle] to the life-span of the Buddhas...
It is impossible to create an obstacle. For this has been said: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that anyone could deprive a Tathāgata of life by means of another's assault.
No one can create an obstacle to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man or the eighty minor characteristics of the Buddhas. No one can create an obstacle to the Buddha-rays.
"These are the four things that are without obstacles.
This concludes the concluding remarks.
Thus far has the commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa* reached its completion.
Adopting the path of the ancient commentaries—
which illuminate the meaning of the Canon and are adorned by a diverse method of interpretation as brilliant as gold—
I have composed this commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*.
Because it completely elucidates the sweet meaning by avoiding all diffuseness,
it is therefore called *Madhuratthappakāsinī*.
On the surface of the earth purified by the falling waters of the Kāvīra river...
In the delightful city of Kāvīrapaṭṭana, crowded with various men and women,
a monastery was caused to be built by the virtuous Kaṇhadāsa, who spoke with gentle words;
it possessed walls of various forms and beautiful gate-towers.
In a place endowed with shade and water, beautiful and delightful,
free from the crowding of wicked people, auspicious and possessing the bliss of seclusion—
there, upon the surface of the eastern palace, most cool;
While dwelling in the lineage of the Buddhas, this commentary has been composed by me.
Just as this commentary on the lineage of the Buddhas has reached successful completion without obstacle,
so may the thoughts of people devoted to the Dhamma attain success without hindrance.
By whatever mass of merit has been acquired by me in composing this commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*,
may the world, through the power of that merit, always certainly attain the eternal, ultimate goal.
May all diseases perish among human beings, and may the gods send down rain at the proper time.
May there be constant, supreme happiness even for those in the hells; may the *pisācas* be freed from their thirst.
May the gods, together with the throngs of *accharās*, long experience happiness in the world of the devas.
May the Dhamma of the Lord of Sages endure for a long time in the world, and may the World-Protectors guard the earth in peace.
The Elder known by the name given by his preceptor as Buddhadatta, having composed the *Madhuratthavilāsinī* commentary,
has placed this manuscript for the benefit of future generations.

"Alas, he has fallen under the power of death, having remained for but a short time"—thus, by way of recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*), there are twenty-six such sections; by way of text (*gantha*), there are six thousand five hundred texts; and by way of syllables (*akkhara*), there are two hundred and three thousand syllables.
That this [work] reached its conclusion without any obstacle—[this is the marvel].
"Likewise, may the intentions of beings who rely upon the Dhamma be fulfilled.
Thus ends the *Madhuratthavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*.
